**COPERNICUS (NICOLAUS) 1473–1543.**

**566. Six Books on the Revolutions of the Celestial Spheres, by Nicolaus Copernicus.** <note>original: "Nicolai Copernici de Reuolutionibus Orbium cœlestium, Libri VI." This is the foundation of modern astronomy, proposing that the Earth revolves around the Sun.</note> In this newly born and published work, diligent reader, you have the motions of the stars, both fixed and wandering, restored from both ancient and recent observations; and furthermore, adorned with new and wonderful hypotheses. You also have most convenient **Tables**, from which you can calculate these motions with the greatest ease for any time. Therefore, buy, read, and enjoy... small folio. *Nuremberg, published by Johannes Petreius*, 1543. <gloss>W. A. S.</gloss> <note>These initials likely refer to a bibliographical assistant or a previous owner.</note>

Woodcut figures and initials. Page of errors <term>errata; a list of corrected printing errors</term> at the end, with the <term>catchword; a word at the bottom of a page that matches the first word of the next page to ensure correct order</term> 'Nicolai' (apparently intended to precede the title-page). Hebrew inscription on the title-page (with a translation on the flyleaf: 'God the Lord—God shall be my lord'); also an inscription 'Library of Marischal College' (see below). Inserted: A manuscript translation of the preliminary matter by Miss E. G. Parker.

The anonymous preface was 'slipped in' by <term>Andreas Osiander; a Lutheran theologian who oversaw the book's printing and added an unauthorized preface claiming the sun-centered system was just a mathematical tool, not physical reality,</term> with the object of avoiding theological criticism.

This original edition has become rare. I missed the only copy sold in London (at auction) in the past twelve years (£22). This one came from Heffer (a bookstore in Cambridge) for £18. It was formerly in Marischal College, and there is no mark indicating it was a duplicate; but I have resisted the prickings of conscience which suggest asking how it got out of the library! For the benefit of the ordinary student, I have had the preface and introduction translated.

Equally in the history of science and of medicine, 1543 is a starred year marked by a revolution in our knowledge alike of the Macrocosm <note>The "Great World," or the universe at large.</note> and the Microcosm <note>The "Little World," or the human body; referring here to Andreas Vesalius's "De fabrica," the foundation of modern anatomy, also published in 1543.</note>. In Frauenburg, the town physician and a <term>canon; a member of a cathedral's administrative clergy,</term> now nearing the <term>Psalmist's limit; a reference to Psalm 90:10, suggesting a human lifespan of 70 or 80 years,</term> and his end, had sent to the press the studies of a lifetime—*On the Revolutions of the Celestial Spheres*. It was no new thought, no new demonstration that Copernicus thus gave to his generation. Centuries before, men of the keenest scientific minds from Pythagoras on had worked out a <term>heliocentric theory; the model where the Sun is at the center of the universe,</term> fully promulgated by Aristarchus, and very generally accepted by the

<column-break/>

<insert>
Pius VII decreed, September 11, 1822, without mentioning Copernicus, that such works on the mobility of the earth should not be prohibited in the future. Consequently, the next "Index" <note>The Index Librorum Prohibitorum, the Catholic Church's list of banned books.</note> of 1835 was the first to omit his works.
</insert>

brilliant investigators of the Alexandrian school; but in the long interval, lapped in oriental lethargy, man had been content to acknowledge that the heavens declare the glory of God and that the firmament shows his handiwork. There had been great astronomers before Copernicus. In the fifteenth century, Nicolas of Cusa and Regiomontanus had hinted at the heliocentric theory; but 1543 marks an epoch in the history of science, since for all time Copernicus put the problem in a way that compelled acquiescence ... We can imagine the touching scene in the little town when his friend Osiander brought the first copy of the precious volume hot from the press, a well enough printed book. Already on his deathbed, stricken with a long illness, the old man must have had doubts (expressed in the preface) how his work would be received, though years before Pope Clement VII had sent him encouraging words. Fortunately, death saved him from the 'rending' <note>Violent criticism or persecution.</note> which is the portion of so many innovators and discoverers ... The church was too much involved in the Ptolemaic system <note>The older model where the Earth is the stationary center of the universe.</note> to accept any change, and it was not until 1822 that the works of Copernicus were removed from the Index. (Compare entry no. 6259, pages 144–145.) In the 1667 Index [entry no. 7125], page 93, may be seen the title of the book with the words after it 'unless it be corrected according to the decree of 1620.' <note>original: "nisi corrigatur juxta decretum 1620." In 1620, the Church allowed the book to be read only if certain passages were altered to present the theory as a mere hypothesis.</note> [W. O.]

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>This page contains the famous "Anonymous Preface" to Copernicus’s work. Although published without a signature, it was written by the Lutheran theologian Andreas Osiander. Osiander inserted this text to protect the book (and its author) from religious or philosophical backlash by arguing that the heliocentric theory—placing the Sun at the center—was merely a mathematical "hypothesis" to make calculations easier, rather than a claim about the physical reality of the universe. This page follows the title page of the 1543 first edition.</meta>

# TO THE READER CONCERNING THE HYPO-
## THESES OF THIS WORK.

<image-desc>A historiated woodcut initial 'N' depicting a scholar or astronomer seated at a desk with books or manuscripts, possibly in a study.</image-desc>

I do not doubt that certain learned men—now that the report has spread regarding the novelty of the hypotheses <term>hypotheses: in this context, the fundamental assumptions or mathematical models used to explain planetary paths</term> of this work, which posits a moving Earth and a stationary Sun at the center of the universe—will be strongly offended, and think that the liberal arts <note>original: "disciplinas liberales"; the traditional core curriculum of education including geometry and astronomy.</note>, established correctly long ago, ought not to be thrown into confusion. But if they wish to weigh the matter exactly, they will find that the author of this work has committed nothing that deserves blame. For it is the astronomer’s unique task to gather the history of the celestial motions through diligent and skillful observation. Then, since he cannot by any means reach the true causes or hypotheses [behind them], he must devise and invent whatever kind of assumptions he can, so that, by assuming them, these same motions can be correctly calculated from the principles of geometry, for both the future and the past. This craftsman <note>A respectful reference to Copernicus.</note> has excellently performed both of these tasks. For it is not necessary that these hypotheses be true, nor even probable; rather, this one thing is sufficient: if they provide a calculation consistent with observations. Unless, perhaps, someone is so ignorant of geometry and optics that they take the <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used in ancient astronomy to explain why planets seem to speed up or slow down</term> of Venus to be probable, or believes it to be the reason why the planet sometimes precedes the Sun and sometimes follows it by forty degrees or more. For who does not see that, if this is assumed, it necessarily follows that the diameter of the star <note>In the 16th century, planets were often called "wandering stars."</note> would appear more than four times larger, and its body more than sixteen times larger, at <term>perigee: the point in an orbit closest to Earth</term> <note>original Greek: "περιγείῳ"</note> than at <term>apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from Earth</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀπογείῳ"</note>? Yet the experience of every age contradicts this. There are other things in this discipline no less absurd, which there is no need to examine for the time being. For it is clear enough that this art is entirely and simply ignorant of the causes of the apparent irregular motions. And if the astronomer devises any through invention—as he certainly devises many—he does not do so in order to persuade anyone that it is so, but only so that they may correctly set up a calculation. Moreover, since various hypotheses sometimes offer themselves for one and the same motion (as in the motion of the Sun, both eccentricity and the epicycle), the astronomer will primarily seize upon that which is easiest to grasp. The philosopher, perhaps, [will seek] probability mo-

<meta>catchword: gis re- [more]</meta>

<summary>This preface argues that Copernicus's heliocentric model should be viewed as a mathematical tool for calculation rather than a literal physical description of the universe. It aims to deflect potential criticism by claiming that astronomers are not concerned with "truth," but only with creating models that match observations.</summary>
<keywords>astronomy, hypotheses, heliocentrism, Nicolaus Copernicus, Andreas Osiander, geometry, epicycle, Venus, perigee, apogee</keywords>

--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This page concludes the "Anonymous Preface" by Andreas Osiander and begins the formal front matter of Copernicus's work with a letter of encouragement from Cardinal Nikolaus von Schönberg. The preface continues to argue that astronomical theories are mathematical tools rather than physical truths, while the Cardinal’s letter (dated 1536, seven years before the book's publication) demonstrates the high-level ecclesiastical support Copernicus received early on.</meta>

[reasoning] requires, yet neither will grasp or hand down anything certain, unless it has been divinely revealed to him. Therefore, let us allow these new hypotheses to become known among the old ones, being no more probable <note>original: "verisimiliores"; Osiander is being provocative here, suggesting Copernicus's theory is just as "unlikely" as the old ones, but more useful for math.</note>, especially since they are at once admirable and easy, and bring with them a vast treasury of the most learned observations. Nor should anyone expect anything certain from astronomy regarding hypotheses, since it can provide nothing of the kind; otherwise, if he takes as true that which was invented for another purpose, he may leave this discipline more foolish than when he approached it. **Farewell.**

# NIKOLAUS SCHÖNBERG, CAR-
## dinal of Capua, to Nicolaus Copernicus, Greetings.

<image-desc>A square decorative woodcut initial C, featuring a seated figure in a garden-like enclosure, perhaps representing a scholar or cleric.</image-desc>
Since the report of your merit reached me some years ago through the constant conversation of everyone, I then began to hold you in higher esteem and even to congratulate our people, among whom you flourished with such great glory. For I had understood that you not only were exceptionally skilled in the discoveries of the ancient mathematicians, but had also established a new system of the world <term>system of the world: "mundi ratio," referring to the structural arrangement of the universe</term>. In this system, you teach that the Earth moves; that the Sun occupies the lowest <note>In the physics of the time, the "lowest" point was the center of the universe.</note> and therefore the middle place of the universe; that the eighth sphere <note>The "sphere of fixed stars," which in ancient astronomy was the outermost shell of the universe.</note> remains motionless and fixed forever; and that the Moon, together with the elements included within its sphere, situated between the heavens of Mars and Venus, revolves around the Sun in an annual course. I also understood that commentaries on this entire system of astronomy have been composed by you, and that you have compiled the movements of the wandering stars <note>The planets.</note>, calculated and reduced into tables, to the greatest admiration of everyone. Therefore, most learned man, unless I am a burden to you, I beg you again and again, most earnestly, to communicate this discovery of yours to scholars, and to send to me at the first possible opportunity your meditations on the sphere of the world together with the Tables, and whatever else you have pertaining to this same matter. I have, moreover, given instructions to Theodoric von Reden <note>A Polish cleric and colleague of Copernicus who acted as an intermediary.</note> that everything be transcribed there at my expense and sent to me. If you grant me this favor, you will understand that you have dealt with a man who is studious of your name and desiring to do justice to such great merit. Farewell. From Rome, November 1st, 1536.

<summary>This page concludes Osiander’s warning that astronomical models are not physical facts and presents a letter from Cardinal von Schönberg urging Copernicus to publish his heliocentric findings.</summary>
<keywords>Osiander's Preface, Cardinal Nikolaus von Schönberg, heliocentrism, astronomical tables, 1536, Theodoric von Reden, Papal circles</keywords>

# TO THE MOST HOLY
# LORD, PAUL III,
# SUPREME PONTIFF,
## The Preface of Nicolaus Copernicus to the Books
## of the Revolutions.

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'S' at the beginning of the text, featuring two figures (scholars or classical figures) seated amidst ornate floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>

I can well enough estimate, Most Holy Father <note>Pope Paul III (reigned 1534–1549), to whom Copernicus dedicated his work seeking protection from critics.</note>, that it will come to pass that as soon as certain people hear that in these books of mine, which I have written about the revolutions of the spheres of the world, I attribute certain motions to the terrestrial globe, they will immediately cry out that I and such an opinion should be hissed off the stage <note>original: "explodendum"; literally "hissed off," as a bad actor would be removed from a Roman stage.</note>. For my own works do not please me so much that I do not weigh what others will judge of them. And although I know that the thoughts of a philosopher are far removed from the judgment of the common people—because his endeavor is to seek the truth in all things, insofar as God has permitted it to human reason—nevertheless, I think that opinions entirely foreign to the truth ought to be avoided. 

Therefore, when I considered with myself how absurd a "recitation" <note>original: "ἀκρόαμα" (akroama); a Greek term for a lecture or a doctrine to be heard.</note> they would think it—those who know that this opinion has been confirmed by the judgments of many centuries, namely, that the Earth is set motionless in the middle of the heaven as its center—if I, to the contrary, were to assert that the Earth moves, I hesitated for a long time whether I should bring to light my commentaries written to demonstrate its motion, or whether it would be better to follow the example of the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the ancient Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who often kept their mathematical and philosophical discoveries secret.</note> and certain others, who were accustomed to pass down the mysteries of philosophy not through writing, but by hand <note>Meaning orally, from teacher to student.</note> only to their relatives and friends. As the letter of Lysis to Hipparchus <note>A famous (likely forged) ancient letter that discusses the importance of keeping philosophical secrets from the uninitiated.</note> testifies. And indeed they seem to me to have done this, not as some think from a certain jealousy of sharing their doctrines, but lest things of such great beauty, investigated with much effort by great men, should be despised by those who either find it tedious to devote honest work to any literature unless it is profitable, or who, if they are stirred by the exhortations and example of others to the liberal study of philosophy, yet because of <meta>The page ends here. The catchword "stupidita" indicates the next word is "stupiditatem" (dullness/stupidity).</meta>

<summary>In this opening dedication to Pope Paul III, Copernicus expresses his fear that his theory of the Earth's motion will be mocked as absurd by those clinging to the traditional belief in a stationary Earth. He reveals that this fear led him to consider keeping his work secret, following the ancient Pythagorean tradition of only sharing knowledge with a select, trusted circle.</summary>
<keywords>Nicolaus Copernicus, Pope Paul III, heliocentrism, Pythagoras, Lysis, philosophical secrecy, Earth's motion, Renaissance science</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues Copernicus’s dedication to Pope Paul III. He is explaining that his fear of being mocked by those who lack mathematical understanding almost led him to suppress his work forever, until his friends—high-ranking church officials and scholars—persuaded him to publish.</meta>

# AUTHOR'S PREFACE.

...stupidity of intellect among philosophers, like drones moving among bees. When, therefore, I weighed these things in my mind, the contempt which I had to fear because of the novelty and absurdity of my opinion had almost driven me to abandon the work I had begun entirely.

But my friends drew me back, though I was long hesitating and even reluctant. Among them, the first was Nicolaus Schönberg <note>A German cardinal and diplomat who was a patron of the sciences.</note>, Cardinal of Capua, renowned in every kind of learning. Next to him was a man who loves me dearly, Tiedemann Giese, Bishop of Kulm <note>A lifelong friend of Copernicus and a supporter of his heliocentric theory.</note>, a most diligent student of sacred and all good letters. For he frequently exhorted me, and sometimes with added reproaches demanded that I publish this book and finally allow it to come to light—a book which had remained hidden away, suppressed by me, not only for nine years <note>A reference to the Roman poet Horace’s advice in *Ars Poetica* to keep a manuscript for nine years before publishing.</note>, but now into a fourth period of nine years <note>original: "quartum nouennium"; Copernicus implies he has held onto the work for thirty-six years.</note>. Not a few other most eminent and learned men did the same with me, urging that I should no longer refuse to contribute my labor for the common benefit of students of mathematics because of the fear I had conceived. They suggested that the more absurd my doctrine about the motion of the earth might seem to most people now, the more admiration and favor it would earn after they saw, through the publication of my commentaries, the fog of absurdity lifted by the clearest demonstrations. Influenced by these persuaders and by that hope, I finally permitted my friends to undertake the publication of the work, which they had long requested of me.

<margin>d|</margin> But perhaps Your Holiness will not wonder so much that I dared to bring these nighttime labors <note>original: "lucubrationes"; refers to work done by candlelight, implying deep and late-night study.</note> of mine to light, after I took so much trouble in working them out that I did not hesitate to commit my thoughts about the motion of the earth even to writing; rather, you expect to hear from me how it came into my mind that I dared to imagine some motion of the earth, contrary to the received opinion of mathematicians and almost contrary to common sense. Therefore, I do not want it to be hidden from Your Holiness that nothing else moved me to think of another way of calculating the motions of the spheres of the world than the fact that I understood that mathematicians are not consistent with themselves in investigating them. For first, they are so uncertain about the motion of the Sun and Moon that they cannot even [determine the length] of the revolving year...

<meta>catchword: your (tuam)</meta>

<summary>Copernicus describes his 36-year hesitation to publish his work due to fear of ridicule, crediting Cardinal Schönberg and Bishop Giese for finally persuading him to release it. He begins to explain that his motivation was the inconsistency and inaccuracy of existing mathematical models regarding the Sun and Moon.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Copernicus’s dedication to Pope Paul III. In the previous section, he described his hesitation to publish due to the potential for ridicule, eventually being persuaded by friends like Cardinal Schönberg and Bishop Tiedemann Giese. Here, he begins to explain his technical dissatisfaction with the existing models of astronomy.</meta>

-># AUTHOR’S PREFACE.<-

ij

...they might be able to demonstrate and observe your magnitude. Next, in establishing the motions of these, as well as the other five wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" or *planetae* known at the time: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, they do not use the same principles and assumptions, nor the same demonstrations of the apparent revolutions and motions. For some use only **homocentric circles** <note>Also called concentric circles; a system where all celestial spheres share the Earth as their exact center.</note>, others use **eccentrics and epicycles** <note>Mathematical devices where a planet moves on a small circle (epicycle) which itself moves along a larger circle (deferent) that is slightly off-center from the Earth (eccentric).</note>, yet they still do not fully achieve what they seek. For those who relied on homocentric circles, although they demonstrated that several different motions could be composed from them, they were nonetheless unable to establish anything certain that would truly correspond to the **phenomena** <note>The observed positions and movements of the stars and planets as seen from Earth.</note>.

However, those who devised **eccentrics**, although they seem for the most part to have resolved the apparent motions with consistent numerical calculations, have nonetheless admitted many things in the meantime which seem to contravene the first principles concerning the uniformity of motion <note>The ancient Greek requirement that all celestial motion must be perfectly circular and uniform (at a constant speed).</note>. They were also unable to find or deduce the most important thing—namely, the **form of the world** and the certain symmetry of its parts. 

Instead, it happened to them just as if someone were to take hands, feet, a head, and other limbs from different places—drawn very well indeed, but not in comparison to a single body—and since they do not correspond to each other in any way, a monster rather than a human would be composed from them. Thus, in the process of demonstration, which they call a <term>methodos</term> <note>original: "μέθοδον"; a systematic way of teaching or investigating.</note>, they are found to have either passed over something necessary or admitted something alien and completely irrelevant to the matter. This would least of all have happened to them if they had followed certain principles. For if the **hypotheses** they assumed were not fallacious, everything which follows from them would undoubtedly be verified. Although these things I am saying now may be obscure, they will become clearer in their proper place.

Therefore, when I had long pondered this uncertainty of the mathematical traditions regarding the calculation of the motions of the spheres of the world, I began to be weary that no more certain system for the motions of the **machine of the world** <note>A common Renaissance metaphor for the universe as a complex, God-designed mechanism.</note>—which was built for our sake by the best and most orderly Creator of all—was available to philosophers, who otherwise scrutinize the most minute things of this world so exquisitely. For this reason, I took it upon myself to reread the books of all the philosophers I could obtain, to investigate whether anyone had ever thought that there were other motions...

<meta>catchword: motions</meta>

<summary>Copernicus critiques previous astronomers for using inconsistent models that fail to explain the universe's unified structure, comparing their disjointed theories to a "monster" made of mismatched body parts. He announces his intent to research alternative theories of planetary motion to find a more harmonious "machine of the world."</summary>

<keywords>astronomy, homocentric circles, eccentrics, epicycles, world-machine, mathematical tradition, planetary motion, scientific method</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues Copernicus’s preface to Pope Paul III. In the preceding text, he explained how the lack of consensus among mathematicians regarding the motions of the celestial spheres led him to investigate alternative theories.</meta>

-># AUTHOR’S PREFACE.<-

...the motions of the world's spheres, than those who profess mathematics in the schools had proposed. And indeed, I first found in the writings of Cicero that Nicetus <note>Copernicus likely means Hicetas of Syracuse, a 4th-century BCE philosopher mentioned by Cicero as believing the Earth rotates.</note> had held the opinion that the Earth moves. Later, I also discovered in Plutarch that others were of the same opinion; I have decided to set down his words here so they may be available to all:

<note>original: "οἱ μὲν ἄλλοι μένειν τὴν γῆν, Φιλόλαος δὲ Πυθαγόρειος κύκλῳ περιφέρεσθαι περὶ τὸ πῦρ κατακυκλῳ λοξὸν ὁμοιοτρόπως ἡλίῳ καὶ σελήνῃ. Ἡρακλείδης ὁ Ποντικός ϗ Ἔκφαντος ὁ Πυθαγόρειος κινεῖσι μὲν τὴν γῆν οὐ μήν γε μεταβατικῶς, τροχοῦ δίκην ἐζωνισμένην ἀπὸ δυσμῶν ἐπὶ ἀνατολὰς, περὶ τὸ ἴδιον αὐτῆς κέντρον."</note>

> Others say that the Earth stands still, but Philolaus the Pythagorean says that it moves around the central fire in an oblique circle, much like the Sun and the Moon. Heraclides of Pontus and Ecphantus the Pythagorean also grant the Earth motion, not by moving it from its place, but by turning it like a wheel on its axle from west to east around its own center.

Taking this as an opportunity, I too began to think about the **mobility of the Earth**. And although the opinion seemed absurd, yet because I knew that others before me had been granted the liberty to imagine whatever circles they pleased to demonstrate the **phenomena** <note>The observed movements of celestial bodies.</note> of the stars, I thought it might easily be permitted to me as well to test whether, by attributing some motion to the Earth, more solid demonstrations than those of my predecessors could be found regarding the revolution of the celestial spheres.

And so, assuming the motions which I attribute to the Earth later in this work, I finally discovered through long and frequent observation that if the motions of the other **wandering stars** <note>The planets.</note> are compared to the circulation of the Earth, and calculated according to the revolution of each star, not only do their observed appearances follow from this, but also the order and magnitudes of all the stars and spheres. Indeed, it binds heaven itself together so closely that in no part of it can anything be shifted without causing the confusion of all the other parts and of the entire universe. 

Therefore, in the progress of this work, I have followed this order: in the first book, I describe all the positions of the spheres along with the motions I attribute to the Earth, so that this book contains the general constitution of the universe, as it were. In the remaining books, I then compare the motions of the other stars and all the spheres with the mobility of the Earth, so that it can be understood to what extent the motions and appearances of the other stars and spheres can be **saved** <note>To "save the appearances" meant to create a mathematical model that accurately predicted observations, even if the physical reality of the model was debated.</note> if they are compared to the Earth’s motions. Nor do I doubt that ingenious and learned mathematicians will agree with me, if—as this...

# AUTHOR’S PREFACE

...**philosophy** <term>Philosophy</term><note>In the 16th century, "natural philosophy" was the term for what we now call science.</note> especially requires, not in passing but deeply, to know and weigh those things which are brought forward by me in this work for the demonstration of these matters. So that the learned and unlearned alike might see that I avoid no one's judgment at all, I preferred to dedicate these my labors to your Holiness rather than to anyone else. This is because, even in this most remote corner of the earth where I live, you are considered most eminent both in the dignity of your rank and in your love for all literature and even **Mathematics**. By your authority and judgment, you might easily suppress the bites of slanderers—although the proverb says there is no remedy against the bite of a **sycophant** <note>A person who uses flattery or malicious distortion to gain favor or attack others; Copernicus is anticipating that people will attack his work out of spite rather than knowledge.</note>.

If there should perhaps be **idle talkers** <note>original: "ματαιολόγοι" (mataiologoi). A Greek term for those who speak nonsense or engage in vain, empty babbling.</note> who, although they are ignorant of all Mathematics, yet take it upon themselves to judge these things, and because of some passage of **scripture**—badly distorted for their purpose—dare to find fault with and attack this my undertaking, I do not care for them. Indeed, I despise their judgment as rash. 

For it is no secret that **Lactantius** <note>Lactantius (c. 250–325 AD) was an early Christian author who famously argued against the idea of a spherical Earth, mocking the idea of people living on the "other side" (the antipodes).</note>, an otherwise celebrated writer but poor mathematician, spoke quite childishly about the **shape of the earth** when he mocked those who declared that the earth has the form of a globe. Therefore, it should not seem surprising to students if some such people mock us as well. 

**Mathematics is written for mathematicians** <note>This is one of Copernicus’s most famous declarations. He argues that scientific arguments should be judged by scientific criteria, not by those outside the field.</note>, to whom these labors of ours—if I am not mistaken—will also seem to contribute something to the **ecclesiastical Commonwealth** <note>original: "Reipub. ecclesiasticæ." This refers to the organizational and administrative body of the Catholic Church.</note>, over which your Holiness now holds leadership. 

For not so long ago under **Leo X**, when the question of **reforming the Church Calendar** was discussed in the **Lateran Council** <note>The Fifth Lateran Council (1512–1517). The Julian calendar was drifting out of sync with the solar year, making it hard to calculate the correct date of Easter.</note>, it remained undecided for this reason alone: that the lengths of years and months, and the movements of the Sun and Moon, were not yet considered sufficiently measured. Since that time, I have focused my mind on observing these more accurately, encouraged by the most distinguished man, **Lord Paul, Bishop of Fossombrone** <note>Paul of Middelburg (1446–1534), a scientist and bishop who was a key figure in the early efforts to reform the calendar.</note>, who then presided over that business. What I have achieved in this matter, I leave to the judgment of your Holiness especially, and of all other learned mathematicians. And lest I seem to promise more to your Holiness concerning the utility of the work than I can perform, I now pass to the undertaking itself.

## BOOK ONE.

### That the universe is spherical. Chapter I.

<margin>
1. Reason

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' containing a man's face in profile surrounded by stylized leaf patterns.</image-desc>
FIRST, we must note that the universe <note>original: "mundus." In the 16th century, this term referred to the entire cosmos or the world-system.</note> is spherical, either because that form is the most perfect of all, needing no joint, a whole complete in itself; or because it is the most capacious of shapes, which most suits that which is to contain and preserve all things; or even because the most finished parts of the universe, I mean the Sun, the Moon and the stars, are seen in such a form; or because all things desire to be bounded by this shape, which is apparent in drops of water and other liquid bodies when they desire to be bounded by themselves. Thus, no one will doubt that such a form is attributed to the celestial bodies.

### That the earth is also spherical. Chapter II.

<margin>
1. Resolves an objection that could have been made.
2. Proves it by the poles [of the stars] of Eridanus.
3.
</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'T' with botanical or decorative strapwork patterns.</image-desc>
The Earth is also spherical, since it presses upon its center from every side. Although a perfect sphere is not immediately apparent because of the great height of mountains and the depth of valleys, these nevertheless vary the universal roundness of the earth very little. This is manifest in this way: for to those traveling everywhere toward the North, that pole of the daily revolution is gradually raised, while the other sinks by the same amount on the opposite side; more stars around the North are seen not to set, and in the South some stars no longer rise. Thus Italy does not see Canopus <note>A bright star in the southern constellation of Carina, visible only from lower latitudes.</note>, which is visible in Egypt. And Italy sees the last star of the River <note>The constellation Eridanus, "the River," which stretches far into the southern sky.</note>, which our region of a colder climate <note>Copernicus lived and worked in Frombork, Poland, a much higher latitude than Italy or Egypt.</note> does not know. Conversely, to those traveling into the South, those stars are raised, while those which are high to us sink down. Meanwhile, even the inclinations of the poles have everywhere the same ratio to the measured spaces of the earth, which...

...this occurs in no other than a spherical figure. From which it is manifest that the earth is also enclosed between its poles, and because of this, it is a globe. Add also that the Eastern inhabitants do not perceive evening eclipses of the Sun and Moon, nor do those living in the West perceive morning ones; while they see those in the middle, the former later, but the latter sooner. <note>Copernicus is explaining how time differences (longitude) prove the Earth's curvature. Conversely, if something shining is placed at the top of the mast, as the ship moves away from the land, it seems to those remaining on the shore to gradually descend until at last it is hidden, as if setting. 

<margin>3</margin>
It is also certain that waters, flowing by their nature, always seek lower places—just as the earth does—and do not press further from the shore than its convexity allows. For this reason, the land is necessarily that much higher wherever it rises out of the Ocean.

## How the earth with the water forms one globe. Chapter III.

<margin>
THE EARTH IS LOFTIER, as argued from the previous point. There, [the mast] would descend, etc.
</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'H' featuring a figure in profile within an ornate rectangular frame, beginning the word "Hic" (This).</image-desc>
This surrounding Ocean, therefore, pouring into seas in various places, fills its deeper descents. Thus there had to be less water than land, lest the water absorb the whole earth—as both strive toward the same center by their weight—but rather so that it might leave some parts of the land for the safety of living things, and all these islands open here and there. For is not the continent itself, the world of lands, anything other than an island larger than the others? Nor should certain of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, who held traditional views on the "four elements."</note> be heard, who declared all the water to be ten times larger than the whole earth. This was because in the transmutation of the elements, they take the conjecture that from one part of earth, ten parts of water are produced in the resolution. They say that the earth sticks out to some extent because, being cavernous, it is not balanced on all sides according to its gravity, and that the center of gravity is one thing, and the center of magnitude <note>The geometric center.</note> is another. But they are deceived by ignorance of the art of Geometry. They do not know that water cannot even be seven times greater without the whole center of gravity being emptied of earth, which would give place to the waters as being heavier than itself. Since spheres are to each other in the triple ratio <note>original: "tripla ratione." In Euclidean geometry, this refers to the ratio of volumes being the cube of the ratio of the diameters ($r^3$).</note> of their diameters.

<meta>This page continues Chapter III of Book I. Copernicus is arguing against the Aristotelian theory that there is ten times more water than earth. He uses recent geographical discoveries, including the Americas, to prove that land and water together form a single sphere with a shared center of gravity.</meta>

### ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK I.
<sig>a ij</sig>

[if the water] were an eighth part <note>Copernicus is responding to a traditional scholastic theory that the four elements exist in a 10:1 ratio, meaning water would be ten times the volume of earth and therefore should completely submerge it.</note>, its diameter could not be greater than the distance from the center to the surface of the waters; so far is it from the case that there is ten times more water than earth. Furthermore, that there is no difference between the earth’s center of gravity and its center of geometric magnitude can be understood from this: the convexity of the land rising out of the ocean does not swell upward in a continuous, ever-increasing heap. If it did, it would push back the sea waters as much as possible and would never allow internal seas or such vast gulfs to break through. Again, the depth of the abyss would not cease to increase as one moved away from the ocean shore; consequently, neither islands, nor reefs, nor any bit of land would be encountered by sailors who had traveled far out.

Now, it is well known that between the Egyptian Sea <note>The Mediterranean</note> and the Arabian Gulf <note>The Red Sea</note>, barely fifteen stadia <note>original: "stadia" — a classical unit of distance; 15 stadia is roughly 1.7 miles, though Copernicus is likely referring to the narrowest part of the Isthmus of Suez.</note> remain in nearly the middle of the world. Conversely, Ptolemy in his *Cosmography* <note>Ptolemy was a 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian geographer whose work was the standard for over a millennium.</note> extended the habitable land as far as the middle circle <note>The Equator</note>, leaving beyond it unknown land. There, more recent explorers have added <term>Cathay</term> <note>Northern China</note> and very extensive regions even up to 60 degrees of longitude. Thus, the land is now inhabited over a greater longitude than what remains for the ocean. 

This will be even clearer if we add the islands found in our own time under the Princes of Spain and Portugal, and especially <term>America</term> <note>Named for Amerigo Vespucci; Copernicus is writing only a few decades after its "discovery."</note>, named after the captain of the ships who discovered it. Because of its as-yet unknown size, they consider it to be another world. Besides this, there are many other previously unknown islands. We should therefore no longer wonder that there are <term>Antipodes</term> <note>People living on the opposite side of the globe</note> or <term>Antichthones</term> <note>literally "opposite-earthers"</note>. Indeed, geometric reasoning forces us to believe that America is located diametrically opposite to India on the Ganges because of its position. 

From all these facts, finally, I think it is manifest that the earth and water together lean upon a single center of gravity, and that this center is the same as the center of the earth's magnitude. Since the earth is heavier, its gaping parts are filled with water; and therefore, there is a small amount of water in comparison to the earth, even though more water may perhaps appear on the surface. For the earth, along with the waters surrounding it, must necessarily have the kind of shape that its shadow reveals: for during an eclipse of the Moon, the earth creates a darkening with the circumference of a perfect circle. 

<margin>
VARIOUS OPINIONS OF PHILOSOPHERS CONCERNING THE EARTH
</margin>

The earth, therefore, is not flat, as <term>Empedocles</term> and <term>Anaximenes</term> thought; nor drum-shaped, as <term>Leucippus</term> held; nor bowl-shaped, as <term>Heraclitus</term> believed; nor hollow in some other way, as <term>Democritus</term> suggested. Nor, again, is it cylindrical, as <term>Anaximander</term> proposed; nor does it extend downward to an infinite thickness with its roots at the bottom, as <term>Xenophanes</term> thought. Instead, it is a perfect roundness, as the Philosophers <note>Referring generally to the Aristotelian/Platonic tradition of the "Physici" or natural philosophers.</note> believe.

<summary>Copernicus argues that the Earth and its oceans share a single center of gravity and form a perfect sphere, refuting ancient theories of flat or hollow shapes by citing recent voyages to America and China. He notes that lunar eclipses prove the Earth's circularity.</summary>

### That the motion of the heavenly bodies is uniform and circular, perpetual, or composed of circular motions. Chapter IV.

<margin>Having proved the principle that the world is spherical, he now proves that its motion is spherical.</margin>
<margin>There are many motions, but all are spherical.</margin>
<margin>Proof that the motion is circular.</margin>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'P' depicting a scholar or astronomer sitting at a desk with an open book, positioned in front of a window showing a landscape with buildings and a tower.</image-desc>After this, we shall call to mind that the motion of the heavenly bodies is circular. For the mobility of a sphere is to revolve in a circle, expressing its very form through this action, in the simplest of bodies, where no beginning or end can be found, nor can one part be distinguished from another, as it moves through the same path into itself. However, there are multiple motions because of the multitude of spheres. The most obvious of all is the daily revolution, which the Greeks call *nycthemeron* <note>original: "νυχθήμερον" — a 24-hour period of day and night.</note>, that is, the span of a day and a night. By this motion, the entire universe is thought to glide from east to west, with the Earth alone excepted <note>Copernicus refers here to the perceived motion of the heavens from the perspective of an observer on Earth, though his revolutionary thesis will eventually argue the Earth itself is moving.</note>. This is understood as the common measure of all motions, since we measure time itself primarily by the count of days. Next, we see other revolutions that are, as it were, striving against this one—that is, moving from west to east—namely, those of the Sun, the Moon, and the five wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" or planets known in the 16th century: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>. In this way, the Sun regulates the year for us, and the Moon the months, which are the most common divisions of time; likewise, each of the other five planets makes its own circuit. Yet, they differ in many ways. First, they do not revolve around the same poles as that primary motion, but travel through the obliquity of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi" — literally the "sign-bearer," the path of the sun and planets across the sky.</note>. Second, in their own circuits, they do not appear to be carried uniformly. For the Sun and Moon are found to be sometimes slow and sometimes faster in their course. As for the other five wandering stars, we perceive them sometimes even moving backward and making stationary points here and there. And while the Sun always proceeds on its own direct path, they wander in various ways, straying sometimes toward the South and sometimes toward the North, which is why they are called "planets" <note>From the Greek word *planētēs*, meaning "wanderer."</note>. Add also that sometimes they become closer to the earth—and are called "perigee"—and at other times further away—and are called "apogee." Nevertheless, it must be admitted that their motions are circular, or composed of several circles, because these irregularities follow a certain law and return to their original states at fixed intervals, which could not happen if they were not circular. For only a circle can bring back what has already passed; for example, by a motion composed of circles, the Sun brings back to us the inequality of days and nights and the four seasons of the year.

<summary>Copernicus argues that celestial bodies must move in circles because the sphere is the most perfect shape, and only circular motion can account for the regular, repeating patterns of the seasons and planetary cycles.</summary>
<keywords>celestial motion, circular motion, daily revolution, planets, zodiac, perigee, apogee, nycthemeron</keywords>

REVOLUTIONS BOOK I.

...times brings it back, in which multiple motions are understood. Since it is impossible that a simple celestial body should move irregularly in a single orbit. For such a thing would have to happen either because of an inconsistency in the moving power <note>original: "uirtutis mouẽtis" — the internal or external force that keeps a planet in motion.</note>—whether that force be an external addition or part of its inner nature—or because of some defect in the body being revolved. Since the human intellect shrinks from both of these ideas, and it is unworthy to imagine such a flaw in things that are established in the most perfect order, it is reasonable to conclude that their uniform motions only *appear* irregular to us. This happens either because the poles of their circles are different, or because the Earth is not located in the center of the circles in which they revolve. To us, looking from the Earth, the passing of these stars appears to vary because of their unequal distances: those closer to us appear larger than those further away (as is demonstrated in the study of optics). Thus, even though the stars travel equal distances along their orbits, they will appear to move at different speeds during equal amounts of time because of the varying distance from our eyes.

<margin>This presupposition serves all the previous axioms.</margin>

For this reason, I think it is necessary above all else that we carefully observe the relationship of the Earth to the heavens. Otherwise, while we wish to investigate the highest things, we might remain ignorant of the things closest to us, and by that same error, attribute to the heavenly bodies things that actually belong to the Earth.

### Whether circular motion belongs to the Earth, and concerning its location. Chapter V.

<image-desc>A decorative initial letter 'I' showing a scholar or authority figure seated in a room, representing the start of a new section of the argument.</image-desc>
Now, because it has been demonstrated that the Earth also has the shape of a globe, I believe we must see whether its motion also follows its shape, and what place it occupies in the universe. Without these facts, it is impossible to find a reliable explanation for the phenomena seen in the heavens. Although authors generally agree that the Earth rests at the center of the world <note>original: "medio mundi" — in the context of the 16th century, "mundus" referred to the entire universe.</note>, so that they think it unthinkable and even ridiculous to hold the opposite view, if we consider the matter more carefully, it will appear that this question is not yet settled, and therefore should by no means be dismissed.

<margin>That the Earth moves.</margin>

For every perceived change in place is due to the motion of the object seen, or of the observer, or certainly to an unequal movement of both. For when two things move equally in the same direction, no motion is perceived—I mean between the thing seen and the one seeing it. Now, the Earth is the place from which that heavenly circuit is observed and reproduced for our sight. Therefore, if any motion is attributed to the Earth...

...be assigned <note>original: "deputetur" — referring back to the motion of the observer discussed on the previous page.</note>, that same motion will appear in everything which is outside of it, but in the opposite direction, as if the objects were passing by. Such is, in the first place, the **daily revolution**. For this appears to sweep along the entire universe, except for the Earth and those things around it. But if you were to grant that the heavens have nothing of this motion, but that the Earth instead revolves from the west to the east—and if you consider this seriously regarding the apparent rising and setting of the Sun, Moon, and Stars—you will find that this is indeed the case. Since it is the heavens which contain and cover all things, the common "place" of the entire universe, it is not immediately clear why motion should not be attributed to the thing contained rather than to the container, or to the thing located rather than to the thing providing the location.

Indeed, the Pythagoreans Heraclides and Ecphantus, as well as Nicetas of Syracuse (as mentioned in Cicero), were of this opinion, depicting the Earth as revolving in the center of the universe. For they believed that the stars set because the Earth's bulk stands in the way, and they rise when the Earth moves aside. If we assume this, another no less important doubt follows concerning the position of the Earth, although almost everyone has now accepted and believed that the Earth is the center of the world. 

For if someone were to deny that the Earth occupies the middle or center of the world, but yet does not admit that the distance is so great as to be comparable to the sphere of the <term>fixed stars</term><note>Stars that appear to stay in fixed patterns (constellations) relative to one another, unlike "wandering" planets.</note>, but is nevertheless notable and evident in relation to the orbits of the Sun and other stars—and if he thinks that their motion appears diverse for that reason, as if they were regulated by a different center than the center of the Earth—he might perhaps be able to provide a sound explanation for the apparent diverse motion. For the fact that the wandering stars <note>original: "errantia sidera" — the planets.</note> are seen closer to the Earth at some times and farther away at others, necessarily proves that the center of the Earth is not the center of those circular orbits. Thus, it is not even certain whether the Earth draws near to them and moves away, or they to the Earth. 

It would not be so surprising if someone, besides that daily revolution, were to imagine another motion for the Earth. Indeed, that the Earth revolves and even wanders with several motions, and is "one of the stars," is a view Philolaus the Pythagorean is said to have held—a mathematician of no ordinary sort, for whose sake Plato did not hesitate to travel to Italy, as those who have written the life of Plato relate. 

However, many have thought it can be demonstrated by geometric reasoning that the Earth is in the center of the world; that it is like a point compared to the immensity of the heavens, occupying the place of a center; and for that reason, it is immobile, because when the universe moves, the center...

### On the Immensity of the Heavens in Relation to the Size of the Earth. Chapter VI.

That the great bulk of the Earth has no significant scale <note>original: "aestimationem" — here meaning comparative value or measurable size</note> compared to the magnitude of the heavens can be understood from the following fact. The "boundary circles"—for this is the meaning of the Greek term *horizons* <note>original: ὁρίζοντας (horizontas)</note>—cut the entire celestial sphere into two equal halves. This could not happen if the size of the Earth were significant when compared to the heavens, or if its distance from the center of the world were notable. For a circle that cuts a sphere into two equal halves must pass through the center of that sphere, and it is the largest of the circles that can be drawn around it.

Let the circle ABCD be the horizon, and let the Earth, from which our vision originates, be at E, which is the center of the horizon that separates the things that are visible from those that are not. Let there be observed through a sighting-tube <term>Dioptra: an ancient Greek surveying instrument used for measuring angles and altitudes</term>, or a "horoscope" <note>here referring to a sighting instrument for determining the ascendant, not a modern birth chart</note>, or a water-level <term>Chorobates: a long wooden tool (about 20 feet long) used by Roman engineers for leveling, similar to a modern spirit level</term> placed at E, the beginning of Cancer rising at point C; at that same moment, the beginning of Capricorn is seen to set at A. Since AEC forms a straight line through the sighting-tube, it is clear that this line is the diameter of the zodiac <term>Signifer: literally "the sign-bearer," the Latin term for the belt of the zodiac</term>, because six signs [of the twelve] define a semicircle, and the center E is the same as the center of the horizon. 

Again, when the revolution has changed so that the beginning of Capricorn rises at B, the setting of Cancer will then also be seen at D. BED will be a straight line and itself a diameter of the zodiac. Now, since it has already appeared that AEC is also a diameter of the same circle, it is evident that their intersection at E is the center. Thus, the circle of the horizon always divides the zodiac—which is the greatest circle of the sphere—into two equal halves. 

But in a sphere, if a circle cuts through the middle of any of the "great circles," the cutting circle itself must also be a "great circle." Therefore, the horizon is one of the "great circles," and its center appears to be the same as the center of the zodiac. This remains true even though a line drawn from the surface of the Earth must necessarily be different from one drawn from its center. Yet, because of the immensity of the heavens in respect to the Earth, these lines become, in a way, like parallel lines which, due to the excessive distance of their endpoint, appear to be a single line; for when the space that contains <note>original: "continet" — the text continues onto the next page</note>...

->**NICOLAUS COPERNICUS**<-

<meta>The text begins mid-word: "continet" (occupies/contains)</meta>
[...the space] it occupies in relation to their length becomes incomparable to the senses, in the manner demonstrated in *Optics* <note>Copernicus refers here to the science of perspective and light, likely drawing on Euclid or Ptolemy to explain why distant objects appear to lose their measurable size</note>. By this argument, it is clear enough that the heavens are immense compared to the Earth, and present an appearance of infinite magnitude. In the estimation of the senses, the Earth is to the heavens as a point is to a body, and as the finite is to the infinite in magnitude.

Yet nothing else seems to have been demonstrated. For it does not follow that the Earth must necessarily rest in the middle of the universe. Indeed, we should wonder even more if such a vastness of the world should revolve in the space of twenty-four hours, rather than its smallest part, which is the Earth.

For as for the claim that the center is immobile and that things closest to the center move the least, this does not prove that the Earth rests in the middle of the world. It is no different than if you were to say that the sky turns while the poles remain still, and those things closest to the poles move the least. In the same way, the Little Bear <note>original: "Cynosura" — the constellation Ursa Minor, which stays near the celestial pole</note> is seen to move much more slowly than the Eagle <note>original: "Aquila"</note> or the Little Dog <note>original: "Canicula" — usually referring to the bright star Sirius</note>, because being near the pole, it describes a smaller circle. Since all these things belong to a single sphere, whose motion ends at its axis, the sphere does not allow for an equal motion among all its parts; nevertheless, the revolution of the whole brings them all back in the same amount of time, though not across an equal distance.

The reasoning of the argument rests on this: as if the Earth were a part of the celestial sphere and shared its nature and motion, so that, being near the center, it would move very little. Therefore, as a body and not the center itself, the Earth would also move, covering similar—though smaller—arcs of a celestial circle in the same amount of time [as the stars]. 

How false this is, is clearer than light! For it would mean that it would always be noon in one place and always midnight in another, so that neither the daily rising nor setting could occur, since the motion of the whole and the part would be one and inseparable. 

However, the nature of things that are distinct is far different: those things enclosed in a smaller circuit revolve more quickly than those which travel a larger circle. Thus, Saturn, the highest of the wandering stars <note>original: "errantium sydus" — the planets were known as 'wandering stars' as they moved against the fixed backdrop of the constellations</note>, completes its revolution in the thirtieth year; and the Moon, which is undoubtedly nearest the Earth, completes its circuit in a month. Finally, the Earth itself will be thought to circle in the space of a day and a night. 

Therefore, the same doubt regarding the daily revolution arises again. But its location is also still being sought, and is even less certain from the things said above. For that demonstration proves nothing else than that the size of the heavens is indefinite compared to the Earth; but how far this immensity extends is not at all clear.

<summary>Copernicus argues that the immense size of the universe makes it more logical for the small Earth to rotate than for the entire heavens to revolve at incredible speeds. He challenges the traditional Aristotelian view that the Earth must be stationary at the center by comparing orbital periods of planets like Saturn and the Moon.</summary>

## Why the ancients thought the Earth remained at rest in the middle of the universe as its center. Chapter VII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing a portrait of a bearded man (likely a philosopher like Aristotle or Ptolemy) wearing a cap and holding an instrument, possibly a compass or astrolabe.</image-desc>

For this reason, the ancient philosophers tried to prove by certain other arguments that the Earth stands in the middle of the universe. They cite as the most powerful cause the principles of gravity and levity <term>levity: in ancient physics, the "natural" quality of lightness that caused elements like fire to move upward, the opposite of gravity</term>. Truly, the element of earth is the heaviest, and all weighty things are carried toward it, striving toward its innermost center. For since the Earth is spherical, heavy things are carried toward it from all sides by their own nature at right angles to its surface. Unless they were held back on the surface itself, they would fall together toward its center; because a straight line, which meets the boundary plane touching the sphere at right angles, leads to the center. It seems to follow that those things which are carried toward the middle should rest in the middle. Therefore, the whole Earth will rest all the more in the middle, and as it receives everything that falls into it, it will remain immobile by its own weight.

In the same way, they also strive to prove this by the reasoning of motion and its nature. For Aristotle <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE) established the physical framework that dominated science until Copernicus's time</note> says that the motion of a single and simple body is simple. Of simple motions, one is straight and the other is circular. Of the straight motions, one is upward and the other is downward. Therefore, every simple motion is either toward the middle (which is downward), away from the middle (which is upward), or around the middle (which is circular). Now, it is appropriate for earth and water—which are considered heavy—to be carried downward, which is to seek the middle. But for air and fire, which are endowed with levity, to be moved upward and away from the middle. It seems consistent that a straight motion is granted to these four elements, but celestial bodies revolve in a circle around the middle. These are the views of Aristotle.

If therefore, says Ptolemy of Alexandria <note>Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE) was the most influential astronomer of antiquity; his *Almagest* defined the geocentric model</note>, the Earth were to revolve—at least with its daily revolution—the opposite of the above would have to happen. For the motion would have to be most rapid, and its speed insurmountable, to carry the whole circumference of the Earth around in twenty-four hours. Now, things that are driven by a sudden whirling seem utterly unfit to be gathered together, and are more likely to be dispersed if they were already united, unless they are held together by some firm coherence. And long ago, he says, the Earth would have been dissipated even into the heavens themselves (which is quite ridiculous

<b>b</b>
<meta>catchword: ridiculous</meta>

### The solution to the stated reasons, and their insufficiency. Chapter VIII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'H' at the start of the chapter, featuring floral or scrollwork ornamentation within a square frame.</image-desc>

For these indeed and similar reasons, they say the Earth rests in the middle of the universe, and that it is undoubtedly so. But if someone should think that the Earth rotates, he will surely say that the motion is natural, not violent <term>natural vs. violent motion: in Aristotelian physics, 'natural' motion is the inherent tendency of an object (like fire rising), while 'violent' motion is forced upon it (like throwing a stone). Forced things break apart; natural things are preserved</term>. Truly, things which happen according to nature produce the opposite effects to those brought about by violence. For things to which force or an impetus is applied must be dissolved and cannot long subsist; but things which happen by nature are rightly ordered and preserved in their best composition.

Therefore, Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE), the Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose geocentric model Copernicus is challenging</note> fears in vain that the Earth and all terrestrial things would be scattered in a revolution performed by the efficacy of nature, which is far different from that of art, or from what human ingenuity can achieve. But why does he not suspect this even more of the universe, whose motion must be as much faster as the heavens are larger than the Earth? Have the heavens become so immense because they are driven away from the center by the unspeakable vehemence of their motion, and would otherwise collapse if they stood still? 

Certainly, if this reasoning held, the magnitude of the heavens would extend to infinity. For the more the motion is carried upward by its own impetus, the faster the motion will be, because of the ever-increasing circumference which must be crossed in the space of twenty-four hours; and conversely, as the motion increases, the immensity of the heavens would increase. Thus, velocity would promote magnitude, and magnitude velocity, into infinity. 

Yet according to that physical axiom, what is infinite cannot be traversed, nor can it be moved by any means; the heavens, therefore, will necessarily stand still. But they say that outside the heavens there is no body, no place, no vacuum, and absolutely nothing, and therefore there is nowhere the heavens could expand; then truly it is a wonder if "something" can be restrained by "nothing." Yet if the heavens were infinite and were only bounded by an inner concavity, it would perhaps be more true that there is nothing outside the heavens, since everything <note>original: "quodqʒ" — catchword for the next page</note>

<summary>Copernicus rebuts the ancient fear that a rotating Earth would fly apart, arguing that natural rotation is stable, whereas a rotating universe would logically have to be infinite and thus unable to move at all.</summary>
<keywords>natural motion, violent motion, Ptolemy, centrifugal force, infinite universe, physics axioms, celestial rotation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Chapter 8, where Copernicus argues that the Earth's rotation is a natural motion that does not cause it to fly apart. He uses the principle of relative motion to explain why the heavens appear to move while the Earth stays still, and addresses the behavior of the atmosphere and falling objects.</meta>

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK I.

...and whatever might be in it, no matter how great its size, while the heaven will remain immobile. For the primary argument by which they strive to prove the universe is finite is motion. Whether the universe is finite or infinite, let us leave that debate to the natural philosophers <term>physiologorum: at this time, people who studied the "physics" or nature of the world</term>; let us hold this as certain: that the Earth is enclosed by its poles and bounded by a spherical surface. Why then do we still hesitate to grant it a mobility consistent with its nature and form, rather than saying that the whole universe—whose limit is unknown and cannot be known—is falling away? Why do we not admit that the appearance of a daily revolution belongs to the heavens, but the reality belongs to the Earth? This is just as the poet Virgil's Aeneas says:

> We sail out of the harbor, and the lands and cities recede. <note>original: "Prouehimur portu, terræq́z urbesq́z recedunt." From the Aeneid, Book 3, line 72.</note>

For when a ship floats along in calm water, everything outside it is seen by the sailors to move in the likeness of the ship's motion, while they, in turn, think they are at rest along with everything with them. In just this way, it can happen with the motion of the Earth that the whole universe is thought to revolve. 

What then should we say about the clouds and other things hanging in the air, or sinking, or rising upward? Only that not only the Earth and the element of water joined to it move in this way, but also a significant part of the air and whatever else has a kinship with the Earth. Either this is because the nearby air, mixed with earthy or watery matter, follows the same nature as the Earth, or because the motion of the air is "acquired"—participating in the perpetual revolution of the Earth through direct contact and without resistance. 

Conversely, they say with no less wonder that the highest region of the air follows the motion of the heavens, as shown by those sudden stars—I mean <term>Comets</term> and what the Greeks call <term>Bearded Stars</term> <note>original: "Pogoniæ"</note>—which they believe are created in that very place, and which rise and set just like other stars. We can say that, because of the great distance from the Earth, that part of the air is deprived of the terrestrial motion. Therefore, the air closest to the Earth will appear tranquil, along with the things suspended in it, unless it is tossed back and forth by wind or some other force, as happens. For what else is wind in the air but a wave in the sea? 

We must admit that the motion of falling and rising bodies is twofold in relation to the universe, being a composite of both rectilinear <note>Straight-line motion</note> and circular motion. Since things which by their own weight <meta>catchword: de (from "deorsum," meaning "downward")</meta>

<summary>Copernicus explains that we perceive the heavens as moving due to the Earth's rotation, much like sailors on a moving ship see the shore receding. He also argues that the atmosphere and objects within it share the Earth's natural circular motion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from Chapter 8, refuting the Aristotelian view that a moving Earth would cause objects to fly off or behave unnaturally. Copernicus explains the relationship between "natural" circular motion and "accidental" straight-line motion.</meta>

<header>NICOLAUS COPERNICUS</header>
<sig>d</sig>
<meta>catchword: fine</meta>

...are pressed downwards, since they are composed mostly of earth; there is no doubt that the parts preserve the same nature as their whole. Nor is it different for those things which are carried into the heights by the force of fire. For even this terrestrial fire is nourished primarily by earthy matter, and philosophers define flame as nothing other than burning smoke. Now, it is the property of fire to expand what it has entered, and it does this with such force that it can be restrained by no means and no machines from breaking its prison and completing its work. This expansive motion is from the center toward the circumference; accordingly, if any earthy part is set on fire, it is carried from the middle up to the heights.

Therefore, as for the saying that "the motion of a simple body is simple" <note>This is a core principle of Aristotelian physics: simple elements like earth or fire have one natural direction—either straight up or straight down.</note>, this is verified primarily regarding circular motion, so long as the simple body remains in its natural place and in its unity. Indeed, in its proper place, there is no motion other than circular motion, which remains entirely within itself, similar to being at rest. But rectilinear <term>rectus: straight-line</term> motion comes upon those things that wander from their natural place, or are pushed out of it, or are in any way outside of it. Nothing, however, is so contrary to the order of the entire world and the form of the universe as being out of one's proper place.

Straight-line motion, therefore, does not happen except to things that are not in a right state and are not perfect according to their nature, while they are being separated from their whole and abandoning its unity. Furthermore, those things that are moved upward and downward, even without circular motion, do not produce a simple, uniform, and equal motion. For they cannot be balanced by their lightness or by the impulse of their own weight. Whatever things fall, beginning with a slow motion, increase their speed as they fall. Conversely, we see this terrestrial fire (for we see no other) immediately lose its strength when carried into the heights, as if acknowledging the cause of the violence done to its earthy matter.

Circular motion, however, always rolls along equally, for it has an unfailing cause. But those other motions have a cause that hastens to an end, for when the objects reach their proper place, they cease to be heavy or light, and that motion ceases. Since, therefore, circular motion belongs to wholes, but straight-line motion belongs to parts as well, we can say that circular motion exists alongside the straight-line motion, just as "animal" exists alongside "sick." <note>original: "sicut cum aegro animal." Copernicus uses a clever analogy: just as being "sick" is a temporary condition that happens to a "living animal," straight-line motion is a temporary "sickness" or accidental state for the "natural" circular parts of the Earth.</note> Surely, even the fact that Aristotle distributed simple motion into three kinds—away from the center, toward the center, and around the center—will be thought of as a mere act of reason. It is much like how we distinguish a line, a point, and a surface, even though one cannot exist without the other, and none of them...

<summary>Copernicus argues that straight-line motion (falling or rising) is a temporary "unnatural" state for objects trying to return to their place, whereas circular motion is the natural, eternal state of "whole" bodies like the Earth. This allows him to reconcile the Earth's rotation with the observed behavior of falling objects.</summary>

<keywords>Aristotle, circular motion, rectilinear motion, simple motion, Nicolaus Copernicus, physics, gravity, natural place</keywords>

Here, he concludes that argument by suggesting immobility is a "divine" state more suited to the universe as a whole than to the Earth, and begins to propose that the Earth has multiple motions, just like the other planets.</meta>

<header>ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK I.</header>

...without a body. To these points we may add that a state of immobility is considered nobler and more divine than one of change and instability; for this reason, instability is more suited to the Earth than to the universe. I add also that it would seem quite absurd to attribute motion to the container or that which provides the place <note>original: "continenti siue locanti." In classical physics, the heavens were seen as the "container" of the Earth.</note>, and not rather to that which is contained and placed, which is the Earth. Finally, since it is manifest that the wandering stars <note>original: "errantia sydera." This is the traditional term for planets, derived from the Greek word *planētēs*, meaning "wanderer."</note> move closer to and further from the Earth, there will also be—even according to those who want the center of the Earth to be the center of the universe—a motion of a single body toward and away from that center. We must therefore understand motion around a center more generally, and it is enough that each motion stays focused upon its own center. You see, then, from all these arguments, that the mobility of the Earth is more probable than its rest, especially regarding the daily revolution, which is most characteristic of the Earth.

### Whether several motions can be attributed to the Earth, and on the center of the universe, Chapter IX.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' containing a seated figure (an astronomer or scholar) at a desk, surrounded by scholarly objects.</image-desc>Since, therefore, nothing prevents the mobility of the Earth, I believe we must now see whether several motions might belong to it, so that it can be considered one of the wandering stars. For that the Earth is not the center of all revolutions is proved by the seemingly unequal motion of the wandering stars and their varying distances from the Earth—phenomena that cannot be understood as circles centered on the Earth. Since there are many centers, one might not unreasonably doubt whether the center of the universe is this center of terrestrial gravity <term>grauitatis terrenæ: the natural tendency of Earth-matter to pull together</term>, or some other point. Indeed, I believe that gravity is nothing other than a certain natural desire <note>original: "appetentiam quandam naturalem"</note> bestowed on the parts by the divine providence of the Maker of all things, so that they may join themselves together in their unity and wholeness by coming together in the form of a globe. It is credible that this same tendency is present in the Sun, the Moon, and the other wandering lights, so that by its power they remain in the roundness they display, even as they complete their circuits in many ways. If, then, the Earth also performs other motions—for instance, around a center—these must necessarily be the motions that appear reflected in many external things, among which we find the annual circuit. For if this motion is shifted from the Sun to the Earth, and immobility is granted to the Sun,

...if granted, the rising and setting of the zodiacal signs and fixed stars, by which they become morning and evening stars, will appear in the same way. ### On the order of the celestial spheres. Chapter X.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'A' featuring foliate and floral motifs within a square border.</image-desc>
I see that no one doubts that the heaven of the fixed stars is the highest of all visible things. But we see that the ancient philosophers wanted to determine the sequence of the wandering stars according to the duration of their revolutions. They assumed the principle that among objects moving at an equal speed, those that are further away seem to move more slowly, as is demonstrated in Euclid’s *Optics* <note>Euclid’s *Optics* (c. 300 BCE) was a foundational text on perspective, explaining how distance affects the perceived size and speed of objects.</note>. Therefore, they believe the Moon completes its circuit in the shortest span of time because, being closest to the Earth, it revolves in the smallest circle. The highest, however, is Saturn, which orbits the largest circuit in the greatest amount of time. Beneath it is Jupiter. After this, Mars.

Regarding Venus and Mercury, however, different opinions are found, because they do not move away from the Sun in every direction <note>Unlike Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, which can appear opposite the Sun in the night sky, Venus and Mercury always stay relatively close to the Sun's position.</note> as the others do. For this reason, some place them above the Sun, as in Plato’s *Timaeus*, while others place them below it, like Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE), whose geocentric model placed the Earth at the center with Mercury and Venus between the Earth and the Sun.</note> and a large number of more recent authors. Alpetragius <note>original: "Alpetragius." The Latinized name of Nur ad-Din al-Bitruji, a 12th-century astronomer who challenged Ptolemy’s use of epicycles.</note> places Venus above the Sun and Mercury below it. Therefore, those who follow Plato—since they believe that all stars (which are otherwise dark bodies) shine with light received from the Sun—argue that if these planets were below the Sun, they would be seen as half-moons or certainly lacking roundness, as they are never very far from it. For they would reflect the light they received upwards, that is, toward the Sun, just as we see in the new or waning Moon. They also say it would be necessary for the Sun to be blocked occasionally by their intervention, and for its light to fail in proportion to their size; since this never appears to happen, they think these planets in no way pass beneath the Sun. Conversely, those who place Venus and Mercury below the Sun base their reasoning on the vastness of the space they find between the Sun and the Moon.
