[revolu]tion. <note>The text completes the word "revolution" from the previous page.</note> For they found that the maximum distance of the Moon from the earth is sixty-four and one-sixth parts, where the radius of the earth is one. They found that this distance is contained nearly eighteen times within the minimum distance to the Sun, which amounts to 1,160 of those same parts. Therefore, between the Sun and the Moon, there are 1,096 parts. Consequently, so that such a vast space would not remain empty, they reasoned from the intervals of the **apsides** <term>apsides: the points in an orbit where a planet is either closest to (perigee) or farthest from (apogee) the center of its motion</term>, by which they calculate the thickness of those spheres. They found that these intervals nearly fill the numbers, so that the lowest point of **Mercury** succeeds the highest point of the Moon, and the highest point of Mercury is followed by the lowest point of **Venus**, which finally, at its highest point, almost reaches the lowest point of the Sun. Indeed, between the apsides of Mercury, they calculate nearly 177 1/2 of the aforementioned parts, and then the remaining space is filled by the interval of Venus, which is nearly 910 parts.

Therefore, they do not admit that there is any opacity in the stars <note>In this period, "stars" often referred to any celestial body, including planets.</note> similar to that of the Moon; rather, they believe the planets shine either by their own light or are saturated with solar light throughout their entire bodies. For this reason, the Sun is not blocked—which would be an extremely rare event—because they are usually positioned away from the Sun's path in latitude. Furthermore, they argue that their bodies are small in comparison to the Sun; since Venus, though larger than Mercury, can hardly cover a hundredth part of the Sun, according to **Al-Battani** <note>original: "Machometus Aracensis." Al-Battani (c. 858–929) was a pioneering Arab astronomer whose observations were more accurate than Ptolemy's.</note>, who estimates the Sun's diameter to be ten times larger. Therefore, he believes such a tiny speck would not be easily seen against that most brilliant light. Nevertheless, **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), the Andalusian polymath.</note> mentions in his commentary on Ptolemy that he remembered seeing something blackish when he found the conjunction of the Sun and Mercury indicated by the calculations. Thus, they conclude that these two stars move below the solar circle. 

But how weak and uncertain this reasoning is, is clear from the fact that while there are 38 parts from the center of the earth to the surface of the nearest Moon according to Ptolemy, a truer estimation shows it to be more than 52 (as will be shown below). Yet, we know of nothing else contained in such a great space except for air and, if one prefers, what they call the *element of fire*. <note>Traditional Aristotelian physics taught that a sphere of fire existed between the upper atmosphere and the sphere of the Moon.</note> Furthermore, the diameter of the circle of Venus—by which it deviates from the Sun by about 45 degrees on either side—must be six times larger than the distance from the center of the earth to its lowest apsis, as will be demonstrated in its proper place. What then will they say is contained in all that space, which is so much larger than what would be required to hold the earth, the air, the ether, the Moon, and Mercury, and furthermore that

<header>NICOLAUS COPERNICUS</header>

...that vast epicycle of Venus would occupy, if it revolved around a stationary earth. Furthermore, Ptolemy’s argument—that it was necessary for the Sun to be carried in the middle, between those planets that diverge from it in every direction and those that do not diverge—is shown to be unconvincing by the fact that the Moon, which itself diverges in every direction, proves its falsehood. <note>Ptolemy argued the Sun must be in the middle of the planetary sequence because some planets (Mercury/Venus) are always near it, while others (Mars/Jupiter/Saturn) can be opposite it. Copernicus points out that the Moon follows none of these rules, yet is placed closest to Earth.</note> Indeed, what reason will those people allege—who place Venus below the Sun, then Mercury, or separate them in some other order—as to why they do not likewise make separate circuits, distinct from the Sun, like the rest of the wandering stars <note>original: "errantium", referring to the planets</note>, provided that the ratio of speed and slowness does not fail the order? Therefore, it will be necessary either that the earth is not the center to which the order of the stars and spheres is referred, or certainly that there is no principle of order, nor does it appear why a higher place should be owed to Saturn more than to Jupiter or any other planet.

For this reason, I think we should by no means disregard what **Martianus Capella** <note>A 5th-century Roman author of an influential encyclopedia; he proposed that Mercury and Venus orbit the Sun, though the Sun still orbited the Earth.</note> (who wrote the *Encyclopedia*) and indeed other Latins were well aware of. For they believe that **Venus** and **Mercury** run around the Sun, which exists in their midst; and for that reason, they think these planets do not diverge further from it than the convexity of their spheres allows, because they do not circle the earth like the others, but have reversed **apsides** <term>apsides: the points in an orbit where a planet is at its maximum or minimum distance from its center of motion</term>. What else, then, do they mean to signify, than that the center of those spheres is around the Sun? Thus, indeed, the sphere of Mercury will be enclosed within that of Venus (which is agreed to be more than twice as large), and it will occupy a place within that very space sufficient for itself.

Taking this opportunity, if someone were also to relate **Saturn**, **Jupiter**, and **Mars** to that same center—provided they understand the magnitude of those spheres to be so great that they contain and surround the earth along with those planets residing within—they will not be in error, as the canonical reasoning of their motions declares. For it is established that they are always closer to the earth around their "evening rising" <note>original: "uespertinum exortum"; this occurs at opposition, when the planet rises as the sun sets</note>—that is, when they are opposite the Sun, with the earth between them and the Sun. Conversely, they are farthest from the earth at their "evening setting," when they are hidden around the Sun, namely while we have the Sun between them and the earth. These things sufficiently indicate that their center belongs more to the Sun, and is the same center to which Venus and Mercury also refer their revolutions. But indeed, since all these things rely on a single middle, it is necessary that the space left between the convex sphere of Venus and the concave sphere of Mars [be] also a sphere...

### ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK 1

...or that a sphere be recognized as sharing a center with them <note>The orbits of Mercury and Venus</note> according to each of its surfaces, which would receive the Earth along with its attendant, the Moon, and whatever is contained beneath the lunar globe. For we can in no way separate the Moon from the Earth—since they are undeniably close to one another—especially since we find a sufficiently fitting and abundant space for the Moon in that region.

Therefore, we are not ashamed to confess that this whole system which the Moon encircles, along with the center of the Earth, passes through that **great orbit** <note>original: "orbem illum magnum"; this refers to the Earth's annual path around the Sun</note> among the other wandering stars <note>original: "errantes stellas", the planets</note> in an annual revolution around the Sun. We confess that the Sun is the center of the world. With the Sun remaining immovable, whatever motion the Sun appears to have is instead verified to be the mobility of the Earth. 

The magnitude of the world is so great, however, that while the distance from the Earth to the Sun has a size quite evident in proportion to the orbits of the other wandering stars, it is as nothing when compared to the sphere of the fixed stars. I think this is easier to grant than to allow the intellect to be distracted by an almost infinite multitude of spheres—which those who have kept the Earth at the center of the world were forced to do. Instead, we should follow the sagacity of nature, which, just as it has been most careful to avoid producing anything superfluous or useless, so it has preferred to enrich a single thing with many effects.

All these things are difficult and almost inconceivable, being contrary to the opinion of many; however, in the following pages, God willing, we will make them clearer than the Sun itself—at least to those who are not ignorant of the mathematical art. Therefore, while the first principle remains intact—for no one will propose a more suitable one than that the size of the orbits is measured by the length of time <note>Copernicus argues that the further a planet is from the center, the longer its "year" should be—a logic that perfectly dictates the order of the planets once the Earth is seen as moving.</note>—the order of the spheres follows in this manner, beginning from the highest:

The first and highest of all is the sphere of the fixed stars, containing itself and all things, and for that reason, it is immovable. It is indeed the place of the universe to which the motion and position of all other stars are compared. As for the fact that some think it changes in some way <note>A reference to "trepidation" or the precession of the equinoxes, which some contemporaries thought involved a physical movement of the outer sphere.</note>, we shall assign another cause for why it appears so in our deduction of the Earth's motion. 

There follows the first of the wandering stars, **Saturn**, which completes its circuit in thirty years. After this is **Jupiter**, moving in a twelve-year revolution. Then **Mars**, which circles in two years. The fourth place in the order is held by the annual revolution...

### BOOK I OF THE REVOLUTIONS.

...in this arrangement we find an admirable symmetry of the universe and a certain harmonious link between the motion and size of the orbits, such as cannot be found in any other way. For here one may observe, if they contemplate it diligently, why the progression and regression <note>original: "progreſſus & regreſſus"; this refers to "retrograde motion," where planets appear to move backward in the sky from our perspective on Earth</note> appears greater in Jupiter than in Saturn, and smaller than in Mars; and again greater in Venus than in Mercury. And why such reversal appears more frequently in Saturn than in Jupiter, but more rarely in Mars and Venus than in Mercury. Furthermore, why Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars are closer to the Earth when they are at their nightly rising <note>original: "acronycti"; the point when a planet is opposite the Sun and rises just as the Sun sets</note> than around the time of their disappearance and reappearance. Most notably, Mars when visible all night seems to equal Jupiter in size, distinguished only by its reddish color; yet elsewhere it is hardly found among stars of the second magnitude, recognized only by those following with diligent observation. All these things proceed from the same cause, which is found in the motion of the Earth.

However, that none of these effects appear in the fixed stars argues for their immense height, which makes even the orbit of the annual motion <note>The Earth’s path around the Sun</note> or its image vanish from our sight. For everything visible has a certain distance of length beyond which it is no longer seen, as is demonstrated in the science of Optics. That there is still a vast distance from the highest of the wandering stars, Saturn, to the sphere of the fixed stars, is demonstrated by their twinkling lights. By this sign they are chiefly distinguished from the planets, as it was necessary for there to be a very great difference between what is moving and what is not. So great indeed is this divine workshop of the Best and Greatest God.

## Demonstration of the Triple Motion of the Earth. Chapter XI.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' depicting a bearded scholar or saint seated at a desk within a room, looking toward a window.</image-desc>Since, therefore, so many and such great testimonies from the wandering stars agree with the mobility of the Earth, we shall now explain that motion in summary, so that the appearances may be demonstrated by it as a hypothesis. We must admit three distinct motions in total. The first is the one we mentioned the Greeks call the <term>nychthēmerinon</term> <note>original: "νυχθημερίνὸν"; meaning "belonging to a day and a night"</note>, the proper circuit of day and night around the axis of the Earth, turning from west to east, just as the universe is thought to be carried in the opposite direction, describing the equinoctial circle, which some call the "equal-day" circle, imitating the meaning of the Greek... <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page</note>

### NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

<meta>catchword: decli-</meta>

...[equinoxes], among whom it is called the **equinoctial** <note>original Greek: "ἰσημεϱινός" (isēmerinos), referring to the celestial equator where day and night are of equal length</note>. The second motion is the **annual motion of the center**, which describes the circle of the signs <term>the zodiac; the path the Sun appears to follow through the stars</term> around the Sun, proceeding from west to east in the order of the signs. As we have said, this path lies between Venus and Mars, along with those things that move with the Earth. Thus it happens that the Sun itself appears to pass through the zodiac with a similar motion. For example, when the center of the Earth passes through Capricorn, the Sun appears to pass through Cancer; when the Earth is in Aquarius, the Sun appears in Leo, and so on, as we have described. Regarding this circle—which is through the middle of the signs—and its surface, it must be understood that the **equinoctial circle** and the axis of the Earth have a variable inclination. For if they remained fixed and simply followed the motion of the center, no inequality of days and nights would appear. Instead, it would always be either the summer solstice, the winter solstice, the equinox, summer, or winter; whatever the quality of the season, it would remain forever the same.

Therefore, the **third motion of declination** follows, also with an annual revolution, but moving in the preceding direction <note>original: "in precedentia"; this means a retrograde motion, or moving "backwards" through the signs of the zodiac (East to West)</note>, which is to say, reflecting against the motion of the center. Because these two motions <note>The Earth's annual orbit around the Sun and this third corrective motion of the axis</note> are nearly equal and opposite, the result is that the axis of the Earth, and the greatest of the parallel circles—the equinoctial—point toward almost the same part of the universe, as if they remained immobile. Meanwhile, the Sun is seen to move through the slant of the **sign-bearer** <note>original: "signiferi"; another term for the zodiac or ecliptic</note> by that same motion with which the center of the Earth moves, exactly as if the Earth were the center of the universe—provided you remember that the distance between the Sun and the Earth has already been surpassed by our sight in the **sphere of the fixed stars** <note>Copernicus reminds the reader that the Earth's orbit is so small compared to the distance to the stars that the Earth's shift in position doesn't change how the stars look to us</note>. 

Since these matters are of a kind that require being placed before the eyes rather than merely spoken of, let us describe the circle **ABCD**. This shall represent the annual circuit of the center of the Earth in the plane of the zodiac, and let **E** near its center be the Sun. I will divide this circle into four parts by the diameters **AEC** and **BED**. Let point **A** represent the beginning of Cancer, **B** of Libra, **C** of Capricorn, and **D** of Aries. Now, let us assume the center of the Earth is first at **A**. Around this, I will designate the earthly equator **FGHI**, but not in the same plane, except that the diameter **GAI** shall be the common section of the circles—that is, of the equator and the zodiac. We shall also draw the diameter **FAH** at right angles to **GAI**, where **F** is the limit of the greatest declination toward the South, and **H** is toward the North. With these things thus arranged, the inhabitants of the Earth will see the Sun near the center **E** under Capricorn, making the winter solstice, with the greatest...

**Alternatively:** Let there likewise be in the underlying plane **ABC** a <term>diameter</term> <note>original: "dimetiens"</note>, which is the common intersection of a circle standing upright to that plane. In this plane, around points **A** and **C** (that is, under the signs of **Cancer** and **Capricorn**), let the circle of the Earth passing through the poles be designated in turn as **DGFI**. Let the Earth’s axis be **DF**: the North pole being **D**, the South pole **F**, and **GI** being the diameter of the <term>equinoctial circle</term> <note>the Equator</note>. 

Therefore, when **F** turns toward the Sun (which is at **E**), and the inclination of the equator is northern according to the angle **FAE**, then the daily rotation around the axis will describe a southern parallel to the equator according to the diameter **KL**; the distance **LI** represents the **tropic of Capricorn** as it appears from the Sun. Or, to put it more accurately: that motion around the axis, relative to the line of sight **AE**, carves out a conical surface with its point at the center of the Earth and its base as a circle parallel to the equator. In the opposite sign <note>Cancer</note>, everything happens in exactly the same way, but reversed. 

It is clear, therefore, how these two motions meeting each other—namely, the motion of the center <note>the Earth's orbit</note> and the motion of inclination <note>the tilt of the axis</note>—force the Earth's axis to remain in the same <term>equilibrium</term> <note>original: "libramento," referring to a steady, balanced orientation</note> and in a consistent position. This makes everything appear as if it were the Sun that was moving. However, we were saying that the annual revolutions of the center and of the declination are *almost* equal. If they were exactly equal, then the equinoxes, the solstices, and the entire <term>obliquity of the zodiac</term> <note>original: "obliquitas signiferi," the 23.5-degree tilt of the Earth's path relative to the equator</note> under the sphere of the fixed stars would never change at all. But because there is a slight <meta>catchword: difference (differentia)</meta>

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK I.

...this difference <note>original: "differentia"</note>, which only becomes apparent as it grows over a long period of time, has been revealed: from the time of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the influential 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer</note> down to our own, it has shifted by nearly 21 degrees. For this reason, some believed that the sphere of the fixed stars also moves. To explain this, they preferred a ninth superior sphere; and when even that was not sufficient, recent authors have added a tenth. Yet they have not reached the goal which I hope we will achieve by means of the motion of the Earth. We shall use this motion as a principle and hypothesis in the demonstrations of other phenomena.

### On the Magnitude of Straight Lines in a Circle. Chapter XII.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap initial "Q" containing a seated figure holding what appears to be a book or an astronomical instrument, possibly representing a scholar or astronomer.</image-desc>

Since the demonstrations which we will use throughout almost the entire work deal with straight lines and arcs, and with plane and spherical triangles—about which much is already clear in the *Elements* of Euclid <note>The standard textbook of geometry from ancient Greece</note>—they nevertheless do not contain what is most sought after here: how the sides can be obtained from the angles, and the angles from the sides. Since an angle does not measure the subtended straight line <note>The "chord" or the line connecting two points on a circle's edge</note>, just as the line does not measure the angle, but rather the arc does. Therefore, a method has been found by which the lines subtending any arc may be known. With their help, one can find the arc corresponding to an angle, and conversely, find the straight line through the arc that subtends the angle. Because of this, it seems relevant to treat these lines here.

We shall also discuss the sides and angles of both plane and spherical triangles, which Ptolemy handed down in a scattered way through examples, so that they may be settled here once and for all, making what we are about to present clearer. According to the common consensus of mathematicians, we divide the circle into 360 parts. The ancients assigned 120 parts to the diameter <term>diameter</term> <note>the distance across the center of the circle</note>. But later scholars, in order to avoid the entanglement of "scruples" <note>minutes or small fractions in the sexagesimal (base-60) system</note> in the multiplication and division of numbers regarding these lines—which are for the most part <term>incommensurable</term> <note>having no common measure, like irrational numbers</note> in length and often in square—set the rational diameter at 1,200,000, others at 2,000,000, and others differently, from the time when the Indian shapes of numbers <note>Hindu-Arabic numerals (0-9), which were much easier for complex calculation than Roman numerals</note> were accepted into use. This number system surpasses any other, whether Greek or Latin, with a certain unique...

...surpasses it in readiness, and adapts itself most fitly to every kind of calculation. For this reason, we too have adopted 200,000 parts of the diameter as sufficient to exclude any obvious error. For in those matters which do not have a ratio like one number to another <note>meaning irrational numbers, which cannot be expressed as simple fractions</note>, it is enough to achieve the closest approximation. We will explain this in six theorems and one problem, following Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, whose *Almagest* provided the standard chord tables for over a millennium</note> for the most part.

## Theorem One.

Given the diameter of a circle, the sides of the triangle, square, hexagon, pentagon, and decagon which the same circle circumscribes are also given. Since the radius <note>original: "quae ex centro", literally "that which is from the center"</note>, being half the diameter, is equal to the side of the hexagon. The square of the triangle's side is triple, and the square of the square's side is double the square made by the side of the hexagon, as has been demonstrated in Euclid’s *Elements*. Therefore, the side of the hexagon is given as 100,000 parts in length; the square’s side as 141,422 parts; and the triangle’s side as 173,205 parts. Now, let the side of the hexagon be AB, which, by the 11th proposition of the second book, or the 30th of the sixth book of Euclid, is divided in extreme and mean ratio <note>the "Golden Ratio," where the ratio of the whole to the larger part is the same as the larger part to the smaller</note> at point C, and let the larger segment be CB, to which is added an equal segment BD.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a horizontal line segment with points labeled A, C, E, B, D from left to right, used to illustrate the division of a line according to the golden ratio (extreme and mean ratio).</image-desc>

Therefore, the whole line ABD will be divided in extreme and mean ratio, and the smaller segment added to it [BD] will be the side of the decagon inscribed in the circle for which AB was the side of the hexagon, as is clear from the 5th and 9th propositions of Euclid's 13th book. Indeed, BD itself will be given in this way: let AB be divided in half at E. It is clear by the third proposition of that same book of Euclid that the square of EBD is five times the square of EB. But EB is given as 50,000 parts in length; its square's fivefold value is given, and EBD itself is 111,803 parts in length. If the 50,000 parts of EB itself are subtracted from this, there remains BD, the sought side of the decagon, at 61,803 parts. Also, the side of the pentagon—the square of which is equal to the squares of the hexagon side and the decagon side combined—is given as 117,557 parts. Therefore, given the diameter of a circle, the sides of the triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, and decagon inscribable in that same circle are given, which was to be demonstrated.

## Porism <note>A "porism" in classical geometry is a corollary or a derived proposition.</note>

Hence it is manifest that when the chord <note>original: "subtensa", literally "the line stretched under" an arc</note> of any arc has been given, that chord is also given which subtends the remainder of the semi-

<meta>This page continues Copernicus's geometric proofs for constructing a table of chords (the basis for trigonometry). Having just calculated the side of a decagon, he is now using the Pythagorean theorem and Ptolemy’s Theorem to find the lengths of other chords.</meta>

REVOLUTIONS BOOK I.

...subtends <note>In geometry, a chord "subtends" an arc if it connects the two endpoints of that arc.</note> in a semicircle. Because an angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle, and in right-angled triangles, the square of the side subtending the right angle—that is, the diameter—is equal to the sum of the squares of the sides enclosing the right angle <note>This is the Pythagorean Theorem applied to a triangle inside a circle.</note>. Since it has been demonstrated that the side of a decagon, which subtends 36 degrees of the circumference, consists of 61,803 parts where the diameter is 200,000, the chord which subtends the remaining 144 degrees of the semicircle is also given as 190,211 of those parts. And through the side of the pentagon, which subtends 72 degrees with 117,557 parts of the diameter, the difference is found: the straight line which subtends the remaining 108 degrees of the semicircle is 161,803 parts.

### Theorem Second.

If a quadrilateral is inscribed in a circle, the rectangle <note>In historical geometry, "the rectangle contained under X and Y" refers to the product of the lengths of those two lines (X times Y).</note> formed by the diagonals is equal to the sum of the rectangles formed by the opposite sides. For let the quadrilateral ABCD be inscribed in a circle; I say that the product of the diagonals AC and DB is equal to the sum of the products of AB times CD and AD times BC. 

For let us make the angle ABE equal to the angle CBD. Therefore, the whole angle ABD will be equal to the whole angle EBC, by adding the angle EBD, which is common to both. Furthermore, the angles ACB and BDA are equal to each other because they are in the same segment of the circle <note>An ancient geometric principle: angles standing on the same arc are equal.</note>. Thus, the two triangles BCE and BDA will be similar and have proportional sides, such that BC is to BD as EC is to AD; and the product of EC and BD is equal to the product of BC and AD. 

But the triangles ABE and CBD are also similar, because the angles ABE and CBD were made equal, and the angles BAC and BDC are equal, as they stand upon the same arc of the circle. Thus, AB is to BD as AE is to CD, and the product of AB and CD is equal to the product of AE and BD. But it has already been established that the product of AD and BC is equal to the product of BD and EC. Taken together, therefore, the product of BD and AC <note>AC is the sum of AE and EC.</note> is equal to the sum of the products of AD times BC and AB times CD. This was the appropriate point to demonstrate this <note>This is now known as Ptolemy's Theorem.</note>.

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram. A circle contains an inscribed quadrilateral ABCD. Two diagonals, AC and BD, are drawn and intersect. A point labeled E is marked on the diagonal AC near the intersection point. This diagram visually represents the proof of Ptolemy's Theorem described in the text.</image-desc>

### Theorem Third.

From these proofs, if the straight lines <note>meaning the chords</note> subtending unequal arcs in a semicircle are given, the chord subtending the arc by which the larger exceeds the smaller is also given. As in the semicircle ABCD, and the diameter...

OF NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...given the diameter AD and the chords AB and AC of unequal arcs. Since we wish to find the chord BC, the chords of the remaining arcs of the semicircle, BD and CD, are given from the principles stated above; thus, a quadrilateral ABCD is formed within the semicircle.

![A geometric diagram showing a semicircle with diameter AD. Inscribed in the semicircle is a quadrilateral ABCD. Chords AB, BC, and CD are shown, along with diagonals AC and BD.](diagram1)

The diagonals AC and BD of this quadrilateral are given, along with three sides: AB, AD, and CD. In this figure, as has already been demonstrated <note>This refers to Ptolemy's Theorem, explained in Theorem 2 on the previous page.</note>, the product of AC and BD <note>original: "quod sub AC & BD," literally "that which is under [the lines] AC and BD," a standard geometric way to describe the area of a rectangle or the product of two lengths.</note> is equal to the sum of the products of AB times CD and AD times BC. Therefore, if the product of AB and CD is subtracted from the product of AC and BD, the remainder is the product of AD and BC. Thus, by using AD as a divisor, the length of the sought-after chord BC is calculated as accurately as possible. Consequently, since the sides of the pentagon <note>A pentagon's side subtends 72°.</note> and hexagon <note>A hexagon's side subtends 60°.</note> are known from the previous sections, this method provides the chord for 12 degrees (the difference between 72° and 60°), which is found to be 20,905 parts where the diameter is 200,000.

### Theorem Fourth.

Given the chord subtending any arc, the chord subtending half of that arc is also given. Let us describe a circle ABC with diameter AC, and let BC be a given arc with its chord. From the center E, let the line EF cut BC at right angles.

![A circular geometric diagram showing a circle with diameter AC and center E. A triangle ABC is inscribed in the upper semicircle. A perpendicular radius extends from center E through point F on chord BC to point D on the circumference. Point G is shown opposite D on the same diameter. Several chords, including AB and BD, are drawn to illustrate the geometric proof.](diagram2)

Therefore, according to the third proposition of Euclid’s third book <note>Euclid's Elements, Book III, Proposition 3, states that a line from the center perpendicular to a chord bisects that chord.</note>, it will cut the line BC into two equal parts at point F, and the arc at point D. Let the chords AB and BD also be drawn. Since triangles ABC and EFC are right-angled and furthermore share the angle ECF, they are similar. Thus, just as CF is half of BC, EF is half of AB. However, AB is given, as it subtends the remaining arc of the semicircle; therefore EF is also given, along with the remainder DF, which is found by subtracting EF from the radius. Let the diameter be completed as DEG, and connect BG. Therefore, in the triangle BDG, the perpendicular line BF descends from the right angle B to the base. Consequently, the product of GD times DF is equal to the square of BD. <note>This is a property of right triangles where the altitude to the hypotenuse creates a relationship between the segments of the hypotenuse and the sides.</note> Thus, the length of BD is given, which subtends half of the arc BDC. Since the chord subtending 12 degrees is already known, the chord subtending 6 degrees is also given as 10,467 parts; for 3 degrees, 5,235 parts; for one and a half degrees <note>1° 30'</note>, 2,618 parts; and for three-quarters of a degree <note>45'</note>, 1,309 parts.

### Fifth Theorem.

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram positioned to the right of the text. It depicts a circle with points A, B, C, D, and E marked on the circumference. Lines connect these points to form an inscribed pentagonal shape (though not regular). Point F is marked at the center where diameters AD and BE intersect. Diagonal chords BD and CE are also drawn.</image-desc>

Again, when the chords of two arcs have been given, the chord that subtends the total arc composed of them is also given. Let the given chords in a circle be AB and BC; I assert that the chord of the entire arc ABC is also given. For, having drawn the diameters <note>A diameter is a straight line passing through the center of a circle.</note> AFD and BFE, let the straight lines BD and CE also be drawn as chords; these are given from the preceding proofs because AB and BC are given, and DE is equal to AB. With CD connected, a quadrilateral BCDE is formed, whose diagonals BD and CE, along with three sides—BC, DE, and the diameter BE—are given. The remaining side CD will also be given by the second theorem, and likewise CA is given as the chord of the remaining part of the semicircle for the whole arc ABC, which was sought.

Furthermore, since we have so far found the chords that subtend three degrees, one and a half degrees, and three-quarters of a degree <note>original: "dodrantem unius," meaning three-quarters of one degree, or 45 arc-minutes.</note>, anyone could construct a table <note>original: "canona," a "canon" or mathematical table used for astronomical calculations.</note> with the most exact reasoning using these intervals. However, if one wishes to proceed degree by degree, joining one to another, or by halves, or in some other way, one will rightly have doubts about the chords of those parts. This is because the geometric <note>original: "graphicæ," referring to proofs based on straightedge and compass construction.</note> methods by which they might be demonstrated are lacking to us. Nevertheless, nothing prevents us from achieving this by another method, without an error noticeable to the senses, and differing minimally from the assumed number. This is what Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Roman-Egyptian astronomer whose "Almagest" was the standard text Copernicus was updating.</note> sought concerning the chords of one degree and half a degree, first advising us of a specific rule.

### Sixth Theorem.

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram positioned to the right of the text. It shows a circle with points A, B, C, and D. A triangle ABC is inscribed in the upper portion. A line segment BD originates from point B, passes through the center F, and extends to point D on the opposite side of the circle. This line BD intersects the chord AC at point E. Chords AD and CD are also drawn. Points H and I are marked on chords AD and CD respectively.</image-desc>

The ratio of the arcs is greater than the ratio of the straight chords of the larger arc to the smaller. Let there be two unequal arcs joined in a circle, AB and BC, where BC is the larger. I assert that the ratio of arc BC to arc AB is greater than the ratio of the chords BC to AB. These chords enclose angle B, which shall be bisected by the line BD, and let AC be joined, which intersects BD at the point marked E. Likewise, join AD and CD, which are equal because of the equal arcs they subtend. Since, therefore, the line BD of triangle ABC bisects the angle, it also cuts the line AC <note>The text ends mid-sentence as it moves to the next page.</note>

<meta>This page continues the geometric foundations of Copernicus's trigonometry. Having previously shown how to calculate chords for sums and differences of arcs, he now provides a rigorous proof for a mathematical inequality: that the ratio of two arcs is greater than the ratio of their corresponding chords. This is a crucial step for the next "Problem," where he begins to approximate the chord of one degree—a value that cannot be derived through simple geometry alone (like the trisection of an angle).</meta>

BY NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

at **B**, the segments of the base will be **BC** to **AB**. And since **BC** is greater than **AB**, and **BC** is also greater than **EA**, let the perpendicular line **DF** be drawn to **AC**. This line will bisect <note>To "bisect" means to cut exactly in half.</note> **AC** at point **F**, which must necessarily be located within the larger segment **BC**. And since—

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circle with a central point D. A horizontal chord AC is bisected by a vertical line DF coming from the center. A triangle ABC is inscribed in the upper part of the circle. Points E, H, and I are marked along the intersecting lines to illustrate the proportional relationships between the sectors and the internal triangles.</image-desc>

—in every triangle, the larger angle is subtended <note>In geometry, "subtended" means to be opposite to an angle or arc.</note> by the larger side, in triangle **DEF**, side **DE** is larger than **DF**, and further **AD** is larger than **DE**. Therefore, with **D** as the center and **DE** as the radius <note>original: "intervallo," referring to the distance or radius used to draw the arc.</note>, let a circle be described; it will cut **AD** and pass through **DF**. Let it cut **AD** at point **H**, and let it be extended in a straight line **DFI**. Since, therefore, the sector <note>A "sector" is a pie-shaped part of a circle defined by two radii and an arc.</note> **BDI** is greater than triangle **BDF**, but triangle **DEA** is greater than sector **DEH**, the triangle **DEF** will have a smaller ratio to triangle **DEA** than sector **BDI** has to sector **DEH**. However, sectors are proportional to their arcs (or the angles at the center), while triangles sharing the same vertex are proportional to their bases. Therefore, the ratio of the angles **EDF** to **ADE** is greater than that of the bases **EF** to **AE**. Thus, when joined, the ratio of angle **FDA** to **ADE** is greater than **AF** to **AE**. In the same way, the ratio of **CDA** to **ADE** is greater than **AC** to **AE**. And by subtraction, the ratio of **CDE** to **EDA** is also greater than **CE** to **EA**. Now, the angles **CDE** and **EDA** are in the same ratio as the arcs **CB** and **AB**. Furthermore, the base **CE** is to **AE** as the chord **CB** is to the chord **AB**. Therefore, the ratio of the arc **CB** to the arc **AB** is greater than the ratio of the chord <note>original: "subtensae," the straight line connecting the two ends of an arc.</note> **BC** to the chord **AB**. This is what was to be demonstrated.

->Problem.<-

**B**ut since an arc <note>original: "circumferentia"</note> is always greater than the straight line subtending it—since a straight line is the shortest distance between two points—nonetheless, this inequality tends toward equality as the sections of the circle grow smaller, until finally, at the ultimate point of contact with the circle, the straight line and the arc coincide. It is necessary, therefore, that before that point, they differ from one another by no manifest distinction. For example, let arc **AB** be 3 degrees and arc **AC** be 1.5 degrees <note>original: "I. s." where "s" stands for "semis," or one half.</note>. The chord subtending **AB** has been shown to be 5,235 parts (where the diameter <note>original: "dimetiens"</note> is set at 200,000), and **AC** is 2,618 of those same parts. And since the arc is double—

<image-desc>A secondary geometric diagram showing a smaller segment of a circle defined by points A, B, and C. It illustrates the chords AB and AC to visually support the discussion of how small arcs and their chords begin to approach a 1:1 ratio.</image-desc>

<meta>catchword: arc AB</meta>

<summary>Copernicus provides a geometric proof that the ratio of two arcs is greater than the ratio of their chords and begins a "Problem" regarding the calculation of very small arcs. He explains that as arcs decrease in size, the difference between the arc length and the chord length becomes negligible.</summary>
<keywords>geometry, trigonometry, chords, arcs, ratios, De revolutionibus, chord table, mathematical proof</keywords>

--- Page 45 ---
<meta>This page continues Copernicus’s derivation of trigonometric values. On the previous page, he established that for very small angles, the ratio of the arcs is nearly identical to the ratio of their chords. Here, he uses that principle to calculate the chord for one degree and its fractions, effectively providing the final steps before presenting his trigonometric table (the "Canon").</meta>

->REVOLUTIONS BOOK I.<-

<margin>d iij</margin>
<meta>catchword: Table</meta>

arc **AB** to arc **AC**; however, the chord <note>original: "subtensa," the straight line connecting two points on a curve.</note> **AB** is less than double the chord **AC**, which adds only one small part to the 2617 parts. But if we take **AB** to be one and a half degrees, and **AC** to be three-quarters <note>original: "dodrantem," a Roman term for three-fourths.</note> of one degree, we will have chord **AB** consisting of 2618 parts, and **AC** of 1309 parts. Although **AC** ought to be [slightly] larger than half of chord **AB**, it nonetheless appears to differ not at all from the half; rather, the ratio of the arcs and the straight lines now appears to be the same. Since, therefore, we see that we have reached that point where the difference between the straight line and the curved line <note>original: "ambitiosæ," referring to the circuitous path of the arc.</note> entirely escapes our senses—as if they had become a single line—we do not hesitate to apply those 1309 parts of the three-quarter degree, by equal proportion, to the full degree and the remaining parts. Thus, by adding a quarter to the three parts <note>Adding 1/4 of the 3/4 value to reach a full 4/4 (1 degree).</note>, we establish one degree at 1745 parts, a half degree at 872½ parts, and a third of a part at approximately 582 parts.

Nevertheless, I think it is sufficient if we record in the table <note>original: "canone." Early mathematicians referred to their reference tables as "canons."</note> only the halves of the lines that subtend double the circumference. By this shortcut, we can include within a single quadrant <note>A 90-degree arc.</note> what otherwise would have had to be spread across a semicircle. This is especially useful because these half-lines <note>These "half-chords of the double arc" are what modern mathematicians call the **sine** of an angle.</note> occur more frequently in demonstrations and calculations than the full lines themselves. 

We have, therefore, set forth the table, increased by sixths of a degree <note>original: "sextantes," meaning intervals of 10 minutes (since 1/6 of 60 minutes is 10).</note>, having three columns. In the first are the degrees (or parts of the circumference) and the sixths. The second contains the numerical value of the half-line subtending the double circumference. The third has the difference between these numbers which lies between each degree; from these, one may add proportionally what is appropriate for individual minutes <note>original: "scrupulis," used here to mean the small fractional parts of a degree (minutes).</note> of the degrees. This, then, is the table.

<summary>Copernicus concludes his geometric proofs by demonstrating that at very small scales, chords and arcs are proportionally indistinguishable. He then introduces his trigonometric table, explaining that he will list "half-chords" (sines) at 10-minute intervals for ease of calculation.</summary>

## On the sides and angles of plane 
## rectilinear triangles. Chapter XIV.

### I.

**If the angles of a triangle are given, its sides are also given.** Let there be, I say, triangle ABC, around which a circle is circumscribed according to the fifth problem of the fourth book of Euclid <note>Euclid’s *Elements*, Book 4, Proposition 5, describes how to draw a circle that touches all three vertices of a triangle.</note>. Therefore, the arcs AB, BC, and CA will be given in the system where 360 degrees are equal to two right angles <note>original: "duobus rectis æquales." Copernicus describes a full circle as having 360 parts, which corresponds to two "straight" angles (180 degrees each) in Euclidean terms.</note>. Since the arcs are given, the sides of the triangle inscribed in the circle are also given as <term>subtended lines</term> <note>These are "chords"—straight lines connecting two points on a curve. In modern trigonometry, this is the basis for the Sine function.</note> by means of the previously set-forth Table, in parts where the diameter is assumed to be 200,000.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a circle containing an inscribed triangle labeled with vertices A, B, and C.</image-desc>

### II.

**But if two sides of a triangle are given along with one of the angles, the remaining side and the remaining angles will also be known.** For the given sides are either equal or unequal. The given angle is either right, acute, or obtuse. Furthermore, the given sides either enclose the given angle or they do not. Therefore, let there first be in triangle ABC two given sides, AB and AC, which are equal and enclose the given angle A. The remaining angles at the base BC, being equal to each other, are also given; they are each half of the remainder when angle A is subtracted from two right angles <note>180 degrees.</note>. And if one of the angles at the base was the one originally given, its pair is immediately known, and the third angle is found by subtracting these two from 180 degrees. But since the angles of the triangle are given, the sides are also given, and the base BC itself is given from the Table in parts where AB or AC (acting as the radius) would be 100,000 parts, or the diameter 200,000 parts.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of an isosceles triangle labeled with vertices A, B, and C.</image-desc>

### III.

**Should the angle BAC be a right angle and enclosed by the given sides, the same result will follow.** For it is very clear that the squares produced from AB and AC are equal to that [square]...

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a right-angled triangle labeled with vertices A, B, and C.</image-desc>

<meta>catchword: ei, [of it]</meta>

<summary>In this chapter, Copernicus explains the foundational rules of plane trigonometry, demonstrating how to solve for unknown sides and angles of triangles using his newly established table of chords and Euclidean geometry.</summary>
<keywords>plane trigonometry, Euclid's Elements, inscribed triangles, chords, isosceles triangles, right-angle theorems, geometric proofs</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Chapter XIV from Book I, concluding the third demonstration regarding right-angled triangles and moving into cases involving acute and obtuse triangles. This mathematical foundation is necessary for the astronomical calculations that follow in the later books.</meta>

<header>BOOK I OF THE REVOLUTIONS</header>

to that [square] which comes from base $BC$; therefore $BC$ is given in length, and the sides themselves are given in ratio to each other. But the segment of a circle that encloses a right-angled triangle is a semicircle, of which the base $BC$ is the diameter. Therefore, in whatever parts $BC$ is 200,000, $AB$ and $AC$ will be given as the lines subtending <note>original: "subtendentes." These are chords—straight lines connecting two points on a curve. This is the precursor to the modern sine function.</note> the remaining angles of $BC$. Therefore, the ratio of the Table <note>original: "Canonis." Copernicus refers to his trigonometric "Canon" or table of chords provided in the previous chapters.</note> will reveal them in parts where 360 degrees are equal to two right angles. The same will result if $BC$ is given along with one of the other sides forming the right angle, which I believe is now clearly established.

### IIII.

Now let the acute angle $ABC$ be given, also enclosed by the given sides $AB$ and $BC$; and from point $A$ let a <term>perpendicular</term> <note>A line falling at a right angle (90°) to another line.</note> $AD$ descend to $BC$ (extended if necessary), depending on whether it falls inside or outside the triangle. This perpendicular distinguishes two right-angled triangles, $ABD$ and $ADC$. Since in triangle $ABD$ the angles are given (for $D$ is a right angle and $B$ is given by hypothesis), $AD$ and $BD$ are therefore given as lines subtending the angles $A$ and $B$, in parts where $AB$, the diameter of the circle, is 200,000 according to the Table. And by the same ratio by which $AB$ was given in length, $AD$ and $BD$ are similarly given; $CD$ is also given, which is the difference between $BC$ and $BD$. Therefore, in the right-angled triangle $ADC$, with sides $AD$ and $CD$ given, the sought-after side $AC$ and the angle $ACD$ are given through the preceding demonstration.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing an acute triangle ABC with vertex A at the top. A vertical altitude AD is drawn from vertex A to the base BC, with point D lying between B and C. This construction creates two adjacent right-angled triangles sharing the side AD.</image-desc>

### V.

It will happen no differently if angle $B$ is obtuse; for a perpendicular line $AD$, drawn from point $A$ to the extended straight line $BC$, creates a triangle $ABD$ with known angles. For the exterior angle $ABD$ to the angle $ABC$ is given, and $D$ is a right angle; therefore $BD$ and $AD$ are given in parts where $AB$ is 200,000. And since $BA$ and $BC$ have a given ratio to each other, $AB$ is also given in the same parts as $BD$ and the whole line $CBD$. Therefore, in the right-angled triangle $ADC$, since the two sides $AD$ and $CD$ are given, the sought-after $AC$ is also given, along with the remaining angle $ACB$ and the angle $BAC$, which were sought.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating an obtuse triangle ABC. The base line BC is extended to the left to a point D. A perpendicular line AD is drawn from the top vertex A down to point D, creating a large right-angled triangle ADC which contains the obtuse triangle ABC and a smaller right-angled triangle ADB.</image-desc>

### VI.

Now let either of the given sides subtend the given angle $B$...

...given, let it be $AC$ with $AB$; therefore $AC$ is given through the Table <note>original: "Canonem." This refers to the trigonometric table of chords Copernicus provided earlier in the book.</note> in terms of the parts where the diameter of the circle circumscribing triangle $ABC$ is 200,000 parts. And according to the given ratio of $AC$ to $AB$, $AB$ is given in similar parts. Thus, through the table, the angle $ACB$ is found, along with the remaining angle $BAC$, through which the chord <note>original: "subtensa"</note> $CB$ is also given. By this given ratio, the sides are given in whatever magnitude desired.

### VII.

**When all sides of a triangle are given, the angles are given.** 
Regarding equilateral <note>original: "Isopleuro"</note> triangles, it is too well known to need pointing out that each of its angles is one-third of two right angles <note>In modern terms, 60 degrees, since two right angles equal 180 degrees.</note>. In isosceles <note>A triangle with at least two equal sides.</note> triangles, it is also clear. For the equal sides are to the third side as the halves of the diameter are to the chord subtending the arc <note>original: "subtendentem circumferentiam"</note>, through which the angle enclosed by the equal sides is given from the Table (where 360 units around the center are equal to four right angles); then the remaining angles at the base are also given from the remainder of two right angles as halves. It remains, therefore, to demonstrate this for **scalene** triangles <note>Triangles where all three sides have different lengths.</note>, which we will likewise divide into right-angled triangles. Let there be, then, a scalene triangle $ABC$ with given sides, and let a

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a triangle with vertices A, B, and C. A perpendicular line (altitude) is drawn from vertex A to a point D on the base line BC. This visual aid demonstrates the decomposition of a scalene triangle into two right-angled triangles, ABD and ADC, to solve for its internal angles based on the lengths of its sides.</image-desc>

**perpendicular** <note>A line falling at a 90-degree angle.</note> $AD$ descend to the side that is the longest, for instance $BC$. Now, the thirteenth [proposition] of the second book of Euclid reminds us that the side $AB$, which subtends an acute angle, is less in **power** <note>original: "potestate." In Euclidean geometry, "power" refers to the square of a side's length.</note> than the other two sides by twice the rectangle contained by $BC$ and $CD$. For angle $C$ must be acute; otherwise, $AB$ would be the longest side, contrary to our hypothesis, as may be observed from the seventeenth [proposition] of the first book of Euclid and the two following it. Therefore, $BD$ and $DC$ are given, and there will be right-angled triangles $ABD$ and $ADC$ with given sides and angles (as has already been repeated many times), by which the angles of the required triangle $ABC$ are also established.

**Otherwise.**

Likewise, perhaps more conveniently, the penultimate [proposition] of the third book of Euclid will show us: if, using the shorter side $BC$ as a radius and $C$ as the center, we describe a circle that cuts both remaining sides or one of them. Let it cut both: $AB$ at point $E$, and $AC$ at $D$. Let the line $ADC$ also be extended to point $F$ to complete the **diameter** $DCF$. With these things thus prepared, it is manifest from that Euclidean precept that since the rectangle under $FAD$ is equal to...

# BOOK I OF THE REVOLUTIONS.

...to that which is formed by the rectangle of $BA$ and $AE$ <note>original: "quod sub B A E." In classical geometry, this refers to the area of a rectangle whose sides are segments $BA$ and $AE$.</note>, since both are equal to the square of the line which is tangent to the circle from point $A$. But the whole line $AF$ is given, since all its segments are given: namely $CF$ and $CD$, which are equal to $BC$ (being radii from the center to the circumference), and $AD$, by which $CA$ exceeds $CD$. 

<image-desc>Two geometric diagrams positioned side-by-side to the right of the following 17 lines of text. The left diagram shows a circle with center C; a line segment AF passes through the circle, intersecting at D and E. A point A lies outside. Therefore, the rectangle formed by $BA$ and $AE$ is also given, and $AE$ itself in length, together with the remaining segment $BE$ which subtends the arc <note>original: "subtendente circumferentiam." This refers to a chord $BE$ that spans the arc $BE$.</note> $BE$. Having joined $BC$, we will have the isosceles triangle $BCE$ with given sides. Therefore, the angle $EBC$ is given; hence, in triangle $ABC$, the remaining angles $C$ and $A$ will be known through the preceding demonstrations. However, if the circle does not intersect $AB$, as in the second figure where $AB$ falls on the convex circumference, $BE$ will nonetheless be given, and in the isosceles triangle $BCE$, the angle $CBE$ is given, as is the exterior angle $ABC$. By exactly the same line of reasoning as before, the remaining angles are given. 

And let these things said concerning rectilinear triangles suffice, in which a great part of geodesy <note>original: "Geodesiæ." The science of measuring and monitoring the Earth's size and shape.</note> consists. Now let us turn to spherical triangles.

### On Spherical Triangles. Chapter XIV.

In this place, we define a convex triangle as that which is contained by three arcs of great circles <note>A circle on the surface of a sphere whose center is the same as the center of the sphere, like the equator on a globe.</note> on a spherical surface. The difference and magnitude of the angles, however, is determined by the arc of a great circle described with the point of intersection as its pole—which arc is intercepted by the quadrants of the circles forming the angle. For as the arc thus intercepted is to the entire circumference, so is the angle of intersection to four right angles (which we have said contain 360 equal parts).

<sig>f</sig>
<meta>catchword: If</meta>

<summary>This page concludes Copernicus's treatment of plane trigonometry, specifically the calculation of angles in scalene triangles, and introduces the principles of spherical trigonometry, defining the nature of spherical triangles and how their angles are measured.</summary>
<keywords>rectilinear triangles, geodesy, spherical triangles, great circles, geometry proofs, trigonometry, 360 degrees</keywords>

--- Page 58 ---
<meta>This page transitions from plane geometry to the foundational principles of spherical trigonometry. It picks up from the previous page's discussion on solving for angles in triangles, now applying those geometric rules to the surface of a sphere. The catchword "autem" (moreover/however) indicates that the final sentence of the geometric proof will continue on the following page.</meta>

->NICOLAUS COPERNICUS<-

### I.

**I**f there are three arcs of great circles of a sphere, any two of which added together are longer than the third, it is clear that a spherical triangle can be formed from them. For what is proposed here regarding arcs, Euclid <note>Euclid of Alexandria, the "Father of Geometry." Copernicus is referencing Proposition 23 of Book XI of Euclid’s *Elements*.</note> demonstrates in the twenty-third proposition of his eleventh book concerning angles; since the relationship between angles and arcs is the same, and great circles are those that pass through the center of the sphere, it is evident that those three sectors of the circles, of which the arcs are parts, form a solid angle at the center of the sphere. Therefore, what was proposed is manifest.

### II.

**E**very arc of the triangle must be less than a semicircle <term>hemicyclio (semicircle)</term>. For a semicircle forms no angle at the center, but instead falls into a straight line. Moreover, the remaining two angles, to which the arcs belong, cannot enclose a solid at the center; therefore, neither can they form a spherical triangle. And I believe this was the reason why Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer. Copernicus is refining the mathematical methods found in Ptolemy's *Almagest*.</note>, in his explanation of this type of triangle—especially regarding the figure of a spherical sector—stipulates that the chosen arcs should not be greater than a semicircle.

### III.

**I**n spherical triangles having a right angle, the chord <term>subtendens (chord)</term> of twice the side opposite the right angle is to the chord of twice one of the sides containing the right angle, as the diameter of the sphere is to the chord of twice the angle enclosed by the remaining side and the first side on a great circle of the sphere.

...moreover, let the intersection of circles <note>original: "ACE & DE sit FE"</note> ACE and DE be line FE, and the intersection of ABD and DE be FD. Furthermore, let FC be the intersection of circles AC and BC. Then, let line BG be drawn at right angles to FA, BI to FC, and DK to FE, and let GI be connected.

Therefore, since a circle that cuts another circle through its poles does so at right angles, the angle contained under AED will be a right angle, as is ACB by hypothesis. Consequently, both planes EDF and BCF are at right angles to the plane AEF. For this reason, if a straight line were raised at right angles from a point in the common segment FKE in the underlying plane, it will also form a right angle with KD, according to the definition of planes that are perpendicular to each other. Therefore, KD itself is also perpendicular to plane AEF, according to the fourth proposition of Euclid's <note>Euclid of Alexandria’s *Elements*, Book XI. Copernicus relies heavily on Euclidean solid geometry to prove his spherical theorems.</note> eleventh book. By the same reasoning, BI is raised perpendicular to that same plane, and thus DK and BI are parallel to each other by the sixth proposition of that same book. Furthermore, since GB is perpendicular to FD (because angles FGB and GFD are right angles), the angle FDK will be equal to GBI by the tenth proposition of Euclid's eleventh book. But the angle FKD is a right angle, as is GIB by the definition of a perpendicular line. Therefore, the sides of these similar triangles are proportional: as DF is to BG, so DK is to BI.

Now, BI is half of the chord <term>subtendentis (chord)</term> of twice the arc CB <note>In the period before modern sine functions were standardized, mathematicians used the "chord of the double arc." By the same reasoning, BG is half the chord of twice the side BA, and DK is half the chord of twice the arc DE—which is the same as the chord of twice the angle A—while DF is half the diameter of the sphere. It is therefore clear that the chord of twice the arc AB is to the chord of twice BC, as the diameter is to the chord that subtends twice the angle A (or the intercepted arc DE). This is what was intended to be demonstrated.

## V.

In a triangle where the angles are given, and one of them is a right angle, the sides are also given.

## IX.

With <term>C</term> acting as a pole, let the arc of a <term>great circle</term> <note>A circle on the surface of a sphere whose plane passes through the center of the sphere, dividing it into two equal hemispheres.</note> <term>DEF</term> be described, and let the <term>quadrants</term> <note>Arcs of 90 degrees, or one-quarter of a circle's circumference.</note> <term>CAD</term> and <term>CBE</term> be completed; also, let the extension of <term>AB</term> intersect <term>DEF</term> at point <term>F</term>.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a spherical triangle ABC. Arc CA extends to point D, and arc CB extends to point E. A larger arc DEF represents a portion of a great circle. Line AB is extended to meet this outer arc at point F. The diagram illustrates how a small spherical triangle can be projected onto larger arcs (quadrants) to solve for unknown angles and sides.</image-desc>

Thus, in triangle <term>ADF</term>, side <term>AD</term> is given as the remainder of a quadrant from <term>AC</term>. Also, angle <term>BAD</term> is known from <term>CAB</term> [as they add up] to two right angles. For the ratio and dimension of angles formed by the intersection of straight lines and planes are the same, and angle <term>D</term> is a right angle. Therefore, through the fourth theorem of this book, the angles and sides of triangle <term>ADF</term> will be determined. And again, in triangle <term>BEF</term>, angle <term>F</term> has been found, and <term>E</term> is a right angle by the intersection at the pole; also side <term>BF</term> [is found] by which the whole arc <term>ABF</term> exceeds <term>AB</term>. Therefore, by the same theorem, triangle <term>BEF</term> will also have its angles and sides determined. From this, side <term>BC</term> is given from <term>BE</term> as the remainder of the quadrant and is the side sought; and from <term>EF</term> the remainder of the whole <term>DEF</term>—which is <term>DE</term>—is the angle <term>C</term>; and through the angle which is under <term>EBF</term>, the angle at the vertex <term>ABC</term> is found. But if instead of <term>AB</term>, side <term>CB</term> is assumed (which is opposite the given angle), the same result will follow. For the remainders of the quadrants <term>AD</term> and <term>BE</term> are given, and by the same argument, the two triangles <term>ADF</term> and <term>BEF</term> have their angles and sides determined, as before; from these, the proposed triangle <term>ABC</term> becomes known in its sides and angles, which was intended.

<summary>Copernicus demonstrates how to solve for all sides and angles of a spherical triangle when two sides and one angle are provided, using the properties of great circles and quadrants.</summary>

## XII.

<image-desc>A spherical geometry diagram illustrating a construction on the surface of a sphere. It shows a triangle ABC with arcs extending to form additional points D, E, and F. The diagram demonstrates the relationship between angles and sides in spherical trigonometry, specifically showing a right-angled construction used in the proof.</image-desc>

**F**urthermore, if any two angles are given along with any one side, the same results will follow. For, keeping the construction of the previous figure, let there be a triangle *ABC*, with two angles *ACB* and *BAC* given, along with side *AC*, which lies adjacent to both angles. Moreover, if one of the given angles had been a right angle, all the rest could be reached by reasoning through the fourth preceding [theorem]. However, we wish this to differ in that the angles are not right angles. Therefore, *AD* will be the remainder of the <term>quadrant</term> <note>An arc of 90 degrees, or one-quarter of a circle.</note> from *CAD*, and the angle under *BAD* is the residue of *BAC* from two right angles, and angle *D* is a right angle. Therefore, by the fourth [theorem] of this [section], the angles and sides of triangle *AFD* are given. And through the given angle *C*, the arc *BE* is given, and the remainder *EF*, as well as the right angle *BEF*, and angle *F* which is common to both triangles. Likewise, by the fourth [theorem], *BE* and *BF* are given, from which the remaining sought-after sides *AB* and *BC* will be established. 

Otherwise, if one of the given angles were opposite to the given side—for example, if angle *ABC* were given instead of *ACB*, with the rest remaining—it will be established by the same demonstration that the entire triangle *ADF* has its angles and sides given, and the particular triangle *BEF* similarly. For because of the angle *F* common to both, and the <term>vertical angle</term> <note>The angle opposite the vertex where two lines cross.</note> *EBF* which is given, and the right angle *E*, it was demonstrated in the preceding parts that all its sides are also given; from which, finally, the same things we have said follow. For all these things are always linked by a mutual and perpetual bond, as befits the form of a globe.

## XIII.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a spherical triangle ABC. Lines are drawn from the vertices A, B, and C toward a common point D within the sphere, intersecting at a point E. This visual represents the geometric proof for determining angles from given sides in spherical geometry.</image-desc>

**F**inally, when all the sides of a triangle are given, the angles are given. Let all the sides of triangle *ABC* be given; I say that all the angles are also found. For either the triangle will have equal sides, or it will not. Therefore, let the sides *AB* and *AC* first be equal. It is manifest that the halves of the <term>chords</term> <note>A straight line segment whose endpoints both lie on the arc of the circle.</note> subtending twice those [arcs] will also be equal. Let these be *BE* and *CE*, which will intersect each other at point *E*, because of their equal distance from the center of the sphere in the common section of the circles *DE*, which is clear from the 4th definition of the third book of <term>Euclid</term> <note>Copernicus refers here to the "Elements of Geometry" by the Greek mathematician Euclid, the standard textbook for over 2,000 years.</note>.

Therefore, angle BEC is the angle of inclination of those planes according to the fourth definition of the eleventh book of Euclid <note>Euclid's *Elements*, Book XI, Definition 4 defines the angle between two intersecting planes</note>, which we shall find in the following manner. But if the triangle is <term>scalene</term> <note>a triangle with three unequal sides</note>, as shown in the second figure, it is evident that the halves of the chords of their double arcs will not meet. For if arc AC is greater than arc AB, the half-chord of the double arc AC (which let be CF) will fall lower. If it is smaller, it will be higher, according to how such lines are made closer to or farther from the center by the fifteenth proposition of the third book of Euclid. 

In this case, let FG be drawn parallel to BE, which cuts the common intersection of the circles BD at point G, and let CG be connected. It is therefore evident that angle EFG is a right angle, namely equal to AEB, and angle EFC is also a right angle, since CF is the half-chord of double arc AC. Therefore, CFG is the angle of the intersection of circles AB and AC, which we therefore also attain. For as DF is to FG, so is DE to EB, because triangles DFG and DEB are similar. 

Therefore, FG is given in the same units in which FC is also given. But DG is to DB in the same ratio; thus DG itself will be given in units where DC is 100,000 <note>original: "100000"; Copernicus uses a large integer base for his trigonometric tables to avoid decimals, representing the radius of the circle</note>. Furthermore, the angle under GDC is given through arc BC. Therefore, by the second proposition on plane triangles, side GC is given in the same units as the remaining sides of the plane triangle GFC. Thus, by the last proposition on plane triangles, we shall have angle GFC—which is the sought spherical angle BAC—and we will then determine the rest by the eleventh proposition on spherical triangles.

[...if the ratio] has been given, the circumferences of the segments themselves will also be given.

For let the circumference ABC be given around center D, which is cut at any point B, provided that the segments are less than a semicircle. Let the ratio of the half-chord of double arc AB to the half-chord of double arc BC <note>original: "dimidiæ sub duplo"; in the trigonometry of Copernicus’s time, the sine of an angle was calculated as half the length of the chord (subtense) of an arc twice as large.</note> be given in length in some way; I say that the circumferences AB and BC are also given.

<note>The diagram shows a circle with center D. A chord AC is intersected by the diameter DEB at point E. Perpendicular lines AF and CG are drawn from the chord to the diameter. K marks the midpoint of chord AC.</note>

For let the straight line AC be subtended <term>subtended</term> <note>a chord is drawn connecting the points</note>, which the diameter cuts at point E. From the endpoints A and C, let perpendiculars AF and CG fall to the diameter; these must be the half-chords of double arcs AB and BC. Therefore, in the right-angled triangles AEF and CEG, the angles at the vertex E are equal, and consequently, the triangles themselves are equiangular and similar; they have proportional sides corresponding to the equal angles. As AF is to CG, so is AE to EC. Therefore, in whatever numbers AF or CG are given, we will have AE and EC in those same units, and from these, the whole line AEC will be given in the same units. 

But the chord subtending the arc ABC is given in the units where the radius is DEB; and in those same units, the half of AC (which is AK) and the remainder EK are also given. Let DA and DK be joined, which will also be given in the same parts as DB, as the half-chord subtending the remaining segment of the semicircle from ABC, contained under angle DAK. Thus, angle ADK is given, which contains half of the circumference ABC. Furthermore, with two sides of the triangle EDK given, and the angle EKD being a right angle, the angle EDK will also be given. From this, the whole angle EDA—containing circumference AB—will be known, through which the remaining arc CB will also be established. This is the demonstration that was sought.

**If all angles of a triangle are given, even if none is a right angle, all its sides are given.**

Let there be a triangle ABC, of which all angles are given, but none of them is a right angle. I say that all of its sides are also given. Therefore, there will also be right angles at F and G. In triangles having a right angle, therefore, the ratio of the half-chord of double arc <note>original: "dimidiæ sub duplo"; this refers to the sine, which Copernicus and his contemporaries calculated as half the chord of twice the angle.</note> AB to the half-chord of double arc EF will be the same as the ratio of the half-diameter of the sphere to the half-chord subtending double angle BAF. Then, by the fifth theorem, we shall obtain sides AB, BC, AC, CD, and the whole of BC.

# NICOLAUS COPER-
## NICUS ON THE REVOLUTIONS
### BOOK TWO.

<insert>Decorative woodcut initial C showing a scholar with a celestial instrument</insert> Since in the preceding book we have set forth the three motions of the Earth in summary, by which we promised to demonstrate all the appearances of the stars, we shall now proceed to examine these individually by parts and investigate them to the best of our ability. We shall begin, moreover, with the most well-known of all, the revolution of the day and night time, which we noted is called the *nychthemeron* <term>nychthemeron</term> <note>original Greek: νυχθήμερον; a period of twenty-four hours, literally 'night-day'</note> by the Greeks, and which we have taken to be most closely and directly associated with the terrestrial globe, since from it months, years, and other periods of many names arise, just as numbers arise from unity. Therefore, we shall say a few things regarding the inequality of days and nights, the rising and setting of the Sun, the parts of the zodiac and the signs, and those things of this kind that follow from this revolution; especially because many have written quite enough about these matters, which nevertheless support and agree with our findings. And it makes no difference if we, taking the opposite view, arrive at the same goal as those who demonstrate these things by means of a stationary earth and a whirling of the universe; since in matters that are relative to each other, it happens that they mutually agree with one another. Nevertheless, we shall omit nothing that is necessary. Let no one wonder, indeed, if we still simply speak of the rising and setting of the Sun and stars, and similar things, but let him know that we are speaking in the accustomed manner, which can be accepted by everyone, yet always keeping in mind that:

> While we are carried by the earth, for us the Sun and Moon pass by,
> and the turns of the stars return, and again recede. <note>Copernicus here adapts a line from Virgil's *Aeneid* (III.72) to explain how the movement of the observer—on the rotating Earth—creates the illusion of the heavens moving.</note>

->On the circles and their names. Chapter I.<-

# BOOK II OF THE REVOLUTIONS.

the circle of signs <note>The Zodiac</note>, under which the center of the Earth itself travels in its annual revolution. But since the zodiac exists at an angle to the equinoctial <note>The celestial equator, which is the Earth's equator projected into the sky</note>, according to the degree of the tilt of the Earth's axis toward it, through the daily rotation of the Earth, it describes two circles touching each other on both sides, like the extreme limits of its slant, which are called the **Tropics**. For the Sun is seen to make its *tropas* <note>original: "tropas", from the Greek τροπάς, meaning 'turnings' or 'reversals'</note>—that is, its turnings—at these points: namely, the winter and summer turnings. Thus, people have become accustomed to calling the northern one the solstitial tropic, and the other, toward the south, the brumal <note>Winter</note> tropic, as was explained above in the summary account of the Earth's revolutions.

Next follows the so-called **Horizon**, which the Latins call the *Finisher* <note>original: "finientem"; that which defines the limit of what is seen</note>; for it defines for us the visible part of the world from that which is hidden. At the horizon, everything that sets appears to rise; it has its center on the surface of the Earth and its pole at our zenith <note>The point directly overhead</note>. But since the Earth is incomparable to the immensity of the heavens—especially because even this whole space between the Sun and the Moon, according to our hypothesis, cannot be compared to the magnitude of the heavens—the circle of the horizon appears to cut the sky into two equal halves, as if through the center of the universe, as we demonstrated from the beginning. 

However, to the extent that the horizon is tilted toward the equinoctial, it also touches two parallel circles on either side: the Northern one, consisting of stars that are always visible, and the Southern one, of stars that are always hidden. These were named the **Arctic** and **Antarctic** by Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek philosopher whose works on the "Sphere" were standard astronomical textbooks in the Renaissance</note> and most of the Greeks; these circles become larger or smaller according to the slant of the horizon or the elevation of the equinoctial pole. 

There remains the **Meridian**, which passes through the poles of the horizon and also through the poles of the equinoctial circle; it is therefore perpendicular to both circles. When the Sun reaches this circle, it indicates midday and midnight. But these two circles that have their center on the surface of the Earth—I mean the Finisher and the Meridian—follow the motion of the Earth entirely, and wherever our sight goes. For the eye everywhere assumes for itself the center of the sphere of all things visible around it. Therefore, all circles established on Earth reflect their similar images of circles in the heavens, as is demonstrated more clearly in Geography <note>original: "Cosmographia"</note> and regarding the dimensions of the Earth. And these are indeed the circles having proper names, while others can be designated in infinite ways and by infinite names.

He emphasizes that because the Earth is effectively a point compared to the vastness of space, the horizon appears to bisect the heavens perfectly.</summary>
