## Chapter II. On the tilt of the zodiac, the distance of the tropics, and how they are measured.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'S' featuring ornate foliage and scrollwork within a square frame.</image-desc>
Since the circle of signs <note>The Zodiac</note> proceeds at an angle between the tropics and the equinoctial <note>The celestial equator</note>, I now consider it necessary to investigate the distance between the tropics themselves, and likewise the size of the angle of intersection between the equinoctial and zodiacal circles. For this must be perceived by the senses and by the skill of instruments. To achieve this best, let a wooden square be prepared, or better yet, one made of a more solid material like stone or metal, lest the wood, being unstable due to atmospheric changes, might deceive the practitioner. Let one of its surfaces be smoothed with the greatest precision, and let it have a width sufficient to allow for markings, such as three or four cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters</note>. Then, using one of the corners as a center, a quadrant <note>A quarter-circle used for measuring angles</note> is marked out to the full capacity of the square and divided into 90 equal parts <note>degrees</note>, which are likewise subdivided into 60 minutes, or as many as the space can accommodate. 

Next, a cylindrical gnomon <term>gnomon</term> <note>The part of a sundial or astronomical instrument that casts a shadow</note> is attached to the center, perfectly turned on a lathe; it should stand perpendicular to the surface and project slightly, perhaps the width of a finger or less. Once this instrument is prepared, it is necessary to lay out a meridian line <note>A north-south line</note> on a floor leveled to the plane of the horizon. This should be leveled as carefully as possible using a water-level <term>Hydroscopium</term> or a chorobates <term>Chorobaten</term> <note>original: "Chorobaten"; a long wooden leveling tool used by Roman engineers</note>, so that it does not tilt in any direction. 

Within a circle described on this level floor, the gnomon is erected at its center. We shall observe at some time before noon where the tip of the shadow touches the circumference of the circle and mark it. We shall do the same after noon, and then bisect the arc of the circle lying between the two marks already noted. In this way, a straight line drawn from the center through the point of bisection will unfailingly indicate North and South for us. 

The plane of the instrument is then erected upon this line as a base and fixed exactly vertical, with its center turned toward the south, so that a line dropped perpendicularly from the center exactly coincides at right angles with the meridian line. In this way, the surface of the instrument occupies the plane of the meridian circle. From this, on the days of the Summer Solstice and the Winter Solstice <note>original: "Solsticii & Brumae"</note>, the midday shadows of the Sun are

...to be observed by that pointer or cylinder falling from the center, using some object around the underlying circumference of the quadrant so that the position of the shadow may be held more surely. We will note down as accurately as possible the middle of the shadow in degrees and <term>minutes</term> <note>original: scrupulis; literally "scruples," referring here to the 60 small divisions of a degree</note>. For if we do this, the arc found marked between the two shadows—that of the Summer Solstice and that of the Winter Solstice <note>original: Brumal</note>—will show us the distance between the tropics and the total tilt of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: signiferi; literally the "sign-bearer," the path of the sun through the constellations</note>. Once we take half of this value, we will have the distance of the tropics from the equator <note>equinoctial</note>, and the size of the angle of inclination of the equator to the circle that passes through the middle of the signs <note>the ecliptic</note> will become clear.

<term>Ptolemy</term> <note>A 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose model Copernicus was updating</note> therefore found this interval between the aforementioned Northern and Southern limits to be 47 degrees, 42 minutes, and 40 seconds—where the full circle is 360 degrees. He found this was also observed before him by <term>Hipparchus</term> <note>The "father of astronomy" (2nd century BCE)</note> and <term>Eratosthenes</term> <note>The Greek scholar who first measured the Earth's size</note>. This value is 11 parts out of 83 parts of a full circle <note>A traditional ratio used in antiquity to express the distance between the tropics</note>. From this, the half-difference, which is 23 degrees, 51 minutes, and 20 seconds, established the distance of the tropics from the equatorial circle (on a 360-degree scale) and the angle of intersection with the zodiac.

Ptolemy thought this value was invariable and would remain so forever. However, since that time, these values are found to have continually decreased until our own day. Indeed, it has been found by us and certain others of our contemporaries that the distance of the tropics is no more than 46 degrees and almost 58 minutes; the angle of intersection is 23 degrees, 28 minutes, and two-fifths of a minute. It is thus clear enough that even the tilt of the zodiac is mobile. We will discuss this more below, where we will also show by a probable enough conjecture that it was never greater than 23 degrees, 52 minutes, nor will it ever be less than 23 degrees, 28 minutes.

which we say reaches the meridian of the sky, which also, in the space of 24 hours, passes through and divides both the **zodiac** <note>original: *signiferum*, literally "the sign-bearer"</note> and the **equator** <note>original: *aequinoctiali*</note>, by cutting their circumferences starting from the vernal or autumnal intersection; in turn, the circumference intercepted between them is divided by those same circles. And since these are all "great circles" <note>circles that share the same center as the sphere, like the equator or meridians</note>, they form a <term>right-angled spherical triangle</term>. This is because the angle where the meridian cuts the equator through the poles is a right angle, as previously defined. Furthermore, they call the arc of the meridian—or of any circle passing through the poles—that is intercepted in this way the <term>declination</term> <note>The angular distance of a point north or south of the celestial equator</note> of that segment of the zodiac. But the arc that corresponds to it on the circle of the equator is called the <term>right ascension</term> <note>The distance measured eastward along the celestial equator from the vernal equinox</note>, which moves out <note>rises</note> simultaneously with its matching arc of the zodiac.

All of these things are easily demonstrated in a convex triangle. For let **ABCD** be the circle passing through the poles of both the equator and the zodiac, which most people call the <term>Solstitial Colure</term>. Let the half of the zodiac be **ABC**, and the half of the equator be **BED**. Let the **Vernal Equinox** be at point **E**, the **Summer Solstice** at **A**, and the **Winter Solstice** at **C**. Let **F** be the pole of the daily rotation, and on the zodiac let an arc **EG** be taken—for example, of 30 degrees. Over this, let a quadrant of a circle **FGH** be drawn. 

Then it is manifest that in the triangle **EGH**, the side **EG** is given as 30 degrees, along with the angle **GEH**. This angle is, at its minimum, 23 degrees and 28 minutes <note>original: *XXIIII. scrup. XXVIII.* The text here reads 24 degrees, but Copernicus’s corrected value for the obliquity of the ecliptic was approximately 23° 28'</note> according to the maximum declination **AB** (where 360 degrees make four right angles), and the angle **GHE** is a right angle. Therefore, by the fourth theorem on spherical triangles, the triangle **EHG** itself will have its angles and sides given. 

For it has been demonstrated that the ratio of the **chord** <note>original: *subtensa*, the straight line connecting the ends of an arc</note> of double the arc **EG** to the chord of double **GH** is the same as the ratio of the chord of double **AGE** (or the diameter of the sphere) to the chord of double **AB**. The halves of these chords behave similarly. Since the half-chord <note>equivalent to the sine in modern math</note> of the radius (double **AGE**) is 100,000 parts, and the half-chord of **AB** is 39,822 of those same parts, while **EG** is 50,000 parts. And since if four numbers are proportional, the product of the means is equal to the product of the extremes, we will have the half-chord of double the circumference **GH** as 19,911 parts. By looking this up in the table <note>the "canon" or table of sines/chords</note>, we find this same **GH** is 11 degrees and 29 minutes, which is the declination corresponding to the segment **EG**. 

Therefore, in triangle **AFG**, they also give the side **FG** as 78 degrees 31 minutes, and **AG** as 60 of the same parts (as the remainders of the quadrants), and angle **FAG** is a right angle. In the same manner, the chords of the doubles of **FG**, **AG**, **FGH**, and **BH** [are calculated]...

Since three of these values are known, the fourth will also be given: **BH**, consisting of 62 degrees and 6 minutes, which is the <term>right ascension</term> <note>The distance measured eastward along the celestial equator</note> from the point of the **solstice**, or **HE**, consisting of 27 degrees and 54 minutes from the vernal **equinox**. Similarly, from the given sides **FG** (78 degrees, 31 minutes) and **AF** (66 degrees, 32 minutes) and a quadrant of the circle, we will find the angle **AGF** to be approximately 69 degrees and 23.5 minutes, to which the vertically opposite angle **HGE** is equal. We shall follow this example for all other cases.

However, it is important to understand that the **meridian circle** cuts the **zodiac** <note>original: *signiferum*, the path the sun appears to follow through the stars</note> at right angles at those signs where it touches the **tropics** <note>The points of the summer and winter solstices</note>. For at those times, as we have said, it cuts the zodiac through its poles. But at the **equinoctial** points, the meridian forms an angle with the zodiac that is smaller than a right angle, specifically by the amount that the **zodiac** deviates from a right angle; thus, at the minimum inclination, the angle is 66 degrees and 32 minutes.

It should also be noted that for equal arcs of the **zodiac** measured from the equinoxes or the tropics, the angles and sides of the resulting triangles are equal. For example, if we describe an arc of the equator **ABC** and an arc of the zodiac **DBE**, intersecting at point **B** where the equinox occurs, and we take equal arcs **FB** and **BG**, and then draw two quadrants of circles through the poles of the daily rotation, **KFL** and **HGM**:

<image-desc>A circular diagram representing the celestial sphere. It features a horizontal equator arc labeled A, B, C and an inclined ecliptic arc labeled D, B, E intersecting at B. Two vertical meridian arcs labeled K, F, L and H, G, M cross both the equator and ecliptic. Points F and G represent specific locations on the ecliptic used for spherical trigonometry calculations.</image-desc>

there will be two triangles, **FLB** and **BMG**, whose sides **BF** and **BG** are equal, and the angles at the vertex **B** are equal, and the angles at **L** and **M** are right angles. Therefore, according to the sixth book of <term>spherical geometry</term> <note>Copernicus refers here to the *Sphaerica* by Theodosius of Bithynia, a standard textbook on the geometry of the sphere</note>, the triangles have equal sides and angles. Thus, the **declinations** <note>Distance north or south of the equator</note> **FL** and **MG** are equal, as are the **right ascensions** **LB** and **BM**, and the remaining angle **F** is equal to the remaining angle **G**.

The same will be evident for equal arcs assumed from the tropical point. For instance, when **AB** and **BC** are equal on either side of the point of contact with the tropic at **B**: if we draw the **quadrants** **DA** and **DB** from the pole **D** of the equator, there will similarly be two **triangles**, **ABD** and **DBC**.

Their bases **AB** and **BC**, and the side **BD** which is common to both, are equal, and the angles around **B** are right angles. By the eighth book of <term>spherical geometry</term>, it will be demonstrated that these triangles have equal sides and angles. <meta>This page continues Copernicus's explanation of celestial geometry. # NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

They will correspond with the quadrants of the whole circle. Following this, we shall provide an example of a **Table** <note>original: *Canonicae descriptione*</note> for reference. In the first column, the parts of the **zodiac** <note>original: *signiferi*, the path of the sun through the constellations</note> will be placed. In the second, the **declinations** <note>The distance north or south of the celestial equator</note> corresponding to those parts. In the third, the **minutes** <note>original: *scrupula*, meaning small parts of a degree</note> by which the specific declinations differ and exceed those that occur under the maximum inclination of the zodiac—the sum of which is 24 minutes. We shall do the same in the table of **ascensions** <note>The position along the celestial equator</note> and angles. For it is necessary that when the **obliquity** <note>original: *obliquitatis*, the tilt of the Earth's axis relative to its orbit</note> of the zodiac changes, everything that follows from it must also change.

Furthermore, in **right ascension** <note>original: *ascensione recta*</note>, the difference is found to be very small, such that it does not exceed one-tenth of a "time" unit, which in an hour's space makes up only 1/150th part. Indeed, the ancients called the parts of the **equinoctial circle** <note>the celestial equator</note> "**times**" <note>original: *tempora*</note>, which rise along with the parts of the zodiac; there are 360 of these in each circle, as we have often said. However, to distinguish between them, most have named the parts of the zodiac "**degrees**" <note>original: *gradus*</note> and those of the equator "**times**," a practice we shall also follow henceforth. 

Since this difference is so small that it can rightly be ignored, it was not a burden to include it here anyway. From these values, the same results will be apparent for any other inclination of the zodiac, if proportional parts are considered for each case, based on the ratio of the excess from the minimum to the maximum obliquity of the zodiac. 

For example: with an obliquity of **23 degrees and 34 minutes**, if I wish to know the declination owed to **30 degrees** of the zodiac measured from the equinox. I find in the **Table** <note>original: *Canone*</note> **11 degrees and 29 minutes**, with a difference of **11 minutes**, which would be added in full at the maximum obliquity of the zodiac (which was, as we said, **23 degrees and 52 minutes**). But it is now assumed to be **23 degrees and 34 minutes**, which I say is **6 minutes** greater than the minimum obliquity—and 6 is one-fourth part of the **24 minutes** by which the maximum obliquity exceeds the minimum. Now, the same proportion of the **11 minutes** of difference is approximately **3 minutes**. When I add these to the **11 degrees and 29 minutes** <note>The OCR reads 11.19, but the calculation requires 11.29 to reach the stated total</note>, I will have **11 degrees and 32 minutes**, which is the declination for 30 degrees of the zodiac from the equinox at that time. One may do the same for the angles and right ascensions, except that for the latter one must always subtract the difference, whereas for the former one must always add it, so that all results may be more accurately produced for the given time.

### How the declination and right ascension of any star situated outside the zodiac circle <note>original: *signifer*, the "sign-bearer," referring to the ecliptic path where the zodiac signs sit</note>—provided its latitude and longitude are established—may be revealed, and with which degree of the zodiac it reaches the meridian. Chapter XIV.

These matters have been set forth concerning the zodiac, the celestial equator <note>original: *aequinoctiali*</note>, and the meridian circle, and their mutual intersections. However, for the study of the daily revolution, it is important to know not only those things which appear along the zodiac itself—which explain the movements of the Sun alone—but also to demonstrate the **declination** <note>the distance of a star north or south of the celestial equator</note> and the **right ascension** <note>the distance of a star measured eastward along the celestial equator</note> for stars outside of it, whether they be fixed stars or wandering stars (planets), provided their longitude and latitude are known.

Therefore, let the circle ABCD be described through the poles of the celestial equator and the zodiac. Let AEC be the semi-circle of the equator around pole F, and BED be the semi-circle of the zodiac around pole G. Let the intersection with the equator be at point E. From pole G, let the arc GHKL be drawn through the star, and let the given position of the star be at point H.

[Image: A geometric diagram showing the intersection of the celestial equator and the ecliptic within a celestial sphere, used to calculate stellar coordinates through spherical trigonometry.]

Through this point H, let the quadrant of a circle FHMN descend from the pole of the daily motion <note>the celestial pole, F</note>. Then it is clear that the star existing at H crosses the meridian at the same time as the two points M and N. The arc HMN represents the **declination** of the star from the celestial equator, and EN is the **right ascension** in a "right sphere" <note>a perspective where the celestial equator is vertical to the horizon</note>, which is what we are seeking.

Since, therefore, in the triangle KEL, the side KE is given, and the angle KEL <note>the obliquity of the ecliptic</note> is known, and EKL is a right angle, the sides KL and EL are therefore given by the fourth theorem of spherical triangles <note>Copernicus refers to the trigonometric rules he established in Book I</note>, along with the remaining angle KLE; thus the entire arc HKL is known.

And for that reason, in triangle HLN, two angles are given—HLN, and the right angle LNH—along with the side HL. Therefore, by the same fourth theorem of spherical triangles, the remaining sides are given: HN, which is the **declination** of the star, and LN. By subtracting LN from the whole, what remains is NE, the **right ascension**, which measures the star's position relative to the equinox.

Or in another way: if from the preceding tables you take the arc KE of the zodiac as though it were the right ascension of LE itself, then LE will be given in reverse from the *Table of Right Ascensions*, and LK will be given as the declination corresponding to LE...

### On the intersections of the horizon. Chapter V.

The horizon circle—the boundary of our sight—is of one kind in a **right sphere** and another in an **oblique sphere**. For in a **right sphere**, the horizon is said to be that to which the celestial equator <note>original: *aequinoctialis*</note> is perpendicular, or rather, it passes through the poles of the celestial equator. However, we call it an **oblique sphere** when the celestial equator is tilted relative to the horizon. Therefore, in a right sphere, all stars rise and set, and the days are always equal to the nights. This is because the horizon cuts all the parallel circles described by the daily motion exactly in half—passing through the poles—and there occur the things we have already explained regarding the meridian. Truly, we define a "day" here as the time from the rising of the Sun to its setting, not simply from light to darkness as the common people <note>original: *uulgus*</note> understand it—which is from dawn until the first lamps are lit—about which we shall say more concerning the rising and setting of the zodiac signs.

On the contrary, where the axis of the earth is perpendicular to the horizon <note>this describes the Earth's poles</note>, nothing rises or sets, but everything revolves in a circle and is always in view or always hidden, unless some other motion should interfere, such as the annual motion around the Sun. From this it follows that at the poles, a perpetual day lasts for a six-month period, and a night for the remaining time; there is no difference other than between winter and summer, since the celestial equator coincides with the horizon there. 

Furthermore, in an oblique sphere, some things rise and set, while others are always in view or always hidden, and meanwhile, the days and nights are made unequal. Where the horizon is oblique, it touches two parallel circles according to the degree of its tilt; of these, the one near the visible pole defines the region of perpetual visibility, and conversely, the one near the hidden pole defines the region of perpetual darkness. Therefore, as the horizon passes through the entire latitude between these limits, it cuts all the parallels in the middle into unequal arcs, except for the equator, which is the largest of the parallels; for two great circles always bisect each other. Thus, the oblique horizon itself divides the larger parts of the parallel circles in the upper hemisphere toward the visible pole, from those toward the South and the hidden...

### What the differences of midday shadows are. Chapter VI.

There are also differences in midday shadows, because of which some people are called **Periscii**, others **Amphiscii**, and others **Heteroscii**.

The **Periscii** <note>literally "around-shadowed"</note> are indeed those we might call "shadow-circlers," who receive the Sun’s shadow on all sides. These are the people whose zenith <note>original: *vertex*, the point directly overhead</note> or pole of the horizon is less than, or no further from the pole of the earth than the distance of a tropic from the equator <note>original: *aequinoctiali*</note>. For there, the parallel circles that the horizon touches—being the boundaries of those things always visible or always hidden—are larger than or equal to the tropics. And consequently, the summer Sun, rising high among the stars that are always visible, casts the shadows of gnomons <term>gnomon|the vertical rod of a sundial that casts a shadow</term> in every direction at that time. But where the horizon touches the tropical circles, they themselves become the boundaries of the always visible and always hidden stars. Therefore, the Sun at the solstice is seen grazing the earth at midnight; at that moment, the entire zodiac <note>original: *signifer circulus*, "the sign-bearing circle"</note> coincides with the horizon, and immediately six signs rise at once, while just as many on the opposite side set at once, and the pole of the zodiac coincides with the pole of the horizon. 

The **Amphiscii** <note>literally "shadowed on both sides"</note>, who cast midday shadows in both directions, are those living between the two tropics—a region the ancients call the "middle Zone" <note>the Torrid Zone</note>. Since the zodiac stands vertically twice over that entire region (as demonstrated in the second theorem of Euclid’s *Phaenomena*), the shadows of gnomons disappear twice there; and as the Sun moves from one side to the other, the gnomons cast shadows sometimes toward the South, sometimes toward the North. 

The rest of us, who live between these two groups, are **Heteroscii** <note>literally "differently-shadowed"</note>, because we cast our midday shadows in only one direction—that is, toward the North. Furthermore, ancient mathematicians were accustomed to divide the world into seven **climates** <term>climata|geographical zones defined by the length of the longest day</term>—for example, through Meroë, Syene, Alexandria, Rhodes, the Hellespont, the middle of the Black Sea <note>original: *Pontum*</note>, the Dnieper River <note>original: *Boristhenem*</note>, Byzantium, and others along individual parallels, based on the difference and increase of the longest days. They also observed the length of shadows cast by gnomons at midday during the equinoxes and both solstices <note>original: *Solis conuersionibus*, "turnings of the sun"</note>, and according to the elevation...

# BOOK II OF THE REVOLUTIONS.

These values, having changed somewhat over time, are not exactly the same as they once were, on account of the changing obliquity of the zodiac <note>original: *signiferi*, referring to the ecliptic or the sun's path</note>, as we have already mentioned, which was hidden from the ancients. Or, to put it more accurately, this is due to the varying inclination of the equatorial circle relative to the plane of the zodiac, upon which those values depend.

But the elevations of the pole, or the latitudes of places, and the equinoctial shadows agree with those recorded in ancient times. This was bound to happen, since the equatorial circle follows the pole of the Earth's globe. Therefore, those regions <note>original: *segmenta*, likely referring to the traditional "climates" or latitude zones</note> are not defined or designated accurately enough by any occurrences of shadows and days, but more correctly by their distances from the equatorial circle, which remain perpetual. However, that change of the tropics, although very small, allows for a slight variation in days and shadows in the Southern regions, but becomes more evident as one travels toward the North.

Regarding the shadows of gnomons <term>gnomon|the vertical rod or pillar of a sundial that casts a shadow</term>, it is clear that for any given altitude of the Sun, the length of the shadow is perceived, and vice versa. 

Just as if there were a gnomon AB, which makes a shadow BC; and since the pointer itself stands perpendicular to the plane of the horizon, it must always form a right angle ABC, according to the definition of lines perpendicular to a plane. Therefore, if AC is connected, we will have a right-angled triangle ABC, and for a given altitude of the Sun, we will also have the angle at ACB. And by the first rule of triangles, the ratio of the gnomon AB to its shadow BC will be given, as well as the length of BC itself. Conversely, when both AB and BC are given, the angle ACB will also be established by the third rule of plane [triangles], along with the elevation of the Sun that produces that shadow at that time. 

In this way, the ancients, in their description of those regions of the Earth's globe, assigned the lengths of the midday shadows for each, both at the equinoxes and at both solstices <note>original: *trope*, meaning "turnings"</note>.

# OF NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

This is because the same parallel circle contains both degrees of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi"; literally 'the sign-bearer,' referring to the ecliptic or the belt of the zodiac</note>, since their declination <note>the celestial equivalent of latitude, measuring distance north or south of the equator</note> is equal and in the same direction. # THE WORKS OF NICOLAS COPERNICUS

Since then they are parallel, according to the definition of Posidonius <note>original: "Posydonij definitionem"; Posidonius was a Greek Stoic philosopher who defined parallels as lines that neither converge nor diverge but maintain a constant distance</note>, which neither converge nor diverge but everywhere maintain equal perpendicular lines between them, the straight line **KE** will be equal to half the chord subtending double the arc **AF** <term>half the chord|subtendentis duplam; a trigonometric method used before the modern "sine" function, where the sine of an angle is half the chord of twice that angle</term>. Similarly, **KN** will be half the chord subtending the circumference of the parallel circle whose radius is **FK**, by which difference the equinoctial day differs from a different [day]. This is because all the semicircles whose common sections these are—namely, **BED** of the oblique horizon, **LEM** of the right horizon <note>the horizon as seen from the equator</note>, **AEC** of the equinoctial, and **F**

[A circular geometric diagram representing the celestial sphere. It contains a horizontal diameter labeled B, E (center), D. A vertical diameter is labeled A, E, C. An oblique line represents the horizon, labeled L, E, M. Chords and segments are marked with points F, G, K, and N, illustrating spherical trigonometry relative to the equator and horizon.]

**x G** of the parallel—are perpendicular to the plane of the circle **ABCD**. And the sections they make among themselves, according to Proposition 19 of the eleventh book of Euclid’s *Elements* <note>this proposition states that if two planes are perpendicular to a third plane, their intersection is also perpendicular to that same plane</note>, are perpendicular to that same plane at points **E**, **K**, and **N**. Furthermore, by Proposition 6 of the same book, they are parallel; and **K** is the center of the parallel circle, while **E** is the center of the sphere. Therefore, **EN** is half the chord subtending double the arc of the horizon, by which the sunrise on a parallel circle differs from the equinoctial sunrise. 

Since the declination **AF** is given, along with the remainder of the quadrant **FL**, the halves of the chords subtending double the arcs—**KE** for **AF**, and **FK** for **FL**—will be known in terms of the units where **AE** <note>the radius of the sphere</note> is 100,000. In the right-angled triangle **EKN**, the angle **KEN** is given by the elevation of the pole **DL**, and the remaining angle **KNE** is equal to **AEB**, because in an oblique sphere the parallels are inclined to the horizon at the same angle. Thus, the sides are given in the same units where the radius of the sphere is 100,000. Therefore, in units where the radius **FK** of the parallel circle is 100,000, **KN** will also be given as half the chord subtending the total difference between the equinoctial day and the parallel [day] in degrees, just as the parallel circle itself is 360 degrees. 

From this it is clear that the ratio of **FK** to **KN** is composed of two ratios: namely, the chord of double **FL** to the chord of double **AF** (that is, **FK** to **KE**), and the chord of double **AB** to the chord of double **DL** (which is as **EK** to **KN**), for **EK** is taken as the middle term between **FK** and **KN**. Similarly, the ratio of **BE** to **EN** is composed of **BE** to **EK** and **KE** to **EN**. In this way, I believe, one can discern not only the inequality of days and nights, but also the segments of the paths of the Moon and stars whose declination is known—circles described by their daily motion—to distinguish those parts above the earth from those below, from which their rising and setting can easily be understood.

NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

## On the hours and the parts of day and night. Chapter VIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' depicting a scholar or astronomer seated at a desk or bench, possibly examining a book or instrument.</image-desc>

From these findings, it is evident that if we take the difference of days <note>This refers to the "ascensional difference" calculated in the previous tables.</note> for a given elevation of the pole and add it to a quadrant of a circle <note>90 degrees</note> for a Northern declination, or subtract it for a Southern declination, and then double the result, we will have the length of that day. The remainder of the circle will be the space of the night. If either of these is divided by 15 temporal parts <note>Since a full circle is 360 degrees, 15 degrees of the Earth's rotation equals one equal hour (360 / 24 = 15).</note>, it will show how many equal hours the day or night lasted. Furthermore, by taking a twelfth part of the total day or night, we obtain the duration of a "temporal hour." 

These temporal hours <note>Also known as "unequal" or "seasonal" hours.</note> take their names from the day to which they belong, of which they are always one-twelfth part. Thus, we find the ancients naming hours as "solstitial," "equinoctial," and "winter" hours. In the beginning, no other hours were in common use but these twelve from sunrise to sunset; the night, however, they divided into four "watches" or "guards." This system of hours lasted for a long time by the silent consent of all nations. For this reason, <term>clepsydrae</term> <note>Water clocks that measured time by the regulated flow of water.</note> were invented; by subtracting or adding the dripping water, people adjusted the hours to match the changing length of the days, so that the division of time would not be lost even under a cloudy sky. 

Later, however, once "equal hours"—which are common to both day and night—were generally accepted as being easier to observe, those old temporal hours became so obsolete that if you were to ask any common person which is the first, third, sixth, ninth, or eleventh hour of the day, they would have no answer, or at least nothing relevant to the matter. Even regarding the count of equal hours, different people follow different customs: some count from noon, others from sunset, others from midnight, and some from sunrise, depending on what has been established by each city.

---

## On the oblique ascension of the parts of the zodiac, and how to find the degree that is at the meridian for any given rising degree. Chapter IX.

<meta>catchword: So</meta>

<summary>Copernicus explains how to calculate the length of days and nights using his tables and discusses the historical shift from "temporal hours" (which varied in length) to the standardized "equal hours" used in his own time.</summary>
<keywords>temporal hours, equal hours, clepsydra, water clocks, day length, night watches, declination, zodiac</keywords>

--- Page 93 ---
<meta>This page follows the discussion of day and night lengths across different latitudes. Copernicus is now moving from the duration of daylight to the timing of when specific parts of the zodiac (the signs) rise above the horizon, a concept essential for casting horoscopes and determining local time by the stars.</meta>

### ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK II.

Now that the lengths and differences of days and nights have been explained, the next logical step is to explain **oblique ascensions**. By this, I mean the periods of time in which the <term>dodecatemories</term> <note>From the Greek *dodekatemorion*, meaning "twelfth part"; these are the twelve 30-degree segments of the zodiac.</note>—that is, the twelve parts of the zodiac—or any other arcs of it, rise above the horizon. For there are no other differences between **right and oblique ascensions** than the differences between the equinoctial and the varying day, which we have already explained. Furthermore, the dodecatemories (which take their names from the constellations of the fixed stars, beginning from the vernal equinox) are called **Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer**, and the rest in their proper order. 

Therefore, for the sake of greater clarity, let us redraw the meridian circle **ABCD**. Let **ABC** be the semicircle of the <term>equinoctial</term> <note>The celestial equator.</note>, and **BED** the horizon, which intersect each other at point **E**. Let the equinox be at **E**, through which the <term>signifer</term> <note>Literally the "sign-bearer," meaning the circle of the zodiac or ecliptic.</note> circle **FHL** passes, intersecting the horizon at **L**. Through this intersection, let a quadrant of a great circle **KLM** descend from the pole **K** of the equinoctial.

<image-desc>A circular astronomical diagram showing a celestial sphere. A main circle is labeled ABCD at the cardinal points (A at top, B at left, C at bottom, D at right). Inside, an arc representing the equinoctial (equator) is labeled ABC. A line representing the horizon is labeled BED, intersecting the equinoctial at point E. Various points E, H, L, and M are connected by arcs and lines to illustrate geometric relationships.</image-desc>

Thus, it is clearly seen that when the arc of the zodiac **HL** rises, it does so along with arc **HE** of the equinoctial. However, in a <term>right sphere</term> <note>The "sphæra recta" refers to the view from the Earth's equator, where the celestial equator rises at a 90-degree angle to the horizon.</note>, it would rise with arc **HEM**. The difference between these is the arc **EM**, which we previously demonstrated to be half the difference between the equinoctial day and the varying day. But what was added there in a Northern declination is subtracted here, and conversely added in a Southern declination, to the **right ascension** so that the **oblique ascension** may be produced. Consequently, the time it takes for a whole sign or any other arc of the zodiac to emerge will be made clear by calculating the ascensions from the beginning to the end. 

From this it follows that when any given degree of the zodiac is known (measured from the equinox) which is rising, the degree which **culminates** <note>Reaches the highest point in the sky, known as the "midheaven."</note> is also known. For since point **L** is given (the degree of the zodiac currently rising), along with its declination according to arc **HL**, its distance from the equinox, and its right ascension **HEM**, the entire semi-diurnal arc **AHEM** is also known. Therefore, the remaining arc **AH** is given, which is the right ascension of the point **FH**. This value is also given through the table, since the angle of the section **AHF** is given along with the side **AH**, and the angle at **FAH** is a right angle. Thus, the entire arc of the zodiac **FHL**, between the degree that is rising and the one at the midheaven, is determined. Conversely, if the degree that is at the midheaven is known first—for example, the arc **FH**—we shall also know the degree that

### Chapter 10. On the angle of intersection of the ecliptic with the horizon.

Furthermore, the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>original: *signifer*; literally the "sign-bearer," the path the sun appears to follow through the zodiac constellations.</note> circle, being tilted relative to the axis of the sphere, creates various angles with the horizon. We have already mentioned, regarding the differences in shadows, that for those living between the tropics, the ecliptic rises perpendicularly to the horizon twice. However, I believe it is sufficient for our purposes to demonstrate only those angles that serve the <term>Heteroscii</term> <note>From Greek *heteros* (different) and *skia* (shadow); these are inhabitants of the temperate zones (like Copernicus in Europe) whose noon shadows always fall in one direction, toward the north or south, unlike those in the tropics.</note>—that is, ourselves—from which the general logic of these angles can be easily understood. 

It is, I think, quite clear that in an <term>oblique sphere</term> <note>A view of the heavens where the celestial equator is tilted relative to the horizon, as seen from anywhere other than the poles or the equator.</note>, when the equinox or the beginning of **Aries** is rising, the ecliptic is more inclined and slants toward the horizon by as much as the maximum southern declination (which occurs at the beginning of **Capricorn**) is added, while Capricorn holds the <term>midheaven</term> <note>The highest point the sun or a star reaches on the meridian.</note>. Conversely, the ecliptic is more elevated and creates a larger eastern angle when the beginning of **Libra** emerges and the start of **Cancer** occupies the midheaven. This is because these three circles—the equinoctial, the ecliptic, and the horizon—meet at the same common intersection in the poles of the meridian circle, and the arcs intercepted by them reveal the size of that eastern angle. 

However, so that the method of measuring may be open for the other parts of the ecliptic as well, let the meridian circle again be **ABCD**, the half-horizon **BED**, and the half-

ecliptic **ABC**, with any degree you like rising at **E**. Our goal is to find the size of the angle **AEB**, based on a system where four right angles equal 360 degrees. Since the rising point **E** is given, it is also known from previous demonstrations which point is at the midheaven, as well as the arc **AE** and the meridian altitude **AB**. Therefore, angle **AEB** itself is also given. But if the degree of the <term>midheaven</term> <note>Latin: *medij cæli*; the point where the ecliptic intersects the local meridian, representing the highest point a star or planet reaches in the sky that day.</note> is given, which we shall call **A**, rather than the degree of the rising point, that rising angle will nonetheless be measured. For with the pole established at **B**, let a quadrant of a great circle **FGH** be described, and let the quadrants **EAG** and **EBH** be completed. 

Since the meridian altitude **AB** is therefore given, as well as the remainder of the quadrant **AF**, the angle **FAG** is also known from the preceding steps, and **FGA** is a right angle. Therefore, the arc **FG** is given, along with the remainder **GH**, which measures the required rising angle. Furthermore, it is also clear here how the degree that is rising is given in relation to the degree that is in the midheaven. This is because the <term>chord</term> <note>Latin: *subtensa*; Copernicus uses the geometry of chords (straight lines connecting two points on a curve) rather than modern sine functions, though they are mathematically related.</note> of twice **GH** is to the chord of twice **AB** as the diameter is to the chord of twice **AB**, as is the case in spherical triangles.

We have also provided three examples of tables for these matters. The first will be of ascensions in a <term>right sphere</term> <note>A view of the heavens as seen from the equator, where the celestial equator stands at a 90-degree angle to the horizon.</note>, beginning from **Aries**, in increments of six degrees of the zodiac. The second is of ascensions in an <term>oblique sphere</term> <note>The view of the heavens from any latitude other than the poles or the equator, where the sky appears to rotate at an angle.</note>, likewise by six-degree increments, starting from the parallel where the pole is elevated by 39 degrees up to the one that has 57 degrees, using three-degree increments for the middle values. The remaining table is for horizontal angles, also by six degrees, under the same seven segments. All of these are calculated according to the minimum <term>obliquity of the ecliptic</term> <note>The angle of the Earth's tilt; Copernicus uses a value of 23 degrees and 28 minutes, which he notes was the standard for his time (the 16th century).</note> of 23 degrees and 28 minutes, which is roughly consistent with our own century.

### Chapter XI. On the use of these tables.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'U' (Latin 'V') featuring a seated scholar or personification of science within a classical architectural frame.</image-desc>The use of the tables is now clear from what has been demonstrated. For if, with the known degree of the Sun, we take the <term>right ascension</term> <note>original: *ascensionem rectam*; the position of a point along the celestial equator</note>, and to it we add fifteen "times" <note>Copernicus uses "times" to mean degrees of time; since 15 degrees of the sky rotate every hour, 15 degrees equals one hour</note> for any equal hour, and subtract 360 parts of a full circle if they exceed that amount, the remainder of the right ascension will show the degree of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: *signifer*, literally the "sign-bearer"</note> that is at the <term>mid-heaven</term> <note>original: *medio caelo*; the highest point the zodiac reaches at a specific time</note> at the proposed hour from noon. 

Similarly, if you do the same regarding the <term>oblique ascension</term> <note>original: *ascensionem obliquam*; the arc of the equator that rises together with a degree of the zodiac at a specific latitude</note> of your region, you will have the rising degree of the zodiac at the hour assumed from sunrise. Furthermore, for any stars which are outside the circle of the signs (the zodiac), and whose right ascension has been established as we taught above, these tables give the degrees of the zodiac which reach mid-heaven with them by the same right ascension from the beginning of <term>Aries</term> <note>The "First Point of Aries" is the traditional starting point for celestial measurements</note>, and by their oblique ascension, the degree of the zodiac that rises with them, just as the ascensions and parts of the zodiac present themselves in the rows of the tables. 

In a similar way, but always using the opposite location, you shall operate regarding the setting of the stars. Moreover, if a quadrant of a circle (90 degrees) is added to the right ascension that is at mid-heaven, the result is the oblique ascension of the rising point. Therefore, through the degree of the mid-heaven, the rising degree is also given, and vice-versa. There follows a table of the angles of the zodiac with the horizon, which are taken by the rising degree of the zodiac; by these it is also understood how much the ninetieth degree of the zodiac is elevated above the horizon, which is a fact most necessary to know in <term>solar eclipses</term> <note>original: *eclipsibus solaribus*</note>.

Thus, <term>F G</term> is also given through the demonstrations of spherical [triangles], as is the remaining <term>G H</term>, the altitude of <term>G</term> itself, along with the angle <term>F G A</term>, which we were seeking. We have gathered these things from <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose work *Almagest* served as the foundation for Copernicus's geometry</note> in passing, concerning the angles and sections around the zodiac; we refer ourselves to the general tradition of spherical triangles, in which if anyone wishes to exercise themselves, they will be able to find for themselves more uses than those we have just treated by way of example.

->### Chapter XIV. On the rising and setting of the stars.<-

The rising and setting of the stars also seem to belong to the daily revolution; not only those simple ones of which we have just spoken, but the ways in which <term>morning</term> <note>original: *matutina*</note> and <term>evening</term> <note>original: *vespertina*</note> [risings and settings] occur. Although these happen through the course of the annual revolution, they will nevertheless be more suitably discussed in this place. The ancient mathematicians distinguish <term>true</term> [risings and settings] from <term>apparent</term> ones. The true morning rising of a star is when it emerges at the same time as the Sun. The true morning setting, however, is when the star sets as the Sun is rising; during the entire middle of this time, the star was said to be "morning-like." But the evening rising is when the star emerges as the Sun is setting. The evening setting is when the star sets at the same time as the Sun is setting; during the middle of this time, it is also called "evening-like," as it

# NICHOLAS COPERNICUS

is established during the day, and that which follows at night. Of the <term>apparent</term> <note>visual phenomena as seen by an observer, rather than purely mathematical positions</note> phenomena, the morning rising of a star occurs when it first brings itself into view at dawn and before sunrise, beginning to appear. The morning setting, however, is when the star is seen to set for the last time just as the Sun is about to rise. The evening rising is when the star first appears to rise during the twilight. Finally, the evening setting is when the star no longer appears after sunset, being hidden from then on by the approach of the Sun, until in their morning rising they bring themselves forward again in their previous order.

These rules apply to the <term>fixed stars</term> <note>original: *stellis haerentibus*; the stars that maintain constant positions relative to one another</note>, and also to the <term>outer planets</term> <note>original: *solutis*; literally "unbound" or "released" planets: Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars</note>, Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars. However, Venus and Mercury make their risings and settings differently; for they are not overtaken by the Sun's approach as the others are, nor are they revealed by its departure. Instead, running ahead of the Sun, they mingle with its brilliance and are snatched away. The outer planets, when making an evening rising and a morning setting, are not hidden at all, but rather remain visible almost the whole night with their own light; but these inner planets hide without distinction from setting to rising, and cannot be seen anywhere.

There is also another difference: for the outer planets, the <term>true</term> <note>calculated geometric positions</note> morning risings and settings occur before the apparent ones, and the evening ones after, insofar as they precede the Sun's rising in the former case and follow its setting in the latter. In the <term>inner planets</term> <note>original: *inferioribus*; literally "inferior" or lower planets</note>, however, the apparent morning and evening risings occur after the true ones, while the settings occur earlier.

The method by which these are determined can be understood from what was said above, where we explained the <term>oblique ascension</term> <note>the arc of the celestial equator that rises with a star in an oblique sphere</note> of any star whose position is known, and with which degree of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: *signiferi*; the "sign-bearer"</note> it rises or sets. If the Sun appears at that degree or its opposite, it will cause the true rising or setting, whether morning or evening, of the star. The apparent phenomena differ from these according to the brightness and magnitude of each star: those which shine with greater light are hidden for shorter periods by the Sun's rays than those which are dimmer.

The limits of hiding and appearance are measured by the arcs of circles below the horizon, passing through the poles of the horizon, between the boundary [the horizon] and the Sun. For the first-magnitude fixed stars, these are nearly 12 degrees. For Saturn, 11 degrees; for Jupiter, 10; for Mars, 11 ½; for Venus, 5; and for Mercury, 10. In the total duration where the remains of daylight yield to the night—which encompasses twilight or dawn—there are 18 degrees of the aforementioned circle. When the Sun has moved away by these degrees, even the smaller stars begin to appear. By this distance...

Therefore, when we know at what degree of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: *signiferi*, literally "the sign-bearer"</note> a star rises or sets, and we know the angle where that zodiac intersects with the horizon in that same region: if we then also find as many degrees of the zodiac between the rising degree and the Sun as are sufficient to account for the Sun's <term>depression</term> <note>original: *profunditatem*; the angular distance of the Sun below the horizon</note> below the horizon (according to the established limits for that specific star), we shall announce that its first appearance or its hiding is occurring. 

What we have explained regarding the altitude of the Sun above the earth in the preceding demonstration applies in every way to its descent below the earth as well; for they differ in nothing but their position. Just as those things that set in the visible hemisphere rise in the hidden one, everything happens in turn and is easy to understand. Therefore, let what has been said about the rising and setting of the stars, and thus about the daily rotation of the terrestrial globe, suffice.

### On seeking the positions of the stars, and the standard description of the fixed stars. Chapter 14.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring foliate ornamentation.</image-desc>

After our explanation of the daily rotation of the globe of the Earth and the phenomena that follow from it, the demonstrations of its annual circuit should now follow. However, since some of the ancient mathematicians judged that the phenomena of the <term>fixed stars</term> <note>original: *stellarum non errantium*; literally "stars that do not wander"</note> should come first as the very foundations of this art, we have decided to follow that opinion. We do this because we have assumed among our principles and hypotheses that the sphere of the fixed stars is entirely immobile, and it is against this sphere that the wandering paths of all the planets are equally compared. 

But let no one wonder why we have adopted this order, when <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer of antiquity</note> in his *Great Composition* <note>original: *magna constructione*; commonly known as the *Almagest*</note> believed that an explanation of the fixed stars could not be provided unless knowledge of the positions of the Sun and Moon had first been established, and for that reason, he judged that matters concerning the fixed stars should be deferred until that point. If you understand this as referring to the numbers by which the apparent motion of the Sun and Moon is calculated, his opinion will perhaps stand. For even Menelaus the Geometer <note>A Greek mathematician and astronomer (c. 70–140 AD) who was the first to recognize geodesics on the curved surface of a sphere as the natural analogs of straight lines</note> attained many stars and their positions through calculations based on lunar <term>conjunctions</term>...

<summary>Copernicus concludes his explanation of how the Sun’s position below the horizon determines the visibility of stars and introduces his catalog of fixed stars. He justifies placing the star catalog before the study of the Sun and Moon, arguing that the immobile stars serve as the necessary backdrop for all planetary motion.</summary>

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...investigated. We shall achieve this much better, however, if with the aid of instruments we take any star by means of the carefully examined positions of the Sun and Moon, as we shall soon teach. The futile efforts of those who thought the magnitude of the solar year should be defined simply from the <term>equinoxes</term> <note>the two times a year when day and night are of equal length</note> or <term>solstices</term> <note>the times when the Sun reaches its highest or lowest point at noon</note>, or even from the fixed stars, also warn us; in this, they have never been able to agree down to our own time, so much so that in no part has there been greater discord. Ptolemy had noticed this, who, having calculated the solar year in his time not without a suspicion of error (which might emerge over time), warned posterity to seek further certainty on this matter hereafter. It therefore seemed worthwhile to us to show how the positions of the Sun and Moon are captured by the skill of instruments—namely, how far they are from the vernal equinox or other cardinal points of the world—which will then provide us with the means for investigating other stars, by which we may also lay out the sphere of the fixed stars woven into constellations, and its image, before our eyes.

By which instruments the distance of the <term>tropics</term> <note>the northernmost and southernmost latitudes where the Sun can be directly overhead</note>, the obliquity of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: *signiferi*, literally "the sign-bearer"</note>, and the inclination of the sphere—or the altitude of the equinoctial pole—might be taken, has been set forth above. In the same way, we can take any other altitude of the midday Sun. This altitude—according to its difference from the inclination of the sphere—will show us how much the Sun <term>declines</term> <note>its angular distance north or south of the celestial equator</note> from the equinoctial circle; through this declination, its position taken from the equinox or solstice will then become even more manifest at noon itself. Now, the Sun appears to traverse nearly one degree in the space of 24 hours; thus, there result about 2 and a half <term>scruples</term> <note>original: *scrupula*; these are minutes of a degree</note> for an hourly portion. From this, its position at any other appointed hour will be easily estimated.

For observing the positions of the Moon and stars, however, another instrument is constructed, which Ptolemy calls an <term>Astrolabe</term> <note>specifically the armillary astrolabe, a model of objects in the sky consisting of a spherical framework of rings</note>. For two rings are fashioned, or rather quadrilateral rims of rings, so that they receive the concave and convex surface at right angles with their flat sides, or "jaws": equal in all respects and similar, and matching in size, lest by excessive size they become less manageable—although a larger size grants more precision to the parts to be divided. Their width and thickness,

...let them be at least a thirtieth part of the diameter. They shall then be brought together and joined to one another at right angles, with their concave and convex parts fitting together as if in the roundness of a single globe. One of these should represent the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: *circuli signorum*, the circle of signs</note>, and the other the circle that passes through both poles—that is, the <term>equator</term> <note>original: *æquinoctialis*</note> and the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>original: *signiferi*, the path of the sun</note>. This zodiacal circle is to be divided along its sides into the usual 360 equal parts, which may be further subdivided according to the capacity of the instrument. On the other circle, once the <term>quadrants</term> <note>90-degree sections</note> have been measured from the zodiac, the poles of that same zodiac are to be assigned. Taking a distance from these poles according to the <term>obliquity of the zodiac</term> <note>the tilt of the Earth's axis relative to the sun’s path</note>, the poles of the equatorial circle should also be marked.

With these preparations completed, two more rings should be fashioned, an outer and an inner one, which will move upon those same poles of the zodiac. These should have a thickness equal to the space between two planes, and their <term>rims</term> <note>original: *maxillarum*, literally "jaws"</note> should have a similar width. They are to be so arranged that the hollow surface of the larger ring touches the convex surface of the zodiac, and the convexity of the smaller ring touches the hollow of the zodiac everywhere. This must be done without hindering their rotation, allowing the zodiac itself and its meridian to pass through easily, and letting the rings move freely against one another. We shall then skillfully drill holes through these rings at the poles of the zodiac along the diameter, and insert <term>axles</term> <note>original: *axonia*</note> by which they may be connected and carried. The inner ring should also be divided into 360 equal parts, so that in each quadrant there are ninety degrees toward the poles.

Furthermore, a fifth ring is to be placed inside the hollow of this ring, rotatable within the same plane. To its rims should be fixed viewing systems having openings along the diameter and <term>sight-holes</term> <note>original: *diaugia* or *specilla*</note> through which the light of a star can enter and exit, as is the custom with a <term>diopter</term> <note>a sighting device for measuring angles</note>. These should be aligned with the diameter of the ring, and pointers should be fitted on either side as indices for the numbers, for the purpose of observing the latitudes on the containing ring.

Finally, a sixth ring is to be applied, which contains and supports the entire <term>Astrolabe</term> <note>an instrument used to model the heavens and measure the positions of celestial bodies</note>. This is suspended from the mountings of the equatorial poles and placed upon a small column, supported and standing upright relative to the plane of the horizon. Once the poles are adjusted to the inclination of the celestial sphere, it should maintain a position similar to the natural meridian and not wobble in the least.

When the instrument has been prepared in this way, and we wish to take the position of any star, in the evening or when the Sun is about to set—and at a time when we also have the Moon in view—we shall align the outer ring with the degree of the zodiac in which...

...since we will have then obtained the Sun’s position, known through previous calculations, we shall turn the intersection of the rings toward the Sun itself, until both of them—namely, the zodiac ring and that outer ring which passes through the poles—cast a single shadow upon one another. Then we also turn the inner ring of the Moon [toward it], and with the eye placed at its plane, where we see the Moon opposite, as if bisected by that same plane, we shall mark the location on the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: *signifero*, the "sign-bearer"</note> of the instrument; for that will then be the Moon’s position according to its observed longitude. For without the Moon, there was no way of determining the positions of the stars, since she alone among all the heavenly bodies partakes of both day and night.

Then, when night comes on and the star whose location we are seeking can finally be seen, we align the outer ring to the position of the Moon. Through this, we check the position of the <term>astrolabe</term> <note>a complex tool used to calculate the positions of celestial bodies</note> relative to the Moon itself, just as we previously did with the Sun. Then we also turn the inner circle toward the star until it appears to cling to the plane of the ring and is sighted through the <term>apertures</term> <note>original: *specilla*, small view-holes or sights</note> contained in the small ring. In this way, we shall have discovered both the longitude and the latitude of the star. While these things are being done, the degree of the zodiac that is at <term>mid-heaven</term> <note>original: *caelum mediat*, the point where a celestial body crosses the observer's local meridian</note> will be visible to our eyes, and therefore the exact hour at which the observation was made will be clearly established.

For example, take Ptolemy. In the second year of the Emperor Antoninus Pius, on the ninth day of Pharmuthi (the eighth month of the Egyptians) in Alexandria, around sunset, he wished to observe the location of the star in the breast of Leo called the <term>Basilisk</term> <note>original: *basiliscus*, another name for the star Regulus</note> or Regulus. Having aligned the astrolabe to the setting Sun, five <term>equinoctial hours</term> <note>standardized 60-minute hours, as opposed to seasonal "unequal" hours</note> having passed since midday, while the Sun was found at 3 degrees and a <term>half-ounce</term> <note>original: *semuncia*, here meaning 1/24th of a degree or 2.5 minutes</note> of Pisces, he found the Moon following the Sun by 92 and 1/8 degrees by using the inner ring. Therefore, the observed position of the Moon was then at 5 degrees and a <term>sixth</term> <note>1/6th of a degree, or 10 minutes</note> of Gemini. 

Half an hour later, when the sixth hour from midday was completed and the star had already begun to appear (with the fourth degree of Gemini at mid-heaven), he turned the outer ring of the instrument to the already determined position of the Moon. Proceeding with the inner ring, he measured the distance of the star from the Moon in the order of the signs as 57 and 1/10 degrees. Since the Moon was found to be 92 and 1/8 degrees from the setting Sun, as was said, this placed the Moon at 5 degrees and a sixth of Gemini. However, it was calculated that in the space of that half hour, the Moon had moved by a <term>quarter of a degree</term> <note>15 minutes of arc</note>, since the hourly movement of the Moon is approximately half a degree; but because of the Moon's <term>parallax</term> <note>original: *commutationem*, the displacement in apparent position when viewed from the Earth's surface versus its center</note> which was subtractive at that time, it ought to have been a little less than a quarter...

<meta>Catchword: which (original: quod)</meta>

<summary>Copernicus explains how to use an astrolabe to determine a star's position by using the Moon as a reference point between day and night. He illustrates this method by citing Ptolemy's 2nd-century observation of the star Regulus in the constellation Leo.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how to determine the positions of the fixed stars using the moon and the sun as reference points, transitioning into Copernicus's justification for his star cataloguing method.</meta>

### ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK II.

which he defined as about a twelfth part <note>original: *uncia*, literally an "ounce," used here as a fractional unit of a degree</note>; whereby the Moon was at 5 degrees and a third of <term>Gemini</term> <note>the Twins</note>. But when we have thoroughly discussed the Lunar parallaxes <note>original: *commutationibus*, the apparent shift in position of the Moon due to the observer's location on Earth</note>, it will appear that the difference was not so great, so that it can be sufficiently clear that the visible position of the Moon exceeded five degrees of Gemini by more than a third, and by barely less than two-fifths. To these were added 57 degrees and one-tenth part, which together bring the position of the star to approximately 2 ½ parts of <term>Leo</term> <note>the Lion</note>, distant from the Sun’s summer <term>solstice</term> <note>original: *aestiva conversione*, the "summer turning point"</note> by 32 ½ degrees, with a northern latitude of one-sixth of a degree. This was the location of <term>Basiliscus</term> <note>original: *Basiliscus*, known today as the star Regulus, the "Little King"</note>, through which the approach to the other fixed stars was opened. This observation by Ptolemy was made in the year of Christ, according to the Romans, 139, on the 24th of February, in the first year of the 229th <term>Olympiad</term> <note>a four-year period used in ancient Greek dating</note>. Thus that most eminent man of Mathematics noted what position each of the stars held at that time relative to the vernal equinox, and he set forth the <term>asterisms</term> <note>constellations or star patterns</note> of the heavenly creatures. By these efforts, he aided our own study not a little and relieved us of a quite difficult labor; for we, who have thought that the positions of the stars should not be referred to the equinoxes (which change over time), but that the equinoxes should be referred to the sphere of the fixed stars, can easily deduce the description of the stars from another immutable principle. We have decided to take this from <term>Aries</term> <note>the Ram</note>, as the first sign, and from its first star, which is in its head, so that in this way a single and absolute appearance always remains for those things which, as if fixed and coherent, are placed in a permanent seat once they have been captured. Indeed, they were arranged into 48 forms by the wonderful care and skill of the ancients, except for those which the circle of stars always hidden from view separated, starting from approximately the fourth <term>climate</term> <note>a geographical zone; here referring to the latitude of Rhodes</note> through Rhodes. Thus the "unformed" stars remained unknown to them. For stars were formed into images for no other reason, according to the opinion of Theon the Younger in his exposition of <term>Aratus</term> <note>a Greek didactic poet who wrote about the stars</note>, than so that such a great multitude of them might be distinguished by parts and could be designated individually by certain names. This is quite an ancient practice, since it is established that even in the time of <term>Job</term> <note>referring to the biblical Book of Job</note> some were already named, and we read of the <term>Pleiades</term>, the <term>Hyades</term>, <term>Arcturus</term>, and <term>Orion</term> mentioned by name in Hesiod and Homer. Therefore, in our description of them according to longitude, we shall not use the <term>dodecatemories</term> <note>original: *dodecatemorijs*, the twelve 30-degree divisions of the zodiac</note> which are derived from the equinoxes and solstices, but the simple and accustomed number of degrees. In other matters we shall follow Ptolemy, with a few exceptions which we have found to be either corrupted or otherwise different. To what extent their distance from those cardinal points may be apparent, we shall teach in the following book.

# On the anticipation of the equinoxes and solstices. Chapter I.
<note>original: "De æquinoctiorum solstitiorúmque anticipatione." This "anticipation" refers to what we now call the precession of the equinoxes, where the positions of the equinoxes gradually shift over time.</note>

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'S'. The illustration within the letter features two figures in Renaissance-era dress; one is seated in the lower loop of the 'S', while the other stands behind the upper curve, possibly engaged in a scholarly or astronomical discussion.</image-desc>**S**ince we have depicted the appearance of the fixed stars, we must now pass on to those matters concerning the annual revolution. For this reason, we shall first treat the change of the equinoxes, because of which even the fixed stars are believed to move. We find that the ancient mathematicians did not distinguish the "turning" or natural year <note>A natural or "tropical" year is measured by the return of the Sun to the same equinox or solstice.</note> from the year that is measured by one of the fixed stars. Consequently, they thought that the Olympic years—which they began at the rising of the Dog Star <note>original: "Caniculæ"; refers to the star Sirius. The ancient Greeks used this to mark the start of their calendar year near the summer solstice.</note>—were the same as those measured from the solstice, as the difference between the two was not yet known. However, Hipparchus of Rhodes, a man of marvelous sagacity, was the first to notice that these differ from each other. While observing the length of the year more attentively, he found it to be longer when compared to the fixed stars than when compared to the equinoxes or solstices. Therefore, he thought that there was some motion in the fixed stars as well, following the order of the signs, but so slow that it was not immediately perceptible. But now, with the passage of time, it has become most evident; we now see a far different rising and setting of the signs and stars than what was prescribed by the ancients. Furthermore, the twelve divisions <note>original: "dodecatemoria"; the twelve equal 30-degree segments of the zodiac circle.</note> of the circle of signs have receded from the constellations of the fixed stars by a considerable distance, though originally they agreed in both name and position. Moreover, the motion itself is found to be unequal. Those wishing to explain the cause of this variation have brought forward different opinions. Some thought it was a certain oscillation <note>original: "libramentum"; this refers to the historical theory of "trepidation," which suggested the equinoxes moved back and forth like a pendulum rather than in a continuous circle.</note> of the hanging world—similar to the motion we find in the planets regarding their latitudes—and they believed that however far it proceeded from certain limits in either direction, it would eventually return. They estimated that its wandering on either side of its midpoint was no more than eight degrees. But this outdated opinion could no longer stand, especially because

<summary>Copernicus begins Book III by discussing the precession of the equinoxes, noting that Hipparchus was the first to distinguish between the solar year and the sidereal year. He mentions that the zodiac signs no longer align with their namesake constellations and introduces the historical (though eventually rejected) theory of trepidation.</summary>
<keywords>precession of the equinoxes, solar year, sidereal year, Hipparchus, zodiac signs, dodecatemoria, trepidation, Sirius, Dog Star</keywords>

<meta>catchword: Historia</meta>

...[while] it is now sufficiently clear that the "head" of the starry constellation Aries is separated from the vernal equinox by more than twenty-four degrees <note>original: "ter octo gradibus"; literally "thrice-eight degrees."</note>, and other stars have shifted similarly, with no trace of a return <note>A reference to the theory of "trepidation," a supposed back-and-forth wobbling of the equinoxes that some medieval astronomers believed in.</note> having been observed over so many centuries. Others believed that the sphere of the fixed stars does indeed advance, but by unequal steps, though they defined no certain rule for this. 

In addition, another wonder of nature appeared: that the obliquity <note>The tilt of the Earth's axis relative to the plane of its orbit.</note> of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi"; the "sign-bearer," referring to the ecliptic or the path of the sun through the constellations.</note> does not appear to us to be as great as it appeared to Ptolemy, as we have mentioned. To account for these things, some devised a ninth sphere and others a tenth, through which they believed these phenomena occurred, yet they could not fulfill what they promised. By now, even an eleventh sphere had begun to emerge <note>Medieval astronomers added extra "spheres" to the Ptolemaic model to account for the slow shifting of the stars and the changing tilt of the Earth.</note>, but we shall easily refute this number of circles as superfluous by means of the motion of the Earth. 

For as we have already partly explained in the first book, the two revolutions—namely, that of the annual declination <note>Copernicus's "third motion," a slow rotation of the Earth's axis that keeps it pointing in roughly the same direction as it orbits the Sun.</note> and that of the Earth’s center—are not entirely equal; thus, the completion of the declination anticipates the period of the center by a small amount. From this it must follow that the equinoxes and solstices <note>original: "conuersiones"</note> appear to anticipate their positions <note>This "anticipation" is the precession of the equinoxes.</note>, not because the sphere of the fixed stars is carried forward, but rather because the equinoctial circle moves backward, being oblique to the plane of the zodiac according to the tilting of the axis of the terrestrial globe. 

Indeed, it would be more appropriate to say that the equinoctial circle is oblique to the zodiac than the zodiac to the equinoctial, when comparing the smaller to the larger. For the zodiac—which is described by the distance between the Sun and the Earth in their annual circuit—is much larger than the equinoctial circle, which is marked out by the daily motion around the Earth’s axis, as has been stated. In this way, these equinoctial intersections, along with the entire obliquity of the zodiac, are seen to advance over time, while the stars appear to fall behind. 

However, the measure and the cause of the variation in this motion remained hidden to our predecessors because the length of its revolution is still unknown due to its incredible slowness; for in all the centuries since it first became known to mortals, it has hardly completed a fifteenth part of a circle <note>A 1/15th part of a 360-degree circle is 24 degrees, matching the "twenty-four degrees" mentioned at the start of the page.</note>. Nevertheless, to the best of our ability, we shall make these matters more certain through what we have received from historical observations down to our own time.

<summary>Copernicus argues that the precession of the equinoxes and the changing tilt of the ecliptic are caused by the Earth's axial motion rather than by the movement of the stars or the addition of extra celestial spheres. He identifies the extreme slowness of this cycle—having moved only 24 degrees in recorded history—as the reason earlier astronomers struggled to understand it.</summary>
