### History of observations proving the unequal precession of the
### equinoxes and solstices. Chapter II.

In the first 76-year period according to Callippus <note>A Greek astronomer who refined the 19-year Metonic cycle into a 76-year cycle to better align the solar year and lunar months.</note>, in its 36th year—which was the 30th year after the death of Alexander the Great—Timochares of Alexandria, who was the first to take care in recording the locations of the fixed stars, reported that Spica, which the Virgin holds <note>The brightest star in the constellation Virgo.</note>, was distant from the solstice point by 82 and one-third degrees, with a southern latitude of two degrees. He also reported that the star in the forehead of Scorpio—the northernmost of the three and the first in the order of that constellation’s formation—had a latitude of one and one-third degrees, but a longitude of 32 degrees from the autumnal equinox. And again, in the 48th year of the same period, he found Spica of the Virgin at a longitude of 82 and a half degrees from the summer solstice <note>original: "aestiva conversione"; literally 'summer turning,' referring to the solstice.</note>, the latitude remaining the same. 

Hipparchus, however, in the 50th year of the third Callippic period—which was the 196th year of Alexander—found the star in the heart of the Lion called Regulus <note>The "Little King," the brightest star in Leo.</note> following the summer solstice by 29 and a half plus one-third degrees [29° 50']. 

Then Menelaus, the Roman geometer, in the first year of the Emperor Trajan’s reign—which was 99 years from the birth of Christ and 322 years from the death of Alexander—reported Spica of the Virgin to be distant in longitude by 86 and one-quarter degrees from the solstice. He recorded the star in the forehead of Scorpio at 36 degrees minus one-twelfth of a degree <note>original: "uncia"; an 'ounce,' used here as a measurement for 1/12th of a degree (5 minutes).</note> [35° 55'] from the autumnal equinox. 

Following these, Ptolemy, in the second year of Antoninus Pius—which was the 462nd year from the death of Alexander—learned that Regulus of Leo occupied 32 and a half degrees from the solstice, Spica 86 and a half degrees, and the aforementioned star in the forehead of Scorpio occupied 36 and one-third degrees of longitude from the autumnal equinox. In all these cases, the latitude was changed in no way, just as was expressed above in the standardized Table <note>original: "expositione Canonica"; referring to the star catalog provided in the previous book.</note>. And these measurements we have reviewed just as they were reported by those men. 

But after a great deal of time, namely in the 1202nd year from the death of Alexander, the observation of al-Battani <note>original: "Machometi Aracensis"; the Latinized name of the influential Arab astronomer al-Battani (c. 858–929 AD).</note> followed, in whom one may place the greatest trust. In that year, Regulus (or the "Little King" of the Lion <note>original: "Basiliscus Leonis"</note>) was at 44 degrees and 5 minutes <note>original: "scrupulus"; literally 'scruple,' used here for minutes of a degree.</note> from the solstice, and the star in the forehead of Scorpio was at 47 degrees and 50 minutes.

<summary>Copernicus catalogs historical star measurements from ancient Greek, Roman, and medieval Arab astronomers to demonstrate that the rate of the precession of the equinoxes has changed over time. By comparing the positions of stars like Spica and Regulus across 1,200 years, he provides the empirical basis for his theory of unequal precession.</summary>

By the 6th proposition of the same book, they are parallel to each other. This is found in the following way: for the angles **OKP** and **AEB** are equal (the exterior angle being equal to the interior and opposite angle), and **OPK** is a right angle. Therefore, the ratio of **OP** to **OK** is the same as the ratio of half the chord of twice **AB**...

For Aristarchus of Samos <note>An ancient Greek astronomer (c. 310–230 BCE) who was the first to propose a sun-centered universe.</note> found the same obliquity of the zodiac and the equinoctial to be 23 degrees <term>partium</term>, 51 minutes <term>scrupulorum primorum</term>, and 20 seconds <term>secundorum</term> as Ptolemy did. In our times, however, it is not found to be greater than 23 degrees and 28.5 minutes. Thus, it is also manifest from this that the motion was minimal from Aristarchus to Ptolemy, but maximal from Ptolemy himself to al-Battani.

### Hypotheses by which the change of the equinoxes, the obliquity of the zodiac, and the equinoctial are demonstrated. Chapter III.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a bearded scholar or astronomer in Renaissance robes holding a quadrant, framed by a border of foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>Since, therefore, it seems clear from these facts that the equinoxes and solstices are changed by an unequal motion, no one will perhaps offer a better cause for this than a certain deflection of the Earth’s axis and of the poles of the equinoctial circle. For this seems to follow from the hypothesis of the Earth’s motion. Since it is manifest that the circle which passes through the middle of the signs <note>The ecliptic, the apparent path of the sun across the celestial sphere.</note> remains forever immutable—as the constant latitudes of the fixed stars attest—but the equinoctial circle changes. For if the motion of the Earth's axis simply and exactly agreed with the motion of the center, no anticipation <term>praeventio</term> <note>Copernicus uses this to describe the precession of the equinoxes, where the equinox occurs slightly earlier each year.</note> of the equinoxes and solstices would appear at all, as we have already stated. But since they differ from one another, though by an unequal difference, it was necessary for the solstices and equinoxes also to precede the locations of the stars by an unequal motion. The same thing happens regarding the motion of declination, which also unequally changes the obliquity of the zodiac <term>signiferi</term> <note>Literally the "sign-bearer," another name for the zodiacal circle.</note>, though this obliquity should more rightly be attributed to the equinoctial. For this reason, one must understand two entirely reciprocal motions of the poles, similar to hanging librations <term>librationibus</term> <note>Oscillating or swinging motions, like a pendulum.</note>, since the poles and circles in a sphere cohere and agree with one another. Therefore, there will be another motion which changes the inclination of those circles,

<summary>Copernicus compares historical measurements of the Earth's axial tilt (obliquity) from antiquity to his own time, noting its gradual decrease. He argues that the precession of the equinoxes is caused by the Earth's axis oscillating like a pendulum rather than remaining perfectly aligned with its orbital motion.</summary>

# BOOK III OF THE REVOLUTIONS.

<sig>f 2</sig>

...the poles being thus moved up and down around the angle of the intersection. There is another motion which increases and decreases the solstitial and equinoctial precessions by a movement made back and forth across the transverse. We call these motions **librations** <note>original: *librationes*; from the Latin *libra* (scales), referring to a swinging or oscillating motion like a balance scale</note>, because, like hanging weights, they move along the same path between two limits, becoming faster in the middle and slowest at the extremes. Such motions frequently occur in the latitudes of the planets, as we shall see in the proper place. These motions also differ in their cycles, in that the irregularity of the equinoxes is completed twice during a single completion of the obliquity <note>The "obliquity" refers to the angle of the Earth's axial tilt.</note>.

Just as in every apparent irregular motion, a certain "mean" <note>An average or middle point used as a mathematical reference.</note> must be understood so that the ratio of the irregularity can be calculated, so too here it was necessary to conceive of **mean poles** and a **mean equinoctial circle**, as well as mean equinoctial intersections and mean points of conversion <note>The solstices.</note>. Under these, the terrestrial poles and the equinoctial circle, though deflecting this way and that, nevertheless make those equal motions appear diverse within their fixed limits. 

Thus, those two librations meeting together cause the poles of the Earth to describe, over time, certain lines similar to a **twisted crown** <note>original: *corollæ intortæ*; a reference to a complex, looping geometric shape often compared to a figure-eight or a garland</note>. But since it is not easy to explain these things sufficiently with words—and I fear they will be understood even less by hearing unless they are also seen with the eyes—let us therefore describe the circle of the signs [the zodiac] on the sphere as **ABCD**. Let its North pole be **E**, the beginning of Capricorn **A**, of Cancer **C**, of Aries **B**, and of Libra **D**. Through the points **A** and **C** and the pole **B**, let the circle **ABC** be described. Let the maximum distance between the North poles of the zodiac and the equinoctial be **EF**, and the minimum distance be **EG**. Consequently, let the **mean pole** be at position **I**. Around this pole **I**, let the equinoctial circle **BHD** be described, which shall be called the **mean equinoctial**, and **BD** shall be the **mean equinoxes**.

All these points are always carried by a steady motion around pole **E** in the direction of the preceding signs <note>That is, westward, or against the natural order of the zodiac signs.</note>; this is a slow motion under the sphere of the fixed stars, as has been said. Now, let us imagine two reciprocating motions of the terrestrial poles, like swinging weights: one between the limits **F** and **G**, which shall be called the **anomaly** <note>A term for the irregularity or "unevenness" in a cycle.</note> of the obliquity; the other moving across, from the preceding to the following and back again, which we shall call the **anomaly of the equinoxes**, which is twice as fast as the first one. Both of these motions, meeting at the poles of the Earth, deflect them in a marvelous way. For first, when the North pole of the Earth is placed at **F**...

### How Reciprocal or Oscillatory Motion is 
### Composed of Circular Motions. Chapter 4.

<image-desc>A woodcut decorative initial 'Q' containing a portrait of a bearded man in academic robes, possibly an astronomer or the author, framed within a circle.</image-desc>
We shall now demonstrate how this motion agrees with the observations. In the meantime, however, someone might ask how the regularity of those librations <term>libration: from the Latin 'libra' (scales); a slow oscillation or "wobbling" motion like a balance scale</term> can be understood, since it was stated at the beginning that celestial motion is uniform, or composed of uniform and circular motions. Yet here, in both cases, two motions appear as one within two limits, where a pause <note>In a back-and-forth motion along a line, an object must momentarily stop at the ends to change direction, which seems to contradict the principle of eternal, constant circular motion.</note> must necessarily occur. We will indeed admit that they are doubled, but they are demonstrated to come from uniform motions in this way.

Let there be a straight line **AB**, which is divided into four equal parts by the points **C**, **D**, and **E**. At **D**, let homocentric <note>Circles that share the same center</note> circles be described in the same plane, **ADB** and **CDE**. On the circumference of the inner circle, let any point **F** be taken, and with **F** as the center and **FD** as the radius, let circle **GHD** be described, which intersects the straight line **AB** at point **H**, and let the diameter **DFG** be drawn.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the conversion of circular motion into reciprocal motion. It shows a large circle with a vertical diameter AB and a smaller concentric circle CDE around center D. An epicycle (circle GHD) is centered at point F on the inner circle's circumference and passes through the center D. A diameter GFD of the epicycle is drawn, and point H is marked where the epicycle intersects the vertical diameter AB. Lines connect D to F, F to G, and F to H.</image-desc>

It must be shown that with the two motions of the circles **GHD** and **CFE** occurring together, the moving point **H** travels back and forth along the same straight line **AB** by a reciprocating motion. This will occur if **H** is understood to move in the opposite direction and twice as fast as **F**. Since the same angle which is under **CDF** at the center of circle **CFE** and on the circumference of **GHD** encompasses both arcs of the equal circles, the arc **GH** is double the arc **FC**. Let it be assumed that at some time, when the straight lines **ACD** and **DFG** were joined, the moving point **H** was at **G**, coinciding with **A**, and **F** was at **C**. Now, however, the center **F** has moved to the right toward **PFC**, and **H** itself has moved along the circumference **GH** to the left, a distance twice as great as **CF**.

It is clear, therefore, that from two circular motions meeting each other in this way, a motion along a straight line is composed. Furthermore, from equal circular motions, a reciprocal and unequal motion <note>The speed of the point along the line is "unequal" because it slows down at the ends and speeds up in the middle, even though the underlying circles turn at a constant speed</note> is created, which was to be demonstrated. From these things it also follows that the straight line **GH** will always be at right angles to **AB**; for the lines will encompass a right angle within the semicircle **DHG**. And therefore **GH** will be half of the chord subtending double the arc **AG**, and **DH** will be the other half of the chord subtending double that which remains from the quadrant of the circle **AG**, because the circle **AGB** is twice the size of **HGD** in terms of its diameter.

...that the motion is slower near the circumference is easily demonstrated. For let there be a semicircle **ABC** with its center at **D** and its diameter **ADC**, and let it be bisected at point **B**. Assume equal arcs **AB** and **BF**, and from points **F** and **E** <note>The point E is established by the context of the diagram as the point on arc AB corresponding to point F on arc BF</note> let perpendicular lines **EG** and **FK** be dropped onto the diameter **ADC**. Euclidis*; this proposition concerns the lengths of lines drawn from a point to the circumference of a circle</note>, is less than **GE**, and therefore it will also be less than **DK**.

With this demonstrated, let the center of the Earth now be taken at **L**, such that the straight line **DL** is at right angles to the plane of the semicircle **ABC**. Through points **A** and **C**, let an arc of a circle **AMC** be described with center **L**, and let the straight line **LDM** be drawn. Accordingly, the pole <term>pole: the highest point or the vertex of the arc</term> of the semicircle **ABC** will be at **M**, and **ADC** will be the common intersection of the circles. Connect **LA** and **LC**, and likewise **LK** and **LG**; let these lines be extended straight to intersect the arc **AMC** at **N** and **O**. 

Since, then, the angle **LDK** is a right angle, the angle **LKD** is acute. Therefore, the line **LK** is longer than **LD**. Even more so in obtuse-angled triangles <note>original: *ambligonijs triangulis*</note>, the side **LG** is greater than side **LK**, and **LA** is greater than **LG**. Thus, a circle described with center **L** and radius **LK** will fall outside the line **LD**, but will intersect the remaining lines **LG** and **LA**. Let it be described and called **PKRS**. 

And since triangle **LDK** is less than sector **LPK**, while triangle **LGA** is greater than sector **LRS**, the ratio of triangle **LDK** to sector **LPK** is less than the ratio of triangle **LGA** to sector **LRS**. Alternately, the ratio of triangle **LDK** to triangle **LGA** will be less than the ratio of sector **LPK** to sector **LRS**. And according to the first proposition of the sixth book of Euclid's *Elements*, just as triangle **LDK** is to triangle **LGA**, so is the base **DK** to the base **AG**. But the ratio of sector to sector is as the angle **DLK** is to angle **RLS**, or as arc **MN** is to arc **OA**. Therefore, **DK** is in a smaller ratio to **GA** than arc **MN** is to arc **OA**. But we have already demonstrated that **DK** is greater than **GA**; therefore, it follows even more strongly that **MN** will be greater than...

## On the uniform motions of the precession of the equinoxes and the inclination of the zodiac. Chapter VI.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' (translated from the Latin 'O' for 'Omnis') with a botanical or floral motif inside a square frame.</image-desc>Every circular motion that appears non-uniform <note>original: *diuersus*; in this context, it refers to motion that seems to change speed from our perspective</note> moves within four limits: there is a point where it appears slow, and another where it appears fast, as if at the extremes; and there are points where it appears at a medium pace, as in the middle. For from the end of a decrease and the beginning of an increase, it passes to a medium pace; from a medium pace, it increases into high velocity; then from high velocity, it tends back toward a medium pace; and from there, the remainder returns from equality back to its previous slowness. From this, it can be understood in which part of the circle the location of the irregularity <term>anomaliæ; the discrepancy between the observed and the calculated mean position of a celestial body</term> was at any given time, and by what signs the completion <note>original: *restitutio*; the point where the cycle returns to its starting position</note> of the irregularity itself is perceived. For instance, in a circle divided into four parts, let *a* be the position of maximum slowness, *b* the increasing medium pace, *c* the end of the increase and beginning of the decrease, and *D* the decreasing medium pace.

Since, therefore, as was recounted above, from *Timocharis* <note>A Greek astronomer of the 3rd century BCE, among the first to record star positions</note> to *Ptolemy*, the apparent motion of the precession of the equinoxes was found to be slower than in all other times; and because for some time it appeared equal and uniform—as shown by the observations of *Aristyllus*, *Hipparchus*, *Agrippa*, and *Menelaus* made during that middle period—it argues that the apparent motion of the equinoxes was simply at its slowest. At that middle time, it was at the beginning of its increase, when the ceasing decrease, joined to the beginning increase, caused the motion to seem uniform for a while through mutual compensation. Therefore, the observation of *Timocharis* must be placed in the final part of the circle in the quadrant *DA*, while that of *Ptolemy* will fall into the first quadrant, *AB*. 

Furthermore, because in the second interval from *Ptolemy* to *Al-Battani* <note>original: *Machometum Aratensem*; the 9th-century Arab astronomer Al-Battani, known for his refined measurements</note>, a faster motion is found than in the third interval, it declares that the maximum velocity—that is, the point *c*—was passed during that second interval of time, and the irregularity has now reached the third quadrant of the circle, *CD*. In the third interval until our own time, the completion of the cycle of the irregularity is almost finished and is returning to the starting point of *Timocharis*. For if we encompass the entire circuit of 360 degrees within the 1,819 years from *Timocharis* to us, we will have, in proportion to the years, a circumference of 85.5 degrees for 432 years. For the 742 years, the arc is 146 degrees and 51 minutes <note>original: *scrupula*; used here as minutes of a degree</note>; and in the remaining 645 years, the remaining circumference is 127 degrees and 39 minutes. Since in 1819 years we had an apparent motion of almost 25 degrees and 1 minute. But from the time of *Timocharis* <note>An Alexandrian astronomer (c. 320–260 BCE) whose star catalog was used by later astronomers to detect the movement of the stars</note> in 102 years (by which 1717 years differ from 1819), the apparent motion should have been about 1 degree and 4 minutes, because it is likely it was a bit larger then, so that in a hundred years it would have completed one degree, since it was still decreasing and had not yet reached the end of its decrease. Therefore, if we take away one degree and one-fifteenth from the 25 degrees and 1 minute, there will remain what we said: in 1717 Egyptian years, a mean and uniform motion, equal to the varying and apparent motion, then leveled out at 24 degrees and 57 minutes. From these, a complete and uniform revolution of the precession of the equinoxes arises in 25,816 years, during which time nearly 15 and 1/28th revolutions of the irregularity occur.

The motion of the obliquity <note>the tilt of the Earth's axis relative to the plane of its orbit, which causes the seasons</note> also adapts itself to this calculation, whose return we said was twice as slow as the precession of the equinoxes. For because *Ptolemy* reported the obliquity as 23 degrees, 51 minutes, and 20 seconds, having been changed not at all from 400 years before him by *Aristarchus of Samos*, this indicates that it then stood nearly at the limit of maximum obliquity; namely, when the precession of the equinoxes was also in its slowest motion. ### ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK III.

...observations of those who preceded us most closely differ very little. Here again, it is most clearly evident that the change in the obliquity <term>obliquity; the angle or "tilt" of the Earth's axis relative to its orbit</term> from the time of Ptolemy over 900 years occurred more rapidly than in any other interval of time. Since we now have the full circuit of the irregularity <term>anomalia; the variation in the rate of motion</term> of the precession in 1,717 years, we will also have, during that same time, half the period of the obliquity, and in 3,444 years <note>While 1717 doubled is 3434, the text reads 3,444 (III. CCCCXXXXIIII), likely accounting for slight adjustments in his data set</note> its complete restoration.

Therefore, if we divide the 360 degrees of a circle by that same number of 3,444 years, or 180 degrees by 1,717 years, there will result an annual motion of the simple irregularity of 6 first minutes, 17 seconds, 24 thirds, and 9 fourths <note>Copernicus uses "minutes, seconds, thirds, and fourths" to represent fractions of a degree in base-60, similar to how we measure time today</note>. These, distributed again over 365 days, yield a daily motion of 1 second, 2 thirds, and 2 fourths. Similarly, when the mean precession of the equinoxes is distributed over 1,717 years—in which time it moved 23 degrees and 57 minutes—there will result an annual motion of 50 seconds, 12 thirds, and 5 fourths; and from this, over 365 days, a daily motion of 8 thirds and 15 fourths.

In order that these motions may become clearer and more readily available when necessary, we will set out tables or "Canons" for them through the continuous and equal addition of the annual motion. We will always carry over any amount exceeding 60 into the next higher unit (minutes or degrees), and we have compiled these up to the order of 60 years for the sake of convenience. For in sixty-year periods, the same pattern of numbers presents itself, with only the denominations of the parts and minutes transposed <note>This is a property of base-60 (sexagesimal) mathematics: multiplying by 60 just shifts the "decimal" place</note>. Thus, what were previously seconds become first minutes, and so on. By using these brief tables as a shortcut, one can easily calculate and collect the mean motions for any given number of years within a 3,600-year span. The same applies to the number of days.

We shall use Egyptian years everywhere in the calculation of celestial motions, for they are the only ones found among civil calendars to be uniform. It is necessary for the measure to agree with what is being measured, which is not the case with the years of the Romans, Greeks, and Persians. In those calendars, intercalations <term>intercalation; the insertion of leap days or months</term> were not handled in one way, but according to the pleasure of each nation. The Egyptian year, however, introduces no ambiguity; it has a fixed number of 365 days, comprising twelve equal months which they call by their own names in order: **Thoth, Phaophi, Athyr, Chiach, Tybi, Mechyr, Phamenoth, Pharmuthi, Pachon, Pauni, Epiphi, Mesori**. These months account for six sets of sixty days, with five remaining days which they call "intercalary" <note>These are the five "epagomenal" days added to the end of the year to bring the 360-day calendar up to 365</note>. For this reason, the Egyptian years are the most suitable for calculating mean motions, as any other calendar can easily be reduced to them by resolving the dates into a total number of days.

## What the greatest difference is between the uniform and apparent precession of the equinoxes, Chapter VII.

Having thus set forth the mean motions <note>original: "Medijs motibus"; referring to the average, uniform rate of movement</note>, we must now investigate how great the maximum difference is between the uniform and apparent motion of the equinoxes, or the diameter of the small circle through which the motion of the anomaly <note>The variation or irregularity in the speed of the precession</note> revolves. For once this is known, it will be easy to discern any other differences in these motions. Since, therefore, as was recounted above, there were 432 years between the first observation of Timocharis <note>An ancient Greek astronomer (c. 320–260 BCE) whose data Copernicus used to calculate long-term changes</note> and that of Ptolemy in the second year of Antoninus <note>Antoninus Pius; the observation occurred in 139 CE</note>: in which time the mean motion is 6 degrees, but the apparent motion was 4 degrees and 20 minutes; the difference between these is one degree and 40 minutes. The motion of the double anomaly was also 90 degrees and 35 minutes. It appeared also that in the middle of this time, or thereabouts, the apparent motion had reached the point of maximum slowness; at this point it is necessary for the apparent motion to coincide with the mean motion, and for the true and mean equinoxes to have been in the same intersection of the circles. Therefore, by making a two-fold distribution of the

[Diagram: A geometric figure illustrating the celestial arcs. A vertical line BF intersects a horizontal arc DBE at point B. Two slanted lines crossing each other at point B extend toward the edges A and C. Intersections of these lines with other arcs or horizontals are labeled G, H, I, and K. This represents the "small circle" model Copernicus used to explain the varying speed of precession.]

motion and the time, the differences between the irregular and uniform motion on either side will be fifty minutes <note>original: "dextantes unius gradus," literally ten-twelfths of a degree</note>, which the circumference of the circle of anomaly covers across 45 degrees 17 and a half minutes on either side. These things being thus established, let the circumference of the zodiac <note>The path of the sun through the constellations</note> be ABC, the mean equinoctial <note>The celestial equator</note> be DBE, and let B be the mean intersection of the apparent equinoxes—either of Aries or of Libra. Let BF descend through the poles of DBE itself. Furthermore, let equal arcs BI and BK be taken on either side of the circumference ABC by fifty minutes <note>ten-twelfths of a degree</note>, so that the whole IBK is one degree and 40 minutes. Let there also be drawn two circumferences of the apparent equinoctial circles, IG and HK, at right angles to FB itself. Now I say at right angles, although...

<summary>In this chapter, Copernicus calculates the maximum difference between the steady, "mean" precession of the equinoxes and their observed, "apparent" movement using historical data from Timocharis and Ptolemy. He introduces a geometric model involving a small circle to explain these variations in speed.</summary>

<keywords>precession of the equinoxes, mean motion, apparent motion, anomaly, Timocharis, Ptolemy, zodiac, geometry of the heavens</keywords>

--- Page 161 ---
<meta>This page continues the geometric demonstration of the variation in the precession of the equinoxes. Copernicus is currently calculating the relationship between the movement of the celestial poles and the shift of the equinoxes, moving from the previous page's discussion of the observation history into specific trigonometry.</meta>

### ON THE REVOLUTIONS Book III.

nevertheless, the poles themselves, $I, G$ and $H, K$, often exist outside the circle $BF$ because the motion of declination <note>The "motion of declination" refers to the wobbling of the Earth's axis, which Copernicus uses to explain the changing tilt of the Earth relative to the Sun.</note> mixes with it, as was seen in the hypothesis. But because of the very small distance—which, even at its greatest, does not exceed the 450th part of a right angle <note>original: "CCCCL partem recti"; this equals 12 minutes of arc ($90^\circ / 450 = 0.2^\circ = 12'$)</note>—we use these as if they were right angles to the senses; for no error will appear because of it. Since, therefore, in triangle $IBG$, the angle $IBG$ is given as 66 degrees 20 minutes <note>original: "scrup. XX"; Copernicus uses 'scruples' for minutes of a degree</note>, because the remainder from the right angle $DBA$ was 23 degrees 40 minutes (the angle of the mean obliquity of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi"; literally the "sign-bearer," a standard Latin term for the zodiac circle</note>), and $BGI$ is a right angle, and also the angle at $BIG$ is almost equal to $IBD$ itself; and the side $IB$ is 50 minutes. Therefore, the arc $BG$—the distance of the mean and apparent poles—is also given as equal to 20 minutes. Similarly, in triangle $BHK$, the two angles $BHK$ and $HBK$ are equal to the two $IBG$ and $IGB$; and side $BK$ is equal to side $BI$, so $BH$ will also be equal to $BG$ itself, namely 20 minutes. But since all these matters concern very small values—inasmuch as they do not even reach one and a half degrees of the zodiac—in which the straight lines subtending the arcs are almost equal to the arcs themselves, and a difference is scarcely found even in the third-order fractions <note>referring to "sixtieths of a minute" or seconds</note>, we shall commit no error if we use straight lines instead of arcs. Let $ABC$ be that portion of the circle of signs <note>the zodiac</note>, in which the mean equinox is $B$. With $B$ taken as the center,

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circular arc ADC (a semicircle) above a horizontal line containing points A, F, B, and C. A vertical radius line connects the center B to the top of the semicircle at point D. A point E lies on the arc between A and D, and a vertical line segment EF descends from E to point F on the horizontal base line.</image-desc>

let the semicircle $ADC$ be described, which cuts the circle of signs at points $A$ and $C$. Let the line $DB$ also be drawn from the pole of the zodiac, which will also bisect the described semicircle at $D$; under which point $D$ the maximum limit of slowness is understood to be, and the beginning of the increase <note>the point where the rate of precession starts to speed up again</note>. In the quadrant $AD$, let arc $DE$ be taken as 45 degrees 17.5 minutes. And through point $E$, let $EF$ descend from the pole of the zodiac, and let $BF$ be 50 minutes. It is proposed from these to find the whole distance $BA$. It is manifest, therefore, that double the length of $BF$ subtends double the segment $DE$. Just as $BF$ of 7107 parts is to $AB$ of 10,000 parts <note>Copernicus is using a table of sines where the radius is 10,000</note>, so are the 50 minutes of $BF$ itself to the 70 minutes of $AB$. Therefore, $AB$ is given as one degree 10 minutes. This is the greatest difference between the mean and apparent motion of the equinoxes which we were seeking, and which is followed by the greatest deflection of the poles of 28 minutes.

### On the particular differences of these motions, and their presentation in tables. Chapter 8.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring an astronomer seated at a desk, looking at an armillary sphere or globe.</image-desc>Since, therefore, line **AB** is given as 70 minutes <note>original: "scrupulorum"; Copernicus uses the term "scruples" to refer to minutes of a degree</note>, and this circumference seems to differ not at all from a straight chord in its length, it will not be difficult to show any other particular differences between the mean and apparent motions. The Greeks call these *Prosthaphaereses* <note>meaning "additions and subtractions"; these are the corrections applied to a mean astronomical model to match observed reality</note>, while more recent writers call them *equations*, for by their subtraction or addition the appearances are made to agree. We shall use the Greek term as more fitting. 

If, therefore, **ED** <note>referring to the position on the small circle of anomaly</note> is three degrees, then according to the ratio of **AB** to the chord **BF**, we will have a *Prosthaphaeresis* **BF** of 4 minutes. If it is six degrees, it will be 7 minutes; for nine degrees, eleven; and so on for the rest. We believe we must proceed in a similar way regarding the change in the obliquity <note>The "obliquity of the ecliptic" is the angle between the Earth's equator and its path around the sun—the "tilt" that causes the seasons</note>, where a difference of 24 minutes was found between the maximum and minimum, as we said. These 24 minutes are completed over a half-circle of simple anomaly in 1,717 years. The mean position, found at a quadrant of the circle <note>at 90 degrees</note>, will be 12 minutes, where the pole of this small circle of anomaly will be at an obliquity of 23 degrees 40 minutes. 

In this manner, as we have said, we will extract the remaining parts of the difference in proportion to those mentioned above, as contained in the Table below. Although the apparent motions can be composed in various ways through these demonstrations, that method was most pleasing by which each particular *Prosthaphaeresis* is taken separately. This makes the calculation of the motions easier to understand and more consistent with the explanations of the things demonstrated. 

We have therefore written a table of 60 rows, increasing by triads <note>groups of three</note> of the degrees of the circle. In this way, it will neither occupy a sprawling space nor seem to have an overly cramped brevity, just as we shall do in other similar cases. This table will have four columns. The first two contain the degrees of both semicircles, which we call the "Common Number," because through the simple number the obliquity of the signs of the circle <note>the zodiac</note> is taken, and the doubled number will serve the *Prosthaphaeresis* of the equinoxes, the beginning of which is taken from the start of the increase...

...is taken. <note>This page begins mid-word, continuing from the previous page's discussion on how values are derived.</note> In the third place, the <term>prosthaphaereses</term> <note>original: "prosthaphæreses"; these are the corrections applied to the mean motion to find the "apparent" or true position observed in the sky</note> of the equinoxes will be arranged, to be added to or subtracted from the mean motion according to their corresponding triple-degree segments. We measure this mean motion starting from the first star in the Head of Aries <note>the star Hamal, a traditional reference point in the zodiac</note> toward the vernal equinox. The corrections are subtractive when the <term>anomaly</term> <note>the angle representing the position in a cycle of irregular motion</note> is in the smaller half-circle—that is, the first order—and additive in the second and following half-circle.

Finally, in the last place, are the <term>scruples</term> <note>original: "scrupula"; here referring to minutes of a degree</note>, called the proportional differences of the <term>obliquity</term> <note>original: "obliquitas"; the angle of the Earth's axial tilt, which causes the seasons</note>, which rise to a total of sixty. Since we set the value of 60 to represent the maximum and minimum variation in the obliquity (which is 24 minutes), we can then coordinate proportional parts for the remaining variations according to a similar ratio. For this reason, we place 60 at the beginning and the end of the anomaly. However, when the variation reaches 22 minutes (as occurs at an anomaly of 34 degrees), we record 55 in its place. Likewise, for 20 minutes we record 50 (as at an anomaly of 28 degrees), and so on for the others, as is clear in the table provided below.

# On the examination and correction of those things set forth concerning the precession of the equinoxes. Chapter IX.

Since we have taken by conjecture that the beginning of the increase in the differing motion occurred midway between the 36th year of the first Callippic period <note>A cycle of 76 years used in ancient Greek astronomy to synchronize the lunar month with the solar year; the 36th year of the first period is roughly 295 BCE.</note> and the second year of Antoninus <note>Refers to the reign of Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius, specifically around 139 CE.</note>, from which point we began the motion of the anomaly <note>A term for the irregular or varying part of a celestial motion.</note>. We must still test whether we have done this correctly and whether it agrees with the observations. Let us recall those three recorded star observations by Timocharis, Ptolemy, and al-Battani <note>original: "Machometis Aratei"; Copernicus refers to the 9th-century Arab astronomer Muhammad ibn Jābir al-Battānī.</note>, and it is clear that in the first interval there were 432 Egyptian years. In the second, there were 742 years. The mean motion in the first span of time was 6 degrees; the varying motion was 4 degrees and 20 minutes; and the double anomaly was 90 degrees and 35 minutes, subtracting 1 degree and 40 minutes from the mean motion. In the second interval, the mean motion was 10 degrees and 21 minutes. The varying motion was 11 and a half <note>original: "s."; abbreviation for "semis," meaning one-half.</note> degrees. The double anomaly was 155 degrees and 34 minutes, adding 1 degree and 9 minutes to the mean motion.

Now let the circumference of the zodiac be ABC as before, and let B be the mean vernal equinox. Taking the pole as a center, let a small circle <term>epicycle<note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle; used here to explain the oscillating motion of the equinoxes.</note></term> ADCE be described with the circumference AB [as radius] of 1 degree and 10 minutes. Let the mean motion of B be understood to move toward A, that is, in <term>precedence<note>Motion from East to West, opposite to the natural order of the zodiac signs.</note></term>, and let A be the western limit where the varying equinox leads the most, and C the eastern limit where the varying equinox follows the most. From the pole of the zodiac, let the line DBE descend through point B; this line, together with the circle of signs <note>The ecliptic, or the path the Sun appears to follow.</note>, will divide the small circle ADCE into four parts, because they intersect each other at right angles through the poles. When the motion is in the semicircle ADC toward the <term>consequence<note>Motion from West to East, following the order of the zodiac signs.</note></term>, and the remainder CEA is toward precedence, the midpoint of the apparent equinox's slowness will be at D, due to the resistance against the progress of B itself; whereas at E, there will be the greatest velocity, as the motions promote each other in the same direction. Let arcs FD and DG be taken before and after D, each being 45 degrees and 17 and a half minutes. Let F be the first limit of the anomaly (which is Timocharis's), G the second (Ptolemy's), and P the third (al-Battani's), through which points the great circles descend through the poles of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi"; literally 'sign-bearer,' meaning the zodiac circle.</note>, FN, GM, and OP, which all [intersect] in the small...

<header>ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK III.</header>

### Chapter X. What the maximum difference is between the intersections of the equator and the zodiac.

In a similar way, we shall prove that the explanations set forth concerning the change in the obliquity <note>obliquity: the tilt of the Earth's axis, which creates the seasons</note> of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi," the "sign-bearer," a common Latin name for the zodiac</note> and the equator are correct. For we have, from the second year of the reign of Antoninus <note>Antoninus Pius, the Roman Emperor; Copernicus is citing an observation by Ptolemy from approximately 139 AD</note> as recorded by Ptolemy, a tested simple anomaly <term>anomaly: a technical term for the position of a celestial body or a theoretical point along its calculated path</term> of 21 degrees and one quarter [21° 15'], at which the maximum obliquity was found to be 23 degrees, 51 minutes, and 20 seconds. 

From that time to our own observation, there are approximately 1,387 years, during which the position of the simple anomaly is calculated to be 145 degrees and 24 minutes; and at that time, the obliquity is found to be 23 degrees, 28 minutes, and nearly two-fifths of a minute. Concerning these values, let the arc ABC of the zodiac be repeated—or a straight line in its place because of its smallness—and upon it, let there be the semicircle of the simple anomaly with its center <note>original: "polo," literally "pole," here used as the center of the geometric figure</note> at B, as before. 

And let A be the maximum limit of declination <note>declination: the angular distance of a heavenly body north or south of the celestial equator</note> and C the minimum, the difference between which we are investigating. Therefore, let the arc AB of the small circle be taken as 21 degrees and 15 minutes, and the remainder of the quadrant <note>quadrant: one-quarter of a circle, or 90 degrees</note> BC will be 68 degrees and 45 minutes. However, the whole arc BDF, according to the numbering of ABC, is 145 degrees and 24 minutes, and the remaining arc DF is 76 degrees and 29 minutes. 

Let EG and FK be dropped as perpendicular lines to the diameter ABC. Now, GK will be the arc of the great circle representing the difference in the obliquities from Ptolemy’s time to ours, which is known to be 22 minutes and 56 seconds. But the line GB, being similar to a straight line, is half of the chord <term>chord: a straight line connecting two points on a curve</term> subtending twice the arc EB, or equal to 932 parts where AC (representing the diameter) is 2,000 parts. 

In these same units, KB would also be half of the chord subtending twice the arc DF, which is 973 parts; thus the whole length GK is given as 1,905 parts where AC is 2,000. But in units where GK is 22 minutes and 56 seconds, AC will be approximately 24 minutes—this is the difference between the maximum and minimum obliquity that we were seeking. By this, it is established that the maximum obliquity between the times of Timocharis and Ptolemy was 23 full degrees and 52 minutes, and that it is now approaching its minimum of 23 degrees...

->On establishing the positions of the uniform motions of the equinoxes and<-
->the anomaly. Chapter 11.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'H' featuring a woodcut portrait of a bearded man's head and shoulders within a square frame with cross-hatching.</image-desc>With all these matters thus settled, it remains for us to establish the positions of the motions of the spring equinox. These positions are called "roots" <term>roots: often called "epochs" in modern astronomy, these are fixed reference points in time used to calculate the positions of celestial bodies for any other date</term> by some, and from them, calculations are derived for any proposed time. For this purpose, Ptolemy established as his primary point of reference the beginning of the reign of Nabonassar <note>Nabonassar: a King of Babylon whose reign, beginning in 747 BC, was used as a standard chronological baseline by ancient astronomers like Ptolemy</note> of the Chaldeans, which among historians is identified with Shalmaneser, King of the Chaldeans. We, however, following more well-known eras, thought it sufficient if we began from the first Olympiad <note>Olympiad: the four-year periods used by the ancient Greeks to mark time, beginning in 776 BC</note>, which is found to have preceded the era of Nabonassar by 28 years. We take our start from the summer solstice <note>original: "aestiua conuersione"</note>, the time when the Dog Star <note>original: "Canicula," referring to the star Sirius</note> rose for the Greeks and the Olympic Games <note>original: "Agon Olympicus"</note> were celebrated, as Censorinus and other reliable authors have recorded. 

Therefore, according to a more exact calculation of time, which is necessary for calculating celestial motions, from the first Olympiad at noon on the first day of the Greek month of Hekatombaion <note>Ecatonbæonos: the first month of the Attic calendar, falling around mid-summer</note> to Nabonassar and noon of the first day of the month of Thoth <note>Thoth: the first month of the Egyptian calendar</note>, according to the Egyptians, there are 27 years and 247 days. From this point to the death of Alexander [the Great], there are 424 Egyptian years. From the death of Alexander to the beginning of the years of Julius Caesar, there are 278 Egyptian years and 118.5 days, reckoned to the midnight before the Kalends of January <note>Kalends: the first day of the month in the Roman calendar</note>, which Julius Caesar made the beginning of the year he established. He instituted this year during his third term as Chief Priest <term>Pontifex Maximus: the highest religious office in Rome, which Caesar held while reforming the calendar</term> and the consulship of Marcus Aemilius Lepidus. 

From this year, thus ordered by Julius Caesar, the subsequent years are called "Julian." From Caesar's fourth consulship to Octavian Augustus, the Romans count 18 years, likewise from the Kalends of January—even though it was on the 16th day before the Kalends of February <note>January 17th</note> that the son of the divine Julius Caesar, the Emperor Augustus, was so named by the Senate and other citizens upon the motion of Munatius Plancus, during his own seventh consulship and that of Marcus Vipsanius [Agrippa]. But the Egyptians, because they had come under the power of the Romans two years earlier, after [the death] of Antony...

### BOOK III OF THE REVOLUTIONS.

...and the fall of Cleopatra <note>Cleopatra VII's death in 30 BC marked the end of the Ptolemaic Kingdom and the beginning of Roman rule in Egypt.</note>, there are 15 years and 246½ days at noon on the first day of the month of Thoth <note>The first month of the ancient Egyptian calendar.</note>, which for the Romans was the third day before the Kalends of September [August 30]. For this reason, from Augustus to the years of Christ (likewise beginning from January), there are 27 years according to the Romans, but according to the Egyptians, there are 29 of their years and 130½ days. From here to the second year of Antoninus <note>Antoninus Pius, Roman Emperor; his second year was roughly 139 AD.</note>, in which Claudius Ptolemy described the locations of the stars observed by him, there are 138 Roman years and 55 days; these years add 34 days to the Egyptian calendar. From the first Olympiad <note>776 BC, the traditional starting point for Greek chronology.</note> up to this point, 913 years and 101 days are collected. During this time, the uniform precession of the equinoxes <note>original: "anteceſsio æqualis"</note> is 12 degrees and 44 minutes <term>minutes: also called "scruples," these are 1/60th of a degree.</term> The simple anomaly <term>simple anomaly: in this context, the irregularity or "wobble" in the Earth's precession over long cycles.</term> is 95 degrees and 44 minutes.

Now, in the second year of Antoninus, as has been recorded, the spring equinox preceded the first of the stars in the head of Aries <note>Aries: the Ram, the first sign of the zodiac. Copernicus uses the stars themselves as a fixed reference point to measure how much the equinox has "precessed" or shifted.</note> by 6 degrees and 40 minutes. And since the double anomaly was 42½ parts, the difference between the uniform and apparent motion was subtractive by 48 minutes. When this is added back to the apparent motion of 6 degrees and 40 minutes, it brings the mean position of the spring equinox itself to 7 degrees and 28 minutes. 

If we add 360 degrees of a full circle to this, and subtract from the sum 12 degrees and 44 minutes, we will have—for the first Olympiad, which began at noon on the first day of the month of Hekatombaion <note>original: "Ecatombæonos"; the first month of the Attic calendar in Greece.</note> among the Athenians—the mean position of the spring equinox at 354 degrees and 44 minutes; namely, that it then followed the first star of Aries by 5 degrees and 16 minutes. In a similar way, if from 21 degrees and 15 minutes of the simple anomaly we subtract 95 degrees and 45 minutes, there will remain for that same beginning of the Olympiads the position of the simple anomaly at 285 degrees and 30 minutes.

And again, through the addition of motions made according to the distance of times—always discarding 360 degrees whenever they exceed that amount—we will have the positions or **roots** for Alexander <note>Alexander the Great; the era often refers to his death in 323 BC.</note>: uniform motion 1 degree, 2 minutes; simple anomaly 332 degrees, 52 minutes. For Caesar <note>Julius Caesar; referring to the reform of the calendar in 45 BC.</note>: mean motion 4 degrees, 5 minutes; simple anomaly 2 degrees, 2 minutes. For the position of Christ: mean position 5 degrees, 32 minutes; anomaly 6 degrees, 45 minutes. And so for any others, taking the starting points of time, we will grasp the roots of the motions.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial letter Q, containing a portrait of a man, likely an astronomer (possibly Copernicus himself), seated at a desk with a globe or armillary sphere.</image-desc>Whenever, therefore, we wish to find the position of the spring equinox <note>The "spring" or vernal equinox is the moment the sun crosses the celestial equator, marking the start of spring.</note>, if the years from our assumed starting point to the given time are unequal—such as the Roman years we commonly use—we shall arrange them into "equal" years, otherwise known as Egyptian years <note>Egyptian years: Unlike the Roman/Julian calendar with leap years, the Egyptian calendar used by astronomers always had exactly 365 days, making it much easier to calculate long-term cycles.</note>. For we shall use no other years in the calculation of uniform motions than Egyptian years, for the reason we have already stated. As for the number of years themselves, insofar as it is greater than sixty, we shall distribute them into groups of sixty. When we enter the tables of motions with these groups of sixty, we shall at first pass over the first position encountered in the motions as if it were a surplus; then, beginning from the second position (the degrees), we shall take the groups of sixty—if there are any—along with the remaining degrees and minutes <term>minutes: original "scrupula," literally "scruples," representing 1/60th of a degree.</term> that follow. 

Then, with the remaining years, we make a second entry into the tables; from the first position as they lie, we shall take the groups of sixty, degrees, and minutes encountered. We shall do the same for days and for groups of sixty days when we wish to add uniform motions <note>Uniform (or mean) motion is the theoretical average speed of a celestial body, before accounting for "wobbles" or irregularities.</note> through the tables of days and minutes. If the double anomaly is less than a semicircle <note>180 degrees.</note>, we shall subtract this prosthaphaeresis from the mean motion. ### On the Magnitude of the Solar Year and its Variation. Chapter XIV.

It necessarily follows that the length of the year, when compared to one of the equinoxes or solstices, is unequal because of the unequal shifting of these boundaries; for these things are interconnected. # BOOK III OF THE REVOLUTIONS.

The temporal year must be distinguished from the sidereal year. We call the "natural" or "temporal" year that which regulates the four annual seasons for us. The "sidereal" year, however, is that which returns to the same position relative to one of the fixed stars <note>original: "stellarum non errantium," literally the stars that do not wander, as opposed to planets.</note>. That the natural year—which they also call the "turning year" <note>original: "annum vertentem"</note>—is of unequal length is shown by the many observations of the ancients. For Calippus, Aristarchus of Samos, and Archimedes of Syracuse defined it as 365 full days plus one-quarter of a day, following the Athenian custom of beginning the year at the summer solstice.

However, Claudius Ptolemy, realizing that the apprehension of the solstices is difficult and prone to error, did not fully trust their observations. He turned instead to Hipparchus, who left behind records not only of solar solstices but also of equinoxes observed in Rhodes; Hipparchus reported that the year lacks a small amount of that quarter-day. Later, Ptolemy determined this deficit to be the 1/300th part of a day, using the following method. 

He takes the autumnal equinox, observed by Hipparchus at Alexandria with the greatest possible accuracy, in the 177th year after the death of Alexander the Great, on the third intercalary day <note>These were "leap days" or extra days added to the 360-day Egyptian calendar to make it 365 days.</note> according to the Egyptians, at midnight, followed by the fourth intercalary day. Then Ptolemy adds the same equinox observed by himself at Alexandria in the third year of Antoninus <note>The Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius.</note>, which was the 463rd year from the death of Alexander, on the ninth day of the Egyptian month of Athyr, nearly one hour after sunrise. 

Therefore, between this observation and that of Hipparchus, there were 285 Egyptian years, 70 days, 7 hours, and a fifth of an hour. These should have been 71 days and six hours if the turning year had been exactly a quarter-day beyond the full 365 days. Thus, in 285 years, there was a deficit of one day minus a twentieth part of a day. From this, it follows that in 300 years, an entire day is lost. 

He draws a similar conclusion from the spring equinox. For he records that Hipparchus noted it in the 178th year of Alexander, on the 27th day of Mechir (the sixth Egyptian month) at sunrise. He himself, in that same 463rd year, found it on the seventh day of the month of Pachon (the ninth Egyptian month), one hour and a little more after midday. In the same way, over 285 years, one day was missing minus a twentieth part. Aided by these signs, Ptolemy defined the turning year as 365 days, 14 <term>minutes</term> <note>original: "scrupulis primis." In this context, 14/60ths of a day.</note>, and 48 <term>seconds</term> <note>original: "scrupulis secundis." In this context, 48/3600ths of a day.</note>. After these men, Al-Battani <note>original: "Machometus." Copernicus refers to the 9th-century Arab astronomer Al-Battani, often Latinized as Albategnius.</note> in Raqqa, Syria...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "natural year" by comparing historical observations of the autumnal equinox. Copernicus is using data from the 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy and the 9th-century astronomer Al-Battani (referred to here as Machometus Aratensis) to demonstrate that the length of the year fluctuates over long periods of time.</meta>

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

With no less diligence, 1,206 years after the death of Alexander, he <note>Al-Battani, a 9th-century Arab astronomer whom Copernicus deeply respected</note> observed the autumnal equinox. He found that it occurred after the seventh day of the month Pachon, in the following night at about seven and two-fifths hours; that is, four and three-fifths hours before the dawn of the eighth day. Therefore, comparing this observation of his to that of Ptolemy (made in the third year of Antoninus, one hour after sunrise at Alexandria—which lies ten degrees to the west of Raqqa), he adjusted it to his own meridian at Raqqa <note>original: "Arata"</note>, where it would have been one and two-thirds hours after sunrise.

Thus, in an interval of 743 equal years, there were 178 extra days, 17 hours, and three-fifths of an hour, whereas the sum of quarter-days <note>the 1/4 day added to 365 days in a standard Julian-style leap year</note> should have totaled 185 days and three-quarters. Since there was a deficit of seven days and two-fifths of an hour, it appeared that the 106th part <note>1/106</note> of a day was missing from each quarter-day. Therefore, he took that deficit of seven days and two-fifths of an hour and divided it by the total number of years (743). The result—14 minutes <note>original: "scrupuli horarii"</note> and 36 seconds—he subtracted from the quarter-day, and he declared that the natural year contains 365 days, 5 hours, 46 minutes, and 24 seconds.

We too observed the autumnal equinox at Frauenburg <note>original: "Fruëburgo," the town in modern-day Poland where Copernicus lived and worked</note> in the year of our Lord 1515, eighteen days before the Kalends of October <note>September 14</note>. This was 1,840 Egyptian years after the death of Alexander, on the sixth day of the month Phaophis, half an hour after sunrise. But since Raqqa <note>original: "Areca"</note> is further east than our region by about 25 degrees—which accounts for two hours minus one-third of an hour <note>1 hour and 40 minutes</note>—the time between our observation and that of Al-Battani <note>original: "Machometi Aratensis"</note>, over a span of 633 Egyptian years, consisted of 153 days and six and three-quarters hours, instead of 158 days and six hours.

From that observation by Ptolemy in Alexandria to the time and place of our own observation, there are 1,376 Egyptian years, 332 days, and half an hour; for we differ from Alexandria by about one hour. Therefore, compared to the time of Al-Battani, five days minus one hour and fifteen minutes would have been lost in 633 years, which is one day every 128 years. From Ptolemy's time, however, in 1,376 years, nearly 12 days were lost—one day every 115 years. Thus, in both instances, the year is shown once again to be of unequal length.

<meta>This page continues Copernicus's investigation into the varying length of the "natural" or solar year. Having previously discussed the autumnal equinox, he now turns to his own observations of the vernal (spring) equinox to show that the timing of the seasons is not as constant as ancient astronomers believed.</meta>

# BOOK III OF THE REVOLUTIONS

We also observed the vernal equinox, which occurred in the year 1516 after the birth of Christ, at four and one-third hours after midnight on the eleventh of March <note>original: "quintum ante Idus Martij" — the fifth day before the Ides of March</note>. From that vernal equinox observed by Ptolemy (taking into account the difference between the meridian of Alexandria and our own), there are 1,376 Egyptian years, 332 days, and 16 and one-third hours. Here, too, it is apparent that the spans of time between the vernal and autumnal equinoxes are unequal. It matters greatly, therefore, whether the solar year—measured in this way—is actually constant.

For in the case of the autumnal equinoxes between Ptolemy’s time and our own, as has been shown, a 115th part of a day was missing from the quarter-day <note>meaning the 365.25 day year was slightly too long by 1/115th of a day</note> according to an equal distribution of years. However, this does not match the equinox of Al-Battani <note>original: "Machometano Aratensi"</note> by half a day. Nor does the interval from Al-Battani to our own time (where a 128th part of a day should have been missing from the quarter-day) agree with Ptolemy. Instead, the calculated number precedes his observed equinox by more than a full day, and precedes Hipparchus’s by more than two days. Similarly, the calculation for Al-Battani, when derived from Ptolemy, exceeds the equinox of Hipparchus by two days.

It is more correct, therefore, to derive the equality of the solar year from the sphere of the "non-wandering" <note>fixed</note> stars. This was first discovered by <term>Thabit ibn Qurra</term> <note>original: "Thebites Choræ filius," a 9th-century Sabian astronomer and mathematician</note>, who found its length to be 365 days, 15 minutes, and 24 seconds <note>these are "hexagesimal" fractions of a day, where 15 minutes = 1/4 of a day</note>. This equals 6 hours, 9 minutes, and 12 seconds. He likely arrived at this by the plausible argument that the year seemed longer when the equinoxes and solstices occurred more slowly, and shorter when they occurred more quickly, according to a certain proportion. This could not happen unless the measurement was made in comparison to the sphere of the fixed stars.

Because of this, we should not listen to Ptolemy on this point. He thought it was absurd and irrelevant to measure the annual equality of the Sun against any return to the fixed stars, claiming it made no more sense than if someone were to measure the year against the position of Jupiter or Saturn. Thus, the reason is obvious why the "temporary" <note>tropical</note> year was longer before Ptolemy’s time, and why it has become shorter after him by a varied difference. But even regarding the <term>sidereal</term> <note>original: "asteroterida," from the Greek for "star-related"</note> or starry year, an error can occur, though a very small one and much less than the one we have just explained. This is because the same apparent motion of the center of the Earth around the Sun is also unequal due to two other variations.

<meta>catchword: Of which</meta>

<summary>Copernicus argues that the solar year (the time between seasons) is inconsistent and should instead be measured against the fixed stars, citing the work of Thabit ibn Qurra. He critiques Ptolemy's rejection of this "sidereal year" and notes that even this measurement has slight complexities.</summary>

<keywords>vernal equinox, solar year, sidereal year, Thabit ibn Qurra, Al-Battani, Ptolemy, Hipparchus, astronomy, duration of the year</keywords>

--- Page 176 ---
<meta>This page continues Copernicus's investigation into the complexities of the solar year. Having previously discussed the observations of earlier astronomers like Ptolemy and Al-Battani, he now begins to explain the specific celestial mechanics that make measuring a "constant" year so difficult, transitioning from observational data to theoretical causes.</meta>

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

Of these differences, the first and simple one completes its cycle annually; the other, which varies by altering the first, is perceived only over a long span of time. Therefore, the calculation of the annual equality is neither simple nor easy to understand. For if anyone simply wishes to determine the year by the known distance of a certain star (which can be done using an <term>astrolabe</term> <note>a historical instrument used to calculate the positions of celestial bodies</note> with the Moon as a middle-man, just as we explained regarding the star <note>original: "Basiliscum Leonis" — the star Regulus, the "Little King," in the constellation Leo</note> Regulus), he will not entirely avoid error, unless at that time the Sun, because of the Earth's motion, either has no <term>prosthaphæresis</term> <note>a technical term for the correction added or subtracted to the average (mean) position of a planet to find its true position</note> or happens to have a similar and equal correction at both ends of the observation. Unless this happens, and if there is some difference regarding their inequality, an equal circuit will certainly not appear to have occurred in equal times. 

But if the total diversity is subtracted or applied according to the ratio at both ends of the observation, the work will be perfect. Furthermore, the understanding of this diversity itself requires a prior knowledge of the average motion, which is why we seek it. Nevertheless, so that we may eventually come to a resolution of this matter, we have found four causes in total for this unequal appearance. 

The first is the inequality of the precession of the equinoxes, which we have already explained. The second is that by which the Sun appears to cover unequal arcs of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi" — the sign-bearer or zodiac</note>, which is almost annual. The third, which also varies this second one, we shall call the "second diversity." There remains a fourth, which changes the <term>apsides</term> <note>the points in an orbit closest to or furthest from the center of motion</note> of the Earth's center, both the highest and lowest, as will appear below. 

Of all these, only the second was known to <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose geocentric model Copernicus was challenging</note>; this alone could not have produced the annual inequality, but when entangled with the others, it does so more significantly. However, for demonstrating the difference between the equality and appearance of the Sun, an extremely exact calculation of the year does not seem necessary; it is sufficient if we take 365 days and a quarter for the magnitude of the year in our demonstration, in which that motion of the first diversity is completed. Since that which differs so little from the whole circle vanishes entirely when subsumed into a smaller magnitude. Yet, for the sake of good order and ease of instruction, we here set forth the equal motions of the annual revolution of the Earth's center, which we shall then establish through necessary demonstrations alongside the differences of equality and appearance.

<meta>catchword: Concerning the equal-</meta>

<summary>Copernicus identifies four distinct celestial causes for why the solar year appears to vary in length, noting that ancient astronomers like Ptolemy only recognized one of them. He proposes using the standard 365.25-day year as a baseline for his upcoming proofs regarding the Earth's motion.</summary>
<keywords>astrolabe, Regulus, prosthaphæresis, Ptolemy, zodiac, apsides, solar year, Earth's motion</keywords>

<page-num>81</page-num>

### On the Uniform and Mean Motions of the Revolutions of the Center of the Earth. Chapter 14.

We have found the length of the year and its uniformity to be only one second and ten thirds greater than what <term>Thabit ibn Qurra</term> <note>original: "Thebith Benchoræ" — a 9th-century astronomer and mathematician from Harran who studied the length of the sidereal year</note> reported. Thus, the year is 365 days, 15 <term>minutes</term> <note>original: "scrup. primorum" — literally "first scruples," the standard division of a degree or hour into 60 parts</note>, 24 seconds, and 10 thirds. This is equal to 6 uniform hours, 9 minutes, and 40 seconds. Its exact uniformity relative to the sphere of the fixed stars is established. 

Therefore, when we multiply the 360 degrees of a single circle by 365 days and divide the product by 365 days, 15 minutes, 24 seconds, and 10 thirds, we obtain the motion for one <term>Egyptian year</term> <note>a standard year used by ancient astronomers consisting of exactly 365 days, which makes calculations of mean motion much simpler</note>. This motion is five <term>sexagenes</term> <note>original: "sexagenis" — units of 60 degrees used in the sexagesimal system; 5 sexagenes equals 300 degrees</note>, 59 degrees, 44 minutes, 49 seconds, 7 thirds, and 4 fourths. The motion for sixty similar years, after casting out the full circles, is 5 sexagenes, 44 degrees, 49 minutes, 7 seconds <note>The Latin text lists this as "scrup. prima," though in this context it refers to the first division of the sexagene</note>, and 4 thirds. 

Furthermore, if we divide the annual motion by 365 days, we obtain a daily motion of 59 minutes, 8 seconds, 11 thirds, and 22 fourths. If we add the mean and uniform <term>precession of the equinoxes</term> <note>the slow westward shift of the equinoctial points relative to the stars</note> to these figures, we will also establish the uniform motion for the <term>solar years</term> <note>original: "annis temporarijs" — the tropical or seasonal year, measured from equinox to equinox rather than against the stars</note>. This annual motion is 5 sexagenes, 59 degrees, 45 minutes, 39 seconds, 19 thirds, and 9 fourths; the daily motion is 59 minutes, 8 seconds, 19 thirds, and 37 fourths. 

For this reason, we can call the first motion of the Sun (to use the common term) "simple uniform motion," and the latter "composite uniform motion." We will set these out in tables in the same way we did for the precession of the equinoxes. To these is added the uniform motion of the <term>Sun's anomaly</term> <note>the variation in the Sun's apparent speed caused by the Earth's eccentric orbit; "anomaly" refers to the angle used to calculate this deviation from mean motion</note>, which we will discuss later.

This can indeed be understood in two ways: either by an **eccentric** circle (that is, one whose center is not the Sun's center) or by an **epicycle** on a **homocentric** <note>A homocentric circle is one that shares the same center as the world or the Sun.</note> circle. <image-desc>A circular geometric diagram labeled with points A (top), B (upper right), C (lower left), and D (bottom). Let its diameter pass through both centers AEFD; let the <term>apogee<note>original: "apogeum," from the Greek for "away from Earth."</note></term> be at A, which is called the **highest apsis** by the Latins—the place farthest from the center of the world—and let D be the <term>perigee<note>original: "perigeum," from the Greek for "near Earth."</note>,</term> which is the nearest point and the **lowest apsis**. For if equal arcs AB and CD are taken, and straight lines BE, CE, BF, and CF are drawn, the angles AEB and CED will be equal, because equal arcs are subtended around the center E. However, the angle CFD, as it is seen [from F], is greater than angle CED (since an exterior angle is greater than the interior one); therefore, it is also greater than angle AEB, which is equal to CED. But since the exterior angle AEB is also greater than the interior angle AFB, then angle CFD is much greater than AFB. Yet each arc was produced in an equal amount of time, because the arcs AB and CD are equal. Therefore, the motion will appear uniform around center E, but unequal around F.

The same thing may be seen even more simply, because the arc AB is farther from F than the arc CD is. For by the seventh proposition of the third book of <term>Euclid’s Elements<note>Euclid was the ancient Greek "Father of Geometry." Copernicus relies on his mathematical proofs to validate how distances affect perceived size and speed.</note>,</term> the lines that contain them, AF and BF, are longer than CF and DF; and as is demonstrated in optics, equal magnitudes that are closer appear larger than those further away. Thus, what is proposed concerning the eccentric circle is clear.

Furthermore, the demonstration is exactly the same whether the Earth were at rest at F and the Sun moved in the surrounding circle ABC (as held by <term>Ptolemy<note>Claudius Ptolemy was the 2nd-century astronomer whose Earth-centered model Copernicus is here revising into a Sun-centered one.</note></term> and others). In ancient astronomy, this was a small circle that rolls around the circumference of a larger one to explain complex planetary paths.</note></term> on a homocentric circle. For let there be a homocentric circle BCD, with the center of the world at E, where the Sun also is. Let the center of the epicycle FG be in the same plane, and let a straight line CEAF be drawn through both centers. Let the apogee of the epicycle be F and the perigee be I. Because if A moves toward B, that is, **in the order of the signs** <note>original: "in consequentia," meaning eastward, following the sequence of the Zodiac.</note>, but the center of the Earth moves from the apogee F **in the preceding signs** <note>original: "in præcedentia," meaning westward or retrograde relative to the stars.</note>, [the Earth] will appear to move faster at B in the <term>perigee<note>The point in an orbit closest to the center of motion.</note></term>, which is I, because the two motions of A and I are in the same direction. This also happens in three ways. First, if the epicycle in the homocentric and the star in the epicycle complete equal revolutions, but with their motions opposing each other, the motion of the star will describe a fixed eccentric, whose apogee and perigee maintain unchangeable positions.

From all these things, it is evident that the same inequality of appearance is always produced, whether through an epicycle on a homocentric circle, or through an eccentric circle equal to the homocentric; and they differ in no way from each other, provided that the distance of the centers is equal to the radius of the epicycle. <summary>Copernicus proves that the epicycle and eccentric models are mathematically interchangeable and produce the same observed phenomena. <meta>This page continues the geometric demonstration of how eccentric circles and epicycles can be used to model the movements of celestial bodies. Copernicus is specifically proving where the maximum "inequality"—the difference between a planet's calculated average position and its observed position—occurs in an orbit.</meta>

->NICOLAI COPERNICI<-

<note>original: "uagantibus eccentrepicyclos accõmodauit."</note> ...he accommodated **eccentric-epicycles** <term>Eccentric-epicycle: A geometric model combining a secondary circle (epicycle) moving along an offset primary circle (eccentric) to account for variations in planetary speed.</term> to the wandering stars. From these it is also easily demonstrated that the greatest difference between uniformity <note>Uniformity refers to the "mean motion," or the steady, average speed a planet would have if its orbit were a perfect circle centered on the observer.</note> and appearance <note>Appearance refers to the "apparent motion," or how the planet actually looks to an observer on Earth, which changes speed as it nears or moves away.</note> is seen when the star appears in the middle place between the **highest and lowest apsis** <term>Apsis: The points in an orbit where a celestial body is at its maximum distance (apogee) or minimum distance (perigee) from the center of motion.</term>, according to the eccentric method; but according to the epicycle method, it occurs at its point of contact, as in **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the influential Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose geocentric model Copernicus was updating.</note>. Through the eccentric, it is shown in this way:

Let there be a circle **ABCD** with center **E**, and diameter **AEC** passing through **F**, the **Sun** <note>original: "Solem." Note that even as he develops his heliocentric theory, Copernicus uses traditional geometric proofs where the Sun is the point of observation or the eccentric focus.</note>, which is outside the center. Let the line **BFD** be drawn at right angles through **F**, and let **BE** and **ED** be connected. Let **A** be the **apogee** <term>Apogee: The point in an orbit farthest from the center (in this case, the Sun at F).</term> and **C** the **perigee** <term>Perigee: The point in an orbit closest to the center.</term>, from which **B** and **D** are the mean appearances. It is manifest that the exterior angle **AEB** contains the uniform motion, while the interior angle **EFB** contains the apparent motion, and their difference is the angle **EBF**. 

I say that no angle greater than these angles at **B** and **D** can be formed upon the line **EF** along the circumference. For if we take points **G** and **H** before and after **B**, and join **GD**, **GE**, **GF**, and likewise **HE**, **HF**, **HD**. Since **FG**, being closer to the center, is longer than **DF**, the angle **GDF** will be greater than **DGF**. But the angles under **EDG** and **EGD** are equal, as the sides **EG** and **ED** descending to the base are equal. Therefore, the angle **EDB**, which is equal to **EBF**, is greater than angle **EGF**. Similarly, **DF** is longer than **FH**, and angle **FHD** is greater than **FDH**. Since the whole angle **EHD** is equal to the whole **EDH** (as **EH** and **ED** are equal), the remaining angle **EDF** (equal to **EBF**) is greater than the remaining angle **EHF**. Therefore, nowhere else than at points **B** and **D** above the line **EF** can a greater angle be formed. Thus, the greatest difference between uniformity and appearance exists in the middle place between the apogee and the perigee.

<meta>This page continues the geometric proof regarding the Sun's eccentricity.
