### ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK III, PAGE 87

...it comprises from the Spring equinox to the summer solstice 94 ½ days; from the solstice to the Autumnal equinox 92 ½ days. Therefore, according to the calculation of time, in the first interval the mean and equal motion <note>Mean and equal motion refers to the steady, average speed the Sun would appear to have if its orbit were a perfect circle centered exactly on the observer.</note> was 94 degrees and 9 minutes. In the second, 91 degrees and 11 minutes. In this way, let the circle of the year be **ABCD**, with **E** as the center; let **AB** be taken for the first space of time as 94 degrees and 9 minutes; **BC** for the second as 91 degrees and 11 minutes. And from **A** let the Spring equinox be seen, from **B** the Summer solstice, from **C** the Autumnal equinox, and what remains from **D**, the Winter solstice. Let **AC** and **BD** be connected, intersecting each other at right angles at **F**, where we place the **Sun** <note>original: "Solem"</note>. Since therefore the circumference **ABC** is greater than a semicircle, and **AB** is also greater than **BC**, Ptolemy understood from these things that the center of the circle **E** is contained between lines **BF** and **FA**, and the **apogee** <term>Apogee: The point in an orbit where the celestial body—in this model, the Sun—is at its maximum distance from the center of motion.</term> is between the Spring equinox and the Summer solstice of the Sun. 

Now let **IEG** be drawn through center **E**, parallel to **AFC**, which will cut **BFD** at **L**; and let **HEK** be drawn parallel to **BFD**, which cuts **AF** at **M**. In this way, the rectangular parallelogram **LEMF** is established, whose diameter **FE**, extended in a straight line, will indicate the line **FEN** as the Earth's greatest distance from the Sun, and the location of the apogee at **N**. 

Since therefore the circumference **ABC** is 185 degrees and 20 minutes, its half **AH** is 92 degrees and 10 minutes. If it is subtracted from the arc **GB**, it leaves the excess **HB** as 59 minutes. Indeed, the half-chord of double **BH** consists of 172 of the same parts. ## NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

If from these are subtracted <note>Referring to the geometric segments calculated on the previous page.</note> **CK** and **DK**, which are equal to **AG** and **HB**, there remains **CD** of 86 degrees 51 minutes; and what remains of **CDA** is **DA** itself, of 88 degrees 49 minutes. But to 86 degrees 51 minutes correspond 88 days and an eighth part of a day <note>One eighth of a day is 3 hours.</note>. To 88 degrees 49 minutes correspond 90 days and an eighth part of a day (which are 3 hours), in which, under the equal motion of the **Earth** <note>Though describing the Sun's apparent path, Copernicus uses "telluris" (Earth) to reflect his heliocentric view that it is the Earth's motion we are actually measuring.</note>, the Sun was seen to pass from the Autumnal equinox to the **Winter Solstice** <term>Bruma: The winter solstice, the point where the Sun reaches its southernmost point in the sky.</term>, and in the remainder of the year to return from the Winter Solstice to the Vernal equinox.

Ptolemy testifies that he found these things just as they had been set forth by Hipparchus <note>Hipparchus (c. 190–120 BCE) was a Greek astronomer whose observations formed the basis for much of Ptolemy's work.</note> before him. For this reason, he believed that for all time to come, the **highest apogee** <term>Highest apogee: The "summa absis," or the point in the orbit where the Earth is farthest from the Sun.</term> would remain at 24 ½ degrees before the summer solstice <note>original: "tropen æstiuam"</note>, and the **eccentricity** <term>Eccentricity: The degree to which the Earth's orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</term> would perpetually remain at the twenty-fourth part of the radius, as was said.

Both of these are now found to have changed, with a manifest difference. **Al-Battani** <note>original: "Machometus Aratensis." A 9th-century Arab astronomer whose high-precision observations often corrected Ptolemy.</note> noted from the Vernal equinox to the Summer solstice 94 days 35 minutes; to the Autumnal equinox 182 days 37 minutes. From these, following Ptolemy's rule, he derived an eccentricity of no more than 347 parts, where the radius is 10,000. **Al-Zarqali the Spaniard** <note>original: "Arzachel Hispanus." An 11th-century astronomer from Toledo whose "Toledan Tables" were famous in the Middle Ages.</note> agrees with this in the ratio of eccentricity, but reported the apogee at 12 degrees 10 minutes before the solstice, whereas it appeared to Al-Battani to be 7 degrees 43 minutes before the same solstice.

By these indications, it is surely understood that there remains yet another difference in the motion of the center of the earth, which is also proven by the observations of our own age. For more than ten years now, since we applied our mind to investigating these matters, and especially in the year of Christ 1515, we found that from the Vernal to the Autumnal equinox 186 days 5 ½ minutes are completed. And so that we might be less deceived in taking the solstices—which some suspect happened occasionally to our predecessors—we called upon certain other locations of the Sun in this business, which were not at all difficult to observe even outside the equinoxes, such as the midpoints of the signs of **Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius**.

We found, therefore, from the Autumnal equinox to the middle of **Scorpio** 45 days 16 minutes; to the Vernal equinox 178 days 54 ½ minutes. Moreover, the equal motion in the first interval is 44 degrees 37 minutes. In the second, 176 degrees [19 minutes. Which...]

### ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK III.

### XIX.

With these things thus established, let the circle **ABCD** be repeated. Let **A** be the point from which the **Sun** appeared at the **Vernal equinox** <note>The spring equinox, around March 21</note>, **B** where the **Autumnal equinox** was observed, and **C** the midpoint of **Scorpio** <note>A specific astronomical observation point used to divide the orbit</note>. Let **AB** and **CD** be joined, intersecting each other at point **F**, which is the center of the **Sun**, and let the line **AC** be drawn.

Since, therefore, the arc **CB** is known—for it is 44 degrees 37 minutes—the angle **BAC** is also given <note>By the geometric principle that an inscribed angle is half the central angle of the arc it subtends</note>, according to a scale where 360 units equal two right angles. And the angle **BFC**, representing the apparent motion, is 45 degrees where 360 units equal four right angles; but on the scale where they equal two right angles, **BFC** is 90 degrees. From this, the remaining angle **ACD** <note>relative to the circumference</note> is 45 degrees 24 minutes. But the entire segment **ACB** is 176 degrees 19 minutes; when **BC** is subtracted, **AC** remains as 131 degrees 42 minutes. This, when combined with **AD**, gives the arc **CAD** as 177 degrees 5 ½ minutes.

Since both segments **ACB** and **CAD** are less than a semicircle, it is clear that the center of the circle is contained in the remaining part **BD**. Let that center be **E**, and let the diameter **LEFG** be drawn through **F**, where **L** is the **apogee** <term>Apogee: The point in the orbit farthest from the Sun.</term> and **G** is the **perigee** <term>Perigee: The point in the orbit closest to the Sun.</term>. Let **EK** be erected perpendicular to the line **CFD**.

Furthermore, the chords of the given arcs are also given by the **Table** <note>original: "Canonem"; referring to the Table of Chords or Sines used for calculations</note>: **AC** is 182,494 and **CFD** is 199,934, where the diameter is set at 200,000. In the triangle **ACF**, with its angles known, the ratio of the sides is also given by the first rules of plane triangles: **CF** is 97,967 where **AC** was 182,494. Because of this, the half-excess over **FD**—which is **FK**—is 2,000 of those same parts.

And since the segment **CAD** falls short of a semicircle by 2 degrees 54 ½ minutes, the half-chord of that shortfall, which is equal to **EK**, is 2,534 parts. Therefore, in the triangle **EFK**, with two sides **FK** and **KE** given as they enclose a right angle, the sides and angles will be known. **EF** is approximately 323 parts, where **EL** <note>the radius</note> is 10,000. The angle **EFK** is 51 and two-thirds degrees (where 360 degrees equal four right angles). Therefore, the whole angle **AFL** is 96 and two-thirds degrees, and the remaining angle **BFL** is 83 and one-third degrees.

However, on a scale where **EL** <note>the radius</note> is 60 parts, **EF** is approximately 1 part 56 minutes. This was the distance of the Sun from the center of the orbit, which has now become barely a thirty-first part <note>Copernicus is noting that the eccentricity—the "off-centeredness" of the orbit—has decreased since the time of the ancient Greeks</note>.

### On the Examination of the Uniform Motion in Longitude. Chapter XVIII.

These things have been explained concerning the annual inequality of the Sun. However, it is not through a simple difference, as it once appeared, but through one that is thus far mixed, which the length of time has revealed. We shall indeed distinguish these from one another hereafter. Meanwhile, the mean and uniform motion of the center of the Earth will be established with numbers that are more certain the more it is separated from the differences of inequality and the longer the interval of time between observations. This, moreover, will be established in the following manner. We have taken that Autumnal equinox <note>The moment in September when day and night are of equal length</note> which was observed by Hipparchus <note>A foundational Greek astronomer from the 2nd century BCE</note> at Alexandria, in the thirty-second year of the third Calippic period <note>A 76-year cycle used in ancient Greek timekeeping</note>. It was distant from the <term>highest apse</term> <note>The apogee, or the point in the orbit farthest from the center</note> by 114 ½ degrees.

## Concerning the Positions and Principles to be Fixed for the Uniform Motion of the Sun. Chapter XIX.

In the time elapsed from the death of Alexander the Great to the observation by Hipparchus, there are 476 years, 362 days, and 27.5 minutes <note>original: "scru. XXVII. s."</note>. In this period, the mean motion <note>The theoretical average speed of the Sun (Earth) if its orbit were a perfect circle</note>, according to calculation, is 312 degrees and 43 minutes. When these degrees are subtracted from the 360 degrees of the 20th circle <note>Copernicus is calculating backward through 20 full orbits or revolutions</note> adjusted for Hipparchus’s observation, there remains for the beginning of the years of the deceased Alexander the Great a position at noon on the first day of the month of Thoth <note>The first month of the ancient Egyptian calendar</note>, the first of the Egyptians, of 225 degrees and 37 minutes. This is calculated for the meridian of Krakow and Frauenburg, the location of our observations.

From here to the beginning of the Roman years of Julius Caesar, in 278 years and 118.5 days, the mean motion—after the completion of full revolutions—is 46 degrees and 27 minutes. These, when added to the figures for the Alexandrian position, produce Caesar's position at midnight on the Kalends of January <note>January 1st, the start of the Roman year</note>, when the Romans are accustomed to begin their years and days, at 272 degrees and 4 minutes. 

Then, in 45 years and 12 days—or from Alexander the Great in 323 years and 130.5 days—there arises the position of Christ at 272 degrees and 31 minutes. And since Christ was born in the third year of the 194th Olympiad <note>A four-year period used by the Greeks for dating</note> (which calculates to 775 years and 12.5 days from the beginning of the first Olympiad), at midnight before the Kalends of January, these similarly report the position of the first Olympiad at 96 degrees and 16 minutes at noon on the first day of the month of Hecatombaeon <note>The first month of the Attic/Greek calendar</note>, the anniversary of which now falls on the Kalends of July according to the Roman years. 

In this way, the principles of the simple solar motion <note>Motion measured against the "fixed" backdrop of the stars</note> have been established relative to the sphere of the fixed stars. The composite positions <note>Motion that includes the "precession of the equinoxes," or the slow wobbling of the Earth's axis</note> are also produced by adding the precession of the equinoxes; accordingly, the position for the Olympiads is 90 degrees 59 minutes; for Alexander, 226 degrees 38 minutes; for Caesar, 276 degrees 59 minutes; and for Christ, 278 degrees 2 minutes. All of these, as we have said, are related to the meridian of Krakow.

### On the Second and Twofold Difference that Occurs Concerning the Sun Because of the Change of the Apsides. Chapter XX.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring two cherubs or putti holding a shield amidst stylized floral vines and foliage.</image-desc>

Now a greater difficulty arises regarding the instability of the solar apogee <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the center</note>. While Ptolemy believed this point to be fixed, others thought it followed the motion of the "eighth sphere" <note>The sphere of the fixed stars; earlier astronomers believed the stars moved slowly, a phenomenon called the precession of the equinoxes</note>, just as they believed the fixed stars themselves moved. Arzachel <note>The Latin name for the 11th-century Andalusian astronomer Al-Zarqali</note> was of the opinion that this motion was also unequal—that is, it could even be seen to move backward. He based this conclusion on the evidence that when "Machometus Aratensis" <note>The Latin name for the 9th-century astronomer Al-Battani</note>, as has been said, found the apogee to be seven degrees and 44 minutes <note>original: "xliiii. scrup."</note> before the summer solstice, it had previously (in the 740 years since Ptolemy) advanced by nearly 17 degrees. Yet, in the 193 years <note>original: "cc. minus vii." (200 minus 7)</note> following Al-Battani, it seemed to have moved backward nearly 4.5 degrees. Because of this, Arzachel thought there was another motion for the center of the annual orbit, moving in a certain small circle. According to this theory, the apogee would deflect forward and backward, and the distance of the center of that orbit from the center of the world <note>the Sun, in Copernicus's model, though he uses the traditional terminology of his predecessors here</note> would become unequal.

This was certainly a beautiful invention, but it has not been accepted because, when compared as a whole, it does not harmonize with other observations. For if the succession of this motion is considered in order—namely, that it stood still for some time before Ptolemy, that in roughly 640 years it passed through 17 degrees, and then in the 200 years following it moved forward another 4 or 5 degrees to our own time—no other regression has been perceived in all that time. Nor have there been the "stations" <note>Points where a body appears to stop moving before reversing direction</note> which must necessarily occur between contrary motions. These things can in no way be understood within the framework of canonical and circular motion. Therefore, it is believed by many that some error occurred in those observations. Both mathematicians <note>Ptolemy and Al-Battani</note> were equal in their zeal and diligence, so it remains a matter of uncertainty whom we should follow.

Indeed, I confess that in no part of astronomy is there a greater difficulty than in grasping the solar apogee, where we reason out great things from very small and barely perceptible details. This is because near the perigee <note>closest point</note> and apogee <note>farthest point</note>, an entire degree of the orbit changes the <term>prosthaphæresis</term> <note>From the Greek for "addition and subtraction"—the correction applied to the mean motion to find the true position</note> by only two minutes, more or less. However, near the "middle apsides" <note>the points halfway between the closest and farthest distances</note>, 5 or 6 degrees pass by for every 1 minute of change. Thus, a slight error can manifest itself in an immense...

He highlights the extreme difficulty of precisely measuring these points because of the minute mathematical differences involved in the Sun's apparent speed at those positions.</summary>

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK III.

...however the Earth moves along the circumference FO of the second and its own <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one</note>, point O will no longer describe an <term>eccentric</term> <note>A circular orbit whose center is offset from the center of the universe</note> whose center lies on the line AC, but rather on a line parallel to DO, such as LP. Furthermore, if lines OI and CP are joined, they will also be equal, but smaller than IF and CM; and the angle DIO will be equal to angle LCP, according to the eighth proposition of the first book of <term>Euclid</term> <note>A reference to Euclid’s *Elements*, the foundational textbook of geometry</note>. For this reason, the Sun's <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the orbit farthest from the Earth</note> will appear to precede the actual point A along the line CP. From this it is also clear that the same thing happens through an <term>eccentric-epicycle</term> <note>A model combining an offset center with a secondary small circle</note>. Since in the pre-existing case of a single eccentric circle—which the epicycle D describes around the center L—the center of the Earth revolves on the circumference FO under the aforementioned conditions (that is, slightly more than one annual revolution), it will introduce another eccentric circle to the first one around the center P, and exactly the same effects will occur. Since so many methods lead to the same numerical result, I could not easily say which one actually exists, except that the perpetual harmony of the numbers and the appearances compels us to believe it is one of them.

## Chapter XXI. How Great the Second Difference of the Solar Inequality Is.

Since it has now been seen that this second <term>inequality</term> <note>A technical term for a variation or irregularity in a planet's motion compared to a perfectly uniform circle</note> follows that first and simple <term>anomaly</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet from its furthest point (apogee)</note> of the tilt of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: "signiferi"; the "sign-bearer" or the path of the sun</note>, or something similar to it, we shall have its definite differences, provided no error from past observers stands in the way. For we shall have the simple anomaly itself in the year of Christ 1515, according to the calculation, as approximately 165 degrees and 39 minutes; its beginning, by calculating backward, was approximately sixty-four years before the birth of Christ. From that time until our own, 1,583 years are collected. At that beginning, the maximum <term>eccentricity</term> <note>original: "eccentrotes"; the distance by which the center of an orbit is offset from the center of the world</note> was found by us to be 417 parts (where the radius of the orbital circle is 10,000), but our own eccentricity, as has been shown, is 323. Now let AB be a straight line, in which B is the Sun and the center of the world. Let the maximum eccentricity be AB, and the minimum be BD; and after a small circle has been described whose diameter is AD, let the circumference AC be taken according to the measure of the first simple anomaly, which was 165 degrees and 39 minutes. Therefore, since AB is given as 417 parts, which at the beginning of the simple anomaly...

...of the <term>anomaly</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet or the Sun from its apogee</note>, that is, it was found at A, but now B C is 323 parts; we will have the triangle A B C, with the sides A B and B C given, and one angle C A D, because the remaining circumference C D from the semicircle is 14 degrees 21 <term>minutes</term> <note>Original: "scrupula." Copernicus uses the Latin term for "scruples" to refer to minutes of an arc.</note>. Therefore, by the demonstrated rules of plane triangles, the remaining side A C will be given, as well as the angle A B C, which is the difference between the uniform and the varying motion of the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the Sun's orbit furthest from the Earth</note>. Insofar as A C subtends the given circumference, the diameter A D of the circle A C D will also be given. For, through the angle C A D of 14 degrees 21 minutes, we will have C B as 2498 parts, where the diameter of the circle circumscribing the triangle is 20000. According to the ratio of B C to A B, the side A B itself is given as 3225 of those same parts, and the side which subtends the angle A C B is 351 degrees 26 minutes. From this, the remainder—since 360 degrees make two right angles <note>In the trigonometric conventions of the time, calculations were often based on a semicircle of 180 degrees, which Copernicus refers to here as "two right angles."</note>—is the angle C B D of 4 degrees 13 minutes, which is subtended by A C of 735 parts. Therefore, where A B is 417 parts, A C is found to be nearly 95 parts; which, according to how it subtends the given circumference, will have a ratio to A D as if to the diameter. Therefore, A D is given as 96 parts, where A B is 417 parts, and the remaining D B is 321 parts—the minimum distance of the <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The distance between the center of the Earth's orbit and the Sun.</note>. Furthermore, the angle C B D, which was found to be 4 degrees 13 minutes as measured on the circumference, is 2 degrees 6.5 minutes when measured from the center. This is the <term>prosthaphæresis</term> <note>A term from Greek meaning "addition and subtraction." It refers to the geometric correction used to account for the difference between a planet's mean (uniform) position and its true (observed) position.</note> to be subtracted from the uniform motion of A B around the center B. Now, let the straight line B E be drawn tangent to the circle at point E, and having found the center F, let E F be joined. Since, therefore, the side E F of the <term>right-angled</term> <note>Original: "orthogonij."</note> triangle B E F is given as 48 parts, and B D F as 369 parts—where F B D, as the radius from the center, is 10000—E F will be 1300 parts, which is half the chord subtending double the angle E B F. This angle is 7 degrees 28 minutes, where 360 degrees equal four right angles. This is the maximum prosthaphæresis between the uniform motion at F and the apparent motion at E. From this, the other specific differences can be established. For example, if we take the angle A F E to be 6 degrees, we will have a triangle with given sides E F and F B, along with the angle E F B, from which the prosthaphæresis E B F of 41 minutes will result.

### Chapter XXII. How the uniform motion of the solar apogee is explained together with the variable motion.

**Since**, therefore, the time in which the maximum <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The measure of how much the Earth's orbit deviates from a perfect circle centered on the Sun.</note> coincided with the beginning of the first and simple <term>anomaly</term> <note>The angular distance of the Sun from its apogee</note> was the third year of the 178th Olympiad <note>Approx. 66 BCE</note>, which was also the 259th year after Alexander the Great according to the Egyptians; and for that reason, the true and mean position of the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the Earth</note> was at 5 ½ degrees of Gemini, which is 65 ½ degrees from the Spring Equinox. # NICHOLAS COPERNICUS

### On the Calculation of the Sun's Appearance. Chapter XXV.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut drop-cap letter 'E' depicting a scholar or astronomer seated at a desk with astronomical instruments.</image-desc>
From what has been said, I believe it is now sufficiently clear how the apparent position of the Sun is calculated for any given time. For at that specific time, one must seek the true position of the Vernal Equinox <note>The point in the sky where the Sun crosses the celestial equator, marking the start of spring.</note>, or its precession, along with its first simple <term>anomaly</term> <note>An "anomaly" in this context is a specific angle used to track a celestial body's position in its orbit relative to its furthest or closest point to the center.</note>, as we have explained above. Next, one finds the simple mean motion of the Earth's center—or you may call it the motion of the Sun—and the annual anomaly using the tables of uniform motions; these are then added to their established starting values. 

Then, with the first simple anomaly and its number found in the first or second column of the preceding table <note>Referring to the tables on the previous pages.</note>, you will find the corresponding <term>prosthaphaeresis</term> <note>original: "prosthaphæresim"; a technical term for the correction value added to or subtracted from the mean (average) motion to find the true position.</note> for the annual anomaly in the third column, along with the subsequent proportional minutes. You must add this correction to the annual anomaly if the first anomaly was less than a semicircle (180 degrees), or if its number was found in the first column; otherwise, subtract it. The result, whether added or subtracted, will be the "equated anomaly" of the Sun.

Using this equated anomaly, you again find the correction for the annual orbit (found in the fifth column) along with the accompanying "excess." If this excess, when multiplied by the proportional minutes saved earlier, produces any value, it is always added to this correction. This results in the "equated correction," which is subtracted from the mean position of the Sun if the annual anomaly was found in the first column (less than a semicircle), or added if it was greater or found in the second column. The remainder or sum thus produced will determine the true position of the Sun as measured from the head of the constellation Aries <note>The starting point of the fixed stellar zodiac.</note>. Finally, if the true precession of the Vernal Equinox is added to this, it will immediately show the Sun's position relative to the equinox itself in terms of the twelve signs of the zodiac <note>original: "dodecatemorijs"; referring to the twelve 30-degree divisions of the ecliptic.</note> and the degrees of those signs. 

If you wish to achieve this in another way, you may take the "composite uniform motion" instead of the "simple motion" and follow the same steps, except that instead of the precession of the equinox, you would only add or subtract its correction as the situation requires. Thus, the theory of the Sun's appearance, based on the mobility of the Earth, is consistent with both ancient and more recent observations—and all the more so for the future.

...it is presumed that provision has been made for the future. Nevertheless, we are also not unaware that if someone should think the center of the annual revolution is fixed, like the center of the world, and the Sun itself were mobile with two motions similar and equal to those we demonstrated for the center of the eccentricity, everything would appear exactly as before, with the same numbers and the same demonstration. Nothing would change except the position itself, especially concerning the Sun. For the motion of the Earth's center would then be absolute and simple around the center of the world, while the other two motions would be granted to the Sun. Therefore, there remains even now a doubt regarding the center of the world—which of those it might be—as we said from the beginning, ambiguously <note>original Greek: ἀμφιβολικῶς</note> whether the center of the world is in the Sun or around it. But we will say more about this question in the explanation of the five wandering stars <note>The five planets known to the ancient world: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, which we will also decide to the best of our ability. For now, we think it sufficient if we have adopted certain and reliable numbers for the solar appearance.

### On the *Nychthemeron* <note>From the Greek meaning a "night-day," a full 24-hour cycle.</note>, that is, the Difference of the Natural Day. Chapter XXVI.

It remains to say something about the inequality of the natural day concerning the Sun. This is the time comprised by the space of twenty-four equal hours, which we have used until now as a common and certain measure of the celestial motions. Some define such a day as the time between two sunrises, such as the Chaldeans and the ancient Jews; others between two sunsets, like the Athenians; others from midnight to midnight, like the Romans; and others from noon to noon, like the Egyptians. 

It is clear, however, that during this time the proper revolution of the globe of the Earth is completed, along with that which is added in the meantime by the annual progress according to the apparent motion of the Sun. That this addition is unequal is shown first by the apparent unequal course of the Sun itself, and furthermore because that natural day pertains to the poles of the equinoctial circle <note>The celestial equator.</note>, whereas the annual motion happens along the circle of the signs <note>The Zodiac or Ecliptic.</note>. For these reasons, that apparent time cannot be a common and certain measure of motion, since day does not agree with day, nor are they consistent with each other in every part. Therefore, it was necessary to choose a certain mean and equal day among these, by which...

# NICHOLAS COPERNICUS

...it might be possible to measure the equality of motion. Since, therefore, within the circuit of a whole year there are 365 revolutions around the poles of the earth—to which, by daily addition through the apparent progress of the Sun, almost one entire extra revolution is added—it follows that a 365th part of that total is what, by an equal measure, completes a natural day. For this reason, we must define and distinguish the **equal day** from the **varying apparent day**. 

We call an **equal day** <note>Also known as a "mean day."</note> that which contains one full revolution of the equinoctial circle <note>The celestial equator.</note> and, in addition, that small portion which the Sun appears to traverse by its equal <note>mean</note> motion during that time. However, we call an **unequal and apparent day** that which comprises the 360 units <note>original: "tempora" — these are degrees of the equator, where 15 degrees equals one hour.</note> of the equinoctial in one revolution, plus whatever extra portion rises on the horizon or meridian along with the Sun's apparent progress. 

The difference between these days, although very small and not immediately noticed, becomes evident when several days are added together. There are two causes for this: first, the inequality of the Sun’s apparent motion, and second, the unequal ascension <note>The way different parts of the zodiac rise over the horizon at different speeds due to the Earth's tilt.</note> of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi," literally the 'standard-bearer' of the constellations.</note>. 

The first cause, which exists because of the Sun's unequal and apparent motion, has already been made clear. This is because in the semicircle where the highest apsis <term>apsis: the point in an orbit furthest from (apogee) or closest to (perigee) the center of motion.</term> is centered, there was a deficit (according to Ptolemy) of 4 and 3/4 units relative to the parts of the zodiac; in the other semicircle, where the lowest apsis was located, there was an excess of the same amount. Therefore, the total excess of one semicircle over the other was 9 and a half units. 

In the second cause, which relates to rising and setting, the greatest difference occurs between the semicircles of the two solstices <note>original: "conuersionis"</note>. This difference, which exists between the shortest and longest day, varies greatly and is specific to each individual region. However, the difference that occurs relative to high noon or midnight is contained everywhere within four limits. 

For from the 16th degree of **Taurus** to the 14th of **Leo**, roughly 88 degrees of the zodiac cross the meridian in 93 units of time; and from the 14th of **Leo** to the 16th of **Scorpio**, 92 parts of the zodiac pass in 87 units of time. Thus, in the latter case, five units are lacking, while in the former, five are in excess. In this way, the days accumulated in the first segment exceed those in the second by ten units, which make up two-thirds of an hour. The same thing happens by turns in the other semicircle within the remaining diametrically opposite limits. It has pleased mathe=

# BOOK III OF THE REVOLUTIONS

<note>original: "mathematicis"</note> ...mathematicians, the beginning of the natural day is taken not from sunrise or sunset, but from noon or midnight. For the difference measured from the horizon is more complex, as it extends to several hours and is not the same everywhere, but varies in many ways according to the tilt of the sphere <note>The "obliquity of the sphere" refers to how the Earth's axis is tilted relative to its orbit, affecting seasonal day lengths at different latitudes.</note>. However, the difference pertaining to the meridian <note>The imaginary line running from North to South through the zenith; when the sun crosses it, it is local noon.</note> is the same everywhere and is simpler.

The total difference, therefore—which is established from both the causes already mentioned (both the Sun's unequal apparent progress and the unequal crossing of the meridian)—used to amount to 8 and 1/3 units <note>original: "tempora" — in ancient and Renaissance astronomy, these are degrees of the celestial equator, where each "time-unit" or degree equals 4 minutes of clock time.</note> before the time of Ptolemy. This difference began to decrease from the middle of Aquarius and increase from the start of Scorpio.

Today, this difference has shrunk to 7 units and 48 minutes <note>original: "scrupula" — literally "scruples," referring here to minutes of a degree.</note>, decreasing from roughly the 20th degree of Aquarius to the 10th degree of Scorpio, and increasing from the 10th of Scorpio to the 20th of Aquarius. For these values also change over time due to the instability of the perigee <term>perigee|The point in an orbit where a celestial body is closest to the center of its motion; in the Copernican system, this relates to the Earth's closest approach to the Sun.</term> and the <term>eccentricity|The measurement of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</term> <note>original: "eccentrotetis"</note>.

Finally, if the maximum difference in the precession of the equinoxes <note>The slow "wobble" of the Earth's axis that changes the positions of the stars over centuries.</note> is also compared to these, the total difference of natural days could extend beyond ten units over a certain number of years.

In this regard, a **third cause of the inequality of days** has remained hidden until now: because the revolution of the equinoctial circle <note>The celestial equator.</note> was found to be equal relative to the mean <note>average</note> equinox, but not to the apparent <note>observed</note> equinoxes, which, as has been made clear enough, are not perfectly regular. Therefore, ten units doubled <note>Representing the full range of the swing.</note> make one hour and one-third, by which the longest days can sometimes exceed the shortest.

Regarding the Sun’s yearly progress and the slower movement of the other stars, these discrepancies might perhaps be ignored without obvious error. But because of the speed of the Moon—which can cause an error of half a degree and a third <note>About 50 minutes of arc in the Moon's position.</note>—they must not be ignored under any circumstances.

The method for coordinating equal time with varying apparent time, so that all the differences agree, is as follows. For any given time, one must find the Sun’s mean position from the equinox at both the beginning and the end of that period (using its mean equal motion, which we have called "composite"), as well as its true apparent position from the true equinox. Then, one must consider how many time-units have passed through the right ascensions...

<meta>This page concludes the technical explanation of how to adjust for the "Equation of Time"—the discrepancy between solar time and uniform clock time. It provides specific historical examples to demonstrate how to synchronize the Sun's position across different eras, transitioning from the study of the Sun to the study of the Moon.</meta>

->NICOLAUS COPERNICUS<-

...around noon or midnight, or the intervals between those points, from the first true position to the second true position. For if these intervals are equal to the degrees that lie between the two mean positions <note>original: "loco medio" — Copernicus is comparing "mean" time (a theoretical perfectly uniform sun) with "true" time (the actual sun seen in the sky).</note>, then the apparent time taken will be equal to the mean time. But if the time-units <note>original: "partes temporales" — in this context, degrees of the celestial equator, where 1 degree equals 4 minutes of time.</note> exceed the mean, the excess itself should be added to the given time; however, if they fall short, the deficit should be subtracted from the apparent time. 

By doing this, using the values that have been added or subtracted, we will have the time converted into uniformity <note>original: "æqualitatem" — also known as Mean Time.</note>. We do this by taking four minutes <note>original: "scrupula horæ" — literally 'scruples of an hour.'</note> of an hour for each time-unit, or ten seconds <note>original: "scrupula secunda"</note> for each sixtieth part of a day <note>A sixtieth of a day is 24 minutes; ten seconds of that 24-minute unit equals 4 minutes.</note>. Conversely, if mean time is given and you wish to know how much apparent time corresponds to it, the opposite must be done. 

We found that at the first Olympiad <note>The first recorded Olympic Games in 776 BCE, a common epoch used by ancient astronomers.</note>, the Sun's mean position—measured from the mean Spring Equinox at noon on the first day of Hecatombaeon <note>original: "Hecatombeonos" — the first month of the ancient Athenian calendar, roughly mid-summer.</note>, the first month according to the Athenians—was 90 degrees and 59 minutes. Measured from the apparent equinox, it was at 0 degrees and 36 minutes of Cancer <term>Cancer|The zodiac sign of the Crab, marking the summer solstice in this coordinate system</term>. 

Furthermore, at the years of Christ <note>the beginning of the Common Era</note>, the mean motion of the Sun was 8 degrees and 2 minutes of Capricorn. Its true motion was 8 degrees and 48 minutes of the same sign. Therefore, in the right sphere <note>original: "recta sphæra" — a perspective where the celestial equator is perpendicular to the horizon, used here for standardizing astronomical measurements</note>, there rise from 0 degrees 36 minutes of Cancer to 8 degrees 48 minutes of Capricorn a total of 188 time-units and 53 minutes. These exceed the distance between the mean positions by 1 time-unit and 53 minutes. This difference amounts to 7 and a half minutes of an hour. 

The same method applies to all other cases, allowing for the most exact examination of the course of the Moon, which will be discussed in the following book.

# THE REVOLUTIONS BY NICOLAUS COPERNICUS
## BOOK FOUR.

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'C' featuring a central figure surrounded by intricate foliate patterns.</image-desc>Since in the previous book we explained, to the best of our modest ability <note>original: "mediocritas" — a common humble rhetorical device used by Renaissance authors to acknowledge the limits of their talent.</note>, those things that appeared to occur because of the motion of the earth around the Sun, and since it is our purpose by that same means to discern the motions of all the wandering stars <note>original: "stellarum errantium" — the planets, from the Greek term meaning 'wanderers.'</note>, now the course of the Moon interrupts our progress. This is necessary because it is chiefly through her—as she participates in both day and night—that the positions of any stars are captured and examined. Furthermore, she alone of all the heavenly bodies refers her revolutions (however diverse they may be) collectively to the center of the earth, and she is most closely related to the earth. For that reason, as far as her own nature is concerned, she indicates nothing regarding the mobility of the earth—except perhaps for the daily rotation. Indeed, it was for this reason that the ancients believed the earth was the center of the universe and the common center of all celestial revolutions. In our explanation of the lunar course, we do not differ from the opinions of the ancients in the fact that it takes place around the earth. However, we shall bring forward certain things other than those we received from our predecessors, which are more harmonious, and by which we shall establish the lunar motion as accurately as is possible.

### Hypotheses of the Lunar Circles according to the Opinion of the Ancients. Chapter I.

<image-desc>A smaller decorative drop cap 'L' depicting a figure in a landscape or scene.</image-desc>The lunar course, therefore, has this characteristic: it does not follow the middle circle of the signs <note>The Ecliptic — the apparent path of the Sun through the constellations of the Zodiac.</note>, but rather its own inclined path, which bisects that circle and is in turn bisected by it; from this path, the Moon migrates into either latitude <term>latitude: the angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the ecliptic.</term>. These movements behave much like the "conversions" <note>original: "conuersiones" — referring to the solstices or the points where the Sun's path turns back toward the equator.</note> in the annual motion of the Sun. This is not surprising, since what the year is to the Sun, the month is to the Moon. The middle points of these intersections are called "ecliptic" points, or by others, "nodes" <note>The points where the Moon's orbit crosses the Sun's path. Eclipses can only occur when the Moon is near these nodes.</note>. And the conjunctions <note>New Moons.</note> and oppositions <note>Full Moons.</note> of the Sun and Moon occurring in these points are called ecliptic...

...are called. For there are no other points common to both circles <note>The intersection of the Moon's tilted orbit and the ecliptic (the Sun's path).</note> besides these, in which eclipses of the Sun and Moon can occur. Indeed, in other locations, the divergence of the Moon causes the lights to hardly interfere with one another; as they pass by, they do not block each other. This oblique orbit of the Moon also moves with its four cardinal points around the center of the earth uniformly, traveling almost three minutes of a degree daily, and completing its revolution in the nineteenth year <note>This refers to the Metonic cycle, a period of approximately 19 years after which the phases of the Moon recur on the same days of the year.</note>. Under this orbit and its plane, the Moon is always seen moving in the order of the signs <note>original: "in consequentia" — moving eastward, following the sequence of the Zodiac signs.</note>, but sometimes at its minimum speed and sometimes at its maximum. For it is slower the higher [farther] it is, and faster the closer it is to the earth. This could be discerned more easily in the Moon than in any other star because of her proximity. They understood, therefore, that this occurred through an <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle (the deferent).</note>, since the Moon, as it ran around that circle, would subtract from uniform motion on the upper circumference but advance it on the lower one.

Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that what occurs through an <term>epicycle</term> can also occur through an <term>eccentric</term> <note>A circular orbit whose center is shifted away from the center of the Earth.</note>. But they chose the <term>epicycle</term> because the Moon seemed to admit a double variation. For when it was at the highest or lowest apse of the <term>epicycle</term>, no difference from uniform motion appeared. But around the contact points of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>The points where the epicycle meets the main orbital path, often called quadratures.</note>, the difference was not of one kind; rather, it was far greater when the Moon was halved [at the first or last quarter], increasing or decreasing, than if it were full or new <note>original: "sitiens" — literally "thirsty," a poetic term used here to describe the thin or new moon "thirsting" for light.</note>, and this happens in a fixed and regular succession. 

For this reason, they judged that the orbit in which the <term>epicycle</term> moves is not concentric with the earth, but is an <term>eccentric-epicycle</term> in which the Moon is carried under the rule that in all mean <term>conjunctions</term> <note>alignments where the Moon and Sun are on the same side of the Earth.</note> and oppositions of the Sun and Moon, the <term>epicycle</term> is at the <term>apogee</term> [farthest point] of the <term>eccentric</term>, but in the middle quadrants of the circle, it is at the <term>perigee</term> [closest point] of the same. Therefore, they imagined two equal motions contrary to each other around the <term>center</term> of the earth: namely, the <term>epicycle</term> moving in the order of the signs [eastward], and the <term>center</term> of the <term>eccentric</term> and its apsides moving in the preceding order [westward], with the line of the mean position of the Sun always mediating between the two. And in this way, the <term>epicycle</term> traverses the <term>eccentric</term> twice a month. 

To make these things visible to the eyes: Let the oblique circle of the Moon, concentric with the earth, be ABCD, divided into four parts by the diameters AEC and BED, with the <term>center</term> of the earth being E. <summary>Copernicus describes the complex geometry of lunar motion, explaining why astronomers use a combination of epicycles and eccentric circles to account for the Moon's changing speed and apparent size. He details how the Moon's speed varies based on its distance from Earth and its phase, requiring a model where the epicycle moves along an eccentric path twice a month.</summary>

# BOOK IV OF THE REVOLUTIONS

[A geometric diagram illustrating the lunar orbit according to a model using epicycles and eccentrics. Within this circle, an eccentric circle is drawn, with its center at point F. Point E is at the center of the large outer circle. ...of the epicycle <term>MN</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle.</note> at the same time. Let the apogee <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> of the eccentric now be moved westward <note>original: "in praecedentia" — against the order of the signs of the Zodiac.</note> by as much as the epicycle moves eastward <note>original: "in consequentia" — following the order of the signs.</note>. Both move uniformly around <term>E</term> <note>The Earth's center in this model.</note> with equal monthly revolutions relative to the mean conjunctions or oppositions of the Sun <note>The New and Full Moons.</note>. Let the line <term>A E C</term> always be the mean position of the Sun, positioned exactly between those two motions, and let the Moon move again westward from the apogee of the epicycle.

For with the model established in this way, they believe the appearances of the Moon agree with the theory. For since the epicycle, in the space of half a year, completes a semicircle relative to the Sun, but a full revolution relative to the apogee of the eccentric, it follows that in the middle of this time—which occurs when the Moon is halved <note>original: "Lunam dividuam" — the first or last quarter phases.</note>—they are positioned opposite each other along the diameter <term>B D</term>. At this point, the epicycle reaches the perigee <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Earth.</note> of the eccentric, as shown at point <term>G</term>. Having been brought closer to the Earth here, it produces greater differences in the Moon's inequality <note>The "inequality" refers to the variation in the Moon's observed speed and size.</note>. For equal sizes, when viewed at unequal distances, appear larger to the eye when they are closer.

Therefore, the differences were at their minimum when the epicycle was at point <term>A</term>, but at their maximum when it was at <term>G</term>. This is because the diameter of the epicycle <term>M N</term> will have its smallest ratio compared to the line <term>A E</term>, but it will have a larger ratio to <term>G E</term> than to any other lines found in other positions. This is because <term>G E</term> itself is the shortest of all possible lines, and <term>A E</term> (or its equal <term>D E</term>) is the longest of those lines that can be extended from the center of the Earth to the eccentric circle.

### On the Flaw in these Assumptions. Chapter II.

The ancients certainly adopted such a arrangement of circles as being consistent with the lunar appearances. But if we weigh the matter itself more diligently, we shall find this hypothesis neither sufficiently suitable nor adequate, a fact we can prove through both reason and the senses. For while they admit that the motion of the center of the epicycle is uniform around the center of the Earth, they must also admit that it is nonuniform in its own orbit <note>The eccentric path it actually describes.</note>. For if, for example, the angle <term>A E B</term> is taken as 45 degrees (that is, half of a right angle), and angle <term>A E D</term> is made equal to it so that the total angle <term>B E D</term> is a right angle, and if the center of the epicycle is taken at point <term>G</term>...

...and let <term>GF</term> be connected. It is clear that angle <term>GFD</term> is greater than <term>GEF</term>, as an exterior angle is greater than the interior and opposite one. For this reason, both the arcs <term>DAB</term> and <term>DG</term>, described in the same period of time, are dissimilar; so that when <term>DAB</term> is a quadrant <note>A 90-degree arc of a circle.</note>, <term>DG</term>, which the center of the epicycle has described meanwhile, is greater than a quadrant of the circle. However, it was evident that in the case of the "divided Moon" <note>The Moon at its first or third quarter, when it appears exactly half-full.</note>, both <term>DAB</term> and <term>DG</term> were semicircles; therefore, the motion of the epicycle on its eccentric path which it describes is unequal.

If this were the case, what shall we say in response to the axiom that "the motion of the celestial bodies is uniform, and only appears unequal to the eye," if the motion of the epicycle, while appearing uniform, were in reality unequal? It would happen that we would adopt a principle entirely contrary to the one established and assumed. 

But if you should say that it moves uniformly around the center of the Earth, and that this is sufficient to maintain the principle of uniformity, then what sort of uniformity will that be in a "foreign" circle <note>Copernicus is arguing that motion should be measured relative to the center of the circle on which the body actually moves, not a distant point.</note> in which its motion does not exist, rather than in its own eccentric? 

Indeed, we are also astonished by the fact that they wish the uniformity of the Moon within its epicycle to be understood not by comparison with the center of the Earth through the line—namely <term>EGM</term>—to which the uniformity ought rightly to be referred (agreeing as it does with the center of the epicycle itself), but rather toward some different point. They place the Earth midway between this point and the center of the eccentric, and use the line <term>IGH</term> as the indicator of the Moon's uniformity in the epicycle. This alone sufficiently demonstrates that this motion is in reality unequal. For the appearances, which partly follow this hypothesis, compel us to admit this. 

Thus, with the Moon traversing its small epicycle unequally, if we now wished to use these inequalities to prove the inequality of the Moon's appearance, one can see what sort of argument that would be. For what else are we doing but providing a "handle" <note>original: "ansam" — an opportunity or excuse for criticism.</note> to those who disparage this art of astronomy? 

Furthermore, experience and the senses themselves teach us that the Moon's parallaxes <note>The apparent shift in the position of the Moon when viewed from different points on Earth; this shift reveals the Moon's distance.</note> do not agree with those which the logic of these circles predicts. These parallaxes—which they call "changes" <note>original: "commutationes" — the technical term for the shift in perspective.</note>—occur because of the Earth's significant size in relation to its proximity to the Moon. For since the straight lines extended from the surface of the Earth and from its center to the Moon no longer appear parallel, but...

<meta>catchword: Sit enim (Let it be indeed)</meta>

with a manifest inclination, they intersect in the lunar body, they must necessarily produce a difference in the Moon's appearance. This causes it to be seen in a different place by those looking at it obliquely from the surface of the Earth than by those who view the Moon from the center [of the Earth] or from their own <term>zenith</term> <note>The point directly above an observer.</note>. Such shifts <note>original: *commutationes*, referring to parallax</note>, therefore, vary according to the ratio of the Moon's distance from the Earth. For by the consensus of all mathematicians, the maximum distance is 64 and one-sixth parts (where one part is the radius from the center of the Earth to its surface); but the minimum distance, according to the symmetry of their model, ought to have been 33 parts and as many minutes. This would mean the Moon would approach us at almost half the previous distance. Consequently, the <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent shift in an object's position when viewed from two different locations.</note> at the minimum and maximum distances ought to differ by nearly double each other.

We, however, see that those parallaxes which occur in the "divided Moon" <note>The Moon at its first or last quarter, appearing half-full.</note> during its waxing and waning phases—even at the <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Earth.</note> of the epicycle—differ very little or not at all from those occurring during solar and lunar eclipses, as we will demonstrate abundantly in the proper place. But the lunar body itself exposes the error most clearly; by a similar reasoning, it should happen that the Moon's diameter would appear twice as large [at its closest] as it does [at its farthest]. Since circles are in a duplicate ratio to their diameters <note>Meaning the area of a circle increases by the square of the diameter.</note>, the Moon would generally appear four times larger in the <term>quadratures</term> <note>When the Moon is 90 degrees from the Sun.</note> when it is closest to Earth than when it is opposite the Sun [at Full Moon], if it were to shine fully. But because it shines "divided" at that point, it would nonetheless shine with twice the light as a Full Moon at its furthest point. 

The opposite of this is obvious to the senses. If someone, not content with simple sight, wishes to test this using <term>Hipparchus's dioptra</term> <note>An ancient sighting instrument used for measuring the angular diameter of celestial bodies.</note> or any other instruments by which the Moon's diameter is measured, they will find that it does not vary, except by as much as the epicycle without that <term>eccentric</term> <note>An off-center circle used in ancient astronomy to explain varying speeds and distances.</note> would require. For that reason, Menelaus and Timochares, in their investigation of the fixed stars using the position of the Moon, did not hesitate to always use the same lunar diameter of half a degree, which is the amount the Moon is generally seen to occupy.

### Another Theory on the Motion of the Moon, Chapter III.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'I' depicting two figures, one seated and one standing, in a detailed landscape background with trees.</image-desc>It appears clearly, then, that there is no eccentric through which the epicycle might appear larger or smaller, but rather another arrangement of circles.

<summary>Copernicus critiques the Ptolemaic lunar model, arguing that its predicted fluctuations in the Moon's distance are not supported by observations of parallax or the Moon's apparent size. He concludes that a new model, involving a different arrangement of circles rather than a simple eccentric, is necessary.</summary>

--- Page 216 ---
<meta>This page continues Copernicus's argument against the Ptolemaic lunar model, specifically focusing on the discrepancy in the Moon's distance and apparent size. On the previous page, he noted that the traditional model predicts the Moon should appear nearly twice as large at its closest point compared to its farthest, which contradicts observation. He now introduces his own "double epicycle" model to resolve this issue.</meta>

-># NICOLAUS COPERNICUS<-

Let there be an epicycle AB, which we shall call the first and larger one; let its center be C, and from the center of the Earth, which is D, let the straight line DC be extended to the highest **apsis** <note>The highest point in an orbit; original: *summam absidem*.</note> of the epicycle. At center A, let another small epicycle EF also be described, and let all these be in the same plane as the Moon’s oblique orbit. 

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the theory of lunar epicycles is situated on the left, with text wrapping around it. The diagram shows a large circle with center point C and a vertical axis line passing through it. At the bottom of the axis is point D (center of the Earth), and point B marks the bottom of the large circle. At the top of the large circle is point A, which serves as the center for a second, much smaller epicycle. Points E, F, and G are labeled along the vertical axis within and above this smaller circle. This figure visualizes the nested circular motions proposed by Copernicus to explain the moon's observed position and parallax.</image-desc>

Let C move **forward** <note>original: *in consequentia*; following the order of the signs of the zodiac.</note>, but let A move **backward** <note>original: *in praecedentia*; against the order of the signs.</note>. Furthermore, let the Moon move from the upper part F of the small epicycle EF in a forward direction, following this order: that whenever the line DC is aligned with the mean position of the Sun, the Moon is always nearest to the center C—that is, at point E—but at the **quadratures** <note>The quarter phases of the moon (first and last quarter).</note> it is farthest away at point F. 

With these arrangements made, I maintain that the Moon's appearances agree with the model. For it follows that the Moon runs around the small epicycle EF twice a month, during which time C returns once to the Sun. Thus, at the new and full moon, it will appear to trace the smallest circle—specifically the one whose radius is CE. In the quadratures, however, it will trace the largest circle according to the distance from the center CF. In this way, it will produce smaller differences of uniform and apparent motion there [at new/full moon] and larger ones here [at the quarters], under similar but unequal arcs around center C. 

And since the center of the epicycle is always on a circle concentric to the Earth, it will not exhibit such diverse **parallaxes** <note>The shift in an object's position when viewed from different locations.</note>, but rather only those conforming to the epicycle itself. The reason will also be clear why the lunar body appears somewhat similar to itself [in size], and all other things observed concerning the Moon's course will happen in this way.

We shall henceforth demonstrate these things through this <term>hypothesis</term> <note>A proposed explanation or model used as a basis for reasoning.</note> of ours, although the same results can be achieved again through **eccentrics** <note>Orbits whose centers are shifted away from the center of the Earth.</note>, as we did regarding the Sun, provided the proper proportion is maintained. We shall begin, however, with the uniform motions, as we did above, without which the non-uniform motion cannot be discerned. 

Truly, a significant difficulty exists here because of the parallaxes we mentioned. For this reason, the Moon's position is not easily observable through **Astrolabes** <note>Handheld instruments used by astronomers to measure the altitude and position of celestial bodies.</note> or any other instruments. But the kindness of nature has provided for human desire even in this respect, so that its position may be detected more certainly through its **eclipses** <note>original: *defectus*; the darkening of the moon or sun.</note> than by the use of instruments, and without the suspicion of error.

He argues that observing the Moon during eclipses is more accurate than using instruments because of the interference of parallax.</summary>

-># ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK IV.<-

For since the other parts of the universe are pure and full of daylight, it is certain that night is nothing other than the shadow of the Earth, which stretches into a conical shape and ends in a point. Falling into this shadow, the Moon is dimmed, and being situated in the midst of the darkness, it is understood to have reached a position directly opposite the Sun. Nor indeed do solar eclipses—which are caused by the Moon moving in front of the Sun—provide a certain argument for the Moon’s position. For it then happens that we see a conjunction of the Sun and Moon which, when compared to the center of the Earth, has either already passed or has not yet occurred, because of the aforementioned cause of **parallax** <term>parallax: the difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight; original: *commutationis*</term>. For this reason, we do not see the same solar eclipse as equal in magnitude and duration in all lands, nor is it similar in its parts. In lunar eclipses, however, no such impediment occurs, but they are similar everywhere. This is because the Earth transmits the axis of that dimming shadow from the Sun through its own center; therefore, lunar eclipses are most perfectly suited for determining the course of the Moon by the most certain reasoning.

## On the revolutions of the Moon and its specific motions. Chapter IV.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' depicting two human figures in a pastoral or garden setting with foliage.</image-desc>
Among the most ancient observers who took care to hand down this matter to posterity in numbers, Meton the Athenian was found, who flourished in the 37th Olympiad. He declared that 235 months are completed in 19 solar years, for which reason that great year was called the **nineteen-year cycle** <note>original: *ἐννεαδεκαετηρίς*</note>, or the Metonic cycle. This number was so pleasing that it was posted in the forum at Athens and other famous cities, and it is even accepted into common use up to the present day, because by it they believe the beginnings and ends of the months are established in a certain order. He also made the solar year of 365 days and a quarter-day commensurable with the months. From this came the Callippic period of 76 years, in which one day is intercalated <note>inserted into the calendar</note> nineteen times, and they called this the Callippic year. But the skill of Hipparchus found that a whole day accumulates over 304 years, and it is only verified when the solar year is a 300th part of a day shorter than 365 and a quarter days. Thus, by some, that great year is named after Hipparchus...

-># NICOLAUS COPERNICUS<-

was born, in which seven hundred and sixty months were completed. These things were said in a simpler and more "rough-hewn" way, as they say <note>original: *crassiori minerva* — a Latin idiom meaning plain or unrefined reasoning, as opposed to mathematical precision</note>. Since the restorations of the **anomaly** <term>anomaly: the irregularity in the Moon’s speed as it moves around its orbit; original: *anomaliæ*</term> and latitude are also being sought, Hipparchus investigated these matters further. Specifically, he compared the records of lunar eclipses which he had observed with great diligence against those he received from the **Chaldeans** <note>The Babylonians, renowned in the ancient world for their long history of astronomical records</note>. He defined the period in which the revolutions of the months and the anomalies return to the same point together as three hundred and forty-five **Egyptian years** <term>Egyptian years: a calendar used by ancient astronomers consisting of exactly 365 days, without leap years</term>, eighty-two days, and one hour. Within that time, four thousand two hundred and sixty-seven months and four thousand five hundred and seventy-three cycles of anomaly are completed. Therefore, when the proposed number of days—which is one hundred and twenty-six thousand and seven days and one hour—is divided by the number of months, one month is found to be equal to twenty-nine days, thirty-one **minutes**, fifty **seconds**, eight **thirds**, nine **fourths**, and twenty **fifths** <term>minutes, seconds, etc.: Copernicus uses sexagesimal (base-60) fractions for extreme precision; original: *scrupula prima, secunda, tertia, quarta, quinta*</term>. By this reasoning, the motion for any given time became clear. For by dividing the three hundred and sixty degrees of one monthly revolution by the time of a month, the daily course of the Moon away from the Sun was found to be twelve degrees, eleven minutes, twenty-six seconds, forty-one thirds, twenty fourths, and eighteen fifths. These, multiplied three hundred and sixty-five times, collect—beyond twelve full revolutions—an annual motion of one hundred and twenty-nine degrees, thirty-seven minutes, thirty-one seconds, twenty-eight thirds, and twenty-nine fourths.

Furthermore, since the four thousand two hundred and sixty-seven months and four thousand five hundred and seventy-three cycles of anomaly are composite numbers—sharing a common measure of seventeen—they can be reduced to their smallest terms as two hundred and fifty-one to two hundred and sixty-nine. In this ratio, according to the fifteenth theorem of the fifth book of **Euclid** <note>Euclid's *Elements*, the foundation of geometry used by Copernicus to calculate proportions</note>, we will have the relationship of the lunar course to the motion of the anomaly. Thus, when we have multiplied the motion of the Moon by two hundred and sixty-nine and divided the result by two hundred and fifty-one, the annual motion of the anomaly results: after thirteen full revolutions, it is eighty-eight degrees, forty-four minutes, eight seconds, forty thirds, and twenty fourths. Consequently, the daily motion is thirteen degrees, three minutes, fifty-four seconds, fifty-six thirds, and twenty-nine fourths.

The revolution of the latitude, however, follows a different principle. For it does not coincide with the pre-defined time in which the anomaly is restored; rather, we understand the Moon’s latitude to have returned only when a later eclipse of the Moon is similar and equal in every way to an earlier one. This occurs when the obscurations on the same side are equal in both magnitude and duration. This happens when the Moon's distances from the highest or lowest **apsis** <term>apsis: the point in an orbit where the celestial body is furthest (apogee) or closest (perigee) to the Earth; original: *abside*</term> are equal; for then it is understood that the Moon has passed through equal shadows in an equal amount of time.

-># BOOK IV OF THE REVOLUTIONS<-

Such a return, according to **Hipparchus** <note>A Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BCE) considered the father of trigonometry and one of the greatest observers of antiquity</note>, occurs in 5,458 months, to which correspond 5,923 revolutions of **latitude** <term>latitude: in lunar theory, this refers to the Moon's north-south position relative to the ecliptic, the Sun's apparent path; original: *latitudinis*</term>. By this same reasoning, the specific motions of latitude in years and days were established, just like the others. For when we have multiplied the Moon's motion from the Sun by 5,923 months and divided the total by 5,458, we will have the motion of the Moon’s latitude. In years, indeed, after 13 revolutions, the motion is 168 degrees, 42 minutes, 46 seconds, 20 thirds, and 3 fourths <note>original: *scrup. prima, secunda, tertia, quart.* — these are sexagesimal fractions used for high-precision math, where each unit is 1/60th of the previous one</note>. In days, however, it is 13 degrees, 13 minutes, 45 seconds, 39 thirds, and 40 fourths. In this way, Hipparchus calculated the uniform motions of the Moon, and no one before him approached the truth more closely; nevertheless, succeeding centuries have revealed that these figures were not yet perfectly absolute in all their numbers.

For **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE), whose *Almagest* was the standard astronomical text for over a millennium before Copernicus</note> found the same mean motion from the Sun as Hipparchus did, but he found that the annual motion of the **anomaly** <term>anomaly: the irregularity or "wobble" in the Moon’s speed as it moves around its orbit</term> fell short of Hipparchus's calculation by 1 second, 11 thirds, and 39 fourths. The annual motion of latitude, however, he found to exceed Hipparchus's by 52 thirds and 41 fourths.

We, however, with much more time having now passed, have found that Hipparchus’s annual mean motion also falls short by 1 second, 7 thirds, and 56 fourths. For the anomaly, only 26 thirds and 55 fourths are missing. The motion of latitude, however, exceeds Hipparchus’s by 1 second, 2 thirds, and 42 fourths. Therefore, the uniform motion of the Moon, by which it differs from the **Earth’s motion** <note>original: *motu terrestri* — Copernicus is calculating the Moon's movement relative to the Earth's own orbital path around the Sun</note>, will be annually: 129 degrees, 37 minutes, 22 seconds, 36 thirds, and 25 fourths. For the anomaly: 88 degrees, 43 minutes, 9 seconds, 7 thirds, and 15 fourths. For the latitude: 148 degrees, 42 minutes, 45 seconds, 17 thirds, and 21 fourths.

--- Page 226 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the mathematical tables of the Moon’s latitudinal motion to a narrative demonstration of the Moon's "first inequality." This refers to the primary variation in the Moon's speed and position that occurs during its monthly cycle. Copernicus begins this chapter by citing historical observations from Ptolemy to validate his own models.</meta>

OF NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

### Demonstration of the first inequality of the Moon, which occurs at the new and full moon. Chapter 5.

We have explained the uniform motions of the Moon as far as they have been able to become known to us until now. Now we must approach the account of the **inequality** <note>In astronomy, an "inequality" refers to a deviation from perfectly uniform circular motion.</note>, which we will demonstrate by means of an **epicycle** <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle (the deferent), used to explain variations in speed and distance</term>, and first that inequality which occurs in the conjunctions and oppositions of the Sun <note>This refers to the New Moon (conjunction) and Full Moon (opposition).</note>. Regarding this, the ancient mathematicians used wonderful ingenuity through "triads" of lunar eclipses. We shall also follow the path prepared for us by them, and we will take three eclipses carefully observed by Ptolemy, with which we will compare another three noted with no less diligence, so that the uniform motions already explained may be examined to see if they are correct. 

In explaining these, we will use the mean motions of the Sun and Moon from the position of the Vernal Equinox as though they were uniform, in imitation of the ancients. This is because the variation which occurs due to the unequal **precession of the equinoxes** <note>The slow "wobble" of Earth's axis that changes the position of the stars over centuries.</note> is not perceived in such a short time, even a span of ten years. 

Therefore, Ptolemy takes the first eclipse as occurring in the 17th year of the Emperor Hadrian, after the 20th day of the month of Pauni according to the Egyptians. In the years of Christ, this was the 133rd year, on the 6th day of the month of May, or the day before the Nones <note>original: "pridie Nonas." In the Roman calendar, the Nones of May fell on the 7th; "pridie" indicates the day before.</note>. It was a total eclipse, the middle of which was three-quarters <note>original: "dodrantem," a Roman fraction representing 3/4.</note> of an equal hour before midnight at Alexandria; but at Frombork or Krakow it would have been one hour and three-quarters before midnight. He says the second eclipse was in the 19th year of Hadrian, after two days of the month of Choiak, the fourth month of the Egyptians. It was in the year of Christ 134, on the 13th day before the Kalends of November <note>October 20th.</note>, and it was eclipsed from the North by ten-twelfths <note>original: "dextantem," a Roman fraction for 10/12 or 5/6.</note> of its diameter. # ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK IV.

In the year 135 <note>original: "cxxxv"</note>, when the 6th of March had passed, the Moon was again eclipsed from the North by half of its diameter. The middle of this eclipse was at Alexandria four equinoctial hours <note>An equinoctial hour is a fixed unit of time equal to 1/24th of a day, unlike seasonal hours which changed based on the time of year.</note> after midnight, but at Krakow it was three hours after midnight; this was on the morning of the Nones of March. At that time, the Sun was in 14 degrees and 12 minutes of Pisces, with a mean motion of 11 degrees and 44 minutes of Pisces. It is clear then that in the middle space of time between the first and second eclipse, the Moon traveled as far as the Sun did in its apparent motion—setting aside full circles—which was 161 degrees and 55 minutes. From the second to the third eclipse, the distance was 137 degrees and 55 minutes. In the first interval, there was one year, 166 days, and 23 and three-quarters hours according to appearance, but 23 and five-eighths hours when precisely examined. In the second distance, there was one year, 137 days, and simply 5 hours, or exactly 5 and a half hours. The equal motion of the Sun and Moon together in the first interval, rejecting full circles, was 169 degrees and 37 minutes, and the motion of the **anomaly** <note>The "anomaly" refers to the Moon's position on its epicycle, which determines its variation from average speed.</note> was 110 degrees and 21 minutes. In the second interval, the equal motion of the Sun and Moon was likewise 137 degrees and 33 minutes. It is therefore evident that in the first distance, 110 degrees and 21 minutes of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>epicycle: a small circle on which a planet or the Moon moves, while the center of that small circle moves along a larger circle around the Earth.</note> subtract 7 degrees and 42 minutes from the Moon's mean motion. In the second, 81 degrees and 36 minutes add 1 degree and 21 minutes.

With these values thus proposed, let the lunar epicycle <term>ABC</term> be described, in which the first eclipse is at <term>A</term>, the second at <term>B</term>, and the remaining one at <term>C</term>, following the order in which the Moon is understood to move forward. Let the circumference <term>AB</term> be 110 degrees and 21 minutes, which subtracts—as we said—7 degrees and 42 minutes. Let <term>BC</term> be 81 degrees and 36 minutes, which adds 1 degree and 21 minutes. The remainder of the circle, <term>CA</term>, will be 168 degrees and 3 minutes, adding the remaining 6 degrees and 21 minutes. Since the highest point <note>original: "absis," referring to the apogee or the point furthest from Earth.</note> of the epicycle is not within the arcs <term>BC</term> or <term>CA</term> (since they are additive and less than a semicircle), it must necessarily be found within <term>AB</term>. Let us then take <term>D</term> as the center of the Earth, around which the epicycle is carried uniformly. From here, let lines be drawn to the points of the eclipses: <term>DA</term>, <term>DB</term>, and <term>DC</term>, and let the chords <term>BC</term>, <term>BE</term>, and <term>CE</term> be connected. Since the arc <term>AB</term> subtends 7 degrees and 42 minutes of the <note>original: "signiferi," the zodiac circle or ecliptic.</note> zodiac, the angle <term>ADB</term> will be 7 degrees and 42 minutes where 180 degrees make two right angles; but where 360 degrees make two right angles, the angle itself will be 15 degrees and 24 minutes.

Likewise, in the second eclipse, the mean motion of the Moon was at 26 degrees 50 minutes of Pisces. In the third eclipse, it was at 14 degrees of Pisces. ...38 minutes. In the second eclipse of those observed in our own time, the motion of the Moon from the Sun was 182 degrees 50 minutes, and the <term>anomaly</term><note>The anomaly refers to the irregularity in the Moon's movement caused by its travel along an epicycle or elliptical path.</note> was 74 degrees 27 minutes.
