The time which passed from the nineteenth year of Hadrian <note>Reigned 117–138 AD; Copernicus uses his reign as a chronological marker.</note>, in the Egyptian month of Chiach, on the second day and two hours before midnight (which the third day of the month followed), until the year of Christ 1522, on the fifth day of September, at one and one-third hours of apparent time—which, when <term>equated</term><note>The process of "equating" time involves converting "apparent time" (sundial time) into "mean time" (uniform time) to account for the Earth's irregular motion.</note>, results in 1,388 Egyptian years, 302 days, 3 hours, and 34 minutes. In this time, after the completion of 17,165 equal revolutions of the months according to Hipparchus and Ptolemy, there would have been 358 degrees 38 minutes. Regarding the anomaly, according to Hipparchus, there would be 9 degrees 49 minutes, but according to Ptolemy, 9 degrees 11 minutes. Therefore, their figures fall short of these motions of the Moon by 26 minutes, and for the anomaly by 38 minutes, which are added to our numbers and agree with the values we have set forth.

In this period, the Lunar motion according to our calculation is 332 degrees 49 minutes, and the anomaly is 217 degrees 32 minutes. Which...

When these [values] have been subtracted from those found in the eclipse, each from its own kind, there remains the mean position of the Moon from the Sun at 210 degrees 58 minutes, and the <term>anomaly</term><note>The anomaly measures the Moon's position on its epicycle, determining how far it has strayed from its average speed.</note> at 207 degrees 7 minutes, at the beginning of the years of Christ, at midnight before the <term>Kalends</term><note>The first day of the month in the Roman calendar.</note> of January. ...and it rises by two-thirds, just as the records of the ancients also state. For they observed the time in which the half-moon reached the middle distance of the <term>epicycle</term><note>A smaller circle that rolls around the circumference of a larger circle (the deferent) to explain the complex loops and speed changes in planetary motion.</note>, and this occurred near the contact point of a line emerging from the center of the earth, which could easily be perceived through the calculation set forth above. And because the Moon itself was then located near the ninetieth degree of the <term>zodiac</term><note>original: "signiferi," the "sign-bearer."</note> as measured from its rising or setting, they avoided the error which <term>parallax</term><note>The apparent displacement of an object when viewed from different positions; here, the difference between the Moon's position as seen from the Earth's surface versus its center.</note> could introduce into the motion of longitude. At that time, the circle passing through the <term>zenith</term><note>The point in the sky directly overhead.</note> of the horizon divides the zodiac at right angles, and it does not allow for any change in longitude, but the entire effect falls instead into latitude. Consequently, by the skill of the <term>astrolabe</term><note>An ancient astronomical instrument used for measuring the altitudes of celestial bodies and calculating positions.</note> instrument, they recorded the position of the Moon in relation to the Sun. Upon making the comparison, the Moon was found to differ from its average position by seven degrees and two-thirds (as we said), rather than the five degrees expected.

Now, let the epicycle *AB* be described, its center being *C*. From the center of the earth, which is *D*, let the straight line *DBCA* be extended; let the <term>apogee</term><note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> of the epicycle be *A*, and the <term>perigee</term><note>The point in an orbit closest to the Earth.</note> be *B*. Let the tangent of the epicycle *DE* be drawn, and let *CE* be connected. Therefore, since the greatest <term>prosthaphairesis</term><note>The mathematical correction added to or subtracted from the mean motion to find the true position.</note> is at the tangent, which in this case is 7 degrees and 40 <term>minutes</term><note>original: "scrupulis," or small parts (scruples), used here for minutes of a degree.</note>, this is also the value of angle *BDE*. The angle at *CED* is a right angle, specifically at the contact point of circle *AB*. For this reason, *CE* will be 1,334 parts, where the distance from the center *CD* is 10,000. 

But when the Moon was at its full phase, the epicycle was much smaller, namely nearly 863 of those same parts. Let *CE* be recalculated, and let *CF* be 860 parts; this will be the radius of the circle that the Moon traveled at the new and full moon. The remaining part *FE*, therefore, being 474 parts, will be the diameter of the second epicycle, and by dividing it in two at center *G*, the whole *CFG* will be 1,097 parts from the center of the circle which the center of the second epicycle described. Thus, the ratio of *CG* to *GE* is established as 1,097 to 237, relative to a *CD* of ten thousand parts.

## Concerning the remaining variation, by which the Moon is seen to move irregularly from the highest point of the epicycle. Chapter IX.

Through this <term>inference</term><note>original: "epagogen," a logical deduction or induction.</note> it is also understood how the Moon moves irregularly within its first <term>epicycle</term><note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle.</note>. The greatest variation in this motion occurs when the Moon is curved into its crescent horns, or when it is <term>gibbous</term><note>A phase where the Moon is more than half full but not yet entirely full.</note> and the orb is half-full. Let us again consider that first epicycle AB, which the center of the second epicycle describes in its mean motion; let its center be C, its highest <term>apsis</term><note>original: "absis," the point in an orbit where a celestial body is at its maximum or minimum distance from the center.</note> be A, and its lowest point be B. Let a point E be taken anywhere on the circumference, and let the line CE be joined. Let the ratio of CE to EF be as 1097 is to 237. With E as the center and EF as the radius, let a second small epicycle be described, and let the straight lines CL and CM be drawn from center C to be tangent to it on both sides.

Let the motion of the small epicycle be from A toward E—that is, moving across the top toward the preceding signs <note>This indicates a westward or counter-clockwise direction in this geometric model.</note>. Let the Moon, however, move from F to L, also in the preceding direction. It is clear, therefore, that while the uniform motion covers the arc AE, the second epicycle adds the arc EL to its path through the distance FL, and subtracts from it through MF. Now, since in triangle CEL there is a right angle at L, and EL consists of 237 parts of which CE was 1097—consequently, if CE were 10,000 parts, EL would be 2,160. According to the <term>Table</term><note>original: "Canonem," likely referring to a table of chords or sines used for trigonometric calculations.</note>, this value subtends an angle ECL of 12 degrees and 28 <term>minutes</term><note>original: "scrupula," literally "scruples," the standard term for 1/60th of a degree.</note>. This is equal to the angle MEF, since the triangles are similar and equal. This is the maximum variation by which the Moon deviates from the highest point of the first epicycle. This happens when the Moon, in its mean motion, stands away from the line of the Earth's mean motion by 38 degrees and 46 minutes, both before and after. Thus it is clearly evident that these maximum <term>corrections</term><note>original: "prosthapharæses," a technical astronomical term for the difference between the mean (average) and true (observed) position of a planet.</note> occur at a mean distance between the Sun and Moon of 38 degrees and 46 minutes, and at the same distance on either side of the mean <term>opposition</term><note>When the Moon and Sun are on opposite sides of the Earth (Full Moon).</note>.

### How the Apparent Motion of the Moon is Demonstrated from Given Mean Motions. Chapter 10.

<image-desc>Decorative initial H featuring a figure, possibly a scholar or astronomer, within a classical frame.</image-desc>With all these things thus provided, we now wish to show how the apparent and mean motion of the Moon is determined from those given mean motions, using a geometric method, and taking an example from the observations of Hipparchus, so that the theory may be confirmed by experiment. In the 197th year after the death of Alexander <note>Alexander the Great. Copernicus often uses the era of Alexander's death (323 BCE) as a chronological anchor.</note>, on the seventeenth day of the month of Pauni (which is the tenth month of the Egyptians), after nine and one-third hours of the day had passed in Rhodes. Hipparchus, through an <term>astrolabic instrument</term><note>A complex tool used by ancient astronomers to determine the positions of celestial bodies and tell time.</note> by observing the Sun and Moon, found that they were 48 degrees and one-tenth apart from each other, with the Moon following the Sun. And since he judged the location of the Sun to be at 11 degrees minus one-tenth of Cancer <note>Approximately 10.9 degrees of Cancer.</note>, it followed that the Moon occupied the 29th degree of Leo. At that same time, the twenty-ninth degree of Scorpio was rising, with the tenth degree of Virgo at the <term>midheaven</term><note>original: "caelum mediante," the point where the ecliptic crosses the local meridian; the highest point in the sky at that moment.</note> in Rhodes, where the North Pole is elevated 36 degrees. From this argument, it was clear that the Moon, being located about ninety degrees along the <term>zodiac</term><note>original: "signifer," the 'sign-bearer' or the circle of the zodiac.</note> from the horizon, admitted no—or certainly an imperceptible—<term>parallax</term><note>original: "uisus commutationē," the shift in apparent position of a celestial body when viewed from different locations on Earth.</note> in longitude. 

Since this observation was made three and one-third hours after noon on that seventeenth day, which in Rhodes corresponds to four <term>equinoctial hours</term><note>Hours of equal length (60 minutes), as opposed to "seasonal hours" which varied with the time of year.</note>, the equinoctial hours in Krakow would have been 3 and 1/6th, according to the distance by which Rhodes is closer to us by a <term>sixth part of an hour</term><note>original: "sextante horario." Copernicus is adjusting the time for the difference in longitude between Rhodes and his own location in Poland.</note> than Alexandria. Therefore, from the death of Alexander, there were 196 years, 286 days, and 3 and 1/6th hours <term>apparent time</term><note>original: "simpliciter," time as measured directly by the Sun's position.</note>; however, by <term>mean time</term><note>original: "regulariter," time adjusted for the Earth's orbital speed variations.</note> it was about 3 and 1/3 hours. In that time, the Sun by its mean motion reached 12 degrees 3 minutes of Cancer, but it appeared at 10 degrees 40 minutes of Cancer; hence it appears that the Moon, according to the truth, was in 28 degrees 37 minutes of Leo. Moreover, the mean motion of the Moon according to its monthly revolution was 45 degrees 5 minutes. The <term>anomaly</term><note>The position of a planet within its own orbital cycle, measured from its furthest point.</note> from the highest <term>apsis</term><note>original: "summa abside," the point in the orbit farthest from the center of motion.</note> was 333 degrees according to our calculation. ->### BOOK IV OF THE REVOLUTIONS<-

<note>original: "ptiora sint"; completing the phrase "utque illa ad usum promptiora sint" from the previous page: "and so that these may be more ready for use."</note> ...more ready for use, we shall set forth the **Table** of the <term>corrections</term><note>original: "prosthaphaereseon"; from the Greek, these are the mathematical adjustments—additions or subtractions—required to convert the "mean" or average position of a planet into its "true" observed position.</note> themselves, which will contain six columns. For, after the two sets of common degree numbers for the circle, in the third column will be the corrections which arise from the small <term>epicycle</term><note>original: "epicyclo"; a "circle-on-a-circle" used to model the variation in a planet's speed and distance.</note>, varying the uniformity of the first <term>anomaly</term><note>original: "anomaliae"; the irregular or non-uniform motion of a celestial body.</note> according to the doubled motion of the months. Then, leaving the next column temporarily empty for future numbers, we will pre-occupy the fifth column. In this, we shall write the corrections of the first and larger epicycle, which occur at the mean <term>conjunctions and oppositions</term><note>original: "coniunctionibus & oppositionibus"; the New Moon and Full Moon, when the Sun, Earth, and Moon are aligned.</note> of the Sun and Moon; the maximum of these is 4 degrees and 56 <term>minutes</term><note>original: "scrupula"; literally "scruples," referring to 1/60th of a degree.</note>.

In the penultimate column are placed the numbers by which the corrections occurring at the <term>half-moon</term><note>original: "diuidua Luna"; literally "the divided moon," referring to the quarter phases or quadratures.</note> exceed those first ones; the maximum of these is 2 degrees and 44 minutes. To ensure that the other remaining excesses can also be determined, the **proportional minutes** were devised, the reasoning for which is as follows. We take those 2 degrees and 44 minutes as 60, in relation to any other excesses occurring at the contact point of the epicycle. 

Just as in the same example, where we had the line *CG* at 1123 units (of which *CD* is 10,000), which results in a correction of 6 degrees and 29 minutes at the contact point of the epicycle. This exceeds that first correction by 1 degree and 33 minutes. Since 2 degrees and 44 minutes is to 1 degree and 33 minutes as 60 is to 34, we therefore have the ratio of the excess occurring in the semi-circle of the small epicycle relative to that under the given circumference of 90 degrees and 18 minutes. We will therefore write 34 minutes in the table in the row for 90 degrees. In this manner, for each individual circumference of the same circle pre-marked in the Table, we will find the proportional minutes to be set out in the fourth column, which was previously left vacant. 

Finally, in the last column, we have added the degrees of Northern and Southern latitude, which we shall discuss below. For the convenience and utility of the operation prompted us to arrange them in this order.

It provides the mathematical offsets needed to correct the Moon's "mean" (average) position to its "true" observed position. Copernicus used two <term>epicycles</term>—mini-orbits attached to a larger orbit—to explain why the Moon appears to speed up, slow down, and change its distance from Earth. "Epicycle a" represents the larger, primary correction, while "Epicycle b" accounts for smaller variations. ### Chapter XII. On the Calculation of the Lunar Course.

The method for calculating the lunar appearance is clear from what has been demonstrated, and it is as follows. We shall reduce the proposed time for which we seek the Moon’s position to uniform motion <note>The "uniform" or "mean" motion is the idealized average speed of the Moon before corrections are applied.</note>. Through this, we will derive the mean motions of longitude, <term>anomaly</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet from its highest point (apogee).</note>, and latitude—which we shall also soon define—just as we did with the Sun, starting from the established epoch of Christ, or another starting point, and we will establish the positions of each for the proposed time. 

Then, we look up the equal lunar longitude, or the doubled distance from the Sun, in the table. We will note the <term>prosthaphaeresis</term> <note>A correction added or subtracted to convert "mean" (average) motion into "true" (observed) motion.</note> found in the third column, and the proportional minutes that follow it. If the number we used to enter the table is found in the first column—that is, if it is less than 180 degrees—we add the prosthaphaeresis to the lunar anomaly. If it is greater than 180 degrees, or found in the second column, it should be subtracted from it. We will then have the "equated" anomaly of the Moon and its true distance from the highest <term>apsis</term> <note>The highest point in the Moon's orbit.</note>. 

By using this equated anomaly to enter the table again, we will take the prosthaphaeresis corresponding to it in the fifth column, and the "excess" that follows in the sixth column—which the second <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger circle.</note> adds over the first. A proportional part of this excess is taken, according to the ratio of the proportional minutes found earlier out of sixty, and is always added to this prosthaphaeresis. 

The resulting sum is subtracted from the mean motion of longitude and latitude, provided that the equated anomaly is less than 180 degrees (or a semicircle), and it is added if the anomaly is greater. In this way, we will have the true distance of the Moon from the mean position of the Sun, and the equated motion of latitude. Therefore, the true position of the Moon will not be unknown, whether measured from the first star of **Aries** <note>The "First Point of Aries" was the traditional starting point for measuring celestial longitude.</note> by the simple motion of the Sun, or from the **Vernal Equinox** by adding its precession. 

Finally, by using the equated motion of latitude, we will find in the seventh and last column of the table the degrees of latitude by which the Moon is distant from the center of the zodiac circle <note>The ecliptic.</note>. This latitude will be Northern <note>original: "Borea"</note> when the motion of latitude is in the first part of the table—

This involves adjusting the mean motions through a series of additions and subtractions based on the Moon's distance from the Sun and its position on its epicycles.</summary>

...found in the column <note>original: "læ reperitur", completing "columnæ" from the previous page</note>, that is, if it is less than 90 or greater than 270 degrees; otherwise, it will follow the Southern latitude. And for that reason, the Moon will be descending from the North until 180 degrees, and from there climbing from the Southern limit until it has completed the remaining parts of the circle. In this way, the apparent course of the Moon has, in a sense, as many complexities around the center of the Earth as the center of the Earth has around the Sun.

### Chapter XIII. How the Motion of Lunar Latitude is Examined and Demonstrated.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' at the start of the chapter, depicting a figure seated in a rural landscape with foliage and distant architecture.</image-desc>

**N**ow an account must also be given for the motion of the lunar latitude, which seems more difficult to determine because it is hindered by more circumstances. For as we said before, if two <term>lunar eclipses</term> <note>original: "defectus Lunae"</note> were similar and equal in every respect—that is, with the eclipsed parts in the same Northern or Southern position, and occurring around the same intersection with the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The path the Sun appears to follow; the Moon's orbit crosses this at an angle.</note> while ascending or descending, and if its distance from the Earth or the highest <term>apsis</term> <note>The point in the orbit furthest from Earth, also called apogee.</note> were equal. Since these factors agree, it is understood that the Moon has completed full circles of its latitude in true motion. 

For since the shadow of the Earth is conical, and if a right cone is cut by a plane parallel to its base, the circular section is smaller at a greater distance from the base and larger at a lesser distance, and likewise equal at an equal distance; so indeed, the Moon at equal distances from the Earth passes through equal circles of the shadow, and presents equal disks of itself to our sight. From this, it follows that when the Moon projects by equal parts toward the same side, according to an equal distance from the center of the shadow, it makes us certain of equal latitudes. From these, it must follow that the Moon, having returned to its previous place of latitude, is also distant by equal intervals from the same intersection with the ecliptic. This is especially true if the position also agrees on both sides, for the approach and withdrawal of the Moon or the Earth changes the entire size of the shadow, in

HEADER: NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...by only a small amount, which can hardly be detected. Therefore, the greater the time interval that mediates between the two observations, the more defined a value we can obtain for the motion of the Moon’s latitude, just as was stated regarding the Sun.

But since it is rare to find two <term>eclipses</term> <note>original: "defectus," literally "failings" or "deficiencies" of the Moon</note> that agree under these specific conditions, none have certainly occurred to us at present. However, we have noticed another way by which this can be achieved. For if the other conditions remain the same, even if the Moon is eclipsed on opposite sides—and around opposite nodes—it will then signify that the Moon in the second eclipse reached a place diametrically opposite the first, and besides complete circles, it has described a semicircle. This will be seen to satisfy the requirements of our investigation.

We have therefore found two eclipses almost suited to these methods. The first occurred in the seventh year of Ptolemy Philometor <note>Pharaoh of Egypt, reigning c. 180–145 BCE</note>, which was the 150th year of the era of Alexander, after 27 days had passed (as Claudius <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer</note> says) of the seventh Egyptian month, Phamenoth. During the night followed by the 28th day, the Moon was eclipsed from the beginning of the eighth hour until the end of the tenth hour, measured in <term>seasonal hours</term> <note>Hours of variable length depending on the season, where the night is divided into 12 equal parts</note> of the night at Alexandria. At most, seven "digits" <note>A unit of measurement for eclipses where 12 digits equal the full diameter of the Moon</note> of the lunar diameter were obscured from the North around the descending node <note>original: "sectionem descendentem," the point where the Moon crosses the Sun's path moving southward</note>. Therefore, the middle of the eclipse was (he says) two seasonal hours after midnight, which make two and one-third <term>equinoctial hours</term> <note>Hours of fixed length (60 minutes), unlike seasonal hours</note>, since the Sun was in the sixth degree of Taurus; but at Kraków, it would have been one and one-third hours.

The second eclipse we observed under the same meridian of Kraków, in the year of Christ 1509, on the fourth day before the Nones of June [June 2nd], with the Sun in the 21st degree of Gemini. The middle of this eclipse was 11 and 3/5 equinoctial hours after midday. In this instance, nearly eight digits of the lunar diameter were eclipsed from the Southern side around the ascending node. 

From the beginning of the era of Alexander, there are, therefore, 149 Egyptian years, 206 days, and 14 1/3 hours at Alexandria; but at Kraków, 14 and 1/3 hours according to appearance, though more precisely 14 1/2 hours. At this time, the position of the <term>mean anomaly</term> <note>The Moon's position in its orbit relative to its furthest point from Earth, calculated as if it moved at a constant speed</note> was, according to our calculation—which agrees closely with Ptolemy—163 degrees and 33 minutes. The <term>prosthaphæresis</term> <note>The geometric correction used to find the actual position from the average or "mean" position</note> was 1 degree 24 minutes, by which the Moon’s true position was less than its mean position. From the second eclipse to the same...

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion where Copernicus began detailing a specific lunar eclipse from the 7th year of Ptolemy Philometor (the 150th year of the era of Alexander) to calculate the Moon's latitude and motion.</meta>

->### REVOLUTIONS BOOK IV.<-

According to the same established starting point of Alexander, there are 1,832 Egyptian years, 295 days, 11 hours, and 45 minutes in apparent time; but in equalized <note>uniform or mean</note> time, it is 11 hours and 55 minutes. From this, the uniform motion of the Moon was 182 degrees and 18 <term>minutes</term> <note>original: "scrupulus," meaning a "small part," here used for minutes of arc</note>. The position of the <term>anomaly</term> <note>The Moon's position in its elliptical or epicyclic path</note> was 159 degrees and 55 minutes, but the equalized <note>corrected</note> position was 161 degrees and 14 minutes. The <term>prosthaphæresis</term> <note>original: "prosthaphæresis," a correction added or subtracted to transform uniform motion into apparent motion</note>, by which the uniform motion was less than the apparent motion, was 1 degree and 44 minutes.

It is clear, therefore, that in both eclipses the distance of the Moon from the Earth was equal, and the Sun was almost at its <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the Earth</note> in both cases, but there was a difference of one <term>digit</term> <note>original: "digitus," a unit representing 1/12th of the diameter of the celestial body's disk</note> in the magnitude of the eclipses. Since the diameter of the Moon usually occupies about half a degree, as we will show later, a twelfth part of it—representing one digit—will be 2.5 minutes. In the oblique circle of the Moon, near the <term>ecliptic intersections</term> <note>The "nodes" where the Moon's orbit crosses the Earth's orbital plane</note>, this corresponds to almost half a degree. By this amount, the Moon was further from the ascending node in the second eclipse than it was from the descending node in the first. From this, it is most clear that the true motion of the Moon's latitude, after complete revolutions, was 179.5 degrees. 

But the lunar anomaly between the first and second eclipse adds 21 minutes to the uniform motion, which is the amount by which the prosthaphæreses exceed each other. We will therefore have a uniform motion of the Moon's latitude, after complete circles, of 179 degrees and 51 minutes. The time between both eclipses was 1,683 years, 88 days, 22 hours, and 35 minutes in apparent time, which agreed with the uniform time. In this time, after 22,577 complete revolutions, there are 179 degrees and 51 minutes. These results agree with our figures, which we have already set forth.

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK IV.

-> [Diagram: A circle representing the Moon's path. Point C is the northernmost point. A and B are the nodes where the path crosses the ecliptic. Points F, K, E, and L mark the positions of the Moon during the two eclipses used for calculation.] <-

`a` is the descending section of the ecliptic <note>original: "sectio ecliptica descendens"; this is the "descending node," where the Moon crosses from north to south</note>, and `b` is the ascending section. Let two equal arcs, AF and BE, be taken toward the southern parts, just as the first eclipse was at point F and the second at point E. Furthermore, let FK be the subtractive <term>prosthaphæresis</term> <note>A geometric correction used to convert the Moon's "mean" or average position into its "true" or apparent position</note> in the first eclipse, and EL be the additive one in the second. 

Since, therefore, the arc KL is 159 degrees 56 minutes, to which are added FK (which was 4 degrees 20 minutes) and EL (which was 4 degrees 28 minutes), the whole arc FKLE will be 168 degrees 43 minutes. The remainder of this from a semicircle <note>180 degrees</note> is 11 degrees 17 minutes. Half of this is 5 degrees 39 minutes, which is equal to both AF and BE, the true distances of the Moon from the segment AB. Because of this, the arc AFK is 9 degrees 59 minutes. From this it is also established that the mean position of latitude from the northern limit—that is, the arc C AFK—is 99 degrees 59 minutes.

At the time and place of that Ptolemaic observation <note>Ptolemy’s 2nd-century record</note>, there are 457 Egyptian years <note>An Egyptian year consists of exactly 365 days</note>, 91 days, and 10 hours by apparent time from the death of Alexander; by mean time, however, it is 9 hours 54 minutes. During this interval, the motion of latitude is 50 degrees 59 minutes. When these are subtracted from 99 degrees 59 minutes, there remain 49 degrees at noon on the first day of the first month, <term>Thoth</term> <note>The first month of the ancient Egyptian calendar</note>, according to the Egyptians, at the beginning of the years of Alexander. 

From here, the positions of the course of the Moon's latitude (taken from the northern limit) are given for other starting points according to the differences in time, from which we derive the motion itself. Since from the first <term>Olympiad</term> <note>A four-year period used by the Greeks for dating; the first began in 776 BCE</note> to the death of Alexander there are 451 Egyptian years and 247 days (during which 7 minutes of an hour are subtracted for the equality of time), the motion of latitude during that time is 136 degrees 57 minutes. Again, from the first Olympiad to Caesar <note>Julius Caesar</note>, there are 730 Egyptian years and 12 hours (but ten hourly minutes are added for the equality of time), during which time the mean motion is 206 degrees 54 minutes. Then, to Christ, there are 45 years and 12 days. 

If, therefore, 136 degrees 57 minutes are subtracted from 49 degrees (after adding 360 degrees of a circle), there remain 272 degrees 3 minutes for noon on the first day of <term>Hecatombæon</term> <note>The first month of the Attic/Greek calendar</note> of the first Olympiad. If to these are again added 206 degrees 54 minutes, the total is 118 degrees 56 minutes for the midnight before the <term>Kalends of January</term> <note>January 1st, the start of the Roman year</note>...

### Construction of the Parallactic Instrument. Chapter 15.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' containing a woodcut portrait of a bearded man, presumably an astronomer, holding a book.</image-desc>Fortune did not grant us the same opportunity to verify that the maximum latitude of the Moon is five degrees (where the circle is 360 degrees) as it did for Claudius Ptolemy, due to the interference of lunar <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent shift in an object's position when viewed from different locations</note>. Ptolemy, working in Alexandria—where the North Pole is raised 30 degrees and 58 minutes above the horizon—observed how closely the Moon could approach the zenith <note>The point directly overhead</note>. He watched for the moment the Moon reached the start of the sign of Cancer and its northernmost limit, points which could be predicted by calculation. He discovered then, by means of a certain instrument which he calls "parallactic"—built specifically to detect the shifting positions of the Moon—that its minimum distance from the zenith was only two and one-eighth degrees. At such a small distance, any effect of parallax would be very slight. By subtracting those two degrees and one-eighth from the 30 degrees and 58 minutes <note>The latitude of Alexandria</note>, there remain 28 degrees and 51.5 minutes. This value exceeds the maximum obliquity <note>tilt</note> of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: "signiferi"; the ecliptic or the path of the sun</note>—which at that time was 23 degrees, 51 minutes, and 20 seconds—by almost five full degrees. This lunar latitude is found to agree with all other specific observations made to this day.

The parallactic instrument consists of three rods. Two of them are equal in length, at least four <term>cubits</term> <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18–20 inches</note> long, and the third is somewhat longer. This longer rod and one of the first two are joined at their ends; the others are joined by skillful drilling and matching pins or pegs so that they move within the same plane at those joints without any wobbling. On the longer rod, a straight line is carved along its entire length starting from the center of its joint. On this line, a distance is marked out that is exactly equal to the distance between the joints of the other two rods. This section is then divided into a thousand equal parts, or more if possible, and this scale is extended further along the rest of the rod...

<meta>catchword: XXVI.</meta>

along these same divisions, until the total length reaches 1,414 parts. This length is significant because it subtends the side of a square inscribed in a circle whose radius is 1,000 parts <note>Using the Pythagorean theorem, the diagonal of a square with sides of 1,000 is approximately 1,414</note>. Any portion of this ruler that remains beyond this point may be cut off as superfluous. On the second ruler, a line should also be drawn from the center of the joint equal to those same 1,000 parts—the same distance that exists between the centers of the joints. This ruler should have sighting holes <term>specilla</term> <note>original: "specilla"; viewing apertures or sights used for alignment</note> fixed to its side, as is common with a <term>dioptra</term> <note>An ancient Greek surveying and astronomical sighting instrument</note>, through which the sight passes. These sights must be so arranged that the line of vision does not deviate at all from the line marked along the length of the ruler, but remains at an equal distance from it.

Care must also be taken so that when the end of this line is extended toward the longer ruler, it can touch the divided scale. In this way, through the arrangement of the rulers, an Isosceles triangle is formed, the base of which will consist of the parts measured on the divided line. Next, a post, well-squared and smoothed, should be erected and fixed firmly. To this post, the instrument is attached by the ruler containing both hinges using certain pivots, so that it can rotate like a door. This must be done so that the straight line passing through the center of the hinges on the ruler always corresponds to a plumb line and stands toward the zenith <note>The point directly overhead</note> of the horizon as an axis.

Therefore, when one wishes to determine the distance of any star from the zenith, once the star itself is held in view through the sighting holes of the ruler, and by adjusting the bottom ruler with its divided line, one will understand how many parts subtend the angle existing between the line of sight and the axis of the horizon. These parts are measured as if the diameter of the circle were 20,000 <note>Copernicus uses a standard circle where the radius is 10,000 for trigonometric calculations</note>, and by consulting a <term>Canon</term> <note>original: "Canonem"; a mathematical table of chords or sines</note>, one will find the desired arc of the great circle between the star and the zenith.

## On the Parallaxes of the Moon. Chapter 16.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'H' featuring a central face mask at the bottom surrounded by ornate symmetrical foliage and floral scrolls within a square frame.</image-desc>Using this instrument, as we have said, Ptolemy determined the maximum latitude of the Moon to be five degrees. Then he turned his attention to perceiving its <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent shift in an object's position when viewed from different locations</note>, and he states that he found it at Alexandria to be one degree and 7 <term>scruples</term> <note>original: "scrupulus"; 1/60th of a degree, or one minute</note>. This observation occurred while the Sun was in 5 degrees and 28 minutes of Libra. At that time, the mean distance of the Moon from the Sun was 78 degrees and 13 minutes. The mean anomaly <note>The position of a planet or moon in its orbit relative to its perigee</note> was 262 degrees and 20 minutes; the motion of latitude was 354 degrees and 40 minutes; and the additive <term>prosthaphairesis</term> <note>original: "prosthaphæresis"; a correction or "equation" used to find the true position of a celestial body from its mean position</note> was 7 degrees and 40 minutes.

XXVI. And therefore, the position of the Moon was at 3 degrees 9 minutes of Capricorn. The mean motion in latitude was 2 degrees 6 minutes. The northern latitude of the Moon was 4 degrees 59 minutes. Its declination <note>The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator</note> from the equinoctial was 24 degrees 49 minutes. The latitude of Alexandria <note>The Egyptian city where Ptolemy made his observations</note> is 30 degrees 58 minutes. He [Ptolemy] says that the Moon was seen almost on the meridian circle through an instrument at 50 degrees 55 minutes from the zenith <note>original: "a uertice horizontis"; the point in the sky directly above the observer</note>. This was one degree and 7 minutes more than the calculation required. Based on the opinion of the ancients concerning the eccentric and the epicycle <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used in ancient astronomy to explain planetary paths</note>, he demonstrates that the distance of the Moon from the center of the Earth was then 39 parts and 45 minutes, where the radius of the Earth is one part.

Following the logic of those same circles, they claim that the Moon at its greatest distance from the Earth—which they say occurs at the apogee <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</note> of the epicycle during the New and Full Moon—is 64 parts and 10 minutes (or one-sixth of a part). Conversely, at its minimum distance, which occurs in the quadratures <note>The phases of the half-moon</note> when the Moon is at the perigee <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Earth</note> of its epicycle, the distance is only 33 parts 33 minutes. From this, he also estimated the parallaxes <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent change in the position of an object when viewed from different locations, used here to measure the Moon's distance</note> which occur at about ninety degrees from the zenith: the minimum being 52 minutes 33 seconds, and the maximum being 1 degree 43 minutes, as can be seen more extensively in what he constructed regarding these matters.

But it is now clear to those who wish to consider it that these things are far otherwise, as we have experienced many times. However, we shall review two observations we have made, which again declare that our hypotheses concerning the Moon are as much more certain as they agree more closely with the appearances and leave no room for doubt.

In the year of our Lord 1522, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October [September 27], five and two-thirds equal hours after noon, around sunset at Frombork <note>original: "Fruenburgi"; the town in Poland where Copernicus conducted his research</note>, we took the center of the Moon on the meridian circle with the parallactic instrument. We found its distance from the zenith to be 82 degrees 50 minutes. Therefore, from the beginning of the years of Christ until this hour, there were 1,522 Egyptian years <note>A year used by astronomers consisting of exactly 365 days, ignoring leap years for calculation consistency</note>, 284 days, and 17 2/3 hours according to apparent time. But in equated time, it was 17 hours 24 minutes. For this reason, the apparent position of the Sun according to our calculation was at 13 degrees 29 minutes of Libra. The mean motion of the Moon from the Sun was 87 degrees 6 minutes. The mean anomaly <note>The position of a celestial body relative to its starting point in its orbit</note> was 357 degrees.

39 minutes, the true motion <note>original: "uera"; likely referring to the true anomaly or position</note> was 358 degrees 40 minutes, adding 7 minutes. And so the true position of the Moon was at 12 degrees 34 minutes of Capricorn. The mean motion of latitude from the northern limit was 197 degrees 1 minute. The true [motion] was 197 degrees 8 minutes. The southern latitude of the Moon was 4 degrees 47 minutes. It declined from the equinoctial <note>The celestial equator</note> by 27 degrees 41 minutes. The latitude of our place of observation <note>Frombork, Poland, where Copernicus performed his research</note> is 54 degrees 19 minutes, which, when combined with the lunar declination, results in a true distance from the zenith <note>original: "à polo horizontis"; the point in the sky directly above the observer</note> of 82 degrees. Therefore, the 50 minutes that remained were due to parallax <note>original: "commutationis"; the shift in the apparent position of the Moon when viewed from the surface of the Earth versus the center</note>, which according to Ptolemy’s tradition should have been 1 degree 17 minutes.

We conducted another observation in the same place in the year of Christ 1524, on August 7th <note>original: "VII. Idus Augusti"</note>, six hours after noon. We saw through the same instrument that the Moon was at 81 degrees 55 minutes from the zenith. From the beginning of the Christian era to this hour, there were 1524 Egyptian years <note>A calculation year used by astronomers consisting of exactly 365 days</note>, 234 days, and 18 hours—exactly 18 hours. Since the position of the Sun according to calculation was at 24 degrees 14 minutes of Leo, the mean motion of the Moon from the Sun was 97 degrees 6 minutes. The uniform <term>anomaly</term> <note>The angular distance of a celestial body from its furthest point in orbit, used to calculate its irregular speed</note> was 242 degrees 10 minutes. The adjusted anomaly was 239 degrees 40 minutes, adding nearly seven degrees to the mean motion. Therefore, the true position of the Moon was at 9 degrees 39 minutes of Sagittarius. The mean motion of latitude was 193 degrees 19 minutes; the true motion was 200 degrees 17 minutes.

The southern latitude of the Moon was 4 degrees 41 minutes. The southern declination was 26 degrees 36 minutes, which, with the latitude of the place of observation (54 degrees 19 minutes), results in a distance of the Moon from the zenith of 80 degrees 55 minutes. But it appeared to be at 81 degrees 55 minutes. Therefore, the one degree in excess passed into the lunar parallax, which according to Ptolemy should have been 1 degree 38 minutes. And this was according to the opinion of those before us, which the harmonic ratio <note>The mathematical proportions established in earlier planetary models</note> following from their hypothesis forced them to admit.

### Chapter XVII. A demonstration of the Moon's distance from the Earth, and the ratio it holds in parts where the distance from the center of the Earth to its surface is one.

From these data, it will now become clear how great the Moon's distance from the Earth is. Without this, no certain calculation of the parallaxes <term>parallax; the apparent shift in the position of a celestial body when viewed from different points, such as the Earth's surface versus its center</term> can be established, for the two are mutually dependent. It shall be demonstrated in this manner: Let A B be the great circle of the Earth, and C its center. Around this, let another circle be described, in relation to which the Earth has a significant size; let this be D E, where D is the pole of the horizon <note>the zenith, or the point directly overhead</note> and E is the center of the Moon, so that D E is its known distance from the zenith.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a small circle (Earth) with center C and points A and B on its perimeter. Outside this is a larger arc containing points D (zenith/pole) and E (the Moon's center). Lines connect C to E, A to E, and D to E, forming a triangle ACE used to calculate parallax and distance.</image-desc>

Since, therefore, the angle D A E in the first observation was 82 degrees 50 minutes <note>original: "scrupula"; small parts or minutes of a degree</note>, and the parallax angle A E C was 50 minutes, we have a triangle A C E with given angles, and consequently, given sides. For on account of the given angle C A E, the side C E will be 99,219 parts (in a system where the diameter of the circle circumscribing triangle A E C is 100,000), and A C will be 1,454 such parts. This means A C goes into C E nearly 68 times, where A C—the radius from the center of the Earth—is defined as one part. This was the distance of the Moon from the center of the Earth in the first observation.

But in the second observation, the apparent angle D A E was 81 degrees 55 minutes, while the calculated angle A C E <note>the true angular distance from the center of the Earth</note> was 80 degrees 55 minutes, and the remaining angle A E C was 60 minutes. Therefore, side E C is 99,006 parts and A C is 1,747 parts, where the diameter of the circle circumscribing the triangle is 100,000. Thus, the distance of the Moon C E was 56 parts and 41 minutes <note>56 and 41/60ths</note>, where the Earth's radius A C is one part.

Now, let the larger epicycle <term>epicycle; a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used to explain variations in planetary speed and distance</term> of the Moon be A B C, with its center at D. Let E be the center of the Earth, from which a straight line E B D A is drawn, so that A is the apogee <note>the point in the orbit furthest from Earth</note> and B is the perigee <note>the point closest to Earth</note>. Let the arc A B C be 242 degrees 10 minutes, according to the calculated uniformity of the lunar anomaly <note>the Moon's position relative to its perigee/apogee</note>. With the center at C, let a second small epicycle F G K be described, whose circumference F G K is 194 degrees 12 minutes—which is double the distance of the Moon from the Sun. Connect D K, which subtracts from the ano- <note>The text continues on the next page with "maliæ", completing the word "anomaliæ" or anomaly</note>

<margin>G K</margin> Therefore, according to this given ratio, when E K is (as has been shown) 56 parts 41 minutes—where the Earth’s radius is one—it follows that D E is 60 parts 18 minutes of those same units. Consequently, D F is 5 parts 11 minutes, and D F G is 8 parts 2 minutes. Just as if the whole E D G were extended in a straight line, it would be 68 and one-third parts, which is the maximum altitude <note>distance from Earth</note> of the half-moon <note>original: "Luna diuiduæ"; referring to the Moon at quadrature or first/last quarter</note>. By subtracting D G from E D, there remain 52 parts 17 minutes for its minimum distance. So also the whole E D F, which is the altitude occurring at the full and new Moon <note>original: "plena ac silente"; the 'silent' moon is a classical term for the new moon when it is invisible</note>, will be 65 and a half parts <note>represented as "LXV. s." where 's' stands for semis, or half</note> at its maximum, and with D F subtracted, 55 parts 8 minutes at its minimum. Nor indeed should it disturb us that others estimate the maximum distance of the full and new Moon to be 64 parts 10 minutes. This is especially true of those who were only able to know the Moon’s parallaxes <term>commutationes; Copernicus uses this term interchangeably with 'parallaxes' to describe the apparent change in position</term> partially, due to the geographical layout of their locations. To us, however, a more complete perception was granted by the Moon’s closer approach to the horizon, where it is well known that parallaxes reach their full extent. Yet, despite this difference in method, we do not find the parallaxes to differ by more than a single minute.

## On the diameter of the Moon and of the Earth’s shadow, at the place where the Moon passes through it. Chapter 18.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap 'P' containing an illustration of a man in robes, possibly an astronomer or scholar, standing in a landscape with hills and trees, holding a staff or measuring instrument.</image-desc>

Along with the distance of the Moon from the Earth, the apparent diameters of the Moon and the shadow vary; therefore, it is necessary to speak of these as well. And although the diameters of the Sun and Moon are correctly measured using the <term>dioptra<note>A classical observational instrument used for measuring angles or altitudes.</note></term> of Hipparchus <note>Hipparchus of Nicaea (c. 190–120 BCE), a Greek astronomer who pioneered the measurement of the distances and sizes of the Sun and Moon.</note>, it is nevertheless thought that this is achieved much more certainly for the Moon through certain partial <term>eclipses<note>original: "defectus"; literally 'failings' or 'defects,' the standard term for eclipses in this period.</note></term> of the Moon. In these cases, the Moon should be equally distant from its highest or lowest <term>apsis<note>The points in an orbit closest to or furthest from the Earth (apogee and perigee).</note></term>, especially if at that time the Sun also positions itself in the same way, so that the circle of the shadow through which the Moon passes is found to be equal on both occasions—except that the eclipses themselves occur in unequal proportions. For it is clear that when the difference between the eclipsed parts and the latitude of the Moon is compared, it shows how much of the circumference around the center of the Earth the diameter of the Moon <term>subtends<note>The angle formed at the eye (or the Earth's center) by the width of the celestial body.</note></term>. Once this is perceived, the semi-diameter of the shadow is immediately understood.

This will become clearer by an example. Suppose that in the middle of a previous eclipse, three <term>digits<note>original: "digiti"; a unit of measure for eclipses equal to one-twelfth of the diameter of the celestial body.</note></term>—or three inches <note>original: "unciae"</note>—of the Moon's diameter were eclipsed, while it had a latitude of 47 minutes 54 seconds. In another eclipse, 10 digits were eclipsed, with a latitude of 29 minutes 37 seconds. The difference between the obscured parts is 7 digits, and the difference in latitude is 18 minutes 17 seconds. Proportional to these are 12 digits to 31 minutes 20 seconds, which subtend the diameter of the Moon. It is evident, therefore, that the center of the Moon in the middle of the first eclipse exceeded the shadow by a quarter of its diameter, which contains 7 minutes 50 seconds of latitude. If these are subtracted from the 47 minutes 54 seconds of the total latitude, there remain 40 minutes 4 seconds for the semi-diameter of the shadow. Likewise, in the second eclipse, in which the shadow occupied more than the Moon’s latitude of 10 minutes 27 seconds for one-third of the lunar diameter; when the 29 minutes 37 seconds are added, they similarly produce 40 minutes 4 seconds for the semi-diameter of the shadow. Such is the opinion of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE), whose geocentric model Copernicus is here refining.</note>; while the Sun and Moon are joined or opposed at their greatest distance from the Earth, the Moon's diameter is... <note>original: "scrup."; an abbreviation for 'scrupulorum' or minutes. The sentence continues on the next page.</note>

<summary>Copernicus explains the methodology for calculating the apparent diameters of the Moon and the Earth's shadow using observations of partial lunar eclipses. By comparing the Moon's latitude and the depth of the eclipse (measured in 'digits'), he derives specific measurements for these celestial dimensions.</summary>
<keywords>lunar diameter, Earth shadow, lunar eclipse, Hipparchus, Ptolemy, angular measurement, astronomical instruments, celestial geometry</keywords>

## How the distances of the Sun and Moon from the Earth, their diameters, the shadow at the place of the Moon’s passage, and the axis of the shadow are demonstrated simultaneously. Chapter 19.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a scholar or astronomer seated at a desk, likely holding a scientific instrument.</image-desc>

First, we shall review Ptolemy’s opinions on these matters and how he demonstrated them, from which we shall extract what seems most true. He assumes the apparent diameter of the Sun to be 31 and 1/3 minutes, a value he uses without variation. To this, he makes the diameter of the Moon equal when it is at its <term>apogee<note>The point in the Moon's orbit where it is furthest from the Earth.</note></term> during a full or new moon, which he says occurs at a distance of 64 parts and 10 minutes, where one part is the Earth's radius. Since indeed $LOP$ and $MR$ are parallel to $KE$ at equal intervals, $LOP$ and $MR$ together will therefore be double $KE$. Furthermore, according to the second proposition of the sixth book of <term>Euclid<note>Euclid's Elements, the standard Greek textbook for geometry, which Copernicus used for his proofs.</note></term>, $EC$ is to $PC$, $KC$ is to $OC$, and $KD$ is to $LD$ in the same proportional ratio as $KE$ to $OP$. Such was the finding of <term>Ptolemy<note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose work formed the basis of the geocentric model.</note></term>.

Others after Ptolemy, however, because they found that these values did not sufficiently agree with the <term>appearances<note>original: "apparentiis"; the observed phenomena or data collected through telescopes and sightings.</note></term>, put forward other views on these matters. Nevertheless, they admit that the maximum distance of the Full and New Moon from the Earth is 64 parts and 10 minutes. They also concede that the apparent diameter of the Sun at <term>apogee<note>The point in the orbit where the Sun is furthest from the Earth.</note></term> is 31 and 1/3 minutes, and they agree that the diameter of the shadow at the place of the Moon’s passage is in a ratio of 13 to 5, just as Ptolemy himself did. But they deny that the Moon’s apparent diameter at that time is greater than 29 and a half minutes; and for that reason, they set the diameter of the shadow at 1 part and 16 minutes with nearly <term>three-quarters<note>original: "dodrante"; a Roman term for 3/4 of a unit.</note></term>. From these figures, they think it follows that the distance of the Sun at apogee from the Earth is 1,146 parts, and the axis of the shadow is 254 parts, where the Earth's radius is taken as one unit.

However, we will use groups of six degrees <note>original: "hexades graduum."</note>, by which the doubled number may be understood, reaching up to ninety degrees from the vertex of the horizon.

We have arranged this Table into nine columns. In the first and second columns will be the common numbers of the circle. In the third, we will place the parallaxes of the Sun. Then come the Lunar parallaxes: in the fourth place are the differences by which the minimum parallaxes (which occur when the Moon is at its apogee <note>The point where the Moon is farthest from the Earth.</note> and at its half-phase) fall short of the following values at the full and new Moon. The sixth column will contain those parallaxes produced by the full or "waning" <note>original: "sitiens," literally "thirsty," a poetic term Copernicus uses here for a specific lunar phase, likely the new moon or a moon approaching conjunction.</note> Moon at its perigee <note>The point where the Moon is closest to the Earth.</note>. The minutes that follow are the differences by which the parallaxes occurring when the Moon is at its half-phase and nearest to us exceed those previously mentioned. Finally, the remaining two spaces are reserved for the proportional minutes. By these, the parallaxes can be calculated between these four limits; we shall also explain these, starting first with the apogee and the limits between the former values, in this manner. Let there be, I say, the circle...

Let the first epicycle of the Moon be **AB**, with its center at **C**. Taking **D** as the center of the Earth, let the straight line **DBCA** be drawn. At the apogee <term>apogæo|The point in an orbit where the celestial body is furthest from the Earth.</term>, with the center established there, let a second small epicycle **EFG** be described. Let the arc **EG** be assumed to be 60 degrees, and let lines **AG** and **CG** be connected. Since it was demonstrated in the preceding sections that the straight line **CE** consists of 5 parts and 11 minutes <note>original: "scrup." abbreviated for *scrupula*, meaning minutes or 1/60th of a degree.</note> (where one part is equal to the Earth's radius), and that **DC** is 60 parts and 18 minutes, and **EF** is 2 parts and 51 minutes. Therefore, in the triangle **ACG**, the sides **GA** (1 part and 25 minutes) and **AC** (6 parts and 36 minutes) are given, along with the angle **CAG** contained by them.

Therefore, through the principles of plane triangles <term>triangulorum planorum|The mathematical rules for solving the sides and angles of triangles on a flat surface, as opposed to spherical geometry.</term>, the third side **CG** will be 6 parts and 7 minutes. Thus, the whole line **DCG** extended, or its equivalent **DCL**, will be 66 parts and 25 minutes. But **DCE** was 65 ½ parts. There remains an excess **EL** of approximately 55 ½ minutes. According to this given ratio, when **DCE** is 60 parts, **EF** will be 2 parts and 37 minutes, and the excess **EL** will be 46 minutes. To the extent that **EF** is 60 minutes, the excess **EL** will be nearly 18. We will record this in the seventh place of the Table <term>Canone|In this context, an astronomical table or reference list of calculated values.</term> opposite 60 degrees.

Similarly, we will demonstrate this regarding the perigee <term>perigæum|The point in an orbit where the celestial body is closest to the Earth.</term> **B**, where the second small epicycle is repeated as **MNO**. With the angle **MBN** at 60 degrees, the triangle **BCN** will be formed with the sides and angles given as before; similarly, the excess **MP** will be nearly 55 ½ minutes, where the Earth's radius is one. But since **DBM** is 55 parts and 8 minutes—which, if set to 60 parts, would make **MBO** 3 parts and 7 minutes—the excess **MP** is 55 minutes. Just as 3 parts and 8 minutes is to 55 minutes, so 60 is to nearly 18, which is the same as before, though they differ by a few seconds. In this way, we shall proceed with the rest, with which we will complete the eighth column of the Table. If we were to use the values set forth in the Table of corrections <term>prosthaphæresium|From the Greek 'prosthaphairesis,' meaning addition and subtraction; these are the corrections applied to the mean motion of a planet to find its true position.</term> instead of these, we would not commit an error, as they are almost the same and concern the smallest matters

<header>BOOK IV OF THE REVOLUTIONS.</header>

### On the calculation of the parallax of the Sun and Moon. Chapter 25.

We shall also briefly explain the method of calculating the parallaxes <note>Parallax is the difference in the apparent position of a celestial object when viewed from the surface of the Earth versus the center of the Earth.</note> of the Sun and Moon by means of the Table [Canon]. Indeed, by doubling the distance from the zenith <note>The "vertex" or zenith is the point in the sky directly above the observer. Doubling the distance is a step in Copernicus's specific trigonometric method.</note> of the Sun or Moon, we shall find the corresponding parallaxes in the table. For the Sun, this is done simply; for the Moon, however, it is done within its four limits. Using the Moon's motion—or its doubled distance from the Sun—we take the "first proportional minutes" <term>scrupula proportionum; these are factors used to interpolate between values in a table</term>. With these, we take the proportional parts of the difference between the first and last terms relative to 60. We always subtract these parts from the next following commutation <note>original: "commutatione," referring to the parallax shift</note>, and we always add the later parts to the value found in the penultimate limit. We will then have two rectified parallaxes of the Moon, one at apogee <note>The point in the orbit furthest from Earth.</note> and one at perigee <note>The point in the orbit closest to Earth.</note>, which the smaller epicycle <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used to explain complex orbits.</note> increases or decreases.

Then, using the lunar anomaly <note>The position of the Moon along its orbital path.</note>, we take the "last proportional minutes," from which we also derive a proportional part from the difference of the parallaxes just calculated. This part we always add to the first examined parallax (the one at apogee), and the resulting value will be the sought-after parallax of the Moon for that specific place and time, as seen in this example:

Suppose the distance of the Moon from the zenith is 54 degrees, the mean motion of the Moon is 15 degrees, and the equated anomaly is 100 degrees. I wish to find the lunar parallax from these values using the Table. I double the degrees of distance, making 108; to this, the Table shows a difference between the first and second limit of 1 minute and 48 seconds. The parallax of the second term is 42 minutes and 50 seconds; the parallax of the third limit is 50 minutes and 49 seconds. The difference between the third and fourth is 2 minutes and 46 seconds, which I shall note individually. The doubled motion of the Moon makes 30 degrees; with this, I find the first proportional minutes to be 5. Using these, I take the proportional part relative to 60, which results in 9 seconds from the first difference. I subtract these 9 seconds from the 42 minutes and 50 seconds of the parallax; there remain 42 minutes and 41 seconds. Similarly, for the second difference (which was 2 minutes and 46 seconds), the proportional part is 14 seconds. I add these to the 50 minutes and 49 seconds of the second parallax, making 51 minutes and 13 seconds. The difference between these two corrected parallaxes is 8 minutes and 32 seconds. After this, using the 100 degrees of equated anomaly, I find the final proportional minutes to be 34. Through these, I take the proportional part of the 8 minute 32 second difference, which is 4 minutes and 50 seconds.

### How the parallaxes of longitude and latitude are distinguished. Chapter 26.

The simple parallax—or the apparent shift between the Sun and the Moon—is distinguished into longitude and latitude by means of the circumferences and angles of intersecting circles: the zodiac <term>signifer; literally "sign-bearer," the circle of the ecliptic where the signs of the zodiac are located</term> and the circle passing through the poles of the horizon <note>This refers to the vertical circle of altitude that passes through the zenith.</note>. For it is evident that when this circle lies at right angles to the zodiac, it produces no parallax in longitude; instead, the entire shift passes into latitude, as the circles of latitude and altitude are then one and the same. On the other hand, when the zodiac happens to stand perpendicular to the horizon and coincides with the circle of altitude, then if the Moon is without latitude <note>Meaning the Moon is positioned exactly on the ecliptic line.</note>, it experiences no parallax other than in longitude. However, if it is shifted in latitude, it will not escape some change in longitude. For example:

[A geometric diagram consisting of a triangle labeled ADE with vertex A at its apex. A vertical line segment AC drops from vertex A, passing through point B, which marks the intersection with the horizontal base line DE, and extending further down to point C. Point D is at the left end of the horizontal base, and point E is at the right end.]

Let ABC be the zodiacal circle standing perpendicular to the horizon, and let A be the pole of the horizon <note>The zenith, or the point directly overhead for the observer.</note>. Therefore, the circle ABC will be the same as the altitude circle for a Moon lacking latitude, whose position is at B. Its total shift <term>commutatio; the term Copernicus often uses for the parallax shift</term> BC will be in longitude. But when it also has latitude, described by the circle DBE passing through the poles of the zodiac, and the Moon’s latitude is taken as DB or BE, it is clear that side AD or AE will not be equal to AB. Nor will the angle at D or E be a right angle, since DA and AE are not circles passing through the poles of DBE itself. Consequently, the shift will partake in some latitude, and even more so the closer the Moon is to the vertex <note>The closer the Moon is to the point directly overhead, the more the angles of these geometric circles change, affecting the parallax calculation.</note>. For while the base DE of triangle ADE remains the same, the shorter sides DA and AE will enclose more acute angles at the base. The further the Moon moves away from the vertex, the more these angles will resemble right angles. Now, let the Moon's altitude circle DBE be oblique to the zodiac ABC, with the Moon having no latitude—as in an ecliptic intersection <note>The point where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic or Sun's path.</note>...

Therefore, since in triangle *bef*, the angle *ebf* <note>Angle EBF is formed by the intersection of the circle of altitude and the circle of latitude.</note> is given (as shown above), and the angle at *f* is a right angle, and side *be* is also given. <margin>A vertical line labeled with points D, B, and C from top to bottom. A second line segment, labeled E, F, and A, intersects or meets the vertical line at point B.</margin>

But since *be*, *bf*, and *fe* differ only by a small and imperceptible amount from straight lines due to their shortness, we will not err if we use the right triangle as if it were a flat <term>rectilineo; a triangle made of straight lines rather than arcs on a sphere</term> triangle; because of this, the calculation becomes easy.

The case is more difficult when the Moon possesses latitude. For let the zodiac <term>signifer; literally "the sign-bearer," the path of the sun/ecliptic</term> *abc* be repeated, upon which the oblique circle *db* falls through the poles of the horizon. Let *b* be the position of the Moon in longitude, with the Northern latitude being *fb*, or the Southern latitude being *be*. From the summit of the horizon (the zenith), which is *d*, let the circles of altitude *dek* and *dfg* descend upon the Moon itself, in which the parallaxes <term>commutationes; the "shifts" or changes in position caused by parallax</term> are *ek* and *fg*. The true positions of the Moon in longitude and latitude will be at points *e* and *f*, but the seen <note>The "apparent" position as observed from the Earth's surface.</note> positions will be at *k* and *g*. From these points, let circumferences be drawn at right angles to the zodiac *abc*; these shall be *km* and *lg*.

<margin>A complex diagram of spherical trigonometry showing a top vertex D (the zenith) with two arcs, DK and DG, descending from it. Therefore, when the longitude and latitude of the Moon are established along with the latitude of the region, two sides *db* and *be* will be known in triangle *deb*, as well as the angle of intersection *abd*. When added to the right angle, the whole angle *dbe* is known, and therefore the remaining side *de*—along with the angle *deb*—will be given. Similarly, in triangle *dbf*, when the two sides *db* and *bf* are given along with the angle *dbf* (which remains after subtracting angle *abd* from a right angle), the side *df* will also be given along with the angle *dfb*. 

From each of these circumferences *de* and *df*, the parallax *ek* and *fg* is given by the Table <note>Copernicus refers here to his previously calculated tables of parallax.</note>, as well as the true distance of the Moon from the zenith, *de* or *df*. Likewise, the observed distances *dek* or *dfg* are found. Furthermore, in triangle *ebn* (formed by the intersection of *de* with the zodiac at point *n*), the angle *neb* is given, and *nbe* is a right angle; with the base *be* known, the remaining angle *bne* will be known, along with the remaining sides *bn* and *ne*. Similarly, in the whole triangle *nkm*, from the given angles at *m* and *n* and the whole side *ken*, the base *km* will be established. This is the observed Southern latitude of the Moon; the amount by which it exceeds *eb* is the parallax of latitude. The remaining side *nbm* is also given, from which if *nb* is subtracted, the remainder *bm* is the parallax of longitude. Just as also in the Northern triangle *bfc*, when the side *bf* is given with the angle *bfc*...

# NICHOLAS COPERNICUS

& *b* is known, the remaining sides *bl* and *lc* are given, as well as the remaining sides of the triangle *fgc* along with the remaining angle *c*. By subtracting *fg* from *fgc*, the side *gc* is left as a known side in the triangle *glc*. This triangle has two known angles, *lcg* and the right angle *clg*; because of this, the remaining sides *gl* and *lc* are given. Then, what remains from *bc* is *bl*, which is the parallax <note>original: "commutatio"; the shift in position due to the observer's viewpoint</note> in longitude, and *gl* is the apparent latitude. The parallax of this latitude is the difference between *bf* (the true latitude) and *gl*.

However, as you see, this calculation involves more labor than benefit, as it deals with such minute values. For it will be sufficient if we use the angle *abd* instead of *dcb*, and if we simply use the mean distances for *db* (as we did before for the arcs *de* and *ef*), ignoring the lunar latitude. No visible error will result from this, especially in the regions of the Northern climate. But in very Southern regions, where the Moon *b* happens to reach the zenith <note>The point directly overhead</note> while at its maximum latitude of five degrees, and with the Moon at its closest point to the Earth, the difference is nearly six minutes <note>original: "scrupulorum"; a 'scruple' or 'minute' is 1/60th of a degree</note>. In solar eclipses, however, where the latitude of the Moon cannot exceed one and a half degrees, the difference can only be about one and three-quarters minutes.

From these things, therefore, it is clear that to the true position of the Moon in the eastern quadrant of the zodiac <term>signifer; the "sign-bearer" or ecliptic path</term>, the parallax in longitude is always added, and in the western quadrant it is always subtracted, so that we may obtain the apparent longitude of the Moon. To find the apparent latitude, we use the parallax in latitude: if the true latitude and the parallax are in the same direction, they are added together; if they are in opposite directions, the smaller is subtracted from the larger, and the remainder is the apparent latitude in the direction of the larger value.

->### ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK IV.<-

The Moon was about to occult the bright star of the Hyades, which the Romans call Palilicium <note>original: "Palilicium"; this is the star Aldebaran</note>. Having waited for this, we saw the star close to the dark part of the lunar body, already hiding between the horns of the Moon at the fifth hour of the night. It was closer to the southern horn by nearly one-third of the lunar width or diameter. Since the star, according to calculation, was at 2° 52′ of Gemini with a southern latitude of 5 1/6°, it was clear that the apparent center of the Moon preceded the star by half a diameter. Therefore, its apparent position in longitude was 2° 36′ and in latitude about 5° 2′. It was, therefore, from the beginning of the years of Christ, 1497 Egyptian years, 76 days, and 23 hours at Bologna; but at Kraków, which is about 9° further east, it was 24 hours and 36 minutes, to which the equation <note>a correction for the difference between mean and solar time</note> adds 4 minutes. For the Sun was at 28 1/2° of Pisces. Thus, the equal motion of the Moon from the Sun was 74°, the equated anomaly <note>term: anomaly; the angular distance of a planet or the Moon from its apogee or perigee</note> was 111° 10′, the true position of the Moon was 3° 24′ of Gemini, and the southern latitude was 4° 35′. For the true motion of latitude was 203° 41′. At that time in Bologna, the 26th degree of Scorpio was rising, with an angle of 59 1/2°, and the Moon was 84° from the zenith of the horizon. The angle of the intersection of the circles of altitude and the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi"; the "sign-bearer" or ecliptic</note> was nearly 29°. The lunar parallax <note>the apparent shift in the Moon's position due to the observer's location on Earth</note> was 1 part: 51 minutes in longitude and 30 minutes in latitude. These values agree very closely with the observation, so that no one should doubt that our hypotheses and the results derived from them are correct.

### On investigating the true conjunctions and oppositions of the Sun and Moon. Chapter XXIX.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring a figure in profile, possibly a scholar or classical figure, seated within a square frame with architectural or celestial elements.</image-desc>

Once we have obtained, as has been said, the time of the mean conjunction or opposition of these heavenly bodies along with their motions, we must find their true distance—by which they either lead or follow one another—in order to find the true [conjunctions or oppositions]. For if the Moon is ahead of the Sun at the time of the [mean] conjunction or opposition, it is clear that the true alignment is yet to come; if the Sun [is ahead], the true alignment we seek has already passed. This will be made manifest by the prosthaphæresis <term>prosthaphæresis; from the Greek for "addition and subtraction," this is a correction value used to account for the difference between a body's average position and its actual position in its elliptical or eccentric orbit</term> of each.

For if the corrections are zero, or if they are equal and of the same type—meaning both are to be added or both are to be subtracted—it is evident that the true conjunctions or oppositions coincide with the mean ones at that same moment. If, however, they are unequal, the difference between them indicates their distance from each other, and shows which heavenly body leads or follows based on which one has the additive or subtractive correction. But when the corrections are in different directions <note>one additive and the other subtractive</note>, the body with the subtractive correction leads by even more, and the two values added together give the total distance between them. 

Based on this distance, we will estimate how many whole hours it might take for the Moon to traverse it, allowing two hours for every degree of distance. For example, if the distance is about 6 degrees, we will assume 12 hours for them. For this time interval thus established, we will seek the true "evection" <note>the lunar elongation or distance</note> of the Moon from the Sun. We can achieve this easily since we know the mean motion of the Moon is completed by one degree and one minute in just under two hours. 

The hourly motion of the anomaly <term>anomaly; the angular distance of the Moon from its furthest point from Earth (apogee), which determines its change in speed</term>, and its true motion near the New and Full Moon, is nearly 50 minutes <note>original: "scrupulorū" (scrupula); minutes of a degree</note>. In six hours, these produce a mean motion of 3 degrees and 3 minutes, and a true progression of the anomaly of 5 degrees. We will then look in the Table of Lunar Prosthaphæreses for the difference between the corrections themselves; we add this to the mean motion if the anomaly is in the lower part of the circle, or subtract it if in the upper part. For whatever is resulting or remaining is the true motion of the Moon in the estimated hours. If this motion is equal to the distance that existed previously, that is sufficient. Otherwise, we multiply the distance by the number of estimated hours and divide by this motion, or by the true hourly motion we have found.

<meta>catchword: simple</note>
