<page-num>137</page-num>
<header>OF THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK IV.</header>

If we divide the distance <note>original: "simplicẽ distantiā"—referring to the distance between the Sun and Moon at the moment of their average alignment</note> by the difference in their hourly speeds, the result will be the true difference in time, in hours and minutes, between the mean and true conjunction or opposition. We add this difference to the time of the mean conjunction or opposition if the Moon was ahead of the Sun (or ahead of the point diametrically opposite the Sun), or we subtract it if the Moon was behind. Thus, we will have the time of the true conjunction or opposition. 

Although we admit that the solar inequality <term>solar inequality; the variation in the Sun's apparent speed across the sky caused by the Earth's eccentric orbit</term> also adds or subtracts a small amount, it is rightly ignored. Indeed, in the entire calculation, even at the greatest distance <note>original: "elongatione"</note>—which extends over seven degrees—it cannot amount to even one minute of time. This method of determining the lunations <note>original: "taxandaru lunationū"—the period between two new moons</note> is more reliable. For those who rely solely on the Moon's hourly motion, which they call the hourly excess <note>original: "superationẽ horariā"—the amount the Moon's speed exceeds the Sun's</term>, are sometimes deceived and are frequently forced to repeat their calculations. For the Moon is changeable even from hour to hour and does not remain the same. 

Therefore, for the time of the true meeting <note>original: "coitus"—conjunction</note> or opposition, we will calculate the true motion of latitude <note>to determine the Moon's height relative to the Sun's path</note> to learn the Moon's actual latitude, and we will find the true position of the Sun from the Vernal Equinox—that is, the sign—which also allows us to understand the Moon's position, whether it is in the same place or opposite. And since this sort of time is understood as mean and uniform time relative to the meridian of Cracow <note>Copernicus lived and worked in Poland, making Cracow his primary reference point for time</note>, we will reduce it to "apparent" time <term>apparent time; time as measured by the actual position of the sun in the sky, which varies slightly from the steady ticking of a "mean" clock</term> by the method handed down above. 

If we wish to set these times for any place other than Cracow, we will consider its longitude. For every degree of longitude, we take 4 minutes of an hour; for every minute of longitude, we take 4 seconds of an hour. We add these to the Cracow time if the other place is further east, and subtract them if it is further west. The resulting remainder or sum will be the time of the conjunction or opposition of the Sun and Moon.

## How the eclipsable conjunctions and oppositions of the Sun and
## Moon are distinguished from others. Chapter XXX.

Whether an alignment will actually result in an eclipse is easily determined for the Moon. If its latitude is less than half the sum of the diameters of the Moon and the [Earth's] shadow, the Moon will undergo an eclipse; if it is greater, it will not. However, regarding the Sun, there is considerably more trouble, as the parallax <term>parallax; the apparent shift in an object's position when viewed from different locations</term> of both bodies interferes. Because of this, the visible conjunction often differs from the true one. When we have investigated...

...[once] we have [determined] what the parallax <note>original: "commutatio," referring to the shift in apparent position</note> is between the Sun and Moon in longitude at the time of the true conjunction, we will similarly seek the visible distance of the Moon from the Sun for the space of one hour preceding the true conjunction in the eastern quadrant of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi," the ecliptic or zodiacal circle</note>, or following it in the western quadrant. We do this so that we may understand how far the Moon is moved from the Sun in one hour according to its appearance <note>original: "secundum uisum," visibly as opposed to its theoretical "true" position</note>. Therefore, when we have divided that parallax of longitude by this hourly motion, we will have the difference in time between the true and the visible meeting <note>original: "coitū," conjunction</note>.

When this difference is subtracted from the time of the true conjunction in the eastern part of the zodiac, or added in the western part (for in the east the visible conjunction precedes the true, while in the west it follows), the result will be the sought-after time of the visible conjunction. At this time, therefore, we will calculate the visible latitude of the Moon from the Sun—that is, the distance between the centers of the Sun and Moon at the visible conjunction—after subtracting the parallax of the Sun. If this latitude is greater than half the combined diameters of the Sun and Moon, the Sun will not undergo an eclipse; if it is less, it will. From this, it is clear that if the Moon at the time of true conjunction does not have any parallax in longitude, then the visible and the true meeting <note>original: "copula"</note> will be one and the same; this occurs around the ninetieth degree of the zodiac, measured from the east or west <note>the "nonagesimal," the highest point of the ecliptic above the horizon</note>.

### How Great the Eclipse of the Sun and Moon Shall Be. Chapter XXXI.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial P featuring a child or cherub-like figure holding onto foliate or architectural scrolls.</image-desc>
Once we have recognized that the Sun or Moon will be eclipsed, we will also easily know how great their eclipse will be. For the Sun, we use the visible latitude between the Sun and Moon at the time of the visible conjunction. If we subtract this latitude from half the sum of the diameters of the Sun and Moon, the remainder is the portion of the Sun's diameter that will be eclipsed. When we multiply this by twelve and divide the result by the Sun's diameter, we will have the number of digits <term>digits; a traditional unit of eclipse magnitude equal to one-twelfth of the diameter of the celestial body</term> eclipsed. If there is no latitude between the Sun and Moon, the entire Sun will be eclipsed, or as much of it as the Moon is able to cover. We proceed in almost the same way for a lunar eclipse, except that instead of visible latitude, we use its simple latitude <note>since the Moon's parallax is much larger than the Sun's, lunar eclipses are calculated using its "true" position relative to Earth's shadow</note>. When this is taken from half the sum of the diameters of the Moon and the shadow, the remainder is the part of the Moon eclipsed, provided the latitude...

### On predicting how long the eclipse will last. Chapter XXXII.

It remains to see how long the eclipse will last. Here it should be noted that we use the arcs that occur between the Sun, the Moon, and the shadow as if they were straight lines, because of their small size, in which they seem to differ in no way from a straight line. Therefore, taking the center of the Sun or the shadow at point A, and the line BC for the passage of the Moon—whose center is touching the Sun or the shadow at the beginning of its falling-in <note>The start of the eclipse.</note> at B, and at the end of its clearing-out at C—let AB and AC be connected, and let the perpendicular AD be dropped to BC itself. It is manifest that when the center of the Moon is at D, it will be the middle of the eclipse; for AD is the shortest of the other lines descending from A, and BD

By connecting AB and AF, it will be shown in the same way as before that ED and DF are the halves of the stay in darkness <note>original: "mora in tenebris"; this refers to the duration of totality when the Moon is completely within the Earth's shadow.</note>, because AD is the known latitude of the Moon, and AE (or AF), which is the radius of the shadow, is greater than the radius of the Moon. Therefore, ED or DF will be established, which, when divided again by the true hourly motion of the Moon, gives us the time of the half-duration that was sought. 

However, it must be noted here that as the Moon moves in its own orbit, it does not cross segments of the zodiac’s longitude <note>The coordinate measuring a celestial body's position along the ecliptic.</note> that are exactly equal to the segments in its own path, as measured through the circles passing through the poles of the zodiac. Yet the difference is very slight; even at the total distance of 12 degrees from the ecliptic intersection <note>The "ecliptic section" refers to the nodes where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's path; eclipses only occur near these points.</note>—which is the furthest limit for eclipses of the Sun and Moon—the circumferences of these orbits do not differ by more than two minutes <term>scruples|From the Latin "scrupulus" (a small pebble), used here to mean "minutes of arc," or 1/60th of a degree.</term>, which would account for only one-fifteenth part of an hour. For this reason, we often use one in place of the other as if they were the same. We also use the same latitude for the Moon at the beginning and end of the eclipse as we do at the middle of the eclipse, even though the Moon’s latitude is always increasing or decreasing. Because of this, the spaces of the falling-in <term>incidentia|The initial phase of an eclipse as the body enters the shadow or begins to be covered.</term> and the clearing-out <term>expurgatio|The final phase of an eclipse as the body leaves the shadow or is uncovered.</term>

<image-desc>

(the Moon). A vertical axis B-E-G-D-I-F passes through the centers E (of the upper circle) and I (of the lower circle). B is the top point of the upper circle and F is the bottom point of the lower circle. G is the bottom point of the upper circle and D is the top point of the lower circle. are not perfectly equal, but the difference is so small that it would seem a waste of time to examine it more precisely. In this way, the times, durations, and magnitudes of eclipses have been explained according to their diameters. 

But since it is the opinion of many that the obscured parts should be determined not by their diameters but by their surface areas—for it is the surfaces that are obscured, not the lines—let ABCD be the circle of the Sun or of the shadow, with its center at E, and let AFCG be the circle of the Moon, with its center at I. Let these intersect each other at points A and C, and let a straight line BEIF be drawn through both centers. Let AE, EC, IA, and IC be connected, and let AKC be drawn at right angles to BF. We wish to find from these how large the obscured surface area ADCG is, and how many twelfths <note>The author is referring to "digits of area," a measurement where the total surface of the disk is divided into twelve parts, as opposed to dividing the diameter into twelve parts.</note> of the whole plane of the Sun's or Moon's disk are missing in that part. Since, therefore, the radii AE and AI of both disks are given from previous calculations, as well as the distance between the centers (the lunar latitude EI), we have a

<meta>This page concludes Book IV, finalizing the geometric calculations for the area of an eclipse. Copernicus transitions from calculating the duration of an eclipse (linear time) to calculating the "obscuration," or the specific area of the celestial body covered by a shadow, using the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter.</meta>

### REVOLUTIONS BOOK IV

The triangle AEI has sides of known lengths, and therefore, as demonstrated previously, its angles are also known; triangle EIC is similar and equal to it. Consequently, the arcs ADC and AGC are known in terms of the 360 degrees that make up a full circle. Furthermore, Archimedes of Syracuse <note>A Greek mathematician (c. 287 – c. 212 BC) famous for his work on the geometry of spheres and circles.</note> established in his work *On the Measurement of a Circle* that the ratio of the circumference to the diameter is less than 3 1/7 <note>original: "triplā sesquiseptimam"</note> but greater than 3 10/71 <note>original: "triplam superpartientem septuagesimas primas decē"</note>. Between these two values, Ptolemy adopts a middle value, where the ratio is 3 units, 8 minutes, and 30 seconds to 1 <note>This is Ptolemy’s sexagesimal approximation of Pi (3 + 8/60 + 30/3600 ≈ 3.14166).</note>. 

Using this same ratio, the arcs AGC and ADC will also be known in the same units as the diameters AB and AI. The areas contained under BA and AD, and under IA and AG, are equal to the sectors ABC and AIC respectively. Moreover, for the isosceles <note>A triangle with at least two equal sides.</note> triangles ABC and AIC, the common base AKC and the perpendicular heights EK and KI are given. Therefore, the area resulting from AK and KG is given, which is the area of triangle ABC; similarly, the area from AK and KI provides the area of triangle ACI. 

When both triangles are subtracted from their respective circular sectors, the circular segments AFC and ACD remain, which together constitute the total area ADCG that we sought. Furthermore, the entire area of the circle—whether contained by BE and BAD in a solar eclipse, or by FI and FAG in a lunar eclipse—is given. Thus, it will be clear how many digits <term>unciarum|Literally "twelfths" or "inches." In astronomy, a "digit" is 1/12th of the diameter of the Sun or Moon, used here to quantify the area of the eclipsed portion.</term> the area ADCG represents, showing how much is missing from the full circle of the Sun or Moon. Let these remarks concerning the Moon suffice for now, as these matters have been treated more extensively by others; for we are now hastening toward the revolutions of the remaining five stars <note>In the 16th century, the "stars" (siderum) referred to the five visible planets: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, which will be discussed in the following books.

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS OF NICOLAUS COPERNICUS
## BOOK FIVE.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'H' set within a square frame, featuring a decorative background of scrolling vines and foliage.</image-desc>So far, we have completed our account of the revolutions of the Earth around the Sun, and of the Moon around the Earth. We now approach the movements of the five wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" are the planets: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury.</note>. The mobility of the Earth itself connects the order and the sizes of their spheres with a marvelous harmony and a certain symmetry, as we briefly reviewed in the first book when we showed that these spheres do not have their centers around the Earth, but rather around the Sun. It remains, therefore, for us to demonstrate all these things individually and more clearly, and to fulfill our promises as far as we are able, especially by applying the observable evidence that we have received both from the ancients and from our own times, by which the logic of their movements may be held with greater certainty. In Plato’s *Timaeus* <note>A famous philosophical dialogue by Plato (c. 427–347 BC) that discusses the nature of the physical world and the cosmos.</note>, these five stars are named according to their individual appearances. Saturn is called *Phaenon*, as if you were to say "shining" or "appearing," for it is least hidden by the others and emerges more quickly after being concealed by the Sun. Jupiter is *Phaeton*, from its brilliance. Mars is *Pyrois*, from its fiery glow. Venus is sometimes called *Phosphoros* <note>original: "φωσφóρος"</note> and sometimes *Hesperos* <note>original: "ἕσπερος"</note>, which is to say "Light-bringer" and "Evening-star," depending on whether it shines in the morning or the evening. Finally, Mercury is *Stilbon*, from its glittering and vibrating light. These planets are also carried in longitude and latitude <note>In astronomy, longitude refers to the position along the ecliptic (the Sun's path), and latitude refers to the distance north or south of that path.</note> with a greater variation than the Moon.

### On their revolutions and mean motions. Chapter 1.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'B' set within a square frame, featuring a decorative background of scrolling floral patterns.</image-desc>Two movements in longitude appear quite differently in these planets. One is due to the movement of the Earth, which we have already discussed. The other is proper to each planet. It has been decided, not without reason, to call the first the "motion of parallax" <note>original: "motum commutationis". This refers to the apparent change in a planet's position caused by the Earth's own movement.</note>, since it is this motion which makes all of them appear to have stations, progressions, and regressions <meta>catchword: makes appear</meta>

<summary>Copernicus introduces the fifth book, shifting his focus to the five planets and explaining that their complex observed movements are actually a result of the Earth's own motion around the Sun. He adopts the classical Greek names for the planets from Plato and introduces the concept of "parallax" to explain why planets appear to stop or move backward in the sky.</summary>
<keywords>planetary motion, heliocentrism, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury, parallax, celestial longitude, Timaeus</keywords>

--- Page 283 ---
<meta>This page continues Copernicus's introduction to Book V, where he transitions from the motion of the Earth and Moon to the movements of the five planets (Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury). He is explaining how the Earth's own movement creates the illusion of planetary retrograde motion.</meta>

->REVOLUTIONS, BOOK V.<-
L ij

it happens to appear so, not because the planet is thus distracted—for it always proceeds in its own motion—but because it appears this way by means of <term>commutation</term> <note>Latin: *commutatio*. Copernicus uses this term to describe the apparent change in a planet's position caused by the Earth’s own orbital motion. Today, we call this effect "parallax."</note>, which the motion of the Earth effects according to the difference and size of those orbits. It is clear, therefore, that the true places of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars only become visible to us when they are <term>rising at sunset</term> <note>original Greek: *ἀκρονύκται* (akronyktai). This refers to a planet being in "opposition," meaning it is directly opposite the Sun from the Earth's perspective.</note>, which happens nearly in the middle of their backward movements. For at that time, they coincide in a straight line with the mean position of the Sun, having been stripped of that commutation. Furthermore, in Venus and Mercury, the reasoning is different. For they are hidden at that time, being <term>under the sun's rays</term> <note>original: *hypaugi*. From the Greek meaning "under the light," referring to planets so close to the Sun that they are lost in its glare.</note>, and they show only the excursions they make to either side of the Sun, so that they are never found without this commutation. Therefore, each planet has its own private revolution of commutation—I mean the motion of the Earth relative to the planet, which they explain between themselves. For we say the motion of commutation is nothing else than that in which the motion of the Earth exceeds their motion (as in Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars) or is exceeded by it (as in Venus and Mercury).

Since, however, such periods of commutation are found to be unequal by a manifest difference, the ancients recognized that the motions of those stars are also unequal, and have <term>apsides</term> <note>The points in an orbit where a planet is at its maximum or minimum distance from the center of its motion.</note> of circles to which their inequality returns; they believed these apsides had perpetual seats in the sphere of the fixed stars. By this argument, the way was opened to learning their mean motions and equal periods. For when they had a record handed down of a planet’s place according to a certain distance from the Sun and a fixed star, and after an interval of time found the star itself had reached the same place with a similar distance from the Sun, the planet was seen to have completed its entire inequality, and to have returned in all things to its prior state relative to the Earth. And so, through the time that passed, they calculated the number of full and equal revolutions, and from these, the specific motions of the star. Ptolemy reviewed these circuits under the number of solar years, just as he admits to have received them from Hipparchus <note>Hipparchus (c. 190–120 BC) was a Greek astronomer whose observations formed the basis for much of Ptolemy's later work.</note>. However, he intends "solar years" to be understood as those measured from the equinox or solstice. But it has now become clear that such years are not quite equal; therefore, we shall use those years taken from the fixed stars, by which we have also restored the motions of these five stars more correctly, just as in our own time...

<meta>This page continues Copernicus's detailed calculations of planetary movements. Having established that the Earth’s motion creates an apparent "commutation" (parallax) for the other planets, he now provides the specific ratios and time periods for Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury to reconcile their observed positions with his sun-centered model.</meta>

### NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...we find that something was missing from them, or was in excess, in this manner. For in the case of Saturn, the Earth completes fifty-seven revolutions—this is what we called the motion of <term>commutation</term> <note>Latin: *motum commutationis*. This is the apparent change in a planet's position caused by the Earth moving in its own orbit. In modern astronomy, this relates to the "synodic period."</note>—in **69** of our solar years, one day, **7** <term>minutes</term> <note>Latin: *scrupulis primis*. Literally "first small parts," or 1/60th of a degree/hour. Copernicus uses a sexagesimal (base-60) system for all measurements.</note>, and approximately **18** <term>seconds</term> <note>Latin: *secundis*. "Second small parts," or 1/60th of a minute.</note>. In this time, the planet completes two of its own proper circuits, with the addition of one degree, approximately **5** minutes, and **50** seconds. Jupiter is overtaken by the Earth **65** times in **71** solar years, minus **5** days, **54** minutes, and **13** seconds; in this interval, the planet revolves six times, falling short by **5** degrees, **41** minutes, and **32** seconds. For Mars, the revolutions of commutation are **37** in **79** solar years, two days, **24** minutes, and **45** seconds. In this time, the planet completes **42** periods in its own motion, adding **2** degrees, **21** minutes, and **43** seconds. Venus exceeds the motion of the Earth five times in **8** solar years, minus **2** days, **26** minutes, and **44** seconds. Certainly, through <note>original: *p*, an abbreviation for *per*</note> this time it circles the Sun **13** times, minus two degrees, **24** minutes, and **29** seconds. Finally <note>original: *demum*, abbreviated in text</note>, Mercury makes **145** periods of commutation in **46** solar years, with the addition of one day and **25** minutes; by these [periods] it also exceeds the motion of the Earth, with which it returns around the Sun one hundred ninety-one times, adding **21** minutes and **53** seconds.

Therefore, the individual circuits of commutation for each [planet] are as follows:
*   For Saturn: **378** days, **5** minutes, **32** seconds, and **42** <term>thirds</term> <note>Latin: *tertijs*. 1/60th of a second.</note>.
*   For Jupiter: **399** days, **54** minutes, **3** seconds, and **58** thirds.
*   For Mars: **779** days, **56** minutes, **13** seconds, and **55** thirds.
*   For Venus: **583** days, **55** minutes, **17** seconds, and **50** thirds.
*   For Mercury: **115** days, **52** minutes, **38** seconds, and **53** thirds.

When we have resolved these into the degrees of a circle and multiplied them by **365**, and divided by the number of their days and minutes, we shall have the annual motion:
*   Of Saturn: **347** degrees, **32** minutes, **3** seconds, **9** thirds, and **4** fourths.
*   Of Jupiter: **329** degrees, **25** minutes, **8** seconds, **15** thirds, and **6** fourths.
*   Of Mars: **168** degrees, **28** minutes, **30** seconds, **36** thirds, and **4** fourths.
*   Of Venus: **225** degrees, **1** minute, **45** seconds, **3** thirds, and **40** fourths.
*   Of Mercury, after three revolutions: **53** degrees, **57** minutes, **23** seconds, **6** thirds, and **30** fourths.

### REVOLUTIONS BOOK V.

...the three hundred sixty-fifth part <note>A 365th part of the annual motion represents the daily motion of the planet.</note> is the **daily motion**. 

For **Saturn**, it is 57 <term>minutes</term> <note>Latin: *scrupula*. Copernicus uses a sexagesimal (base-60) system. A "minute" here is 1/60th of a degree, followed by seconds (1/60th of a minute), thirds, and fourths.</note>, 7 [seconds], 43 [thirds], 5 [fourths]. 
For **Jupiter**, 54 minutes, 9 [seconds], 3 [thirds], 49 [fourths]. 
For **Mars**, 27 minutes, 41 [seconds], 40 [thirds], 22 [fourths]. 
For **Venus**, 36 minutes, 59 [seconds], 28 [thirds], 35 [fourths]. 
For **Mercury**, 3 degrees, 6 minutes, 23 [seconds], 13 [thirds], 40 [fourths]. 

These are set out in the following tables, modeled after the <term>mean motions</term> <note>The average speed of a planet, ignoring the slight speeding up and slowing down caused by its elliptical path.</note> of the Sun and Moon. However, we have considered it superfluous to expand upon their own "proper motions" <note>The actual orbital motion of the planet around the Sun, as opposed to the "motion of commutation" which is the apparent motion caused by the Earth's movement.</note> in this same way. For those motions are established by subtracting these values from the mean motion of the Sun, which they compose, as we have already stated. 

But if someone is not content with this, they may calculate them according to their own pleasure. For the **annual proper motion** of Saturn relative to the sphere of the <term>fixed stars</term> <note>original: *non errantium stellarum sphaeram*. Literally "the sphere of the non-wandering stars."</note> is 12 degrees, 12 minutes, 45 seconds, 57 thirds, 24 fourths. 
For Jupiter: 30 degrees, 19 minutes, 40 seconds, 51 thirds, 58 fourths. 
For Mars: 191 degrees, 16 minutes, 18 seconds, 30 thirds, 36 fourths. 

Regarding **Venus** and **Mercury**, however, since their own proper motions are not apparent to us <note>Because Venus and Mercury are "inner" planets, their individual orbital progress is tied closely to our view of the Sun.</note>, the motion of the Sun itself serves in their place and provides the means by which their appearances are understood and demonstrated, as seen below.

# NICHOLAS COPERNICUS

### Demonstration of the Uniformity and Appearance of These Stars, According to the Opinion of the Ancients. Chapter II.

Since their mean motions <note>Mean motion refers to the average speed of a planet, assuming it moves in a perfect, centered circle.</note> are as previously described, let us now turn to their apparent inequality. The ancient mathematicians, who held that the Earth was immobile, imagined for Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, and Venus a system of epicycles on eccentrics <term>eccentrepicyclos: a model where a planet moves on a small circle (epicycle), which itself moves along a larger circle (eccentric) whose center is not the Earth</term>. Furthermore, they imagined another eccentric circle according to which the epicycle—and the planet within that epicycle—would move uniformly.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a large circle representing an eccentric orbit with a vertical diameter labeled A at the top and B at the bottom. Point C is the center of this circle. Below it on the diameter is point E, and further down is point D (the center of the Earth). A second circle (epicycle) is drawn centered at point H on a line passing through C. Several lines (IHC and LHME) connect points on the epicycle to centers C and E. Points F and G mark the intersection of an outer concentric circle with the vertical axis.</image-desc>

For example, let there be an eccentric circle AB with center C. Its diameter is ACB, upon which lies the center of the Earth, D, so that the apogee <note>original: "apogæum" — the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</note> is at A and the perigee <note>original: "perigæum" — the point in an orbit closest to the Earth</note> is at B. Let line DC be divided equally at point E. With E as the center, let another eccentric circle FG be described, equal to the first. On this circle, let the center of an epicycle IK be placed at any point H, and let the straight line IHC be drawn through its center, as well as the line LHME. 

Furthermore, let these eccentrics be understood as inclined to the plane of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi" — the "sign-bearer" or the path of the sun and planets through the constellations</note>, and the epicycle inclined to the plane of the eccentric, because of the latitudes <note>The vertical "up and down" motion of the planets relative to the Earth's orbital plane.</note> which the planet creates; however, for the sake of the convenience of this demonstration, let us treat them as if they were in a single plane. They [the ancients] say, therefore, that this whole plane moves around point D (the center of the circle of the signs) along with points B and C, according to the motion of the fixed stars. By this, they mean to imply that these points have fixed positions in the sphere of the non-wandering stars. They also say that the epicycle moves in the order of the signs <note>Eastward motion</note> along the circle FHG, but according to the line IHC, and the star itself revolves uniformly within the epicycle IK. 

However, it is established that the uniformity of the epicycle's motion must occur relative to point E (the center of its "deferent" or carrying circle), and the revolution of the planet must occur relative to the line LME. They therefore concede that, in this case, the uniformity of a circular motion can occur around a center other than its own. Similarly, they claim this occurs even more so in the case of Mercury. But we have already sufficiently refuted this idea regarding the Moon. These and similar problems provided us the opportunity to think about the mobility of the Earth and other ways in which uniformity and the principles of the art of astronomy might be preserved, and the reason for the apparent inequality might be rendered more consistent.

->General<-

He argues that these inconsistencies led him to propose the Earth's motion as a more mathematically sound alternative.</summary>

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK V.

### General demonstration of the apparent inequality caused by the Earth’s motion. Chapter III.

There being two causes for the apparent inequality <note>By "inequality," Copernicus means the observed changes in speed and direction (like retrograde motion) that make planetary orbits look irregular.</note> of a planet's uniform motion—one due to the Earth's motion and the other due to the planet's own motion—we shall explain both generally and separately with a visual demonstration, so they may be better distinguished from one another, beginning with the one that affects all of them due to the Earth's motion. 

And first regarding Venus and Mercury, which are contained within the Earth's circle. Let the eccentric circle be AB, centered at C, which the center of the Earth describes in its annual circuit, according to the method delivered above. Now let us assume for a moment that the planet had no other inequality except this one; this would occur if we made its orbit, say DEB, homocentric <term>homocentric: having the same center</term> to AB. This circle represents either Venus or Mercury, which, because of its latitude <note>In historical astronomy, "latitude" refers to the north-south position of a celestial body relative to the ecliptic, or the Earth's orbital plane.</note>, must be tilted relative to AB. 

But for the sake of a simpler demonstration, let them be imagined as if they were in the same plane. Let the Earth be at point A, from which the lines of sight AFL and AGM are drawn, touching the planet’s circle at points F and G, with diameter ACB being common to both. Let the motion of both—I mean the Earth and the planet—be in the same direction, that is, in succession <note>original: "in consequentia" — moving in the order of the signs of the Zodiac (west to east).</note>, but with the planet moving faster than the Earth. 

Therefore, the center C and the line ACB will appear to move according to the mean motion of the Sun, with the eye being carried along at point A. The star <note>Copernicus frequently uses "sidus" or "stella" (star) to refer to any celestial body, including planets.</note> on circle DFG will traverse the arc FDG in succession in a longer time than it takes to traverse the remaining arc GEF in precedence <note>original: "in præcedentia" — moving against the order of the Zodiac signs; this is retrograde motion.</note>. In the first case, add the entire angle FAG to the mean motion of the Sun; in the second, subtract it. Therefore, when the subtractive motion of the star—especially around the perigee <note>The point in the orbit where the planet is closest to the observer.</note> E—is greater than the additive motion of C (as the star overtakes the Earth), it seems to move backward relative to A. This happens for those stars where the ratio of line CE to line AE is greater than the ratio of the Earth's motion at A to the planet's course, according to the demonstrations of Apollonius of Perga <note>Apollonius was a 3rd-century BC Greek mathematician whose work on epicycles and eccentrics laid the groundwork for Ptolemaic and Copernican astronomy.</note>, as will be mentioned later. But where the subtractive motion is equal to the additive motion, they cancel each other out [each other...]

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a large outer circle (the Earth's orbit) and a smaller inner circle (the planet's orbit). The center is labeled C. Point A represents the Earth at the bottom of the diameter. Tangent lines AFL and AGM extend from the Earth (A) to the edges of the planet's orbit at F and G. Points D and E mark the top and bottom of the planet's orbit along the central axis.</image-desc>

<summary>Copernicus provides a geometric proof for how the Earth's motion creates the illusion of irregular planetary speed and retrograde motion, focusing specifically on the inner planets, Venus and Mercury.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the geometric proof of how the Earth's annual motion creates the illusion of planetary "stations" (stopping) and "retrogradations" (moving backward). Copernicus is transitioning from discussing the inner planets (Venus and Mercury) to the superior planets (Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars).</meta>

->NICHOLAS COPERNICUS<-

to one another, it will appear to stand still, all of which matches the appearances. If, therefore, there had been no other variation in the motion of the planet, as Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Perga (c. 240 BC) was a Greek mathematician who proposed the use of epicycles and eccentrics, which Copernicus is here attempting to simplify using the Earth's motion.</note> believed, these things could have sufficed. But the greatest elongations from the mean position of the Sun—which are understood by the angles FAE and GAE, occurring in the morning and evening for these stars—are not found to be equal everywhere, neither in relation to each other, nor when taken together. This leads to the evident conclusion that their paths are not in circles concentric <term>homocentric: having the same center</term> with the Earth's orbit, but in certain others by which they produce a second variation. The same is also demonstrated for the three superior planets—Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars—which surround the Earth on all sides. For, repeating the previous circle of the Earth, let an outer concentric circle DB be assumed, as if in the same plane, in which 

->[IMAGE: A geometric diagram showing a small inner circle representing the Earth's orbit around center C, and a point D representing a superior planet. Lines DF and DG are tangents to the Earth's orbit. The diameter is labeled DACBE.]<-

the position of the planet is taken at any point, marked D. From this point, let straight lines DF and DG be drawn, touching the Earth's orbit at points F and G, with DACBE as the common diameter. It is clear that from position A alone, the true position of the planet will appear on line DE, representing the mean motion of the Sun, at which time the planet is "acronychal" <term>acronychal: from the Greek 'akronykos,' referring to a planet rising at sunset, being in opposition to the Sun, and thus closest to Earth</term> and at its nearest point to Earth. For at the opposite point B, with the Earth located there, although it is on the same line, the planet will be least visible, having become "hypaugus" <term>hypaugus: a term for a planet being hidden or 'under the rays' of the Sun's glare during conjunction</term> because of its proximity to the Sun at that position. But because the Earth’s own path is larger, whereby it exceeds the motion of the planet, through the "apogeal" <note>original: "apogæam"; here meaning the arc furthest from the planet's perspective</note> circumference FBG, it will seem to add the entire angle GDF to the motion of the star; conversely, in the remaining arc GAF, it will seem to subtract that same angle. However, this occurs in a shorter time along the smaller arc GAF. And where the subtractive motion of the Earth exceeds the additive motion of the star—especially around point A—the star will seem to be left behind by the Earth and move "into the preceding signs" <note>This refers to retrograde motion, where a planet appears to move backward against the background of the stars.</note>, and it will appear to stand still at the point where the difference between these contrary motions is least to the sight. Thus, it is again manifest that all these things occur through the single motion of the Earth, which the ancients sought to explain through the epicycles <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; a complex tool of Ptolemaic astronomy</term> of each individual planet. But since the motion of the star is not found to be uniform (contrary to the opinion of Apollonius and the ancients), as revealed by the Earth's uniform revolution relative to the star, the planets are therefore not carried in a concentric circle, but in another way, which we shall demonstrate immediately.

### In what ways the proper motions of the wandering stars appear unequal. Chapter 4.

Since the proper motions <note>The individual movement of a planet against the background of the stars.</note> of the wandering stars <note>original: "errantium" — the word "planet" comes from the Greek word for "wanderer."</note> in longitude follow almost the same pattern—except for Mercury, who seems to differ from them—those four will be treated together. A different place has been assigned to Mercury. Because the ancients placed a single motion in two eccentrics (as has been recounted), we believe there are two equal motions by which the appearance of inequality is composed, 
<column-break/>
whether by an eccentric on an eccentric, or by an epicycle <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one</term> on an epicycle, or even by a mixture of an eccentric and an epicycle, which can produce the same inequality, as we demonstrated above regarding the Sun and Moon. Therefore, let there be an eccentric circle AB around center C, with the diameter ACB representing the mean position of the Sun <note>Copernicus uses the "mean Sun" as the reference point for the center of the universe.</note> passing through the highest and lowest apsides <term>apsis: the highest (apogee) or lowest (perigee) point in an orbit</term> of the planet, in which the center of the Earth's orbit is D, positioned at the highest apse A. 

<image-desc>An astronomical diagram illustrating a geometric model of planetary motion. It features a large main circle (the deferent) with center C and a vertical diameter ACB. Below the center C is point D, representing the center of the Earth's orbit. At the top of the large circle (point A), a smaller circle (epicycle) is drawn and labeled with points E and F. On the left side, another epicycle is centered on point G and labeled with points H and I. The diagram is crisscrossed with several lines connecting labeled points including N, M, S, T, O, P, K, and L, which serve to calculate the variations and inequalities in planetary movement.</image-desc>

At a distance of a third part of CD, let an epicycle EF be described, in whose perigee <note>original: "perigæo" — the point of the epicycle closest to its center of rotation.</note>, which is F, the planet is placed. Furthermore, let the motion of the epicycle along the eccentric AB be in the order of the signs <note>original: "in consequentia" — this indicates prograde motion, moving forward through the zodiac.</note>. Truly, the motion of the planet in the upper circumference of the epicycle is similarly in...

<summary>Copernicus explains that the perceived unequal speeds of the planets (except Mercury) can be modeled using a combination of circular motions, specifically through epicycles and eccentric orbits. He introduces a geometric diagram to demonstrate how these combined motions account for the planet's varying distance and speed relative to the Earth's orbit.</summary>

--- Page 300 ---
<meta>This page continues the geometric demonstration of planetary movement. The catchword from the previous page "atur au=" likely completes a word such as "sequatur autem" (let it follow however), leading into the description of the directions of motion.</meta>

->NICOLAI COPERNICI<-

[moving] in the order of the signs <note>original: "consequentia" — moving forward through the zodiac (Eastward).</note>, and in the rest toward the preceding signs <note>original: "præcedentia" — moving backward (Westward), often called retrograde.</note>, and for both the epicycle, I say, and the planet in equal revolutions with each other. It will happen, therefore, that when the epicycle is at the highest apse <term>apse: the highest or lowest point in an orbit</term> of the eccentric, and the planet is at the perigee <term>perigee: the point in an orbit closest to the center</term> of the epicycle from the opposite side, they will be exchanged into opposite parts with each other, once each has completed its half-circle [hemicyclium]. But in both middle quadrants, each will have its middle apse; and then only the diameter of the epicycle will be along the line AB, and again, when these are halved, it will be perpendicular to the same line AB. Furthermore, it is always nodding toward and away <note>Copernicus is describing a "libration" or oscillating movement.</note>, all of which are easily understood from the sequence of their motions.

From this it will also be demonstrated that the star <note>original: "sidus" — while we call them planets today, Copernicus often uses "star" or "wandering star."</note>, by this combined motion, does not describe a perfect circle according to the opinion of the ancient mathematicians, though the difference is imperceptible. For let the same epicycle be repeated at center B, which shall be KL. And having taken a quadrant of the circle AG, let there be an epicycle HI at point G itself; and with CD divided into three parts, let CM be one-third, equal to GI itself. Let GC and IM be connected, intersecting each other at Q. Therefore, since the circumference AG is similar to the circumference HI by the rule, and the angle which is under ACG is a right angle, then the angle HGI is also a right angle. And those angles at the vertex Q are also equal; therefore, the triangles GIQ and QCM are equiangular, but also of equal sides, one to the other. Since the base GI is assumed equal to the base CM, the side QI is greater than GQ, just as QM is greater than QC. Therefore, the whole IQM is greater than the whole GQC. But FM, ML, AC, and CG are equal to each other. Therefore, a circle described around center M through the points F and L—and thus equal to the circle AB—will cut the line IM. In the same way, it will be demonstrated from the opposite side and in the other quadrant. The planet, therefore, through the equal motions of the epicycle on the eccentric, and the planet itself within the epicycle, does not describe a perfect circle, but something like it, which was to be demonstrated.

Now let the annual orbit of the Earth be described around center D, which shall be NO, and let IDR be extended; moreover, let PDS be parallel to CG. ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK 5.

[Move]s <note>The text continues from the previous page: "Let the first epicycle move..."</note> forward in the order of the signs <note>original: "in consequentia" — moving Eastward through the zodiac.</note>, and the second moves just as much in the opposite direction, upon which finally the planet is reflected by a doubled motion, the same results that we have already described will occur. This is not much different than what we noted regarding the Moon, or indeed through any of the other methods mentioned above. But we have chosen here the epicycle of an eccentric <term>eccentric: a circular orbit where the center of the orbit is not the center of the Earth/Universe</term>, because while the distance between the Sun and the center remains constant, the point D is found to have changed in the meantime, as was shown in the appearances of the Sun. Since the other planets do not follow this change in the same way, it is necessary that some difference follows in them, which, although very slight, is perceived in Mars and Venus. Therefore, we shall henceforth demonstrate from observations that these hypotheses are sufficient for the appearances, and we shall do this first for Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars. In these cases, the most important and most difficult task is to find the location of the apogee <term>apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from the center</term> and the distance CD <note>The distance between the center of the planet's orbit and the center of the Earth's orbit.</note>, since through these the rest are easily demonstrated. In these matters, we shall use almost the same method we used for the Moon. Namely, by comparing three ancient solar oppositions to three new ones, which the Greeks call *acronychal* <note>original: "acronychias" — a planet's rising at sunset, meaning it is directly opposite the Sun and visible all night.</note> flashes. We call them the "deeps of the night," specifically when the planet falls upon the straight line of the Sun's mean motion, being opposite the Sun; at this point, all that difference introduced by the motion of the Earth is stripped away. Indeed, such positions are captured from observations using astrolabe instruments, as explained above, with the calculation of the Sun also applied until it is established that the planet has reached its opposite point.

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK V.

...then there is no way of distinguishing them, but a difficulty occurs here that is no less than that which Ptolemy faced in this section. For if the given angle *n e o* encompassed the given arc *a b*, and [angle] *o e p* encompassed the arc *b c*, the path would already be open to demonstrating those things which we seek. But while the arc *a b* is known, it subtends an unknown angle *a e b*; and similarly, beneath the known arc *b c*, the angle *b e c* lies hidden. However, it was necessary for both to be known. 

But neither can the differences of the angles *a e n*, *b e o*, and *c e p* be perceived unless the arcs *a f*, *f b*, and *f b c*—which are similar to those of the epicycle <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one</term>—are first established. Indeed, these factors are so dependent on one another that they are either hidden or revealed together. Therefore, those [astronomers] who were deprived of direct means of demonstration relied on *a posteriori* reasoning <note>original: "à posteriori"; reasoning from observed effects back to their causes.</note> and roundabout paths to reach those results which could not be accessed directly or *a priori* <note>original: "à priori"; reasoning from theoretical principles or causes to their effects.</note>. 

Thus Ptolemy, in carrying these out with lengthy discourse, poured himself into a vast multitude of numbers, which I consider troublesome and unnecessary to review, especially since we are about to imitate nearly the same method in our own work that follows. 

And at last, through a revision of the numbers, he found the arc *a f* to be 57 degrees, 1 minute <note>original: "scrupuli"; literally "scruples," used here to mean minutes of a degree.</note>; arc *f b* to be 18 degrees, 37 minutes; and arc *f b c* to be 56.5 degrees. The distance between the centers, however, was 6 degrees, 50 minutes, in a system where the radius of the orbit *d f* is 60. But in our numerical system, where the radius *d f* is 10,000 units, that distance is 1,016. 

From these values, we took three-quarters <term>dodrans: a three-fourth part</term> for the distance *d e*, being 854 parts, and we assigned the remaining quarter <term>quadrans: a one-fourth part</term> of 285 parts to the epicycle. ## On three other acronychal risings of Saturn observed more recently. Chapter 6.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial "C" depicting a bearded man, likely a representation of Saturn or Father Time, holding a scythe.</image-desc>Since, however, the calculation of Saturn's motion handed down by Ptolemy <note>Ptolemy was a 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose models dominated for over 1,000 years.</note> differs not a little from our own times, and it could not be immediately understood in which part the error lay hidden, we were forced to employ new observations, from which we again obtained three of its nightly culminations <note>original: "extremitates nocturnas", referring to acronychal risings—the moment a planet is exactly opposite the Sun and thus at its brightest and best position for measurement.</note>. The first was in the year of Christ 1514, on the third day before the Nones of May [May 5], at one and one-fifth hours before midnight, in which Saturn was found at 205 degrees, 24 minutes. The second was in the year of Christ 1520, on the third day before the Ides of July [July 13] at noon, at 272 degrees, 25 minutes. The third also in the year 1527, on the sixth day before the Ides of October [October 10], at six and two-fifths hours after midnight, at 7 minutes of one degree from the horn of Aries <note>The "horn of Aries" refers to a specific star used as a reference point in the constellation Aries.</note>.

There are, therefore, between the first and second observations six Egyptian years <term>Egyptian year: a calendar of exactly 365 days, used by astronomers for its consistency regardless of leap years</term>, 70 days, and 33 minutes <note>Copernicus expresses fractions of a day in "minutes," where 60 minutes equals one full day.</note>. In this time, Saturn moved according to appearance 78 degrees, 1 minute. From the second to the third observation, there are seven Egyptian years, 89 days, and 46 minutes, and the apparent motion of the star <note>meaning the planet Saturn</note> was 86 degrees, 42 minutes. And the mean motion <term>mean motion: the theoretical average speed of a planet, assuming its orbit was a perfect, uniform circle</term> in the first interval was 75 degrees, 39 minutes. In the second, it was 88 degrees, 29 minutes.

Therefore, in the investigation of the highest apsis <term>apsis: the point in an orbit where a planet is at its maximum or minimum distance from the center of its motion</term> and the eccentricity, we must first proceed according to the instruction of Ptolemy, as if the star moved in a simple eccentric circle. Although this is not sufficient, yet having been brought closer to the matter, we reach the truth more easily.

Let the center of the Earth be taken within it at point *D*, to which lines *AD*, *BD*, and *CD* are connected. Let any one of these be extended in a straight line to the opposite side of the circumference, such as *CDE*, and let *AE* and *BE* be joined. 

Since, therefore, angle *BDC* is given as 86 degrees, 42 minutes, of which 180 degrees make two right angles at the center, the remaining angle *BDE* will be 93 degrees, 18 minutes. # On the Examination of Saturn's Motion. Chapter VII.

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap letter 'O' containing an illustration of a landscape with a town, trees, and a celestial horizon.</image-desc>It has been shown, moreover, that at the time of the last of Ptolemy’s three observations, Saturn was at 174 degrees 44 minutes according to its motion of **parallax** <note>original: "commutationis"; in the Copernican system, this refers to the Earth's motion relative to the planet, which creates the appearance of retrograde motion.</note>. The position of the **highest apse** <note>The apogee, or the point in the orbit furthest from the sun.</note> of the eccentric was at 226 degrees 24 minutes from the head of the constellation Aries. It is clear, therefore, that in the middle time between both observations, Saturn completed 1,344 equal revolutions of its parallax, minus a quarter of one degree. Now, from the 20th year of the Emperor Hadrian, on the 24th day of the Egyptian month Mesori, one hour before noon, until the year of Christ 1527, on the sixth day before the Ides of October <note>October 10th</note>, at six hours, the time of this observation consists of 1,392 Egyptian years, 75 days, and 48 minutes <note>Copernicus uses "minutes" (scrupula) to represent fractions of a day.</note>. If we wish to calculate the motion itself from the tables for this period, we will similarly find five units of sixty degrees <note>300 degrees</note> plus 59 degrees and 48 minutes, which are the remainder beyond the 1,324 complete revolutions of parallax. Therefore, what has been set forth concerning the mean motions of Saturn is correct. In this same period, the simple motion of the Sun is 82 degrees 30 minutes; when 359 degrees 45 minutes are subtracted from this, there remain 82 degrees 45 minutes for the mean motion of Saturn, which now amounts to its 47th revolution, consistent with the calculation. In this interval, the position of the **highest apse** of the eccentric has also advanced 13 degrees 58 minutes under the sphere of the fixed stars. Ptolemy believed this point to be fixed in the same way, but it now appears that it moves approximately one degree every hundred years.

XLIX. The position for the distance between the Sun’s mean place and Saturn’s mean place is the motion of **parallax** <note>original: "commutatiõis"; in the Copernican system, this refers to the apparent displacement of a planet caused by the Earth's motion in its own orbit</note> at midnight on the Calends of January <note>January 1st</note>. ### On the Parallaxes of Saturn, which arise from the Earth's annual orbit, and what its distance is. Chapter IX.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'M' featuring ornate foliage and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>

**M**otions of Saturn in longitude, both the equal and the apparent, have been demonstrated in this manner. For the other appearances that happen to it are **parallaxes** <note>original: "commutationes"</note> which, as we have said, arise from the annual orbit of the Earth. Just as the size of the Earth creates parallaxes relative to the distance of the Moon, so too does the orbit in which the Earth revolves annually create effects regarding the five wandering stars <note>The planets: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>; but because of the great size of this orbit, the effects are far more evident. However, such parallaxes cannot be grasped unless the altitude <note>The distance of the planet from the Sun/center</note> of the star has first become known. It is possible, nonetheless, to determine this through any single consideration of the parallax. We had such an observation regarding Saturn in the year of Christ 1514, on the sixth day before the Calends of March <note>February 24th</note>, at five equinoctial hours after the preceding midnight. Saturn was seen in a straight line with the stars which are in the forehead of the Scorpion—namely, the second and third stars—which, having the same longitude, are at 209 degrees of the sphere of the fixed stars. Therefore, the position of Saturn was also made clear through those same stars. ### Chapter XI. On three other acronychal risings of Jupiter more recently observed.

Having once published and arranged the three positions of the star of Jupiter in this manner, we shall substitute three others, which we ourselves have observed with the greatest diligence at the acronychal rising of Jupiter. The first was in the year of Christ 1520, on the day before the <term>Calends</term> <gloss>The first day of the month in the Roman calendar.</gloss> of May <note>April 30, 1520</note>, 11 hours before the preceding midnight, at 200 degrees and 18 minutes of the sphere of the fixed stars. The second was in the year of Christ 1526, on the fourth day before the Calends of December <note>November 28, 1526</note>, three hours after midnight, at 48 degrees and 34 minutes. The third indeed was in the year 1529, on the Calends of February itself <note>February 1, 1529</note>, 19 hours after midnight, at 113 degrees and 44 minutes.

### Verification of the Uniform Motion of Jupiter. Chapter XII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'A' with a background of floral and leafy scrollwork.</image-desc>
But it has already been seen above that in the last of the three "night-long" <term>oppositions</term> <gloss>The "acronychal" position where the planet is directly opposite the Sun from the Earth's perspective, appearing at its brightest.</gloss> <note>original: "summae noctis stationum"</note> observed by Ptolemy, the star of Jupiter was in its mean motion at 4 degrees, 58 minutes, with an anomaly of parallax of 182 degrees, 47 minutes. The time, however, which intervened from the first year of [the Emperor] Antoninus, on the 20th day of the Egyptian month Athyr, five hours after the following midnight, until the year of Christ 1529, on the very Kalends [1st] of February, 19 hours after the preceding midnight, is 1,392 Egyptian years <note>An Egyptian year is exactly 365 days, used by astronomers for ease of calculation.</note>, 99 days, and 37 <term>scruples</term> <gloss>Small units of time or measurement; here, 37/60ths of a day.</gloss> of a day. To this time, according to the calculation set out above, there similarly corresponds one degree, 5 minutes after the complete revolutions, by which the Earth, in its uniform cycles, has overtaken and passed Jupiter 1,237 times. Thus, the numerical calculation is found to be certain and verified, agreeing with what was discovered by visual observation. During this time, it is also clear that the highest and lowest <term>apsides</term> <gloss>The points in an orbit closest to and farthest from the center.</gloss> <note>original: "summa infimaq; absis"</note> of the eccentric have shifted forward by 4 and a half degrees. This adjusted distribution grants approximately one degree every three hundred years.

From that point, over the course of 451 descending years and 247 days, the motion increases by 110 degrees 52 minutes. These, combined with the position at the Olympiad, result in 138 degrees 10 minutes for the position of <term>Alexander</term> <gloss>The era of Alexander the Great, which astronomers used as a chronological milestone starting in 323 BCE.</gloss> at noon on the first day of the month of <term>Thoth</term> <gloss>The first month of the ancient Egyptian calendar.</gloss> among the Egyptians; and in this same manner for any other dates.

### On perceiving the parallaxes of Jupiter, and its altitude according to the ratio of the Earth's orbital revolution. Chapter 14.

<margin>B F</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'V' with floral and scrollwork motifs.</image-desc>
**T**o perceive the other appearances of Jupiter which involve <term>parallax</term> <gloss>The apparent shift in a planet's position caused by the Earth's own movement around the Sun.</gloss> <note>original: "commutationis"</note>, we observed its position very diligently in the year of Christ 1520, on the 19th of February <note>original: "XII. Calend. Martij," the 12th day before the Calends of March. Because 1520 was a leap year, this corresponds to February 19th.</note>, six hours before noon. We saw through the instrument that Jupiter preceded the first star in the "brow" of <term>Scorpio</term> <gloss>The constellation Scorpius.</gloss>—the brighter one <note>Likely the star Beta Scorpii, also known as Graffias.</note>—by 4 degrees and 31 minutes. Since the position of that fixed star was at 209 degrees 40 minutes, it is clear that the position of Jupiter was at 205 degrees 9 minutes relative to the sphere of the fixed stars.

Therefore, from the beginning of the years of Christ to the year 1520, there are 62 equal days and 15 minutes <note>Copernicus uses sexagesimal fractions (1/60ths) for days as well; 15 "minutes" of a day equals 6 hours.</note> up to the hour of this observation. From this, the mean motion of the Sun is derived as 309 degrees 16 minutes, and the anomaly of parallax at 111 degrees 15 minutes. By these, the mean position of the star Jupiter is established at 198 degrees 1 minute. And since the position of the <term>highest apsis</term> <gloss>The apogee, or the point in the orbit farthest from the center of motion.</gloss> <note>original: "summæ absidis"</note> of the eccentric was found in our time to be at 159 degrees, the <term>anomaly</term> <gloss>The angular distance from the apogee.</gloss> of Jupiter’s eccentric was 39 degrees 1 minute.

Furthermore, let the angle *D B F* be made equal to the angle *A D B*, and

By this amount, the angle of the apparent position **D E M** is smaller than the uniform motion <note>original: "aequalitati"</note> under angle **F D C**. This gives angle **D E N** as 13 degrees 40 minutes, which almost exactly matches the appearance observed between the second and third acronychal <term>acronychal: the position of a planet when it is directly opposite the sun</term> observations. Since the star of Mars appeared in this place (as we have narrated) at 133 degrees 20 minutes from the head of the constellation Aries <note>original: "à capite Arietis stellati"</note>, and the angle **F E N** has been shown to be approximately 13 degrees 40 minutes.

It is manifest, by counting backward, that the location of the apogee <term>apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from the center</term> of the eccentric in this last observation was at 119 degrees 40 minutes in the sphere of the fixed stars. Ptolemy, in the time of Antoninus, found this to be at 108 degrees 50 minutes; therefore, in the time between him and us, it has shifted 10 degrees and ten-twelfths <note>original: "dextante"; a Roman fraction meaning 10/12 or 5/6</note> of one degree in the direction of the signs <note>original: "in consequentia"; following the order of the zodiac signs</term>. We also found a smaller distance between the centers, namely 40 parts, where the radius of the eccentric is 10,000. This is not because Ptolemy or we have erred, but it is a clear proof that the center of the great orbital circle of the Earth has approached the center of the orbit of Mars, while the Sun remains meanwhile immovable. For these values correspond to each other almost exactly, as will appear more clearly than light hereafter.

Now, let the Earth's annual orbital circle be set out around center **E**, with its diameter **S E R** parallel to **C D** because of the equality of their revolutions. Let **R** be the mean apogee <note>original: "apogæum æquale"</note> relative to the star, **S** the perigee, and **T** the Earth. The line **E T** being extended, the line of sight to the star **C D** will intersect at **X**. But the line of sight to the star toward the parts of the longitude was, as was said in this last place, 133 degrees 20 minutes at **X**. The angle **D X E** has also been demonstrated to be 2 degrees 56 minutes; for it is the difference by which the angle **X D F** is greater than the angle **X E D** (the mean motion relative to the apparent). But the angle **S E T** is equal to the alternating angle **D X B**, and is the parallax adjustment <term>prosthaphaeresis of commutation: the correction needed to account for the Earth's own motion in its orbit</term>. When this is subtracted from a semicircle, there remain 177 degrees 4 minutes as the uniform anomaly of commutation <term>anomaly of commutation: the angular distance of a planet from its mean position of opposition</term> calculated from the apogee of its uniform motion at **R**. 

Thus we have demonstrated here that in the year of Christ 1523, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March <note>February 22, 1523</note>, seven equinoctial hours before noon, the star of Mars was in its mean motion of longitude at 136 degrees 16 minutes; its uniform anomaly of commutation was 177 degrees 4 minutes, and the highest apse <term>apse: the highest or lowest point in an orbit</term> of the eccentric was at 119 degrees 40 minutes. These were the things to be demonstrated.

## Demonstration of the Motion of Mars. Chapter 17.

It was shown above that in the last of Ptolemy's three observations, Mars was at a mean course of 244 degrees 30 minutes <note>original: "CCXLIIII.s."; the 's' stands for 'semis,' meaning one-half or 30 minutes</note> and the anomaly of commutation <term>anomaly of commutation: the angular distance of a planet from its apogee, used here to calculate the planet's position relative to the Earth's motion</term> was 171 degrees 26 minutes. Therefore, in the intervening time, after completing full revolutions, an excess of 5 degrees 38 minutes occurred. 

This period spans from the second year of Antoninus <note>Antoninus Pius, Roman Emperor; the observation dates to 139 AD</note>, on the twelfth day of the Egyptian month Epiphy, 9 hours after noon—which is 3 equinoctial hours before the middle of the following night relative to the meridian of Cracow—until the year of Christ 1523, on the 8th day before the Calends of March <note>February 22, 1523</note>, 7 hours before noon. This total duration is 1,384 Egyptian years, 251 days, and 19 minutes <note>scrupula: Copernicus uses 'scruples' to represent fractions of a day or degree, where 60 scruples make one unit</note>. In this time, according to the numbers set forth above, the anomalies of commutation amount to 5 degrees 38 minutes, after completing 648 full revolutions. Furthermore, the assumed uniform motion of the Sun is 257 degrees 30 minutes; when the motion of commutation of 5 degrees 38 minutes is subtracted from this, there remains 251 degrees 52 minutes, which is the mean motion of Mars in longitude. All of these figures almost entirely agree with what has just been presented.

## Establishing the Positions of Mars. Chapter 18.

We count from the beginning of the Christian era to the second year of Antoninus, the 12th day of the Egyptian month Epiphy, 3 hours before midnight, a span of 138 Egyptian years, 180 days, and 52 minutes. The motion of commutation during this time is 293 degrees 22 minutes. When these are subtracted from the 171 degrees 26 minutes of Ptolemy's last observation (borrowing one full revolution for the calculation), there remain 238 degrees 22 minutes as the position for the first year of Christ, at midnight on the Calends of January <note>January 1st</note>. 

From the first Olympiad <term>Olympiad: a four-year period used in ancient Greek dating; the first began in 776 BC</term> to this point, there are 775 Egyptian years and 12 and a half days, during which the motion of commutation is 254 degrees 1 minute. When these are likewise subtracted from 238 degrees 22 minutes (again borrowing a full circuit), they leave the position for the first Olympiad as

### On the Planet Venus. Chapter XX.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'T' depicting a seated figure, likely a scholar or shepherd, in a pastoral landscape with a tree and distant hills.</image-desc> Having explained the motions of the three superior planets—Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars—which surround the Earth, it now occurs to us to speak of those which the Earth itself circles. And first of Venus: which allows for a demonstration of its motion that is easier and more evident than the others, provided that the necessary observations of certain locations are not lacking. For if its maximum distances from the mean position of the Sun <note>original: "à loco Solis medio"</note>—both in the morning and evening—are found to be equal to each other, we then know for certain that the highest or lowest apogee of the eccentric orbit of Venus lies exactly halfway between those two solar positions. These points are distinguished by the fact that such equal elongations <term>elongation: the angular distance between a planet and the Sun as seen from Earth</term> become smaller near the apogee and larger at the opposite point. Finally, in other locations, through the differences by which they exceed one another, one can perceive without doubt how far the orbit of Venus is from the highest or lowest apogee, as well as its eccentricity <term>eccentricity: the degree to which an orbit deviates from a perfect circle</term>. These matters were most clearly handed down by Ptolemy, so there is no need to repeat them one by one, except insofar as they are applied to our hypothesis of the Earth's mobility using those same observations by Ptolemy. The first of these observations he took from Theon the Mathematician of Alexandria, made (as he says) in the 16th year of Hadrian, on the 21st day of the month of Pharmuthi, at the first hour of the following night—which was in the year of Christ 132, at twilight on the eighth day before the Ides of March. Venus was seen at its maximum evening distance of 47 degrees from the mean position of the Sun.

### On the twofold motion of Venus. Chapter XXII.

However, the uniform motion of Venus around center **D** is not simple, as is shown by the evidence of two of Ptolemy’s <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Alexandrian astronomer whose observations Copernicus is refining.</note> most important observations. He made the first one in the 18th year of the Emperor **Hadrian**, on the second day of the Egyptian month of Pharmuthi; according to the Roman calendar, this was the year **134** after the birth of Christ, at dawn on the **12th day before the Kalends of March** <note>February 18, 134 AD</note>. At that time, while the Sun’s mean motion was at **318** degrees and five-sixths <note>original: "dextante," meaning 10/12 or 50 minutes</note>, Venus appeared in the morning at **275** and a quarter degrees of the zodiac <note>275° 15'</note>. It had reached the extreme limit of its elongation <term>elongation: the angular distance between a planet and the Sun as seen from Earth</term> at **43** degrees <note>The OCR reads "LXIIII" (64), but the calculation (318°50' - 275°15') confirms this must be 43.</note> and **35** minutes. He took the second observation in the 3rd year of **Antoninus**, in the same month of Pharmuthi, on its fourth day according to the Egyptians; this was the year of Christ **140** according to the Romans, in the twilight of the **12th** day before the Kalends of March <note>February 18/19, 140 AD</note>. At that time, the mean position of the Sun was also at **318** degrees and five-sixths, while Venus was at its maximum evening distance from it of **48** and one-third degrees, appearing at a longitude of **7** degrees and five-sixths <note>318° 50' + 48° 20' = 367° 10', or 7° 10'</note>.

With these facts established, let us take point **A** on the same Earthly orbit where the Earth is located, such that **AC** is a quadrant of a circle <note>90 degrees</note>, through which the Sun (seen from the opposite side in both observations according to its mean motion) was seen to precede the apogee <term>apogee: the point in an orbit furthest from the center</term> of Venus's eccentric orbit. Let **GC** be joined, and let **DK** be drawn parallel to it. Let the lines **GE** and **GF**, which are tangent to the orbit of Venus, be connected, along with **DE**, **DF**, and **DG**.

But at the mean apsis <note>The points halfway between the highest and lowest points of the orbit.</note>, such as when the center of the orbit is at point **G**, it reaches point **D** and the maximum distance **CD**. From this, it is understood that in the time it takes the Earth to complete one circuit of its orbit, the center of the planet's orbit makes two revolutions around center **N**, moving in the same direction as the Earth—that is, forward <note>original: "in consequentia," following the order of the signs of the zodiac.</note>. For by such a hypothesis concerning Venus, the uniform motion and the observed appearances agree in every way, as will soon be shown. Moreover, all these things which have been demonstrated regarding Venus so far are found to be consistent with our own times; whereas the total [eccentricity] was previously 416 parts, it is now 350, as many of our observations teach us.

...believing that the Earth is motionless and that Mercury moves in its great epicycle through an eccentric. Since they realized that one simple eccentric could not satisfy these appearances—even if it were granted that the eccentric itself moved not around its own center but around a foreign one—they were forced to admit that this same eccentric moved on another small circle carrying the epicycle, similar to the one they admitted for the Moon's eccentric. Thus, although there were three existing centers—namely, one for the eccentric carrying the epicycle, another for the small circle, and a third (which the moderns call the <term>equant</term><note>The equant was a mathematical point used by Ptolemy to explain the observed speed changes of planets. This was completely foreign to the true center and its logic, as well as to both pre-existing centers.

Nor indeed did they think the appearances of this star could be preserved in any other way, as is explained more fully in the **Ptolemaic construction**. But in order that this final star may also be vindicated from the injuries and opportunities of detractors, and that its regularity may appear no less than that of the others preceding it under the **mobility of the Earth**, we shall also assign to it an eccentric-of-an-eccentric in place of what antiquity considered an epicycle. However, in a different manner than in **Venus**, a certain small epicycle moves nonetheless within the eccentric itself, in which the planet is carried not along the circumference but along its diameter, moving up and down; this can also occur from uniform circular motions, as was explained above regarding the **precession of the equinoxes** <note>In Book I, Copernicus explained how two circular motions could result in a straight-line "libration" or oscillation.</note>. By all these means, its appearances will be demonstrated.

### On the position of the highest and lowest apsides of Mercury. Chapter XXVI.

### On the more recent motions of Mercury observed. Chapter XXX.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'H' featuring a male figure's head centered in the top border of the letterframe.</image-desc>
**H**aving indeed shown us this way of examining the course of this star, the ancients were aided by a clearer sky—specifically where the Nile, so they say, does not breathe out such mists as the Vistula does for us. For nature has denied that convenience to us who inhabit a more frozen region, where the tranquility of the air is rarer; furthermore, because of the great obliquity of the sphere <note>Meaning the high northern latitude, which makes the path of planets like Mercury appear very low on the horizon</note>, the sky rarely permits one to see Mercury. For even at its greatest distance from the Sun, if it is in Aries or Pisces, it does not rise to our sight, nor does it set when it is in Virgo or Libra. Indeed, it does not show itself in any way in Cancer or Gemini, when there is only the twilight of night or the break of dawn; it never appears at night unless the Sun has moved back into a good part of Leo. For these reasons, this star has tortured us with many complexities and much labor so that we might scrutinize its wanderings. We have therefore borrowed three positions from those which were diligently observed at Nuremberg. The first was by Bernhard Walther, a disciple of Regiomontanus <note>A famous 15th-century German mathematician and astronomer</note>, in the year of Christ 1491, on the 5th Ides of September <note>September 9th</note>, five equal hours after midnight, using armillary astrolabes <note>An instrument of nested rings used to measure celestial coordinates</note> aligned to the Palilicium <note>The star Aldebaran, the "eye" of Taurus</note>; and he saw Mercury at 13 and a half degrees...

At that time, the star <note>Mercury</note> was at the beginning of its morning setting, having steadily decreased its morning appearance through the preceding days. Therefore, from the beginning of the years of Christ, there were 1,491 Egyptian years <note>A year of exactly 365 days used by astronomers for ease of calculation</note>, 258 days, and 12 and a half scruples <note>original: *scrupula*; here meaning minutes of an hour or a degree</note>. The second observation was in the year of Christ 1504, on the 5th day before the Ides of January <note>January 9</note>, at 6 and a half hours after midnight, while the midheaven at Nuremberg was at 10 degrees of Scorpio.
