According to the calculation, the mean position of the Sun from the Vernal Equinox was at 27 degrees and 7 minutes of Aquarius, which Mercury preceded as a morning star by 23 degrees and 42 minutes.

The third observation was also by the same **Johannes Schöner**, in the same year 1504, on the 15th day before the Calends of April <note>March 18</note>. On this day, he found Mercury at 26 degrees and one-tenth of a degree of Aries, with a northern latitude of nearly 3 degrees, while the midheaven at Nuremberg was at 25 degrees of Cancer, determined by armillary spheres <note>A model of the celestial sphere used for observation</note> compared to the same parallactic star <note>original: *pallalitiū*; likely referring to a reference star used to account for parallax or relative position</note>, at 7 and a half hours after noon. At that time, the mean position of the Sun from the Vernal Equinox was 5 degrees and 39 minutes of Aries, from which Mercury, as an evening star, was 21 degrees and 17 minutes.

Therefore, from the first position to the second, there are 12 Egyptian years, 125 days, 3 minutes, and 45 seconds. In this time, the simple motion of the Sun is 120 degrees and 14 minutes, and the anomaly of commutation <term>anomaly of commutation: the angular distance of a planet from its apogee in its epicycle, or its position relative to the Earth's orbit</term> of Mercury is 316 degrees and 1 minute. In the second interval, there are 69 days, 31 minutes, and 45 seconds. The mean simple position of the Sun is 68 degrees and 32 minutes, and the mean anomaly of commutation of Mercury is 216 degrees.

From these three observations, we wish to examine the course of Mercury for the present time. In these, we think it must be granted that the proportions of the circles have remained from the time of **Ptolemy** even until now, since in other cases the previous good authors are not found to have erred in this part. If we also have the position of the apsis of the eccentric <term>apsis: the point in an orbit where the planet is at its maximum or minimum distance from the center</term>, nothing further would be desired regarding the apparent motion of this star as well. We have assumed the position of the highest apsis <note>apogee</note> at 211 and a half parts—that is, at 28 and a half degrees of the sign of Scorpio—for it was not possible to accept a smaller value without prejudice to the observations. ### On Establishing the Positions of Mercury. Chapter XXXI.

Since, therefore, from the beginning of the Christian era until the final observation, there are 1,504 Egyptian years <note>astronomers used Egyptian years of exactly 365 days to avoid the complications of leap years in long-term calculations</note>, 87 days, and 48 minutes, during which time the motion of the anomaly of commutation <note>the planet's position relative to its mean motion</note> of Mercury is 63 degrees and 13 minutes—after discarding the full revolutions. When these are subtracted from 109 degrees and 38 minutes, there remain 46 degrees and 24 minutes: the position of the anomaly of commutation for Mercury at the beginning of the Christian era. From that point, going back to the beginning of the first Olympiad <note>776 BCE, a common chronological marker in Renaissance astronomy</note>, there are 775 Egyptian years and 12.5 days, in which 95 degrees and 3 minutes are counted after the full revolutions. When this is deducted from the position at the time of Christ (borrowing one full revolution), there remains for the first Olympiad the position of 311 degrees and 21 minutes. By a similar calculation for the time of Alexander's death <note>323 BCE, another "Epoch" or reference point for tables</note> over 451 years and 247 days, the position is calculated as 213 degrees and 3 minutes.

# NICOLAI COPERNICI
### [ON THE REVOLUTIONS]

...of the circles is carried around center **F** in direct motion <note>original: *in consequentia*; the direction following the order of the zodiac signs</note>, along with its sections **GFR** and **HFP**, daily by about 2 degrees and 7 minutes. This is precisely the amount by which the motion of commutation <term>commutation: the planet’s motion relative to the Earth as it "catches up" or passes it</term> of the star exceeds the motion of the Earth in the zodiac, from the apogee <note>the point in an orbit farthest from the center</note> of the star’s eccentric. Meanwhile, the star completes the remaining motion from sign **G** through the circle **OR**, which is its own circle of commutation, in a motion nearly similar to the Earth’s. It is also assumed that in this same annual revolution—that is, the period of the center of the circle **OR** which carries the star—it is carried by a motion of libration <note>original: *motu liberationis*; a back-and-forth oscillation along a straight line</note> along the diameter **LFM**, twice as large as what we previously set, reciprocating as was said above.

When these things are so established, and we have placed the Earth in its mean motion moving against the apogee of the star’s center, at that time the center of the circle carrying the star is at **L**, and the star itself is at sign **O**. At that point, being at its minimum distance from **F**, it will describe the smallest circle by its total motion, the radius of which is **FO**, and so on for what follows. 

When the Earth is near the middle apsis <term>apsis: the highest or lowest points (apogee or perigee) in an orbit</term>, the star falling into sign **H**, following its greatest distance from **F**, describes the largest arcs, specifically according to the circle whose center is **F**. For then the carrying circle **OR** coincides with the circle **GH** because the centers unite at **F**. From here, as the Earth proceeds toward the perigee <note>the point in an orbit closest to the center</note> and the center of circle **OR** moves to the other extreme, which is **M**, the orbit itself is raised above **GK**, and the star at **R** again falls into the minimum distance from **F**, and the same things happen as at the beginning.

Here, indeed, three revolutions coincide and are equal to each other: that of the Earth relative to the apogee of Mercury’s eccentric orbit, the libration of the center along the diameter **LM**, and the movement of the planet from the line **G**. These differ only from the motion of the sections **GH** and **KP** from the apsis of the center, as we have said. 

->So indeed, nature has played around this star with such wonderful variety, which it has nonetheless confirmed with a perpetual, certain, and immutable order.<-

For if, for example, the center remained at **L** while the star proceeded from **O**, it would admit the greatest difference near **H** according to the proportion...

### On the tables of the prosthaphaereses of the five wandering stars. Chapter XXXIII.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'H' featuring a central bearded face within a circular medallion, flanked by scrolled leaf designs.</image-desc>

These matters concerning the uniform and apparent motion of Mercury and the other wandering stars <note>planets; from the Greek *planētēs*, meaning 'wanderer'</note> have thus been demonstrated and set forth in numbers. From these examples, the way to calculate the differences of the motions for any other locations will be open. For this use, we have prepared Tables <term>Tables: original "Canones," meaning rules or mathematical tables used for calculation</term>, specific to each planet, having six columns and 30 rows, using increments of three degrees as is our custom. 

First, two columns will have common numbers for both the eccentricity anomaly and the commutations <term>commutation: the motion of the planet relative to the Earth's position</term>. The third contains the combined prosthaphaereses <term>prosthaphaeresis: the mathematical correction added or subtracted to the mean motion to find the planet's true position</term> of the eccentric—I mean the total differences that fall between the uniform and diverse motion of those circles. The fourth contains the proportional minutes <term>proportional minutes: "scrupula proportionum," small fractions (sixtieths) used to scale the calculations based on the planet's changing distance from Earth</term>, which are sixtieths, by which the commutations are increased or decreased due to the greater or lesser distance of the Earth. The fifth contains the prosthaphaereses themselves, which are the commutations occurring at the highest apsis <note>apogee; the point farthest from the center</note> of the planet's eccentric, resulting from the great circle <note>the Earth's orbit</note>. The sixth and last contains the excesses by which those corrections occurring at the lowest apsis <note>perigee; the point closest to the center</note> of the eccentric surpass the others. And these are the Tables.

<summary>Copernicus concludes his geometric model of Mercury, noting that its orbital complexities are often hidden by the Sun's glare, and introduces the structure of his new astronomical tables for the five planets.</summary>
<keywords>Mercury, prosthaphaereses, astronomical tables, commutation, apsis, orbital eccentricity, planetary motion</keywords>

## How the positions of these five planets in longitude are calculated. Chapter 34.

Through these <term>Tables</term><note>original: "Canones." In this context, Copernicus refers to the mathematical data tables he has calculated for planetary motions.</note> thus set forth by us, we shall calculate the positions in longitude of these five wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" are the planets: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury.</note> without difficulty. For in all of them, the method of computation is nearly the same; however, the three outer planets differ somewhat from Venus and Mercury. Therefore, let us first speak of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars.

The calculation for these is as follows: for any proposed time, one must seek the <term>mean motions</term>—namely, the simple motion of the Sun and the <term>commutation</term><note>original: "commutationis." This refers to the planet's parallax, or the change in its apparent position relative to the Sun as seen from Earth.</note> of the planet—using the method delivered above. Next, the position of the <term>highest apse</term><note>original: "summæ absidis." The point in the planet's orbit furthest from the center of its motion (aphelion).</note> of the planet's eccentric is subtracted from the simple position of the Sun. From what remains, subtract the <term>anomaly of commutation</term>. What is then left is the <term>anomaly of the star’s eccentric</term>. 

We seek the value of this anomaly among the "common numbers" in either of the first two rows of the table. Opposite it, in the third column, we take the <term>equation of the eccentric</term> and the following <term>proportional minutes</term><note>original: "scrupula proportionum." These are used to adjust for the varying distance of the planet's epicycle from the Earth.</note>. We add this equation to the anomaly of commutation and subtract it from the anomaly of the eccentric if the number by which we entered the table was found in the first series; conversely, we subtract it from the anomaly of commutation and add it to the anomaly of the eccentric if it held to the second row. Whatever is thus collected or left over will be the <term>equated anomalies</term> of commutation and of the eccentric, while we save the proportional minutes for the use soon to be mentioned.

Furthermore, we seek the anomaly of commutation thus equated also among the first "common numbers." In the fifth column, we take the <term>parallax correction</term><note>original: "prosthaphaeresim." A Greek term for the correction added or subtracted to the mean motion to find the true position.</note> of commutation along with its "excess" placed at the end. From that excess, we take a proportional part according to the number of proportional minutes, which we always add to the parallax correction. This will produce the true commutation of the planet, which is to be subtracted from the equated anomaly of commutation if it is less than a semicircle [180°], or added if it is greater than a semicircle. For thus we shall have the true and apparent distance of the star from the mean position of the Sun in <term>precedence</term><note>original: "in præcedentia." This refers to movement in the order of the zodiac signs (westward), as opposed to "consequence" (eastward).</note>. When we subtract this from the Sun's position, the sought-after position of the star remains.

the sought-after position, relative to the sphere of the fixed stars <note>original: "non errantium sphæram." Copernicus uses the fixed stars as a stable reference frame for his calculations.</note>. If to this the precession of the equinoxes is finally applied, it will determine the planet's position starting from the vernal intersection <note>The vernal equinox point.</note>. For Venus and Mercury, we use the <term>anomaly of the eccentric</term>—that which exists from the <term>highest apse</term> <note>The aphelion, or the point in the orbit furthest from the sun.</note> to the mean position of the Sun—by which anomaly we adjust the motion of <term>commutation</term> <note>original: "commutationis." If, however, they are of different types, the smaller is subtracted from the larger, and with the remainder, one follows the instruction just given, according to the additive or subtractive property of the larger number; the result will be the apparent position of the planet being sought.

### On the stations and retrogradations of the five wandering stars. Chapter 35.

It also seems to belong to the logic of motion in longitude to understand the stations, regressions, and <term>retrogradations</term> <note>original: "repedationibus." The "backward" motion of planets as viewed from Earth.</note>—specifically where, when, and how great they become. Mathematicians have treated these extensively, especially <term>Apollonius of Perga</term> <note>A 3rd-century BC Greek geometer known for his work on conic sections and planetary models.</note>. But they did so as if the stars were moved by only a single inequality—that by which the stars move in respect to the Sun, which we have called the <term>commutation</term>, caused by the motion of the Earth's "great orbit." For if the circles of the stars were <term>homocentric</term> <note>Sharing the same center.</note> with the Earth's great orbit, and all the stars were carried at unequal speeds in the same direction (that is, in order of the signs), and a star in its own orbit—whether inside the great orbit like Venus and Mercury, or outside—were faster than the Earth's motion; then, if a straight line drawn from our point of sight (the Earth) should cut the star's orbit in such a way that half the section intercepted within the orbit has the same ratio to the line extending from our sight to the lower and retrograding circumference of the cut orbit as the Earth's motion has to the star's velocity; then the point made by the line so drawn to the <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in the orbit closest to the center of motion.</note> of the star's circle distinguishes the retrogradation from the progression, such that a star situated in that place would appear to be at a station. Similarly in the other three outer planets, whose motion is slower than the speed—

This nevertheless agrees with our principles on the mobility of the Earth, and therefore we shall also use it. We can express it in this form: If the longer side of a triangle is divided such that one of the segments is not smaller than the side adjacent to it, the ratio of that segment to the remaining segment

This is demonstrated in the following way: Let the parallelogram ADCB be completed, and let the extended lines BA and CE meet at point F. Since side AB is not smaller than side AC, a circle described with center A and distance AB will pass through C or above it. For now, let it pass through C, and let the circle be GBC. Since triangle AEF is greater than the <term>sector</term> ABG <note>A "pie-slice" piece of a circle.</note>, while triangle ABC is smaller than the sector AEC, triangle AEF has a greater ratio to triangle ABC than sector ABG has to sector AEC. But as triangle AEF is to triangle ABC, so is the base FE to EC; therefore FE has a greater ratio to EC than the angle FAB has to the angle BAC. But as FE is to EC, so is CD to DB; for angle FAB is equal to angle ABC, and angle EAC is equal to angle BCA. Therefore

### BOOK V OF THE REVOLUTIONS

...and $CD$ to $DB$ has a greater ratio than angle $ABC$ has to angle $ACB$. It is evident, moreover, that the ratio will be much greater if $CD$ is assumed not to be equal to $AC$ (which is $AB$), but is set larger than it.

Now, let $ABC$ be the circle of Venus or Mercury around the center $D$. Outside this circle, let the Earth $E$ move around the same center $D$. From our point of vision at $E$, let a straight line $ECDA$ be drawn through the center of the circle. Let $A$ be the place farthest from the Earth <note>The apogee.</note> and $C$ the place nearest to the Earth <note>The perigee.</note>. Let the ratio of $DC$ to $CB$ be greater than the ratio of the motion of our sight <note>The Earth's orbital velocity.</note> to the velocity of the planet. 

It is therefore possible to find a line $EFB$ such that half of the segment $BF$ has the same ratio to $EB$ as the motion of our sight has to the course of the planet. For as the line $EFB$ moves away from the center $D$, the segment $FB$ decreases while $EF$ increases, until the required ratio is met.

I maintain that the planet, when positioned at point $F$, will present to us the appearance of a station. Furthermore, however small an arc we take from either side of point $F$: if taken toward the apogee, we shall find the motion to be progressive <note>Moving forward in the order of the zodiac signs.</note>; but if taken toward the perigee, we shall find it to be regressive <note>Retrograde motion, appearing to move backward.</note>.

To prove this, first let the arc $FG$ be taken toward the apogee. Draw the line $EGK$, and connect $BG$, $DG$, and $DF$. 

->[Diagram showing the circular orbit of an inner planet with Earth at point E and various lines of sight and geometric points.]<-

Since in the triangle $BGE$, the side $BE$ is larger than the other sides, the segment $BF$ is greater than $BG$. Thus, $BF$ has a greater ratio to $EF$ than angle $FEG$ has to angle $GBF$. Consequently, half of $BF$ to $FE$ has a greater ratio than angle $FEG$ has to double the angle $GBF$—which is to say, angle $GDF$. 

However, the ratio of half of $BF$ to $BE$ is the same as the ratio of the Earth’s motion to the course of the planet. Therefore, the ratio of the Earth's motion to the planet's velocity is less than the ratio of angle $FEG$ to angle $GDF$. Let there be an angle $FEL$ that is equal to this ratio. In the time, therefore, in which the planet has traversed the arc $F$ of its orbit, the line of sight will appear...

<summary>Copernicus applies a geometric lemma to the orbits of Venus and Mercury to determine the exact point where they appear stationary from Earth. He demonstrates that the appearance of standing still or moving backward depends on the ratio between the planet's orbital speed and the Earth's motion.</summary>

<keywords>Venus, Mercury, planetary stations, retrograde motion, apogee, perigee, geometric proof, orbital velocity</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the geometric proof of the stationary points and retrograde motions of the planets (specifically the inner planets, Venus and Mercury), using the ratios of the Earth's orbital velocity to the planet's orbital velocity.</meta>

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...our sight has traversed the space opposite to that which lies between lines $EF$ and $EL$. It is clear that in the same time in which the arc $GF$ has moved the star forward <note>original: "in praecedentia"; this refers to movement against the order of the zodiac signs, which we call retrograde motion</note> in our vision under the smaller angle $FEG$, the Earth's motion has drawn it back in the following direction <note>original: "in consequentia"; movement with the order of the zodiac signs, or direct motion</note> under the larger angle $FEL$. Thus, the star is left behind under the angle $GEL$, and being delayed, it does not yet seem to have come to a stop.

It is also clear that the opposite will be demonstrated by the same means. If, in the same diagram, we set half of $GK$ to $GE$ to have the same ratio that the motion of the Earth has to the velocity of the planet, but we take the arc $GF$ toward the perigee <note>The point in the orbit closest to the Earth.</note> from the straight line $EK$, then by connecting $KF$ and forming the triangle $KEF$ (in which $GE$ is designated as larger than $EF$), the ratio of $KG$ to $GE$ will be less than the ratio of angle $FEG$ to angle $FKG$. 

Thus, also, half of $KG$ to $GF$ has a smaller ratio than angle $FEG$ has to double the angle $FKG$—that is, to angle $GDF$ in turn, as was demonstrated before. And it will be concluded by the same means that angle $GDF$ has a smaller ratio to angle $FEG$ than the velocity of the star has to the velocity of our sight. Therefore, since they have the same ratio, when the angle $GDF$ is made larger, the star will complete a greater step forward <note>Original: "in praecedentia"; retrograde movement</note> than its progression requires.

From these things it is also clear that if we assume equal arcs $FC$ and $CL$, the second station will be at point $L$. Indeed, if the line $ELM$ is drawn, the ratio of half of $LM$ to $LE$ will be the same as the ratio of the Earth's velocity to the star's velocity, just as half of $BF$ was to $FE$. Therefore, the points $F$ and $L$ encompass both stations and define the entire arc $FCL$ as retrograde, and the remainder of the circle as progressive.

It also follows that at whatever distances the ratio of $DC$ to $CB$ is not greater than the ratio of the Earth's velocity to the planet's velocity, it will not be possible to draw any other straight line in a ratio equal to this; nor will the star appear to stand still or move backward. For when the line $DC$ is assumed in triangle $DEG$ to be smaller than $EG$, the ratio of angle $CEG$ to angle $CDG$ will be less than the ratio of the line $DC$ to $CB$. But the ratio of $DC$ to $CB$ is not greater than the ratio of the Earth's velocity to the star's velocity; therefore, the angle $CEG$ will also have a smaller ratio to $CDG$ than the velocity of the Earth to the velocity of the star. When this occurs, the progression...

Furthermore, if the orbits on which the planets travel were centered on the same point as the Great Orbit <note>original: "homocentrici"; having the same center</note>, the things promised by the demonstrations would be easily established, as the ratio of the star's speed to the speed of our sight would always remain the same. When these are subtracted from 27 degrees 15 minutes, there remain 8 degrees 8 minutes from one of the stations to the <term>acronychal</term> point. In approximately 36 and a half days, those 19 degrees, 6 minutes, 39 seconds of longitude are completed, and thereafter the total regression is 16 degrees and 16 minutes completed over 74 days.

These calculations apply to the mean distances of the <term>eccentric</term> <note>A circle whose center is offset from the center of the universe (the Sun, in Copernicus's system).</note>. Similar demonstrations are made in other locations, but the specific velocity of the star must always be applied according to what the location itself provides, as we have said. 

Furthermore, the same method of demonstration is clear for **Saturn**, **Jupiter**, and **Mars**, and no less for **Venus** and **Mercury**, provided we take the sight for the star and the star for the sight. This occurs because the motions are reversed in the orbits that are surrounded by the Earth compared to those that surround the Earth. Therefore, so that we do not repeat the same song again and again, let these things suffice. 

However, since the variable motion of those stars according to our sight and the ambiguity of the stations bring no small difficulty—from which the assumption of <term>Apollonius</term> <note>Apollonius of Perga, a 3rd-century BCE mathematician who studied epicycles and stationary points.</note> does not relieve us in the least—I do not know if someone might not do better to approach the stations simply and from the nearest place. In this way, we may find the <term>conjunction</term> of the acronychal star with the line of the mean motion of the Sun, or the meeting of any stars from the known numbers of their motions, which we leave to the pleasure of anyone who wishes.

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS’S SIXTH BOOK ON THE REVOLUTIONS.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a central face within a circular border and elaborate scrollwork.</image-desc>We have indicated, as best as we were able, what power and effect the assumed revolution of the Earth would have on the apparent motion in <term>longitude</term> <note>The position of a planet measured along the ecliptic.</note> of the wandering stars <note>original: "errantium siderum"; the planets.</note>, and into what order it forces all these things—namely, a certain and necessary one. It remains for us to occupy ourselves with the crossings of those stars by which they deviate in <term>latitude</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic plane.</note>, and to show how, in these matters as well, the same mobility of the Earth exercises its command and has prescribed laws for them in this part too. Moreover, this part of the science is necessary because the deviations of these stars cause no small difference regarding their risings and settings, appearances, occultations, and other phenomena which have been generally set forth above. Furthermore, their true locations are only said to be known when the longitude is established together with the latitude from the <term>circle of the signs</term> <note>original: "signorum circulo"; the Zodiac or ecliptic.</note>. Therefore, what the ancient mathematicians thought they demonstrated here through the stability of the Earth, we are going to do perhaps with greater brevity and more appropriately through its assumed mobility.

### General exposition on the deviation in latitude of the five wandering stars. Chapter I.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' containing a seated human figure.</image-desc>The ancients found twofold expansions of latitude in all these planets, corresponding to the twofold <term>inequality</term> <note>Irregularities in observed planetary motion.</note> of the longitude of each of them. They found that one deviation occurs by reason of the <term>eccentric orbits</term> <note>Orbits whose center is not the center of the universe.</note>, and the other by the <term>epicycles</term> <note>Small circles whose centers move around the circumference of larger circles.</note>; in place of which epicycles we have accepted the one <term>Great Orbit</term> <note>original: "orbem terræ magnum"; the Earth's annual orbit around the Sun.</note> of the Earth, as has already been frequently repeated. It is not that the orbit itself [of the Earth] in any way declines from the plane of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: "signiferi plano"</note> once it has been forever established—since they are the same—but because the orbits of those stars incline toward this...

...is changed by a non-fixed obliquity. Indeed, this variation is regulated according to the movement and the revolutions of the <term>great orbit</term> <note>original: "orbis magni"; in the Copernican system, this is the Earth's orbit around the Sun.</note> of the Earth. Since, however, the three superior planets—Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars—move in <term>longitude</term> <note>The position of a planet along the ecliptic.</note> according to certain laws different from the remaining two [Venus and Mercury], they also differ significantly in their motion in <term>latitude</term> <note>The north-south deviation from the ecliptic plane.</note>. Therefore, astronomers first investigated where and how great their furthest limits of northern <note>original: "Boreae"</note> latitude were. Ptolemy found these to be in Saturn and Jupiter around the beginning of Libra, but in Mars around the end of Cancer, nearly at the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit furthest from the center of motion.</note> of the eccentric. In our own times, however, we have found these northern limits to be at 7° of Scorpio for Saturn, 27° of Libra for Jupiter, and 27° of Leo for Mars, just as the apogees have also shifted down to our time.

For the inclinations and the <term>pivots</term> <note>original: "cardines"; the nodal points or turning points where latitude changes direction.</note> of latitude follow the movement of those orbits. Between these limits, through the quadrants of the circles according to equal or apparent distances, the planets seem to make no departure in latitude at all, wherever the Earth happens to be at that time. In these middle longitudes, therefore, they are understood to be in the common intersection of their orbits with the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: "signifero"</note>, no differently than the Moon in its ecliptic intersections, which Ptolemy calls the <term>nodes</term> <note>The two points where a planet's orbital plane intersects the ecliptic.</note>: the ascending node, from which the star enters northern parts, and the descending node, through which it crosses over into the southern <note>original: "Austros"</note> regions. 

It is not that the great orbit of the Earth, always remaining in the same plane of the zodiac, brings any latitude to them; rather, all departure in latitude comes from the planets themselves. This latitude varies most in other places; when the Earth approaches them and they appear opposite the Sun and <term>acronyct</term> <note>original: "acronycti"; meaning a planet is at opposition, rising just as the Sun sets and visible all night.</note>, they always deviate with a greater departure than in any other position of the Earth: in the northern hemisphere <note>original: "hemicyclio Boreo"</note> they move north, and in the southern, south. This occurs with a greater difference than the approach and retreat of the Earth alone would require. On this basis, it has been recognized that the inclination of those orbits is not fixed, but changes by a certain motion of <term>libration</term> <note>An oscillatory or swinging motion, like a pendulum, which Copernicus uses to explain periodic variations in orbital tilt.</note> proportional to the revolutions of the great orbit of the Earth, as will be explained a little further below.

Venus and Mercury, however, seem to deviate in certain other ways, yet observing a fixed law regarding their middle, highest <note>original: "extremas"</note>, and lowest <term>apsides</term> <note>The points in an orbit where the planet is at its maximum or minimum distance from the Sun.</note>. For in their middle longitudes—namely, when the line of the Sun’s mean motion is distant by a <term>quadrant</term> <note>A 90-degree angle, or one quarter of a circle.</note> from their highest or lowest apsis, and the stars themselves are distant from that same line of mean motion by the quadrants of their orbits, [as] even[ing stars]...

Yet, in both these places, they found the Northern departure of Venus to be always greater than the Southern, and the Southern departure of Mercury greater than the Northern. For this reason, they reasoned that there is a double latitude in this place, and three in total. The first, which occurs at the middle longitudes, they called **Inclination** <note>original: "Inclinationem"</note>. The second, which occurs at the highest and lowest apsis, they called **Obliquity** <note>original: "Obliquationem"</note>. And the remaining one, joined to this, they called **Deviation** <note>original: "Deviationem"</note>; this is always Northern for Venus and Southern for Mercury. Between these four limits, these motions mix with one another, and alternately increase and decrease, giving way to each other; for all of which we shall assign appropriate causes.

...variable but regular. Since in Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, the angle of the intersection <note>The angle where the planet's orbital plane meets the plane of the Earth's orbit (the ecliptic).</note> undergoes a certain **libration** <term>libration</term> <note>A slow oscillation or "wobbling" motion, like a swinging balance scale.</note> around that intersection as if on an axis, similar to what we demonstrated regarding the **precession of the equinoxes** <note>The slow change in the orientation of Earth's rotational axis.</note>. Thus, whenever the Earth is closest to the planet—namely, at **opposition** <note>original: "acronycto"; the point when a planet is opposite the Sun in the sky and nearest to Earth.</note>—the greatest inclination of the planet’s orbit occurs; in the opposite position <note>Solar conjunction, when the Earth is furthest from the planet.</note> it is at its minimum, and in the middle it is at a mean value. So, when the planet is at the limit of its greatest **Northern** <note>original: "Borea"</note> or **Southern** <note>original: "Austrinæ"</note> latitude, its latitude appears much greater when in proximity to the Earth than at its greatest distance. And although this unequal distance from the Earth could by itself be the cause of this variation—given that closer things appear larger than more remote ones—the latitudes of these stars increase and decrease by a greater difference [than distance alone explains]. This cannot happen unless their orbits also **oscillate** <note>original: "librentur"</note> in their tilt. But as we said before regarding things that oscillate, one must assume a certain mean between the extremes.

### ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK VI. ###

GB and DL are straight lines. Therefore, while the star <note>Copernicus frequently uses "stella" (star) to refer to planets.</note> is carried under the circle O P, and occasionally coincides with the plane F K by the **motion of libration** <term>libration</term> <note>A slow oscillation or "wobbling" motion.</note>, it migrates into both parts <note>i.e., North and South of the ecliptic plane</note>, and because of this, it makes the latitude appear to vary. For let the star first be at its maximum **Northern** <note>original: "Borea"</note> latitude under the sign O, nearest to the Earth, which is at position A; the latitude of the star will then increase according to the angle O G F of the maximum inclination of the circle O G P. Since the motion of its approach and retreat is, by hypothesis, **commensurable** <note>Moving in a proportional or synchronized ratio.</note> with the **motion of commutation** <term>commutation</term> <note>The relative motion between the Earth and the planet.</note>, if the Earth is then at B, O will coincide with F, and the latitude of the star will appear smaller in the same place than before. It will appear much smaller still if the Earth is at the sign C; for then O will migrate to the extreme and opposite part of its libration, and will leave only as much as remains from the subtractive libration of the Northern latitude—namely, from an angle equal to O G F.

From there, through the remaining semicircle C D A, the Northern latitude of the star (being around F) will increase until it returns to the first sign A, from which it departed. The same process and manner will apply to a **Southern** <note>original: "meridiana"</note> star positioned around the sign X, taking the starting point of the Earth's motion from C. But if the star is at either node G or L, whether it is at **opposition** <term>acronyctos</term> <note>original: "acronyctus"; when a planet is opposite the Sun and at its brightest.</note> or hidden under the Sun, even though the orbits F K and O P are then at their greatest inclination to one another, no latitude of the star will be perceived, as it occupies the common intersection of the orbits. From these facts, I believe, it is easily understood how the Northern latitude of a planet decreases from F to G, and the **Southern** <note>original: "Austrina"</note> increases from G to K, which vanishes entirely at L and passes into the North.

These three superior planets behave in this manner. Venus and Mercury differ from them in latitude no less than they do in longitude, because they have the common intersections of their orbits located through their **apogees** <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the Earth/Sun.</note> and **perigees** <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in the orbit closest to the Earth/Sun.</note>. Their maximum inclinations, however, are turned toward the middle **apsides** <term>apsides</term> <note>The turning points of an orbit (the apogee and perigee).</note> and are changeable by a libration, just like those of the superior planets; but these planets undergo another libration in addition, which is unlike the first. Both librations, however, are commensurable with the revolutions of the Earth, though not in the same way. For the first libration has this property: when the Earth has revolved once to the planets' apsides, the motion of the libration itself has revolved twice, having a permanent axis at the intersection we mentioned through the apogees and perigees. Thus, whenever the line of the mean motion of the Sun is at their perigee or apogee, the greatest angle of intersection occurs; but in the middle longitudes, it is always at its minimum.

<meta>This page continues Copernicus’s complex geometric explanation of the latitudes of the inferior planets, Venus and Mercury. # NICOLAUS COPERNICUS #

The second **libration** <term>libration</term> <note>From the Latin "libra" (scale), referring to a rhythmic, oscillating motion like a balance scale.</note>, however, occurring in addition to the first, differs from it in this respect: because it has a movable axis, it ensures that when the Earth is positioned at the mean longitude, the planet—whether Venus or Mercury—is always on the axis, which is the common intersection of this libration. It is most **deviant** <note>original: "deuius"; referring to the planet's furthest distance from the ecliptic or "path of the sun."</note>, however, when its **apogee** <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> or **perigee** <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Earth.</note> faces the Earth. In this case, Venus is always toward the **North** <note>original: "Boream"</note>, as was said, and Mercury is always toward the **South** <note>original: "Auſtrum"</note>; and yet, because of the first and simple inclination, they should have lacked any latitude at that time.

For example: when the mean motion of the Sun is at the apogee of Venus and the planet itself is in the same place, it is clear that according to the first simple inflection and libration, it would have admitted no latitude at the common intersection of its orbit with the plane of the **zodiac** <note>original: "ſigniferi," literally the "sign-bearer."</note>. But the second libration imposes its greatest deviation upon it, having its intersection or axis through the transverse diameter of the eccentric orbit, cutting the line through the highest and lowest **apsides** <term>apsides</term> <note>The two points—apogee and perigee—where a planet is at its maximum or minimum distance.</note> at right angles. If, however, at the same time the planet is in either quadrant, and around the mean apsides of its orbit, then the axis of this libration will coincide with the line of the mean motion of the Sun. Venus will then add the greatest **Northern** deviation to the reflection, while it will subtract from the **Southern** <note>original: "Auſtrinæ"</note> reflection, leaving it smaller; and in this way the libration of the deviation is **commensurable** <note>Proportional or synchronized.</note> with the motion of the Earth.

A vertical line segments the circles from A to C, and a horizontal line from B to D.

So that this may be even more easily understood, let the **great orbit** <note>The Earth's orbit around the Sun, which Copernicus calls the "orbis magnus."</note> ABCD be repeated. Let the orbit of Venus or Mercury be eccentric and oblique to the circle ABC, according to an equal inclination FG, KL. Let their common intersection be FG, passing through the apogee of the orbit, which we call F, and the perigee, G. ...the common intersection is changed according to the motion of the **perigee** <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Earth.</note> and **apogee** <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note>. While the Earth is in this [intersection], namely at *a* or *c*, and the planet is on the same line, it is clear that it would produce no latitude then, since all latitude is [measured] from the sides. In the semicircles GKF and FLG, the planet makes its approach toward the **North** <note>original: "Boream"</note> or the **South** <note>original: "Austros"</note>, as has been said, according to the measure of the inflection of the circle FKG itself to the plane of the zodiac.

Astronomers call this digression of the planet **obliquation** <term>obliquation</term> <note>A "slanting" or tilting of the orbital plane.</note>, others **reflection** <term>reflection</term>. But when the Earth is at *b* or *d*, that is, at the **mean apsides** <term>mean apsides</term> <note>The points halfway between the closest and farthest distances from the center.</note> of the planet, these same latitudes above and below FKG and GLF occur, which they call **declinations** <term>declinations</term> <note>A "sloping away" from the ecliptic.</note>. Thus they differ more in name than in reality from the former, with which names they are also mixed in the intermediate positions.

But since the angle of inclination of these circles is found to be greater in the **obliquation** than in the **declination**, they understood this to happen through a certain **libration** <term>libration</term> <note>From the Latin "libra" (scale), referring to a rhythmic, oscillating motion like a balance scale.</note>, tilting itself on the intersection FG as an axis, as was said in the previous sections. Since, therefore, we have the known angle of such an intersection in both cases, we can easily understand from their difference how great that libration was from the minimum to the maximum.

Now, let another circle of **deviation** <term>deviation</term> be understood, oblique to the circle GKFL itself. It is **homocentric** <term>homocentric</term> <note>Sharing the same center.</note> in the case of Venus, but **eccentric** <term>eccentric</term> <note>Having a center offset from the main center of motion.</note> to the eccentric in the case of Mercury, as will be said later. Let their common intersection be RS, serving as the axis of this libration, which is movable in a circuit. This is done in such a way that while the Earth is at A or B, the planet is at the extreme limit of its deviation, wherever it may be in the sign $\tau$. And as much as the Earth has progressed from *a*, so much the planet is understood to be removed from $\tau$, while the obliquity of the circle of deviation decreases in the meantime. 

Thus, when the Earth has measured out the quadrant AB, the planet is understood to have reached the **node** <term>node</term> <note>The point where the orbit crosses the plane of the ecliptic.</note> of this latitude, that is, at R. But since the planes coincide at the middle moment of the libration and then strive in opposite directions, the remaining semicircle of deviation, which was previously **Southern** <note>original: "Austrinum"</note>, breaks out into the **North** <note>original: "Boream"</note>. Succeeding into this [semicircle] and neglecting the South, Venus seeks the North again, never destined to seek the South through this libration. In the same way, Mercury, by following the opposite parts, remains **Southern**; he also differs in this, that he oscillates not in a circle homocentric to the eccentric, but in an eccentric [circle] of the eccentric. For this purpose, we used an **epicycle** <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one.</note> in the demonstration of longitudinal inequality. But since there [we discussed] longitude without latitude, and here [we discuss] lati...

...since then these two [motions] are considered without longitude, and one and the same revolution encompasses and returns them both equally, it is clearly evident that there is one motion and the same **libration** <term>libration</term> <note>An oscillation or rocking motion, like a balance scale, used here to describe how the orbital plane tilts up and down.</note> which could produce both variations, existing as both **eccentric** <term>eccentric</term> <note>Off-center; describing an orbit whose center does not coincide with the center of the Earth (or Sun).</note> and **oblique** <term>oblique</term> <note>Slanted or tilted relative to the Earth's orbital plane.</note> at the same time. ### How Great the Inclination of the Orbits of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars is. Chapter III.

After explaining the hypotheses regarding the wandering <note>original: "digressionum"</note> of the five planets, we must now descend to the facts themselves and distinguish each part. First, we must determine how great the inclinations of the individual circles are. We calculate these by means of a great circle that passes through the poles of the tilted circle and is drawn at right angles to the one passing through the middle of the signs <note>The "middle of the signs" refers to the ecliptic, the Sun's apparent path across the sky.</note>; it is along this circle that the shifts in latitude are observed. Once these are understood, the way to know the latitudes of each planet will be opened. 

Beginning again with the three superior planets <note>Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, which orbit further from the Sun than the Earth does.</note>, we find that in the **Ptolemaic** <note>Referring to Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose geocentric model Copernicus is here revising.</note> exposition at the furthest southern limits of latitude, the departures of Saturn when **acronychal** <term>acronychal</term> <note>From the Greek for "at nightfall"; occurring when a planet is opposite the Sun and rises just as the Sun sets. This is when the planet is closest to Earth.</note> are 3 degrees and 5 **minutes** <term>minutes</term> <note>original: "scrupula" (scruples). In astronomy, these are 1/60th of a degree.</note>; Jupiter's are 2 degrees and 7 minutes; and Mars' are 7 degrees. However, in the opposite positions—namely, when they are traveling [in conjunction] with the Sun—Saturn's is 2 degrees and 2 minutes, Jupiter's is 1 degree and 5 minutes, and Mars' is only 5 minutes, so that it almost touches the circle of the signs <note>The ecliptic.</note>, as could be noticed from the latitudes observed during their disappearances and appearances. 

Having established these points, let there be a plane at right angles to the circle of the signs, and let the common section of the zodiac be A B. Let the section of the **eccentric** <term>eccentric</term> [orbit] of any of the three superior planets be C D, passing through the maximum Southern and Northern limits. Let E be the center of the zodiac, and let F E G be the diameter of the **Great Circle** <term>Great Circle</term> <note>The *Orbis Magnus*, which in the Copernican system refers to the Earth's orbit around the Sun.</note> of the Earth. Let D be the Southern latitude and C the Northern. Join C F, C G, D F, and D G. 

Now, the ratios of the Earth's orbit E G to the planet's eccentric orbit E D have been demonstrated above for any given position. Furthermore, the positions of the maximum latitudes are given from observations. Therefore, since the angle B G D of the maximum Southern latitude is given, the exterior angle of the triangle E G D will also give—by the demonstration of plane triangles—the interior and opposite angle G E D, which is the maximum Southern **inclination** of the eccentric orbit to the plane of the zodiac. Similarly, through the minimum Southern latitude, we will demonstrate the minimum inclination, namely through the angle

This also reveals to us the angle CGE of Northern latitude as nearly 6 minutes. 

Therefore, when we subtract the minimum inclination from the maximum—that is, 9 minutes from 1 degree 51 minutes—the remainder is 1 degree 42 minutes. The libration of this inclination (and its half) is nearly 50 minutes. In the same way, the angles of inclination for the other two planets, Jupiter and Saturn, were made clear along with their latitudes. Specifically, the maximum inclination of Jupiter is 1 degree 42 minutes, and the minimum is 1 degree...

### SIXTH BOOK OF THE REVOLUTIONS

...for example, while it is distant from point **B**, the point nearest the Earth, by 45 degrees. We have chosen this, following Ptolemy, so that it may appear whether the inclination of the orbit <term>inclination</term> <note>The angle at which the planet's orbital plane is tilted relative to the Earth's orbital plane (the ecliptic).</note> produces any variation in the longitude of Venus or Mercury. Indeed, such differences ought to be most visible around the midpoints between the boundaries **D, E, F, G**, especially because the planet, when positioned at these four boundaries, produces the same longitudes it would produce without any declination, as is self-evident.

Let us therefore take the arc **BH**, as stated, to be 45 degrees. Let the perpendiculars be drawn to **BC**, namely **HK**, and to the underlying plane of the ecliptic <term>ecliptic</term> <note>original: "signiferi"; the "sign-bearing" circle or the path the Sun appears to follow through the constellations.</note> **KL** and **HM**. Let **HB, LM, AM, and AH** be connected. We will have the quadrilateral parallelogram and rectangle **LKHM**, because **HK** is perpendicular to the plane of the ecliptic; for the angle **LAM**, the correction <term>correction</term> <note>original: "prosthaphaeresis"; the geometric adjustment needed to convert a planet's mean motion into its observed position.</note> of longitude, contains the side itself, while the passage of latitude is the angle under **HAM**, since **HM** also falls perpendicular to the same plane of the ecliptic.

Therefore, since the angle **HBE** is given as 45 degrees, **HK** will be half the chord of double **HB**, which is 7071 where **BE** is 10000. Similarly, in triangle **BKL**, the angle **KBL** is given as 2 ½ degrees <note>The text reads "11. s." which is a common early modern printing of "II s." or 2 and a half.</note>, and **BLK** is a right angle, and the chord **BK** is 7071 where **BE** is 10000. The remaining sides will also be of the same units: **KL** is 308, and **BL** is 7064. But since **AB** is to **BE**, from what was previously shown, approximately as 10000 to 7193, the remaining parts in the same units will be **HK** = 5086, **HM** (equal to **KL**) = 221, and **BL** = 5081. From this, the remaining distance **LA** is 4919.

Now also in triangle **ALM**, with sides **AL** and **LM** (equal to **HK**) given, and **ALM** being a right angle, we will have the chord **AM** = 7075, and the angle **MAL** = 45 degrees and 58 minutes <term>minutes</term> <note>original: "scrupula"; the 60 subdivisions of a degree.</note>, which is the great correction or parallax of Venus according to the calculation. Similarly, in the triangle with sides **AM** = 7075 and **MH** (equal to **KL**) given, the angle **MAH** will be 1 degree and 47 minutes of the latitude of declination.

If it is not too much trouble to weigh what this inclination of Venus brings in the way of longitudinal variation, let us take triangle **ALH**, understanding that **LH** is the diameter of the parallel **LKHM**. For it is 5091 units where **AL** is 4919; and **ALH** is a right angle, from which the chord **AH** is calculated to be 7079. With the ratio of the sides given, therefore, the angle **HAL** will be 45 degrees and 58 minutes. But **ALM** was shown to be 45 degrees and 57 minutes. Thus, there is an increase of only 2 minutes, which was to be demonstrated. Again, in Mercury, by a similar...

In a similar way, we will demonstrate the latitudes of declination through a diagram similar to the previous one, in which the arc **BH** is set at 45 degrees. Similarly, in triangle **AMH**, two sides **AM** and **MH** (which is equal to **KL**) are given, encompassing a right angle; the angle **MAH** will be established as 2 degrees and 16 minutes, which is the latitude we were seeking. 

If we wish to investigate how much is due to the difference between the true and apparent <term>prosthaphæresis</term>, let us take the diameter of the parallelogram **LK**, which we calculate from the sides to be 2,811 parts, and **AL**, which is 7,186 parts. These will show the angle **LAH** to be 21 degrees and 24 minutes, which is the apparent adjustment. This exceeds the previously calculated value by nearly 7 minutes, which was what we intended to demonstrate.

...at the greatest distances from the sun in the morning and evening, as we have said. For Mercury, however, the southern latitudes were nearly one and a half degrees greater than the northern ones. But wishing to accommodate the difficulty and labor of the calculations, he accepted, according to a certain average ratio, two and a half degrees <note>original: "sestertia graduum"; literally "two and a half of degrees."</note> for the various parts of the latitude, which degrees the latitudes themselves subtend at a right angle to the zodiac around the earth, by which the latitudes are defined; especially because he thought that no obvious error would result from this, as we will also show shortly. It must first be shown, therefore, that the maximum extent of this latitude occurs around the points of contact with the eccentric circle, where the corrections <term>prosthaphæreses</term> <note>original: "prosthaphæreses"; from the Greek, meaning the geometric adjustments added or subtracted to find a planet's true position relative to its average path.</note> for longitude are also at their maximum.

...which are under <note>The Latin 'sub' here refers to the angles subtended by the lines mentioned.</note> DAM and EAN. From this it is clear that of the differences in longitude produced by this inclination <note>original: "obliquatione"; referring to the tilting of the planet's orbital plane.</note> among the corrections, the greatest is that which is determined at the maximum transit around point E. For because of the equal angles they subtend, HD, KE, and LF are proportional to HM, KN, and LO. Since the ratio of these to their excesses remains the same, it follows that the excess of EK and KN has a greater ratio to EA than the others have to their counterparts like AD. From this it is also manifest that whatever ratio the maximum longitudinal correction has to the maximum latitudinal transit, the longitudinal corrections of the segments of the eccentric circle will have that same ratio to the latitudinal transits. For as KE is to EN, so are all lines similar to LF and HD to those similar to FO and DM, which were the things proposed to be demonstrated.

Those things which happen between these four limits could indeed be explained by the subtlety of the mathematical art from the proposed hypothesis of circles, though not without labor. Ptolemy, however, being as concise as possible everywhere, saw that both types of these latitudes increased and decreased proportionally according to their whole and in all their parts, just like the lunar latitude. Therefore, by taking any twelve parts of it (because its maximum latitude is five parts, and the number twelve is the 12th part of 60), he established from them <term>proportional minutes</term><note>original: "scrupula proportionum"; scaling factors used to adjust the maximum latitude based on the planet's current position in its orbit.</note>, which he thought should be used not only for these two stars, but also for the three superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>, as will be seen below.

### On the third type of latitude for Venus and Mercury, which they call deviation. Chapter VIII.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'Q' featuring a man, presumably an astronomer or Nicolaus Copernicus himself, seated at a desk with a book and an astronomical instrument, enclosed within a square frame with floral motifs.</image-desc>

Having explained these things as well, it still remains to say something about the third motion of latitude, which is the <term>deviation</term><note>original: "deuiatio"; a small additional northward or southward shift in the planet's position that previous astronomers struggled to explain with simple circles.</note>. The ancients, who keep the Earth in the middle of the world, think this occurs through the tilt of the <term>eccentric</term><note>original: "eccentri"; a circular orbit whose center is offset from the Earth.</note> together with the <term>epicycle</term><note>original: "epicycli"; a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle (the deferent).</note> around the center of the Earth, especially when the epicycle is positioned at the <term>apogee</term> or <term>perigee</term>. In the case of Venus, this is always by a <term>sixth part</term><note>original: "sextantem"; one-sixth of a degree, or 10 minutes of arc.</note> of a part, and always toward the North. For Mercury, it is always by <term>three-quarters</term><note>original: "dodrantem"; three-quarters of a degree, or 45 minutes of arc.</note>, always toward the South, as we said before. However, it is not sufficiently clear whether they intended such an inclination of the orbits to always be equal and the same, for their numbers indicate this when they command that a sixth part of the proportional minutes always be taken for the deviation of Venus, and three-quarters for Mercury. ### Chapter 9: On the calculation of the latitudes of the five planets. <note>original: "quinqʒ errantium," literally "the five wandering stars," the classical term for planets.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'M' inside a square frame with ornate floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>

The method for calculating the latitudes of the five wandering stars <note>planets</note> by means of these tables is as follows. For Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, we compare the <term>adjusted eccentricity anomaly</term> <note>This refers to the planet's position in its own elliptical-like orbit, corrected for various factors.</note> to the common numbers: for Mars, using the value as it is found; for Jupiter, after first subtracting 20 degrees; and for Saturn, after adding 50 degrees. We will then take note of the <term>proportional minutes</term> <note>original: "scrupula proportionum." These are scaling factors used to adjust the calculations based on the planet's distance.</note> located in the last column that correspond to these numbers. Similarly, using the adjusted <term>anomaly of parallax</term> <note>original: "anomalia commutationis." This is the planet's position relative to the Earth's motion.</note>, we will take the adjacent latitude specific to each planet's number. We take the first and Northern <note>original: "Boream"</note> latitude if the proportional minutes are in the upper section, which occurs when the eccentricity anomaly is less than 90° or more than 270°. We take the Southern <note>original: "Austrinam"</note> and subsequent latitude if the proportional minutes are in the lower section—that is, if the eccentricity anomaly used for entry was between 90° and 270°. If we then multiply either of these latitudes by its proportional minutes, the result will be the distance from the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>original: "circulo signorum," the "circle of signs" or the sun's apparent path.</note> toward the North or South, according to the designation of the circles assumed.

But for Venus and Mercury, three latitudes must first be taken using the adjusted anomaly of parallax: those of the <term>declination, obliquity, and deviation</term> <note>These represent the three distinct ways the orbits of the inner planets tilt or "deviate" from the Earth's orbital plane.</note> as they occur, and these should be noted separately. However, for Mercury, one-tenth of the obliquity is subtracted <note>original: "reiiciatur," rejected or cast out.</note> if the eccentricity anomaly and its number are found in the upper part of the table, or that same amount is added if found in the lower part; the resulting remainder or sum is then kept. Their designations, whether they are Northern or Southern, must be distinguished. For if the adjusted anomaly of parallax is in the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the center of motion.</note> semi-circle—that is, less than 90° or more than 270°—and the eccentricity anomaly is also less than a semi-circle <note>less than 180°</note>; or again, if the anomaly of parallax is in the <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in the orbit closest to the center of motion.</note> circumference—namely, more than 90° and less than 270°—and the eccentricity anomaly is greater than a semi-circle, then the declination of Venus will be Northern and Mercury’s will be Southern. If, however, the anomaly of parallax is in the perigee circumference and the eccentricity anomaly is [less than] a semi-circle...

[The previous page ended mid-sentence regarding the calculation rules; this text continues the conditions for determining whether a planet is north or south of the ecliptic.]

...is smaller, or the <term>anomaly of parallax</term> <note>original: "commutationis anomalia." This refers to the apparent shift in the planet's position caused by Earth's own motion.</note> is in the part farthest from Earth, and the <term>eccentricity anomaly</term> <note>The planet's position along its own specific orbital path.</note> is more than a semicircle [180°], then in turn the declination of Venus will be Southern and that of Mercury Northern. In the matter of the <term>slant</term> <note>original: "obliquatione," referring to the tilting of the planet's orbit.</note>, if the anomaly of parallax is less than a semicircle and the eccentricity anomaly is at its farthest point from Earth, or if the anomaly of parallax is greater than a semicircle and the eccentricity anomaly is at its closest point to Earth, the slant of Venus will be Northern and that of Mercury Southern; these also reverse if the conditions are opposite. The deviations, however, always remain Northern for Venus and Southern for Mercury.

Furthermore, when the eccentricity anomaly has been determined, let the <term>proportional minutes</term> <note>original: "scrupula proportionum." These are scaling factors used to adjust the calculated values based on the planet's distance.</note> be taken; these are common to all five planets, although they were originally listed for the three outer planets. These should be assigned to the slant, and the final ones to the deviation. After this, by adding 90 degrees to that same eccentricity anomaly, one finds the common proportional minutes for the resulting sum and applies them to the latitude of the declination.

With all these things thus set in order, let each of the three latitudes described be multiplied by its respective proportional minutes, and the resulting values will be the fully calculated latitudes for that specific place and time. Finally, to obtain the total sum of the three latitudes for these two stars <note>Copernicus refers to planets as "stars" in the classical sense.</note>, if they are all of the same name [e.g., all Northern], they are added together. If not, at least the two that share a name are joined; then, depending on whether that sum is larger or smaller than the third latitude of a different name, the smaller is subtracted from the larger, and the remaining dominant latitude will be the one sought.

# To the Reader
## Concerning the Hypotheses of this work.
<margin>Slipped in by Osiander <note>Andreas Osiander (1498–1552) oversaw the printing of Copernicus's book and added this unsigned preface without the author's permission to avoid religious censorship.</note></margin>
->[Anonymous; authored by Andreas Osiander]<-

I do not doubt that certain learned men will be much annoyed <insert>at</insert> the common report of the newness of the arguments of this work, namely, that the earth is movable, but that the sun is immovable in the middle of the universe, and will think that noble doctrines <note>Refers to the long-held Aristotelian and Ptolemaic views that the Earth was the stationary center of the universe.</note> rightly established in the past should not be disturbed. But if they will consider the matter closely, they will find that the author of this work has done nothing worthy of blame. For it is the part of an astronomer to draw up an account of the celestial movements from earnest and skilful observation. Then since he cannot by any theory arrive at the true causes of these things, or invent or discover any hypotheses whatsoever, but taking them for granted, these same motions may be rightly calculated both <insert>for</insert> the future and <insert>in</insert> the past, by the principles of geometry. 

Now this writer greatly excels in each of these points. For it is not necessary that these hypotheses should be true, or even very probable, but this one thing is sufficient, that they must put forward a calculation agreeing with the observations. Unless by chance anyone be so very ignorant of geometry and optics that he holds the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used in ancient astronomy to explain the complex movements of planets.</note> of Venus to be probable, or believes that it is the cause of its being in forty parts, and still further that it sometimes precedes and sometimes follows the sun. For who does not see, when this is taken for granted, that it necessarily follows that the diameter of a star when nearest the earth is greater by more than fourfold, and <strike>the same body</strike> <gloss>it</gloss> is greater by sixfold than it appears when furthest from the

<summary>This page contains the controversial, anonymous preface to Copernicus's masterwork, arguing that the sun-centered model is merely a mathematical hypothesis for easier calculation rather than a claim of physical reality. This "instrumentalist" approach was intended to protect the work from being condemned as heretical or physically impossible.</summary>

earth, which however the experience of all the ages contradicts? And there are other things not less absurd in this teaching, which it is not necessary to discuss here. For it is clear enough that this art entirely and simply ignores the causes of ~~visible~~ <gloss>apparent</gloss> <note>The author uses "apparent" to distinguish between the visual movement of planets and their actual physical path.</note> unequal motions. And if he devises these causes by invention, as he certainly does very many, by no means however does he discover this, that he can convince anyone that they are true, unless they rightly form a calculation. When various <term>hypotheses<gloss>In 16th-century science, a "hypothesis" was often viewed as a mathematical model to "save the appearances"—calculating positions without claiming to describe physical reality.</gloss></term> of one and the same motion, <gloss>sometimes</gloss> offer themselves (as in the motion, the <term>eccentricity<gloss>The distance between the center of a planet's orbit and the central point (like the Sun or Earth) around which it revolves.</gloss></term>, and <term>epicycle<gloss>A small circular orbit whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle; a primary tool of Ptolemaic astronomy.</gloss></term> of the sun) the astronomer will choose for preference that one which is most easily understood. The philosopher perhaps will require a greater exactitude; neither however will understand or propound anything true unless it has been revealed to him by divine providence. Let us therefore allow these new hypotheses to be known as no less probable than the old ones, particularly as they are at the same time wonderful and easy, and bring with them a huge treasury of most learned observations. Let no one expect anything true, pertaining to hypotheses, from astronomy, for it can show nothing of the sort, lest taking false things for true in some other use, he depart from this teaching more foolish than he came. Farewell.

## To the most Holy Lord Pope Paul III. The Preface
### of Nicholas Copernicus on the Books of the Revolutions.

I can see clearly enough, O most holy Father <note>original: "Sanctissime Pater." Copernicus addresses Pope Paul III directly to seek protection and legitimacy for his controversial work.</note>, that it will happen that certain people, while approving of my attributing certain motions to the globe of the earth, will yet exclaim that I ought to be reproved for such an opinion in these my books concerning the **Revolutions** <term>Revolutions<gloss>From the Latin "De revolutionibus," referring to the rotating motion of the celestial spheres.</gloss></term> of the spheres of the universe. But as my own things do not please me, so I do not consider what others may judge concerning them. And although I know that the reflexions of the philosopher are far removed from the understanding of the common man, because his work is to find the Truth in everything, as God has allowed to human reason, yet I think strange doctrines, far removed from truth, should be avoided.

Thus I thought to myself what an absurd report they would think it, who do not know the opinion confirmed by the judgment of many centuries, that the earth is immovable in the middle of the heavens, being as it were in the centre of it, if I should assert on the contrary that the earth moved; thus for a long time I hesitated whether I should publish my commentaries on its movement, or whether indeed it would be better to follow the example of the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, known for keeping their mathematical and philosophical discoveries secret within their own community.</note> and some others, who used not to transmit the mysteries of philosophy by letters, but by word of mouth to their neighbours and friends, <gloss>only</gloss> as the letter of Lysis to Hipparchus <note>Lysis was a student of Pythagoras; the letter mentioned was a well-known historical example of the Pythagorean warning against making philosophy accessible to the "unworthy" masses.</note> shows. And indeed this seems

<summary>Copernicus addresses Pope Paul III, explaining his apprehension about publishing his theory of the Earth's motion. He describes his fear of being mocked for contradicting centuries of established geocentric thought and mentions his initial preference for the Pythagorean tradition of keeping scientific knowledge secret.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Copernicus's dedication to Pope Paul III. In the preceding text, Copernicus mentioned the Pythagorean tradition of only sharing philosophical secrets with close friends and family to prevent sacred knowledge from being degraded by the unlearned.</meta>

...to me to have been done, not as some think from a certain jealousy of communicating their theories, but lest the noblest things, studied by great men with much care, should be despised by those who are too indolent to expend much labour on any work except for gain; or by those who, even if they are stimulated by the exhortation and example of others to the study of philosophy, yet by the dulness of their wit would remain among philosophers like drones among bees. When therefore I thought on these things, the contempt which I feared on account of the novelty and absurdity of my opinion almost compelled me to discontinue this treatise altogether.

But as I hesitated and resisted for a long time, my friends urged me on. Among these, the first was **Nicholas Schönberg** <note>A German cardinal and diplomat who was deeply interested in Copernicus's work and had previously written to him requesting a copy of his findings.</note>, Cardinal of Capua, famous in every kind of learning. Next to him was my most loving friend **Tideman Gisius** <note>Tiedemann Giese (1480–1550), the Bishop of Culm and a close lifelong friend of Copernicus who championed the publication of the heliocentric theory.</note>, Bishop of Culm, who was as learned in the sacred writings as he was in all <gloss>the</gloss> other sciences. For he again and again exhorted and entreated me with reproaches for a long time to publish this book, and allow it to be brought into the light, which I had <gloss>lain</gloss> hidden ~~within~~ me, <gloss>not only</gloss> for ~~nine~~ years, <gloss>but for four times nine</gloss> <note>Copernicus refers to the Roman poet Horace’s advice to keep a manuscript for nine years before publishing; Copernicus, however, had delayed for thirty-six years.</note> and had <margin>kept back for twenty-seven years</margin> ~~kept back for twenty seven.~~ <gloss>(i.e. 36 years) even into the fourth novennium [i.e. more than 27 years]</gloss> <term>Novennium<gloss>From the Latin "novem" (nine) and "annus" (year), referring to a nine-year period.</gloss></term>. Many other very eminent and learned men did the same, praying me no longer <gloss>to</gloss> refuse, on account of imaginary fears, to deliver up the fruits of my labours for the common good of students of mathematics. For the more absurd my theory of the motion of the earth appeared to be, so much the more admiration and favour would it have when the mist of absurdity was cleared away by the clearest proofs, once my commentaries were published.
